part_subtitle: The road remembers what people deny.

chapters.chapter_title: THE VILLAGE THAT DID NOT USE A NAME
paragraphs: Buck refused the bridge before the village refused its name.

I have trusted horses longer than I have trusted men, which is not a confession of wisdom so much as a record of repeated disappointment. Men lie because they can imagine profit. Horses lie only when oats are involved, and even then they lack the imagination to be dangerous about it. So when Buck stopped with both forehooves in the brown water where the road had sunk, ears flat and wet mane stuck to his neck, I let him tell me what the signpost had already failed to say.

Rain moved over the valley in long patient sheets. Not storm rain. Storms have the decency to declare themselves, break branches, frighten hens, then pass on to bully another field. This was steadier and worse: soft weather that made mud out of roads, soup out of graves, and bad philosophy out of men. The river below the bridge smelled of thawed earth, old reeds, and something warmer underneath, a buried breath rising where no breath had any right to be.

The signpost at the fork had been hacked clean. Someone had taken an axe to the village name and left only the direction marks: north to Crow's Perch, south to the crossing, east to a place no one wanted to admit existed. Fresh cuts showed pale under the rain-dark surface, raw as bone under peeled skin. Fresh damage still wants witnesses.
"You saw it first," I told Buck.

He moved one ear. From Buck, that was practically a signed affidavit. He had carried me through three flooded ditches, one abandoned Nilfgaardian camp, and a toll bridge where two men in mismatched mail had spent half an hour arguing whether a witcher counted as taxable livestock. Buck had taken the ditches, hated the camp, tried to bite one taxman, and now would not set a hoof on a bridge made of old pine and older guilt.

I dismounted. Mud accepted my boots with a soft pull, like a mouth considering whether to keep what it had been given. My Wolf medallion lay heavy against my chest. It did not tremble. The other thing I wore beneath the armor, the barbed star I had possessed before I possessed a name, lay colder against my skin.
That one had always known how to be silent.

At Kaer Morhen, that silence had become instruction long before I left at nineteen. Vesemir never explained the necklace. He only taught me, in the tone he used for cliffs, venom, and kings, never to let a mage hold it under glass, never to sleep where a clerk could inventory my belongings, and never to answer questions about it for the price of being polite.

I remembered one winter evening because memory, like damp, prefers old stone. I had been twelve, still narrow at the shoulders and angry that the world kept refusing to explain itself. The necklace had slipped free during sword drills, and a younger version of me had asked what it was in front of the wrong wall. Vesemir closed my fist around it before the last word finished leaving my mouth. Not hard. Hard would have been easier to hate. His palm was warm, scarred, smelling of blade oil and onion soup, and he held my fingers shut until I stopped looking at the thing and started looking at him. Geralt stood in the doorway behind us, apparently examining a cracked lintel with the full attention of a man who heard every breath in the room. Vesemir said only that some objects became dangerous once named aloud. Then he sent me to clean tack that had already been cleaned. Care, at Kaer Morhen, often arrived disguised as chores.

Four years on the Path had refined the rules. Leave before healers grew curious. Leave before candle flames bent twice toward the same charm. Leave before a village secretary discovered that crimson eyes made a better report than a monster did. I knew I was strange. I had survived by treating that as weather; I did not yet know why the weather had begun keeping records.

The bridge had been repaired in five places. Not maintained. Repaired. Different wood, different hands, different seasons, each layer set over rot instead of cutting it out. I crouched and pressed two fingers to the boards. The surface was cold with rain. The seam between planks breathed warmth.
Buck snorted.
"I said I saw it. I didn't say I liked it."

The village waited beyond the bridge with the careful stillness of places that had rehearsed innocence. Smoke climbed from chimneys, but no one stood under the eaves. A red hen scratched beside a trough and pretended not to notice the three faces watching from behind a shutter. The houses leaned inward around a lane paved in broken stone. At the far end, where the ground dipped toward the river, an old mill turned with no grain in its throat.
The wheel moved slowly, pushed by water black under the sky. It creaked once every turn. The sound arrived late, which is a bad habit in noises and a worse one in people.

I led Buck across by the reins. Halfway over, he stopped again and put his weight backward. I did not pull. Pulling a frightened horse is for fools, noblemen, and men who later wonder why they woke without teeth. I waited until Buck placed one hoof forward, then another, and the warmth under the bridge shifted against the soles of my boots as if the river had rolled over in its sleep.

The first man to meet me had alderman's hands, soft at the knuckles with ink in the nail beds. He wore a fur hat too fine for the weather and a belt with a brass buckle polished bright, implying honest administration, which is rarely a sign of honest administration. Behind him came a young priest with a candle lantern and two villagers carrying boar spears. The spears had been cleaned. The men had not.
"Witcher," the alderman said.
I looked past him to the shuttered windows, the mill, the child watching from behind a broken door, and the black river sliding under its skin of rain. "That was on the notice."
The alderman blinked. "I am Odrik, elected alderman by common assent, royal continuance, and settlement terms left standing after the late war."
"Congratulations."
The man with the left spear coughed into his fist. The priest did not smile. Priests train themselves for such hardships. I respect it in the way I respect a locked door.
"You came quickly," Odrik said.
"Your notice said livestock first. Then two missing men. Then a child. Notices get more expensive when they improve."
"The child came back," the priest said.

His voice was soft and dry. He was young in his piety and old in his use of it as furniture. The candle in his lantern burned yellow and untroubled despite the rain. I watched the flame lean toward the mill.
"Alive?" I asked.
"In body."

The priest looked toward the child after saying it and then away again, as if the phrase had become visible between them. The priest looked away from the child. Odrik feared blame. The priest feared the old name. Neither fear made them villains. That was the trouble. Villains are easier. They stand in the right place for a blade.
"Try not to be poetic until after I know who is paying me."

The spear-man coughed again, worse this time, hiding a laugh badly enough to make me almost like him. Odrik turned a look on him that would have fined him if looks carried seals. I had seen villages arrange themselves by fear, hunger, old women, pigs, priests, and once by a goose with a talent for violence. This one was arranged by what it would not call itself.
"Payment is as posted," Odrik said. "Seventy crowns on proof of removal. Additional ten if the mill is preserved."
"No."
"No?"
"No additional ten. If the mill is part of it, the mill goes where it needs to go."
"The mill belongs to five families."
"Then five families should have built it somewhere else."
The priest lifted the lantern a fraction. "The mill is old. Older than most claims."
"So is rot." I nodded toward the hacked signpost behind me. "What's the village called?"
Three faces vanished from three windows.

Odrik's mouth tightened. The priest lowered the lantern. The child in the broken doorway remained where he was, thin as a post, hair too light for his dirty face, one hand clenched around a wooden toy horse. Buck blew air through his nose and turned his head toward the boy. The boy did not move.

Miro's cuffs were soaked to the elbow though the rain had not reached that doorway. Mud lived under his fingernails in black crescents. One trouser knee had been torn and mended badly with thread too white for the cloth, the sort of repair done quickly by hands that shook and then pretended they had not. He held the toy horse too tightly around its middle, not like a child afraid of losing a toy, but like a man gripping a rail while the floor moved. The villagers gave him space. Too much space. Returned children frighten people because they come back carrying an answer no adult wants to be asked for.
"We do not use the name," Odrik said.
"I noticed the axe work."
"Superstition," Odrik said too quickly. "After the war people became suggestible."
"Respect for the dead," the priest said.
"Those are different lies."
"Superstition sounds lighter on a ledger," I said.
Odrik drew himself up with the practiced exhaustion of men who had spent years being responsible for too little food and too many graves. "A village survives by choosing which truths it can afford."
The priest looked older for one breath. "And sometimes by not calling the dead loudly enough for them to answer."
There it was. Not innocence. Not guilt clean enough to hang. Administrative fear on one side, spiritual fear on the other, both sheltering under the same leaking roof and calling it necessity.
The rain filled the space after that. A dog barked once behind the houses and then thought better of the matter.
Odrik reddened in a disciplined way. "You were hired for a monster, not for an inquiry into local grief."
"I charge extra when grief bites."

The priest faced me properly then. He saw past the swords, past the dark leather, past the white hair wet against my brow. His gaze caught on my eyes and stopped. People always got there eventually. They saw the crimson, the slit pupils, the way low light gathered in them as if invited, and remembered that hiring a witcher meant bringing another frightening thing close enough to speak.

"The first cow vanished six nights ago," he said. "Then two goats. Then Toman the miller's nephew. Then Berek, who went looking for him. The child, Miro, was taken yesterday before dawn. He returned before noon and has not spoken since."
"Where was he found?"
The priest did not answer. Odrik looked toward the mill.
"Useful," I said. "We're improving."

The woman at the mill watched me from the open half of a stable door. She was old, but not with the fragility city folk enjoy imagining when they use the word. She had river-old shoulders, hands bent by work, and the kind of eyes that had outlived pity because pity had never carried water or buried a son. A blue kerchief held back hair the color of stove ash. She did not cross herself. She did not spit. She watched Buck's hooves first, then my hands, then the place under my collar where the hidden necklace lay.
"Who is she?" I asked.
"Edda," Odrik said. "The miller's widow."
"Which miller?"
The priest's fingers tightened around the lantern handle.
I turned to the old woman. She gave me no answer. That, at last, was something honest.

The mill yard had been churned by men trying to look brave after the useful part of fear had passed. Tracks overlapped tracks, boot heels through goat blood, spear-butts in mud, ash scattered in clumsy circles around the threshold. Someone had poured salt at the door, then crossed it twice. Someone else had nailed three horseshoes over the lintel in three directions, which proved the village had at least three opinions and no plan.

I walked the perimeter first. I did not ask questions while the ground was still speaking. Mud keeps better records than frightened men. A dragged mark began at the goat pen, stopped near the well, resumed ten paces away, and vanished not at the river but at the mill's north wall. The gap mattered. Gaps are where lies stand when they have no boots.

The missing cow's blood had not dried properly. It had steamed in cold air, leaving a dark crust around the stones. The mill wheel creaked once. Beneath it, faint and out of rhythm, something clicked as if teeth were being counted.
I knelt beside the well. The rope was scorched halfway down.
"Lightning," Odrik said behind me.
"In a covered well?"
"It was during a storm."
"Storms have standards. Low ones, but standards."
The spear-man made a small sound again. Odrik turned to him. The spear-man became fascinated by his boots.

I drew a knife and scraped the scorched fibers into a fold of oilcloth. The burn smelled wrong: not woodsmoke, pitch, or witchfire, but hot iron and wet stone. I put the oilcloth away and went to the mill wall, where frost clung in sheltered cracks despite the thaw. My medallion twitched once, not a proper warning, more like a sleeping dog kicking at a dream.
I watched the difference.

The wolf medallion knew curses, monsters, and magic that had the manners to announce itself. It shook for ordinary wrongness. The barbed star did not shake. It waited cold against my sternum as if recognition required no movement. One warned. One remembered. I disliked the distinction before I understood it, which is usually the honest order of learning.

Inside, the mill had the warm damp smell of grain gone sour. The grindstones sat silent though the wheel moved outside. Flour dust lay over the floor in old drifts, disturbed by boot marks, animal tracks, and one broad smear where something heavy had been pulled inward. I followed the smear to a trapdoor hidden beneath sacks and a floor plank newer than the others. The iron ring had been wrapped in cloth to keep it quiet.
"Cellar?" I asked.
"Storage," Odrik said.
"For what?"
"Grain. Tools. Winter stores."
I lifted the cloth from the ring. The iron had been handled recently.
"And guilt."
The priest drew a breath. Outside, Edda spat into the yard.
I looked at her through the doorway. "How many times has the mill been rebuilt?"
No one answered.
"Three," Edda said at last.
"Edda," Odrik said.

"Four, if you count the war winter," she said. Her voice had the flatness of river stones. "But they don't count that. Didn't get permits for war work. Hard to file improvements when half the men have run to the woods and the other half are hiding grain from whichever army asks politely with torches."
The priest closed his eyes.
"Who died under it?" I asked.
Edda studied the trapdoor. "Depends which prayer you believe."
"I don't use prayers for counting."

"Seven men during the old fire. Two deserters, one tax rider, one girl dressed as a boy, three we never named. Later, when the foundations sank, we built over them. Priest before this one said disturbance would invite worse. Alderman before this one said digging cost money. Both were right, which is how wickedness usually survives."
Odrik's face had gone the color of old pork. "Those are not established facts."
"No," I said. "Established facts cost money."
Edda almost smiled. It did not improve her face. It only made it less lonely.

The trapdoor opened with a sigh of stale heat. The smell rising from below was not decay. Decay is generous. It announces itself and makes a fair effort to be understood. This smell was cooked mud, iron, split roots, and old grain fermented in something that had once been a body. I took a cat potion from my belt, rolled the vial between gloved fingers, and hesitated because the boy Miro had appeared in the doorway.

No one had heard him cross the yard. He stared at the trapdoor with all of his thin body, not only his eyes. Each time the wheel creaked, his head tilted with it, as if some part of him still answered the sound. The wooden horse hung from his hand by one leg.
"He shouldn't be here," I said.
"He follows the sound," the priest said.
"Then stop making the sound."
"What sound?"

I studied the mill wheel. It turned and creaked, turned and creaked. Miro's gaze followed each turn before mine did, and the hidden clicking beneath it softened as if something below had learned to listen.
"Clear the mill."
Odrik lifted both hands. "Now, witcher, if this is a bargaining posture, it is a poor one. We cannot empty five households because a hired mutant dislikes a noise."

I unsheathed my steel sword. The clean sound did more for persuasion than reason ever had. "Clear the mill. Clear the houses nearest the river. Put everyone uphill. No lamps near the ground floors. No children near wells. Tie your pigs or lose them. If anyone stays because they think property outweighs breath, I charge the same to carry what remains."

For a moment the room held its shape around the threat. Then Edda moved first. She took Miro by the shoulder, not gently, but with the competence of someone who knew the difference between care and softness. The spear-men followed. The priest lifted his lantern, looked at Odrik, and finally said the most useful thing he had said all morning.
"Do as he says."
Odrik did. He made it sound like his own decision, which is one of the privileges of office.
Before the hunt, I walked the hill where the villagers had gathered and made them show me what fear had edited from their first telling.

It took an hour. It should have taken ten minutes. People make poor witnesses when they are frightened and worse ones when they are ashamed, because shame gives them energy to arrange facts into furniture. Toman had not gone into the mill alone. He had gone with two friends to pry old iron from the lower supports, because iron sold well after armies passed and hunger makes thieves of sons whose fathers once called thieves vermin. Berek had not gone looking for him out of bravery. Berek had gone because Toman owed him money for a pig, and money makes grief practical to approach.

Miro had been playing near the old sluice when the ground opened. No one said playing. Odrik said trespassing. The priest said wandering. Edda said the boy had been watching the mill because everyone watched what they were told not to watch, children simply had less training in pretending otherwise. I listened to all three and took the useful portion from each: the sluice mattered, the boy had seen something, and the adults had spent more effort controlling his location than understanding his survival.

The child would not answer questions. I did not force him. Men with authority force speech and then mistake the result for truth. Instead I crouched near the stone wall, held Miro's wooden horse by its carved tail after he pushed it toward me, and examined the mud packed in its wheels. The toy had been dragged through warm silt. Not river mud. Not yard mud. The silt under the mill had small black grains in it that glittered when broken open, as if coal dust had learned to grow.
"He took it down there," Edda said.
"No. It was returned with him."

The priest made the sign of the flame by habit, remembered which goddess his village officially favored, and changed the gesture halfway through. It did not improve the theology. Odrik saw me notice and looked away.
"Something brought the boy back," I said.
"Mercy," the priest said.
"Wrong smell."
Edda's gaze sharpened. "Then why?"

I turned the toy horse over. Under the belly, in the place where a child's thumb had worn the wood smooth, a streak of black silt formed a crooked line. Not a rune. Not even a mark, perhaps. Only pressure and dirt. Still, the barbed star under my shirt chilled as I studied it, and Buck stamped once behind me.
"It returned him because it had learned him," I said.
No one liked that. It is useful to know which truths make a crowd stop breathing.

By dusk, the village that did not use its name had climbed the hill above itself. Rain thinned into mist. Lamps burned behind blankets in upper rooms. Animals complained from fences dragged uphill. Odrik stood under a bent apple tree with a ledger held beneath his coat, trying to record an evacuation as if records could make it orderly. The priest moved among the villagers with his candle lantern and murmured comforts I could not hear. Edda sat beside Miro on a stone wall and watched the mill. Buck stood near them, wet and offended, one rein looped around a dead branch.
He had refused the old stable so violently that I respected the opinion.

I worked alone. I salted the yard where salt mattered and ignored the horseshoes. I set three snares of chain and hooked them to the mill's support beams, then cut two beams halfway through with measured strokes. I wedged an old plough-blade under the wheel brace, coated the trapdoor ring with oil, and laid a path of pig blood from the cellar mouth toward the marsh beyond the north field. The marsh was a skin of reeds and black water over ground that had forgotten whether it was land. It would hold weight badly. That made it useful.
Useful things often have poor manners.
Odrik came down once before full dark, carrying a purse and a face arranged around official concern. "If the mill is destroyed without necessity, we shall have to revisit the terms."
I did not look up from sharpening the last stake. "Bring a shovel when you revisit."
"I am trying to preserve what little these people have left."
"No. You're trying to preserve what proves you didn't know."
Odrik went quiet. Rain ticked on the broken boards. The wheel creaked behind us, slower now.
"My father built one of those beams," he said.
"Your father built over a grave."
"Men did what they had to do during the war."
I tested the edge of the stake with my thumb and watched a thin line of blood appear. "They always do. That's why the ground keeps accounts."
He left with the purse still under his coat. The extra ten crowns would not survive the night. I had known that from the bridge.

When darkness came, it came from the river first. It moved up through the reeds, took the yard, climbed the walls, and sat under the eaves. I drank the cat potion and felt the world sharpen with its usual cruelty. Darkness turned blue and silver. Raindrops became needles. The floor showed faint lines where old repairs met new boards, not with light but with wrongness. My pulse slowed. My mouth filled with the bitter mineral taste of alchemy.
I opened the trapdoor.
Heat breathed up. Below, something clicked twice in answer.
"Come on, then," I said.
The mill answered by stopping.

The silence was immediate and muscular. All day the wheel had given the place a false heart, a sound people could pretend belonged to water and work. Without it, the mill became a mouth held open. Under the floor, mud shifted. The sacks along the far wall sagged inward though nothing touched them. A thin crack ran across the flour-dust floor and closed again.
I stepped backward along the blood path, sword low. The cellar remained black. Then the trapdoor frame buckled upward and something that had learned the shape of roots reached out.

It was not large at first. That was the insult of it. A narrow head pushed through, blind and pale, plated in patches of mud-hard skin and old wood slivers. Its mouth opened sideways. Too many small teeth clicked against one another with the sound I had heard beneath the wheel. Two forelimbs followed, one ending in claws, the other in a flattened digging plate wrapped in rope fibers and bone. The plate found seams instead of boards, levering the floor by what it felt through pressure. It had built itself from survival, pressure, and everything the villagers had given the ground by refusing to open it.
The creature paused at the threshold. It tasted the air. Then it turned its head toward the hill where the villagers waited.
"No."
It came for me instead.

The first rush broke the trapdoor apart. I cut across the plated snout and felt steel scrape without biting deep. The creature recoiled, not from pain, but calculation. It had fought men with spears. It had pulled goats through walls. It knew resistance as a pattern and had learned that anything standing its ground could be undermined. The floor under my left boot softened.
I moved before it opened.

The boards collapsed where I had stood. Mud erupted, warm and black, swallowing the stake I had left there. I rolled across flour dust, came up beside the first chain snare, and drove the hook into the creature's digging limb as it lunged. The chain snapped taut. The beam groaned. Above me, the cut I had made in the support began to widen.
The creature clicked. The sound changed pitch.

I had thought it angry. Anger I could use. Anger narrows a creature, makes it predictable, makes it spend strength for insult. The change in pitch was not anger. It was speech, or close enough to make no difference, and it was not speaking to me.
It was calling the warm seam under the mill.
From the hill, someone shouted. The creature turned toward the voice again. I cut the blood path with my own palm and let fresh blood fall onto the floor.
The barbed star under my armor went cold until it hurt.
I nearly stopped there. Songs rarely keep that part. Aard should have been simple: breath, fingers, will, shove. The Sign waited in my hand and did not feel like enough.

For one breath, the barbed star did not wake; it went colder, warning. The older pressure under my ribs pulled toward the buried place beneath the mill, toward heat, bone, and all the names left under boards. My vision reddened at the edges. I tasted ash. The dead did not speak. The ground pressed its grief against me and waited for my hand to agree.
Then the creature lunged.

I threw Aard. Something answered through it. The Sign broke from me with a red pulse that turned the rain outside to steam and slammed the creature backward through the north wall. The first chain held. The second caught. The third tore free and whipped past my face close enough to kiss the scar on my cheek. The mill screamed in timber-language. The cut beams gave way.
"Stay," I muttered, though Buck was too far to hear and too wise to obey if he chose otherwise.

The north frame collapsed and dragged the creature halfway into the yard. Mud swallowed its flattened limb. The plough-blade jammed under the wheel brace. The old wheel shuddered, jumped, and turned against itself. The floor beneath me tilted. I ran along the sagging boards, silver drawn now, because some things require the right tool and some require the merciful one.

The creature tried to burrow. The marsh took its weight badly, just as I had asked it to. Reeds bent inward. Black water climbed its plated ribs. Its blind head snapped toward me, mouth clicking open. I drove silver through the hinge of that sideways mouth and down into whatever passed for a brain in a thing made of rot, heat, hunger, and bad municipal decisions.
It died with a sound like wet grain being ground between stones.

I stayed on one knee until I was certain. Cat potion made the villagers on the hill too clear: Odrik with both hands over his mouth, the priest's lantern lifted, Edda standing now, Miro beside her with his wooden horse pressed to his chest. My palm burned where I had cut it. My thigh had opened on something jagged. The red pressure in the air faded slowly, reluctantly, like a beast called back to heel.

I wanted to stand before they saw the tremor. Pride is a stupid animal, but it is loyal. I got one foot under me, failed, and stayed down. The mud did not care whether I looked like a legend. It took my knee and kept it.
Miro saw. So did Edda. So did Odrik, and I hated that most because the man already mistook survival for a negotiable clause.
The mill finished collapsing behind me.

When villagers finally came down, they did it the way people approach a grave they have ordered someone else to dig. Odrik looked at the ruin and understood the extra ten crowns had died bravely. The priest knelt near the marsh and prayed over a thing he had no name for. Edda came last, with Miro behind her, and studied the broken cellar mouth under the mill.
"Will it come back?" she asked.
"No."
"You're certain?"
"No," I said. "But I know what to burn. That's better."
We burned the root remains, the scorched rope, three sacks of old grain, and the portion of the foundation that had been built over bodies no one wanted counted.
Before sunrise, Edda made the village count the bones.

She did it without ceremony. Ceremony would have given Odrik somewhere to hide. She took a shovel, put it into the hands of the spear-man who had laughed at the wrong moments, and told him to dig where the foundation had sagged before the war winter. Then she told the priest to stop blessing air and begin naming what could still be named. The man obeyed with the shaken expression of someone discovering that faith, when cornered by an old woman, was expected to become labor.

Seven sets of remains came out of the mud. Four were nearly whole. Two had been mixed by water and years of shifting boards. The last was only a jaw, three ribs, and a length of plaited cord that might once have been a girl's belt. Odrik tried to call them unconfirmed dead for the ledger. Edda looked at him until the phrase went back into his mouth and died there.

Miro watched from the stone wall with his wooden horse pressed under his chin. I should have sent him away. I knew that. Children do not need more evidence that adults build houses over the things they fear to name. But when I moved toward him, his fingers tightened around the toy and he shook his head once.
"It clicks when I close my eyes," he said.

I had a clean answer ready. Witchers collect those the way soldiers collect scars, because a clean answer lets a man sound useful while failing to help. It is dead. It cannot come back. Sleep anyway. I almost said one of them. Edda saved me by arriving with a strip of cloth and a cup of water.
"Then keep your eyes open until they grow bored," she said.

Miro considered this as if it were sound medical counsel. From Edda, it might have been. She wrapped the cloth around the toy horse's broken leg and gave it back to him. The boy touched the knot, then looked at me as though I had been asked a question and failed the exam.
He was right.
"Burning helps," I said at last. "Naming helps more. Neither is quick. Anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. Usually candles."
Miro did not smile. He was too tired for mercy.
Edda did. Very slightly. "There," she said. "A witcher can learn after all."
"Slowly," I said.
"Most men do. The trick is keeping them alive long enough for it to matter."

By dawn, the village had seven old bones laid on a blanket and one new ruin where a mill had stood. That did not make the place clean. Clean is a fantasy invented by people who have never lifted floorboards. But it made the lie smaller, and sometimes that is the only honest work left.

By dawn, the village had regained enough courage to become cheap. Odrik tried to pay sixty, citing damage, irregular conduct, and the difficulty of proving the dead thing had been the only cause of structural failure. I let him explain the position for a while. Men who enjoy the sound of their own reason should be allowed to spend it.
Then I rested one hand on my sword and told him the corpse was still warm enough to put in his bed.
He paid seventy.
Miro followed me to the bridge when I led Buck out. He placed the wooden horse in my gloved hand, then changed his mind and took it back. Good. Surviving children should keep what survived with them.
"It knew my name," he whispered.
His voice was small from disuse, but it did not break. I crouched so my eyes were lower than his. Children are already short. Men with swords do not need to remind them.
"Then don't give it another one," I said.
He considered that. "Do you have one?"
"A name?"
He nodded.

I thought of Vesemir finding me in a ruined keep with a barbed star at my throat and no memory behind my eyes. I thought of Kaer Morhen, of cold walls, hot decoctions, Geralt's silence, and the kind of protection that begins as love and becomes architecture. I thought of the way strangers looked at my eyes and decided my name could not possibly be enough.
"Several," I said. "Most of them unhelpful."
Miro looked at the ruined mill. "Will the village use its name again?"
"Not soon."
"Should it?"
"A name won't save it. But hiding a wound teaches the ground to remember for you."
He looked too serious for a child. That was not my doing. The world had reached him first.
Edda stood by the road with a linen bundle. Inside were bread, hard cheese, and the sort of dried sausage that proves affection by threatening the teeth. "For the road," she said.
"I was paid."
"So were the men who built over the dead. Take it before I decide you're rude."
I took it.
The road took me before gratitude could.

By the time the first version reached the next village, the mill had been swallowed whole by a red wolf with a sword in its teeth. By the time it crossed the river, the wolf had spoken the dead name and the earth had obeyed. By the time a clerk in a brown coat wrote it down on poor paper with expensive ink, the witness was described as reliable, the phenomenon as localized, the witcher as unidentified, and the ground itself as responsive under pressure.
Under remarks, the clerk added one line and sanded it dry.

Subject displays unusual field effect in post-contact witness narrative. Crimson pressure described by multiple observers. Recommendation: retain statement pending narrative correction. Potential recurrence should be observed under controlled contract conditions. Cross-check unresolved barbed-star continuity index if active.
The first repeated phrase appeared on a whitewashed post outside a hamlet that had lost three geese, one drunk, and its sense of proportion.

I read the notice while Buck cropped dead grass from the ditch and pretended the geese were not staring at him. The paper had been nailed too high for most villagers and too low for officials with self-importance, which meant the man who placed it had wanted travelers to see it, not locals. The handwriting was neat. The spelling was better than the hamlet deserved. At the bottom, beneath the usual promise of payment upon proof, someone had written localized instability in a style that belonged nowhere near missing poultry.

The words bothered me before the corpse did. That should have warned me. Monsters leave marks on mud, bone, thresholds, livestock, and the men who lie about where they were after dusk. Offices leave marks on language. One can be tracked with a good knife and bad knees. The other follows you while pretending to describe the weather.

I had been written down before. Witchers are always being written down by people who want danger at a safe grammatical distance: mutant, vagrant, blade-for-hire, tolerated contamination, tax question. Those words smelled of fear and bad education. This was different: same dry phrasing, same polite ownership, same terms wearing local seals as masks. Ordinary hatred shouts. Organized hunger edits.
"Geese," I said.
Buck chewed.
"Localized instability."
Buck swallowed and reached for another mouthful.
"You're right. Geese explain most of it."

The geese did not explain the drunk. That is the trouble with honest mockery. It rarely survives the corpse. The drunk had been found in a drainage ditch at dawn, emptied of blood with two fingers missing and his boots arranged neatly beside him. Folk insisted he had been a harmless man, which meant he was either loved, recently dead, or had owed money to everyone equally.

The alderman of that place was a woman named Branka, wide in the shoulders and narrow in patience. She met me under the post with three farmers, two boys, and a goose that had appointed itself witness. Branka had the direct stare of someone who had spent twenty years telling men where to move stones and had not yet forgiven them for needing instruction.
"You the witcher?"
"I practice."
"Notice said one."
"Then we are both relieved."
She studied my eyes, then my swords, then Buck. The goose hissed at him. Buck ignored it with the dignity of a horse who understood that war with geese has no winners.
"Payment is forty crowns," Branka said. "Five extra if you find the drunk's fingers. Widow wants them for burial."
"Fingers usually go where the mouth goes."
"That meant to comfort me?"
"No."
"Good. I dislike being comforted by men with cat eyes."
I liked her immediately, which was unwise. Liking people on the Path is a fine way to start collecting grief in places grief should not fit.

The ditch ran along the north edge of the hamlet, carrying rainwater, kitchen scraps, and the private ambitions of every latrine uphill. I found the marks where the drunk had fallen, or been pulled. The mud showed one man's staggered prints, then a second pattern that looked like knuckles, claws, and the dragging of a wet sack. Under the bridge stones, something had scraped the limewash from the culvert and left black flecks in the cracks. I touched one with the tip of my knife.

Not garkain. Not exactly. Something feeding like one, moving like one, and leaving behind the bitter cave stink of old blood and damp fur. Monster names comfort people because names sound like borders. The world is less polite. Things breed with curses, hunger, magic, and war refuse. Then some poor fool with a sword gets asked to classify the result.

I lay on my back in six inches of black water for twenty minutes while the thing crawled above me through the culvert. It had folded itself flat enough to pass under the stones, its skin grey and hairless, its ribs moving like fingers under wet leather. Its eyes were clouded white. Its mouth had split too far up one cheek. Around its neck was a strip of official black ribbon tied in a knot too neat for accident.
"There you are," I whispered.
It heard me, which was careless of it.

The fight did not last seven breaths. I wanted it to, which is not the same thing. The creature dropped from the culvert ceiling, all elbows, teeth, and old blood, and I put silver where its throat should have been. The blade slid along bone instead of into it. That was my first mistake. My second was trying to curse in a space too narrow to draw breath.

It hit me hard enough to drive the back of my head against the stone. Ditch water filled my mouth. For one unpleasant moment I was a boy under Kaer Morhen again, pinned under a training frame while Lambert laughed from somewhere safe and Vesemir told me panic was just a body voting against its owner. My body voted loudly. I swallowed mud, got one knee under me, and felt claws rake through leather along my ribs.

I tried Aard. The Sign struck the culvert roof and threw grit into my eyes. Useful, if I had been trying to blind myself before being eaten. The thing came again, and I saw too late that it was not defending a den. It was driving me toward the wider drain where it could unfold. Branka saved me by accident or judgment. A pitchfork punched through the side grate behind the creature, not deep, but enough to make it twist.

I took the ugly second she bought me. Silver went under the jaw this time, then up. Igni followed, not the heroic tavern kind that lights a monster in clean orange flame, but a cramped, mean burst of heat that boiled ditch water and filled the culvert with stink. The creature screamed once. Three geese answered from the road, offended by amateur competition.
When it died, one of the missing fingers slid from its mouth.

I crawled out on my elbows because standing had become a negotiation and I was losing it. Branka looked down at me, then at the dead thing, then at the pitchfork in her hands as if surprised to find herself in possession of courage.
"Do not tell anyone I helped," she said.
"Why?"
"They will ask for a discount."
I coughed ditch water from my lungs and decided I liked her less safely than before.
"Four crowns," Branka said later, looking at the finger wrapped in cloth. "Each finger worth two and a half by agreement."
"You offered five for fingers. I found one."
"Plural."
"Do I look like a grammarian?"

She paid three. I accepted because blood loss makes philosophers generous and because the widow cried when Branka gave her the cloth. Tears do not increase payment, but sometimes they make bargaining feel like theft.

That was another mistake. Not the mercy. The speed. I should have cleaned the cut properly, asked who had handled the ribbon, and made Branka close the road until the dead thing burned. Instead I let coin and fatigue make a small decision for me. Small decisions are where large nets learn the shape of a man.

I was cleaning the wound behind the stable when a man in a clerk's brown coat found me. He had a narrow face, tired eyes, and the expression of someone who had misplaced a moral principle and kept finding paperwork in its place. He held his cap in both hands as if it might confess for him.
"Master witcher?"
"Depends who's asking."
"Rian Wedeck. District copyist. Formerly assistant registrar, temporarily attached to damage compensation review, occasionally messenger by abuse of rank."
"You collect titles the way dogs collect burrs."
His mouth twitched and failed to become a smile. "After the war a man takes the title that arrives with bread."
That could stand without help. I tightened the linen over my side and nodded toward the notice on the post. "You wrote that?"
"I copied it."
"There's a difference?"
"There used to be."
Useful answer. Dangerous man. Not because he was brave, but because he still knew the shape of honesty and had not yet learned to hate it enough to survive.

Rian looked at the dead thing laid out near the ditch. The villagers had come to stand at a distance and say helpful things like never seen the like and my cousin said plague pits glow when you lie near them. Someone had thrown a blanket over the corpse. The blanket had immediately begun to lose the argument.
"That ribbon," Rian said.
"You recognize it."
"No."
"You answered too quickly."
He swallowed. "I recognize the ink on it. Black preservative. Used for field packets that might get wet. Or burned. Or buried badly."
"You people plan for everything except decency."
"I am not people," he said, then flushed. "I mean, I am people, obviously. I meant I am not those people. Not exactly."
"Best kind of denial. Half-built and already collapsing."
Rian took a sealed packet from inside his coat. The wax was black, not red, pressed with no crest I knew. Only a small square mark, four lines crossing. A cage pretending to be a signature.

"There were three notices," he said. "Same phrasing. Localized instability. Same ribbon after the body was collected from the plague pit near Murn. Same instruction to retain witness statements pending correction. I thought it was disease mapping at first. After the war, offices bred like flies around corpses. But then your description appeared. Crimson eyes. Wolf medallion. White hair. Scar along left cheekbone. It was not a full conspiracy to me then. It was only paperwork leaning too hard in one direction."
I looked at him until he remembered how breathing worked.
"I did not write that report," he said. "I copied it."
"Comforting. A knife is much kinder if the handle didn't forge itself."

"I came because someone else is copying faster than I am." He held out the packet. His hand shook, but not enough to make him useless. "There's another notice. Bigger payment. Broken Crown. North road. I think they are putting contracts where you will see them."
"Why warn me?"

"Because I watched a woman die in a fever shed last winter after her compensation claim was corrected from civilian injury to transport irregularity. Her husband received nothing because the paper decided she had not been where her body was found." Rian's throat moved. "I kept the first draft. It did not save her. I would like once, before I die, for stolen paper to be useful before someone is buried."
The wind moved over the ditch and stirred the dead thing's blanket. A goose hissed again, perhaps at the state of government.
"Who gets these reports?" I asked.

"District medics. Field assessors. Auditors. Some military offices. A senior examiner named Sorel Veyrane signed the guidance I saw. There is also a medical addendum network. I don't know how high it goes. I only know my desk touches one belt of the machine."
"High enough to stay dry in rain."
"Usually."
I took the packet. The wax felt cold even after I held it.
"You should leave," I said.
"I should never have come."
"Wiser. Less useful."

Rian gave a tired little nod, as if usefulness had long ago become a disease he could not afford treatment for. "There is a medic in Devenford. Mara Veyr. Not kin to Sorel, I think. At least not closely. She receives the guidance sheets as medicine, not orders. She may know more. She may not know what she has been handed."

That, at least, gave his courage a route instead of making it look like a sudden fever. Rian had not found me because fate had grown sentimental. He had copied three contracts with the same clean phrase, seen the same waterproof packet move through two offices that claimed not to share records, and noticed that every notice along my road paid too much for ordinary work while asking too carefully for witnesses afterward. Mara entered the matter because medicine had become the door polite men used when chains would look premature. If her notes already touched the file, then she was not outside the trap. She was one of its hinges.
"Why bring this to me instead of her?"
His eyes moved to my wound and away. "Because if I am wrong, you leave town and curse me. If I am right, she may already be inside the machinery without knowing where the teeth are."
I disliked him then. Not because he was wrong. Because he had found the one honest reason to stay.
"You trust her?"
"She once reset my fingers after a cavalryman broke them for asking him to sign the correct requisition. She charged him for the splint."
"That is not trust."
"No," he said. "But it is promising."

Branka returned before the fire took the corpse properly. She came with a bucket of sand, two boys carrying dry brush, and the expression of a woman who had learned that men make worse decisions when flames are involved. Her gaze moved from the dead thing to Rian, then sharpened.
"District copyist," she said.
Rian went still. "Mistress Branka."
"You corrected my brother."

The sentence landed harder than accusation. Rian looked at me once, not for help, but because men who have spent too long inside offices sometimes forget whether a witness is allowed to bleed in public.
"I copied a correction," he said. "I did not make it."
"You put it in the hand that killed the pension."
"Yes."
No excuse came after it. That surprised her. It surprised me too, though I would not have paid to admit it.

Branka's brother had died two years earlier, pinned under a wagon during a forced evacuation after a cavalry column changed its mind about which road belonged to whom. The first report called him civilian dead in military movement. The second called him transport irregularity under local responsibility. The third called him nothing payable at all. Somewhere between the second and third, Rian's hand had copied the words that starved a widow through winter.
"I kept the first draft," Rian said.
Branka's jaw worked. "Did it feed her?"
"No."
"Then do not bring me paper and call it repentance."
He nodded. "I wasn't."
That was the first moment I truly believed he might be useful. Not innocent. Innocence has poor endurance. Useful.
Branka looked at me. "If dry-cloak men come asking, I saw you bleeding and unpleasant. Nothing more."
"That is generous."
"It is accurate." She pointed at the corpse. "Burn the ribbon separate. Don't let the smoke touch the geese. They have enough opinions."
Rian stared at her as she turned away. "Why help?"
She stopped. "Because the men who corrected my brother were dry when they arrived and dry when they left. You at least look ruined by the weather."
It was not forgiveness. That would have been too cheap for the shape of the wound. It was a small practical mercy with teeth in it, which is often the only kind that survives contact with government.

I burned the creature before sunset. It smoked green at the joints, then black where the ribbon curled. The villagers stood downwind until they understood their mistake. Branka paid the agreed forty crowns, minus what she described as reasonable adjustment for property damage after my Igni cracked part of the culvert wall. I considered arguing. Then the goose bit her boot and she forgot to look official.
Buck and I left richer than when we arrived, which is not the same as paid well.

At the ferry road, a boy with a split lip asked whether I was the red-eyed witcher from the white post. He had no reason to know the phrase except that someone had paid him to practice it. His questions came too neatly: where I was bound, whether my wounds smoked, whether the horse disliked black ribbon. I gave him a copper for his trouble and an answer worth less. Behind him, a man in a brown coat examined a broken wheel with the intensity of someone who had never repaired anything heavier than a sentence. Clean boots. Dry cuffs. A little leather tube under his arm. When I looked back from the bend, he was speaking to Branka's youngest boy and pointing not at the corpse smoke, but at my tracks. I did not know Black Ink then. I knew only that someone had begun paying strangers to notice the road after me.

Devenford smelled of vinegar, wet wool, and people pretending the war had ended because banners had been folded. It had a market square with two gallows, one church with three saints in competition, and a medical house behind a cooper's yard where the barrels leaked less than the patients. I found Mara Veyr washing blood from a saw.

She was thirty, perhaps a little older, with dark hair pinned carelessly and sleeves rolled past the elbow. Not pretty in the decorative sense merchants pay poets to lie about. Better than that. Her face had work in it: decisive mouth, tired eyes, a small scar near the chin, hands that knew how to touch pain without apologizing to it. She looked at my side before she looked at my face.
"If you came here to die, use the back room," she said. "The front table is clean."
"I was aiming for mildly inconvenienced."
"Men with ribs showing always are. Sit."
"Witcher."
"I have eyes. Sit."

I sat because the room had leaned slightly to the left, and because any woman who opened with that much contempt usually knew something useful. She cut the bandage away and examined the wound without the flinch civilians like to pretend they do not have.
"Garkain?" she asked.
"Garkain-adjacent."
"That is not a medical category."
"Give government time."
Her fingers paused. "You have seen the sheets."
"I have seen enough paper to know when it wants a body under it."
Mara cleaned the wound with something that hurt more than the claw, which is how I knew it was proper medicine. "You tore this open riding."

Pain made the room briefly smaller. The saw, the basin, her sleeves, the rain at the cooper's yard, all of it tightened around the place her hands worked. I caught the edge of the table before my fingers reached for her wrist. A man can be trained not to flinch from knives and still dislike being cared for by someone who is not afraid of him.
"The road was enthusiastic."
"The road did not decide to bleed through leather. Hold still."
I held still. Holding still is a skill witchers learn early. The Trials teach boys many things, most of them rude, but the first is that panic rarely improves the knife.

She worked in silence for a while. Rain began outside, tapping on the cooper's yard and running in silver lines down the window. The infirmary smelled of lye, bitter herbs, warm iron, and Mara's soap, which had rosemary in it. That detail annoyed me. Pleasantness is suspicious in a room where saws are washed.
"Rian sent you," she said.
"Rian pointed. I walked."
"That sounds like him. Brave in the least efficient manner available."
"He says you receive guidance sheets."

"I receive many things. Wounded farmers, rotten boots, accusations of witchcraft, three jars of pickled eels from a patient who thinks gratitude should threaten the tongue." She reached for a hooked needle. "Which guidance sheets?"
"The ones that call dead geese instability."
The needle stopped.
There. Bodies lie less than mouths.

"I thought they were contamination advisories," Mara said. "After the war, there were fevers in the river camps, mutations in livestock, corpse-bloat that walked when it should not. Some of it needed tracking. Some of it needed burning."
"And some of it needed a witcher with crimson eyes."

She looked at me then. Properly. Like the priest in the unnamed village, but without the comfort of theology. Her gaze moved over the slit pupils, the scar, the white hair, the medallion, then dropped to the old barbed-star chain where it had slipped above my collar while she worked. She did not touch it.
That made her smarter than most.
"May I?" she asked, nodding toward the chain.
"No."

She accepted the answer without injury. Another promising sign. "Then let me say this: your wound is warmer than it should be, but you have no fever. The tissue response is too fast. Not normal witcher fast. Too fast. If I had seen you brought in unconscious, I would have written it down."
"Would you have sent it?"
Her mouth tightened.
Better than a lie. Worse than comfort.

"I don't know," she said. "Three months ago, yes. A month ago, perhaps. Today, after Rian came in looking like a man who had learned bureaucracy could grow teeth, no. I treated a patient first, and the report can go hungry for once."

Mara set the needle down then, not because her hands had failed, but because the answer had weight and she preferred not to drop it while holding steel. "I did not ask Rian to bring me an interesting witcher," she said. "I asked him why three medical sheets described routes before wounds. You arrived after the question, not before it. Remember that if you decide to make yourself the center of my bad judgment."

I believed her. Not because innocence sat comfortably on her, but because guilt did not. Mara had the face of a woman discovering that competent notes could become a leash in hands she would never invite into the room. That did not clean her hands. It did make them human.
"Convenient timing."
"Most morality is. People like to imagine courage arrives fully armed at birth. Usually it arrives late, underfed, and asking where to stand."
I almost smiled. It would have hurt the wound and perhaps encouraged her, so I saved myself the trouble.
Mara finished stitching and pressed a clean cloth over the cut. "You need rest."
"I need answers."
"Then rest with questions. You cannot interrogate a filing network while leaking on my floor."
"I've done worse things bleeding."
"Men always have. That is why medicine exists."

Rian came after the garkain-adjacent corpse had finished burning in the square. He entered with a sealed packet and the look of a man trying to decide whether loyalty belonged to law, fear, or the woman who had once set his fingers. Mara saw the packet and closed the shutters.
"No," she said.
Rian held it out anyway. "You should see this."

The packet contained copied notices, field summaries, and one page of irregular guidance written in a hand so clean it felt scrubbed of personhood. Key terms repeated across the sheets: host suitability, reactive field expression, controlled contract conditions, narrative correction, public-risk anomaly. A phrase on the last page made Mara go still.
Voluntary cooperation preferred.
"That means arrest," I said.
Rian nodded miserably. "In polite shoes."
Mara read the page again. "This is not medicine."
"No," Rian said. "It is medicine after someone important asks what a body can do for policy."

The room held the three of us in different kinds of guilt. Mine had older teeth. Rian's kept apologizing for itself. Mara's had just learned her handwriting might have carried men to doors they never walked out of again.
"Who is Sorel Veyrane?" I asked.
Rian licked his lips. "Senior examiner. Special authority under provisional reconstruction. He signs corrections that other offices obey before they understand them."
"Which is to say he writes reality slowly enough that people think they agreed."
"Yes."
Mara folded the paper with care. "You are in danger."
"I was in danger yesterday. This is paperwork."
"Paper outlives knives," she said. "I have seen men die because one clerk wrote livestock where prisoner should have been. Do not look at this as ink. Look at it as a road being built toward you."

I looked at the rain sliding down her window, at Rian's shaking hands, at Buck visible in the yard with his head under a sagging roof, offended by weather and government alike. My side burned. The barbed star under my shirt felt cold enough to numb.
"The Broken Crown," I said. "Where is it?"
Rian closed his eyes briefly. "North of Heddel's Ferry. Old hill-fort. Bad stones. Worse memories."
Mara looked at him. "You gave him the next notice?"
"I warned him. There is a difference."
"A bureaucratic one?"
"I deserved that."
"Yes."
I stood. Mara placed one hand against my chest, not softly. It was not an intimate gesture. It was a professional barricade.
"If you ride tonight, you will reopen the wound, bleed into your armor, frighten your horse, and perhaps die in a ditch with impressive discipline."
"Buck won't be frightened. He'll be angry."
"Two hours," she said.
"No."
"One."
"No."
"Half an hour, and I give you the copied sheet I should burn."
Bargaining is a vice. So is survival. I sat.

Mara worked by lantern light while Rian sorted the papers into piles: true, dangerous, already known, and likely fatal to possess. His labels were not as neat as his handwriting. Mara gave me broth I did not ask for and watched until I drank it. The wound in my side closed too much while she watched, which was rude of it. Her face changed by half a breath. Not fear. Recognition.
"That is not ordinary," she said.
"I get that often."
"Don't perform. Not with me."

The words struck more cleanly than I liked. I had not thought of it as performance, but men with unusual eyes learn young that silence can be armor, economy can be mystique, and contempt can keep curiosity at a civil distance. I had worn all three so long I sometimes forgot where skin ended and manner began.
"No," I said. "It isn't ordinary."
Mara's fingers rested near the bandage, not touching. "Does it hurt?"
"Usually."
"Comforting word. Sounds as if the impossible has habits."
"Everything has habits. Monsters. Men. Paper."
"And you?"
"Especially me."

That was where the room changed. Not by much. A lantern guttered once and recovered. Rain softened against the cooper's yard until the whole town seemed to be holding its breath. Rian, suddenly discovering the genius of cowardice, announced that he needed to check whether the stable roof leaked directly onto Buck's saddle. Buck had no saddle on, but I admired the effort. He left with enough dignity for a man fleeing two people and a question.
Mara tied off the last bandage. The knot pulled against my ribs, neat and unforgiving. "You should leave before dawn."
"That's the plan."
"Plans are just lies men tell the next hour."
"You collect sayings too?"
"Only the ones that survive patients."

She should have moved away then. I should have let her. Instead she stayed close enough for the warmth of her hands to remain in the air between us. Her fingers smelled of spirits, rosemary soap, and the iron ghost of my blood. Mine rested on the table edge because I did not trust them to behave like hands and not arguments.

The room had become too small for cleverness. The saw lay clean beside the basin. The papers lay folded under a stone cup. Rain touched the window in thin silver lines. Mara looked at my mouth, then at the bandage she had tied, then back at my mouth, which was worse than if she had stared without shame.

I took the knife from my belt and set it on the table beside the saw, handle toward me, blade away from her. It was a small thing, almost absurd. Men who had survived their own bad instincts often made ceremonies out of moving sharp objects three inches. Mara noticed. Of course she did.
"If this is pity," I said, "say so now."
Her eyes lifted to mine. The tiredness in them stayed. It made room for something warmer and more dangerous. "Pity does not make me reckless. Exhaustion might. Wanting does."

That was a clean answer. A dangerous one. I stood before sense could recover enough breath to argue and closed the small distance between us. Slowly, because she had earned the right to stop me before my shadow touched her. Deliberately, because I was tired of letting every other hand in the world decide whether my body was patient, problem, witness, or property.

Mara did not step back. Her chin rose by a fraction, not challenge exactly, not permission cheaply given. More like a woman bracing one hand against a door she had already chosen to open. I stopped close enough to smell rosemary soap beneath the spirits on her fingers.
"Tell me if I hurt you," she said.
"You first."
That surprised her. Good. Surprise is one of the few honest things left in a room after fear has made furniture of everything else.

Her hand rose and stopped before it touched my face. I caught it gently by the wrist, not holding it prisoner, only steadying the tremor she had hidden badly enough for a witcher to notice. The pulse beneath my fingers beat too fast for professional concern. Mine was no better, which annoyed me because bodies have never respected a man's private dignity.
"Yes," I said.

Her fingers reached my jaw. Lightly at first. The old scar, the new bruise, the place where a man learns not to flinch because people call it discipline when what they mean is damage trained into obedience. Her thumb brushed the corner of my mouth. The contact was small enough to be denied and warm enough to make denial foolish.
I bent first.

The kiss did not arrive like a song or a tavern lie. It arrived like a decision made in a room full of evidence. Her mouth met mine carefully, bitter tea and smoke and rosemary, soft only where softness had cost her something. I felt her breath catch against my lips, a caught human sound she swallowed almost immediately, as if even that might be written down if she let it live too long.
I drew back a finger's breadth. "Too much?"
"No." Her answer came quick and practical, almost irritated by the need to say it. "Do not make me file a complaint against caution."
"I'd hate to burden the office."
"Then do better."

I did. My hand settled at the back of her neck with more certainty this time, fingers closing in the damp hair that had escaped its pins. Mara came closer of her own will, one knee brushing mine, one hand flat against my shoulder where armor and wet cloth made a poor barrier. She did not melt. Mara was not the melting sort. She leaned in as if testing a splint under weight, and when it held, she trusted it with another inch.

Heat moved between us slowly, through leather, bandage, linen, and the stubborn layer of sense neither of us had fully abandoned. I kept the kiss careful, not timid. There is a difference. Timidity asks the other person to carry the choice alone. Carefulness carries half of it and leaves the door open.
Her fingers found the strap over my ribs and stopped. "That pulls."
"Most things do."
"Unhelpful."
"Accurate."

She made a small sound into my mouth, not quite laughter, not quite surrender. It startled her enough that she broke the kiss and looked annoyed with herself. I touched the loose strand of hair at her cheek and put it back. Her eyes closed for half a breath.
"You are thinking," she said.
"I was admiring your diagnostic method."
"Liar."
"Only partly."

She pressed her forehead against my chin, and the gesture did what the kiss had not. It made the room quiet. Not safe. Safe is a word people use when they want danger to feel insulted and leave. Quiet, though, sometimes happens. Quiet can hold.

I slid my hand from her neck to her shoulder and felt the tension there, the day's work knotted under skin and wool. I rubbed once with my thumb. Mara exhaled, low and involuntary, then caught my wrist before I could move away.
"There," she said, voice rougher than before. "Not because you are weak. Because you are allowed to be tended."
That should not have hit like a blade. It did.

I kissed her again, firmer, answer instead of evasion. The stool scraped when she shifted between my knees, still careful of the wound, still Mara enough to keep one hand near the bandage as if desire had no right to excuse negligence. Her other hand slid into my hair. The pressure of it changed, less question now, more choice.

For a few breaths, neither of us pretended this was only medicine, only comfort, only an error born from candlelight and exhaustion. It was wanting with blood under its nails. It was care standing too close to evidence and refusing to look away. It was not enough to ruin us, which made it more dangerous than something larger would have been.
When she drew back, her face had color in it. One of her pins had surrendered completely. I wanted her badly enough to notice the fact and still not reach for more.
"There," she said softly. "That is why half an hour."
"You kissed me to improve patient compliance?"
"I considered nailing your sleeve to the table."
"Less intimate."
"Less paperwork."

She smiled then, small and tired and more expensive than the contract outside Heddel's Ferry would ever be. I stayed because I am not always wise. I stayed because she made room without making a cage of it. I stayed until the rain thinned, until her hands stopped shaking, until the papers on the table remembered they were dangerous and I remembered leaving was not the same as protecting her.
I left before dawn because I am not entirely stupid.

I told myself the kiss changed nothing. The lie lasted approximately eight steps down the stairs. By the time I reached Buck, it had become less useful and more obvious. He looked at me once, smelled the rosemary soap on my collar, and made the kind of sound horses reserve for men whose plans have begun leaking.
In the morning, the wound had closed too much.
Mara noticed. Rian noticed the missing corner of one copied notice. Buck noticed my mood and tried to kick the stable door. Everyone, in their own profession, proved competent.

Field Observation, District Medical Addendum. Subject: unnamed Wolf School witcher, probable age twenty to twenty-five. Wound response exceeds expected witcher range after garkain contact. Tissue heat persistent. No fever presentation. Eye coloration anomalous. Attending medic's terminology may be interpreted as reactive field expression. Recommend cross-reference with host suitability vocabulary in irregular field guidance. Do not disclose to local authority pending internal custody review.
The contract for the Broken Crown arrived on dry paper in a town where every roof leaked.

That was the first insult. Rain had followed me for nine days, softening roads, swelling streams, turning graves into soup and soup into arguments. Paper suffers in such weather. Notices curl. Ink runs. Seals bleed. Honest village complaints become dark smears under thumb marks. This notice remained crisp on the board outside Heddel's Ferry, its corners square, its ink black, its seal pressed deep into red wax that smelled faintly of cloves.
Buck smelled it and sneezed.
"Agreed," I said.

The notice offered one hundred and twenty crowns for removal of a subterranean threat beneath the hill-fort locally known as the Broken Crown. That was too much. It specified metallic auditory phenomena, livestock distress, and localized structural hazard. That was too clean. It requested that witnesses be held for statement collection after contract resolution. That was too familiar.
I took the notice down. The nail came out smoothly, as if it had been waiting for me.

Inside the nearest tavern, the roof leaked into six buckets and one bald man's soup. The innkeeper was a woman with forearms like cured ham and the tranquil expression of someone who had once broken a soldier's nose and found the memory spiritually nourishing. I placed two coppers on the bar.
"Hill north of here," she said. "Old fort. Bad stones. Worse memories."
"Specific."
"Specific requires another coin."
I added one. She regarded it as if it had insulted her lineage. I added another. She decided my character might yet be improved.

"Broken Crown was a hill-fort before any king with clean boots claimed the road. Then it was a storehouse. Then a prison. Then a place officers used when they wanted men forgotten without leaving the district. After the war, shepherds brought sheep there because sheep don't care about history and the grass is good. Now the sheep won't go near it."
"What came out?"
"Nothing. That's the problem. Things go in, nothing comes out, and at night the hill sounds like someone closing gates under it."
"Who posted the notice?"
She looked at the door, the roof, the buckets, and finally at me. "Man with a clean cloak. Not a soldier. Too dry."
"Dry men are dangerous."
"So are wet ones with two swords, but you paid."
Outside, a boy ran through the rain and handed me a folded strip of oilcloth. He vanished before I could ask who sent him. I opened it under the tavern eave and recognized Mara's hand.

They sent a query after the garkain report. Then another after the mill story. Then one asking whether your eyes were naturally crimson or reactive under stress. If you are going north, do not let them isolate witnesses. Do not bleed near prepared surfaces. If that sounds impossible, take comfort that I also think it is impossible. Come back alive anyway. M.
I read it twice, then burned it in the tavern's hearth before the ink had a chance to become anyone else's property.

The road north climbed through wet fields where old siege lines had become ditches full of brown water. Blackened stakes jutted from one hill like rotten teeth. A shrine to a local saint had been repaired with Nilfgaardian plank wood and Temerian nails, proving peace can be built from anything if you do not ask the dead for commentary. The Broken Crown rose beyond the fields, three shattered towers leaning inward around a hill split by a narrow cleft. From a distance, the ruin looked like a broken jaw trying to close.

Witnesses waited under a canvas awning at the base of the hill: a shepherd with a beard full of rain, two charcoal burners, a clerk with a portable writing desk, and a girl of twelve holding a lamb on a rope. The lamb looked more sensible than the clerk. This was not difficult.

The girl saw me first. She did not flinch at my eyes. Children either stare until adults slap them or understand quickly which monsters are hired and which wear clean boots. She had the second kind of face.
"Name?" I asked.
"Nessa."
"The lamb?"
"Breakfast if he doesn't stop chewing my sleeve."
"Practical."
"Mother says sentiment makes poor stew."
I looked at the shepherd. "Your daughter?"
"Niece," he said. "And she's not coming up."
"No."
The clerk cleared his throat. "The notice requires witnesses to remain accessible for statement collection."
"Accessible is downhill. Alive is better."
"I have instruction."
"So does my horse. He ignores half of it and remains useful."
Buck, tied to a warped post, showed the clerk his teeth with admirable timing.

Before entering the fort, I made the witnesses tell me the hill's stories separately. The shepherd heard gates. The charcoal burners heard chains under the stone. The clerk heard metallic resonance consistent with structural instability, which meant he had heard chains and hoped promotion preferred longer words. Nessa heard a woman singing in a language she did not know. She also saw lights move inside the cleft where no lantern could stay lit.
The drainage cut gave me the first honest sign that the hill had been prepared for my arrival.

Fresh mud lay under the bramble, yes, but mud only says someone passed. The stranger detail sat beneath it: four thumb-wide stripes of black resin painted along the inner stone, each one thin enough to miss if rain had not gathered on it differently. I touched the nearest stripe with the back of my knife. It pulled in a thread, sticky and dark, then snapped back to the rock. Not pitch. Not tar. Something treated, preserved, and meant to survive damp.
I smelled cloves under it.

Mara's note returned with the unpleasant timing of useful advice. Do not bleed near prepared surfaces. I had thought she meant laboratory tables, ward circles, examination cloths, the sort of clean places where frightened men try to make cruelty look hygienic. I had not imagined old stones under bramble, marked in the rain by someone who knew I would look for hidden ways in.
That was my third mistake of the day, and the sun had not yet earned noon.
The clerk saw me looking and decided silence might save him. Silence rarely saves men with writing desks. It only gives them time to sweat.
"Assessment marks," he said.
"I did not ask."
"Preliminary safety assessment. The hill was considered unstable."
"So you painted black bait in the drainage cut. For safety."
He swallowed. "I am not party to technical procedure."

That phrase had the clean shine of a borrowed coin. I let it pass because the hill was already breathing warmth through the gate and Nessa was watching us both. Sometimes an answer can wait. Sometimes waiting is how it becomes expensive.

I scraped a curl of the resin into oilcloth and tied it shut with my teeth. The taste of cloves clung to the air. Prepared surfaces. Witnesses retained. Payment too high. A child who heard the song best. The shape was not complete, but it had enough edges to cut a man who held it carelessly.
I held it carelessly anyway.

The bad part is that I knew I was doing it. Pride does not always feel like arrogance. Sometimes it feels like obligation wearing the right boots. The witnesses were behind me. The monster, or whatever the hill was feeding, was below. The officer with the clean cloak had not yet shown his face. The surface answer was simple enough for a tired man to trust: go down, kill the thing, collect the coin, keep the child away from the cleft.
Simple answers are where traps begin paying rent.

I walked the outer ring twice before going in. Not for mood. Mood is what poets call evidence when they do not know how to charge for it. The old fort had three usable approaches: the fallen gate, the sheep track along the west slope, and a drainage cut hidden under bramble on the east side. The clerk knew about the first because it was visible. The shepherd knew about the second because sheep lack respect for architecture. No one mentioned the third until I found fresh boot mud under the bramble and turned to look at them.

The clerk blinked too often. Not guilt. Fear of being caught outside his instructions. The charcoal burners had not used the drainage cut. Their boots were ash-stained and split at the heel. The shepherd could not have bent low enough without leaving half his coat on the thorns. That left the clean-cloaked man I had not yet seen, or someone like him, already moving around the hill while I asked honest questions of honest frightened people.
"Someone else has been here," I said.
The clerk hugged his writing desk tighter. "Authorized preliminary assessment."
"By whom?"
"I was not given the full designation."
"You were given enough to obey and not enough to sleep well."
He looked at the ground. That answered more cleanly than courage would have.
"What color?" I asked.

The clean-cloaked man was not among the witnesses then. I knew that later. I remember looking at the clerk, at his desk, at the shepherd's staff, at Nessa's lamb chewing rope with the serenity of doomed creatures everywhere, and thinking the danger was under the hill. A bad assumption. Some dangers prefer daylight, dry paper, and other men's authority.
"Red," she said.
The barbed star chilled under my shirt.
"Like fire?"
"No. Like looking through your eyelids when the sun is behind them."

I should have sent her away then. Not downhill. Away. A mile, two miles, far enough that no man with instructions could decide her fear had evidentiary value. I did not. I had a contract, a bell, a plan, and enough confidence to mistake all three for control.
Useful child. Dangerous child. The world is often fond of making those the same.

I entered the ruin alone. The lower gate had fallen inward years ago. Rain pooled in the courtyard and reflected the broken towers in strips, so that the place seemed to sink before it stood. Old tool marks scarred the stones. Later hands had tried to hide them. Iron rings had once been set into the walls at intervals, not for doors, not for torches. Restraints. Some had been pried out. Some remained, rusted black, each one a small confession no one had scraped away.

The courtyard slowed me down. That annoyed me until I admitted why. Too many restraints. Too many places where a man could be kept standing while another man decided whether he still counted as one. I had seen prisons, dungeons, mines turned into cells, and army stockades where old law had rotted into habit. This was older in feeling, not in stone. Not cruelty for punishment. Cruelty for use.

On the inner wall, under lichen and rain, someone had carved a tally with a nail or a knife. Twenty-one marks, then a gap, then three more cut deeper. I touched the last one and the barbed star chilled hard enough to make my teeth meet. I took my hand away. Some evidence does not need interpretation. It needs burial.

People like to say monsters move into ruins. It comforts them. It lets them believe ruins begin innocent, empty, waiting for fangs. The facts are usually meaner. Ruins are built by people, filled by people, misused by people, abandoned by people, and then monsters arrive late enough to be blamed for the smell.

The cleft opened beneath the central tower, a slit in the hill lined with stone old enough to resent mortar. Cold air should have risen from it. Instead warmth breathed out in slow pulses. My medallion trembled properly now. Not fear. Warning. It knew enough to be rude.

I marked the entrance with chalk, oiled silver, and left a tripline tied to a bell at the mouth. Not because bells kill monsters. Bells keep people from lying about whether they followed instructions. I have a professional affection for simple devices that expose stupidity.

Twenty paces down, the passage narrowed. Thirty, the rain sound vanished. Forty, the stone changed. The walls had been cut, not by chisels alone, but by heat. Old runnels had cooled in the rock like black wax. Iron bars had been set across side chambers and later torn away from inside. I found bones in one chamber, then more in another. Not all human. Not all animal. Some had been gnawed. Some had been arranged.
That is a bad difference.

The metallic sound began when I reached the throat of the hill. Gates closing. Chains dragged through wet stone. A woman's song threading between them, soft enough to be mistaken for memory if one had memories generous enough to sing. Mine do not.
I took another cat potion and went deeper.

The cavern under the fort should have been natural. It was not. Men had widened it, braced it, carved channels through the floor, and set iron plates in a circle around a black pit at the center.
