The plates were old, older than the prison, perhaps older than the fort. Each carried a mark that had been hammered nearly smooth. Barbs. A star. Lines arranged not as decoration, but as argument.

I counted the plates because counting keeps dread from becoming poetry. Twelve in the ring. Eight still fixed. Two cracked. One overturned. One missing, leaving a socket in the stone where the dust had gathered in a shape too deliberate to be natural. Around the socket, newer tool marks crossed the old. Someone had pried out more than iron. Someone had taken a piece of a lock and left the door offended.

That was the moment I should have climbed out and dragged every witness down the road at swordpoint. Instead I stayed because the creature moved in the pit and because I could hear Nessa's song-word echoing inside the stone. I told myself the danger had to be understood before it could be ended. Pride often dresses itself as method.
My hidden necklace pressed cold against my sternum.
"Of course," I said. "Why be simple?"
Something moved in the pit.

The creature rose slowly, as if dignity mattered to it. It had once been built like a kikimore, perhaps, or like the memory of one explained badly to a fever. Chitin plates covered a body too long for its limbs. Iron bands had grown into its shell. Human finger bones hung from the bands in little clusters. Its head had no eyes, only a crown of sensory tendrils that opened and closed like black flowers. When it breathed, the plates in the floor answered with a low red heat.
Not a monster in a ruin. A lock being fed.

It struck before I could decide whether that thought was useful. The first limb hit my Quen and broke yellow light into shards. The second caught my thigh and threw me against the wall. I heard something in my shoulder complain. I ignored it, as one does with most complaints that happen during active murder.

Then the wall breathed behind me. Not moved. Breathed. The old prison had lungs made of pressure, and when they filled, every chain mark along the stone shone dull red. My Quen snapped out. Air left me. For half a second I could not remember the next Sign. Witchers are expensive to make, hard to kill, and still, at the worst moments, ridiculous machines made of meat and panic.

I cut one tendril away. Black fluid hit the floor and steamed. The creature recoiled, then struck the nearest iron plate with its forelimbs. The sound rang upward through the hill. Above, bells began to answer. My tripline bell first. Then something larger. Something deeper.
The gates in the walls opened.

The creature had not been trying to kill me quickly. I understood that late, which is the traditional time to understand anything useful. It wanted me near the old plates, bleeding, burning, carrying the barbed star close enough for the hill to taste. I had come to cut a monster out of a ruin. Something under the ruin had invited me to stand where a key should stand.

They were not real gates. That did not improve the situation. Memory can kill a man if the magic is old enough and the man stands in the wrong shape of it. Figures moved in the side chambers: prisoners, soldiers, a girl dressed as a boy, a tax rider with his throat open, men with burned hands, women with bags over their heads. Not ghosts. Not exactly. Stored pressure. Suffering given architecture.
The creature fed on their recurrence. Every time the hill remembered closing, the thing grew stronger.
I heard Nessa scream above.

For one stupid, tactical heartbeat, I considered staying. Kill the feeder, collapse the recurrence, save everyone at once. A clean report would say that. The body tells a meaner story. My thigh was wet, my shoulder was half numb, and the passage above me had begun to ring like a struck helmet. If I stayed, Nessa might die before my cleverness found its way uphill.
That was the clerk's fault. I knew it before I climbed. Men with instructions treat children like evidence and then act surprised when evidence bleeds.

I drove Igni into the pit to slow the creature, threw Yrden at the mouth of the chamber, and ran uphill with silver in one hand and fury in the other. The passage tried to lengthen. Old magic does that when it lacks imagination. I bled from the thigh into the dust, leaving a trail I did not like leaving. The barbed star burned cold enough to make each breath taste of snow.
I emerged into rain and stupidity.

The clerk had brought Nessa to the cleft mouth because she had heard the singing most clearly. The shepherd lay on the stones with two armed men standing over him. A clean-cloaked officer held Nessa by the wrist and looked irritated by her terror.
"Step away from the child," I said.

The officer turned. He had one of those faces that seemed designed by a committee of cautious men: pale, narrow, unmemorable, difficult to punch in a way that would feel poetic. "Witcher. You were instructed to resolve the threat, not interfere with witness procedure."
"You were instructed by whom?"
"Authority sufficient for compliance."
"Pretty phrase. Means nothing, but it is pretty."

One armed man stepped forward. I shifted my weight. Buck, who had somehow freed himself because gates offend him, bared his teeth yellow and exact. The armed man discovered an interest in remaining stationary.
Nessa looked at me. "It's singing louder."
The hill rang beneath us.

I did not ask permission. I grabbed the officer's wrist and bent it until he released the girl. He made a neat sound. Not loud. Administrative men often suffer quietly, perhaps because they are used to doing harm in rooms where shouting would be vulgar.
"Run downhill," I told Nessa.
"Uncle?"
"Take him too."
She ran. The shepherd staggered after her with rain in his beard and murder in his eyes. Good. Murder sometimes keeps a man upright.

The creature burst from the cleft behind me, dragging half the old throat with it. Stone flew. The clerk screamed and protected his writing desk, which told me everything I needed to know about his priorities. The creature's tendrils opened toward Nessa's fleeing back. The iron bands in its shell glowed red. It had found the witness that resonated best with the prison's memory and wanted to add her to the song.

The sight of it above ground was worse. Underground it had belonged to darkness, iron, and bad decisions. In the rain it looked unfinished, a thing dragged from a crime before anyone had agreed what to call it. Its legs struck stone with frantic precision. It did not roar. Roaring is for beasts that want to be feared. This thing clicked and sang and reached.
I planted myself between them.
The first blow broke Quen. The second drove me to one knee. The third did not land because Buck charged the creature and bit a tendril clean through.
There are heroic horses in songs. Buck is not one. He is malicious, opinionated, and personally offended by most of creation. This makes him more reliable than heroism.

The creature recoiled. I used the opening, rolled under its limb, and drove silver into the joint where iron had grown through chitin. The blade stuck. It screamed, not in pain but in many remembered voices closing at once. The Broken Crown answered. The three towers leaned inward. Rain hissed into steam before it touched the stones.
The barbed star opened inside my chest.

That is the only way I can describe it, and even that is a poor map. It did not open like a door. Doors ask to be crossed. It opened like a wound remembering it had once been a lock. Red pressure moved through my ribs, down my arm, into the sword. My medallion thrashed against my chest. My eyes burned. The world narrowed to the creature, the iron, the old plates under the hill, and the child running with the song still hooked in her fear.
I pulled.

The red heat burst outward. Not fire. Not spell. The lamps shattered. The rain turned white. The broken towers groaned, leaning toward the cleft as if bowing or being dragged. The creature came apart in pieces that did not fall so much as lose permission to remain assembled. Iron bands snapped. Chitin split. The old prison-song tore free and spent itself in one long metallic note that shook teeth in skulls and sent every bird in the fields screaming into the sky.
Then silence.

I woke on my knees with silver in my hand and blood in my mouth. The creature lay in a circle around me, dead in portions. My palm was burned with red lines where the sword hilt had heated through the glove. In the cleft below, the iron plates were cold.

No one cheered. That is one blessing of true fear. It has better manners than admiration. The shepherd had one arm around Nessa and one hand still reaching for the rock she would not drop. The clerk had ink on his face. The clean-cloaked officer had seen too much and, worse, had survived to describe it.

I tried to sheathe the sword and missed the scabbard mouth twice. The third time, Nessa stepped forward and guided the blade with the rock still clutched in her other hand. I should have thanked her. I said nothing because my tongue was busy being ashamed of how badly my hand shook.
Nessa stood in the rain, alive, furious, and holding a rock in both hands as if willing to finish what I had started. Good child.
The clean-cloaked officer nursed his wrist and tried to recover authority from the mud. Authority, like dignity, becomes difficult after one has made a small sound.
"We will require immediate custody of the manifestation site," he said.
"You can have the site after payment."
"This event exceeds ordinary contract terms."
"Payment first. Classification later."
The old order and the new one, briefly forced to share a road.

The district clerk approached first. He had lost his hat and gained humility, both temporary conditions. He counted one hundred and twenty crowns into my hand. None clipped. I had to admit, in that narrow matter, the paperwork had manners.
"We will require a statement," the officer said.
"You have witnesses."

The officer looked at Nessa. She looked back with the expression of a child learning that adults can be monsters without changing shape. I stepped half a pace to block his view and almost fell. The shepherd moved beside me without being asked. Between us we made a wall of one wounded witcher, one old man, one furious girl, and one horse who had decided laws were edible.
"Witnesses are unstable."
"So are hills when you drag children into them."
His jaw tightened. "Your name."

The rain struck the stones between us. I could have lied. I have lied for smaller reasons and with better weather. But Nessa was watching. The shepherd was watching. Rian had risked stolen paper. Mara had written come back alive. Vesemir had once given me a name because a boy found in ruins should not have to answer only to what others feared.
"Jack Morningstar," I said.
The officer went still.
There are names people hear. There are names people file. Mine had apparently become the second kind.
"Wolf School?" he asked.
"Enough."
"Registered?"
"With my horse."
Buck snorted in a manner that did not suggest institutional confidence.
The officer opened a black tube and withdrew a dry sheet. Rain touched the paper and did not sink in. That angered me more than the armed men.
"Voluntary cooperation is preferred," he said.
"There it is."
"You are not accused of any crime."
"Neither is a bridge before an army crosses it."
His eyes narrowed. "You do not understand your public risk."
"I understand public men who risk children. Step aside."
One guard looked at the officer. The officer looked at my eyes. Whatever he found there was not worth a wrist and two dead colleagues. He stepped aside.
Nessa caught my sleeve as I passed. "Was it a monster?"
"Yes."
"Only a monster?"
I looked at the broken fort, the old restraints, the iron plates, the officer hiding pain behind rank, the clerk wiping mud from a desk before blood from his hand.
"No," I said.
She nodded as if I had confirmed something she already knew. Smart children are often cheated of childhood by accuracy.

I left the Broken Crown with one hundred and twenty crowns, a burned palm, a reopened thigh, and my name in the mouth of dry paper. Behind me, the officer began correcting witness statements before the creature had finished steaming.

Nessa followed three steps after me until the shepherd called her back. I heard the call, heard her stop, heard the rock drop into mud. It landed with a small sound. That sound stayed with me longer than the hill's last note. Children should not have to set down weapons after being saved by men who arrived late.

Two versions were born before I reached the road. The first came from a charcoal burner who had seen the red pressure strike the creature and insisted, accurately and uselessly, that it had come through me rather than from me, as if the difference could save anyone once an office learned to spell it. The clerk wrote uncontrolled discharge because frightened men prefer phrases that make their own stupidity look passive. The shepherd told anyone near enough that the clean-cloaked officer had dragged Nessa toward the cleft. Three listeners heard him. One nodded. One looked at the officer's purse. One decided old men misremembered when money asked politely. By the time Buck shouldered me past the last broken wall, the officer had found two boys willing to carry a better story downhill: witness preservation, hazardous instability, witcher interference, child removed from threat area by authorized hand. Their pockets clinked as they ran. Silence would not hold this. It had too many paid holes in it.

By nightfall, the event had become a hill-fort instability with anomalous thermal displacement. By dawn, it had gained a subject. By noon, three witness statements had been corrected for hysteria, one girl's account had been retained under restricted access, and one shepherd's statement had been marked unreliable due to age, local superstition, and repeated use of the phrase paper-faced tick in reference to authorized personnel. A rumor had become a file with witnesses.
In a clean office two districts away, a clerk copied the senior examiner's initials at the bottom of the page.

Preliminary Field Classification. Subject: Jack Morningstar, unregistered Wolf School derivative, status irregular. Associated manifestation: crimson thermal-pressure event, non-standard Sign, non-standard curse, non-standard sorcery. Public-risk anomaly confirmed. Senior review requested under S. Veyrane. Recommended language pending: voluntary cooperation preferred, containment viability undetermined.
Mara Veyr had moved the infirmary before I returned, which meant she had expected me to survive or feared I would.

Both possibilities irritated me. Hope makes people careless. Fear makes them thorough. The new room stood behind a cooper's shop in Devenford, above a yard full of barrel staves and rainwater hoops. It smelled of oak shavings, boiled vinegar, bruised mint, and the dry mineral odor of powdered medicines. A narrow window overlooked the alley. A second door opened onto stairs leading to the yard. Mara had chosen well. Two exits, poor sight lines from the street, no loose boards near the bed, knives within reach of the table but not the patient.

I had reached Devenford by back roads, avoiding the main toll not because I feared tolls but because toll collectors remember faces for coin and faces for men who pay them to remember. The ride had opened the Broken Crown wound twice. My palm was worse. It did not bleed much after the first day, but the red lines under the skin pulsed whenever my hidden necklace went cold, which was often enough to make me disagree with my own hand.
Buck tried to refuse the alley. I let him. He had opinions about ambushes and had been right too often to punish. I tied him in the yard where he could see both gates and threaten both worlds.

Climbing the stairs took longer than it should have. Each step reminded me that bodies are ledgers too, less polite than clerks but more accurate. Mara opened the door before I knocked. Her hair was down. A knife was in her right hand. The knife lowered when she saw me; her expression did not soften until after she had looked behind me.
"Alone?" she asked.
"Unless the wound learned to walk."
"Do not joke before I decide whether to be relieved."
"Fine. Not planning to."
She stepped aside. "Bed. Coat off. If you fall before reaching either, I will make the autopsy insulting."
"That's your medical oath?"
"No. My oath has more threats."
I sat because the room had begun leaning toward me. Mara crossed to the shutters and latched them. Then she came back, cut the bandage from my thigh, and swore with admirable economy.
"You fought after this opened."
"Yes."
"You rode after it opened."
"Yes."
"You bled into a boot and kept going."
"I disliked the alternative."
She looked up. "Dying?"
"Waiting."
Mara's mouth tightened. "Those are not opposites."

She cleaned the wound with heated spirits and a controlled anger that did more to keep me still than kindness would have. The room's lamplight turned her face gold at the edges. Rain worked at the roof. Somewhere below, a cooper laughed once and stopped, as if laughter had been caught without proper papers.
"Rian is hiding," she said.
"Good."
"Badly."
"Less good."

"He came two nights ago. He had a copied preliminary classification with your name on it. Jack Morningstar." She said it carefully, not as if testing ownership, but as if testing damage. "He said the Broken Crown witnesses were being reworked. The girl too."
"Nessa."
"You remember her name."
"Children are safer when someone does."
Mara's hands slowed. "And yours?"
"Mine has become less useful."
"That is not what I asked."
No. It was not. Questions that mean what they say are the most dangerous sort.

I looked past her to the table. A traveling bag stood underneath, half-filled with rolled linen, jars, two shirts, a packet of coins, and a stack of medical notes tied with black thread. She had been packing before I arrived. Not fleeing. Preparing to flee, which is a different illness and often more fatal.
"You should leave Devenford," I said.
"I know."
"Soon."
"I know."
"Not with me."
That stopped her hands.

I should have let the sentence stand. Men who say sensible things should not immediately murder their own work with explanation. Unfortunately, sense and silence have never been reliable companions in me when a woman with tired eyes is holding my blood in a cloth.

"They are mapping who knew," I said. "Rian. You. Branka if they bother. Odrik if he can be made frightened enough to feel important. The girl. The shepherd. Everyone who saw something before correction. If you travel with me, you become evidence that moves. They will like that."
"And if I stay?"
"You become evidence that waits."
"You paint choices beautifully."
"I didn't make them."
"No," she said. "You only attract them."

I thought I had offered her distance. She heard abandonment wearing a practical coat. The hurt crossed her face quickly enough that a less interested man might have missed it. I did not miss it. I simply failed to do anything useful with the knowledge.
Her bitterness was not unfair. That made it less pleasant.

She finished cleaning the thigh, wrapped it, then took my burned palm. The red lines had faded at the edges but held their shape under the skin, branching like cracks through hot lacquer. Mara set my hand on a folded cloth and traced near the burn without touching it.
"Does this respond to pain?"
"Everything responds to pain."
"Try not to answer like a haunted door. Does it worsen when you use Signs?"
"After Broken Crown, yes."
"And before?"
"It wasn't there before."
She looked at the barbed-star chain where it showed above my collar. "But something was."
I did not answer.
Mara let the silence live. That was one of her more dangerous skills. Most people see silence as a thing to fill. She treated it as a patient that might yet tell her where it hurt.

"Rian found a dead researcher's name," she said eventually. "Not a full record. A reference. Morningstar under a restricted index, years old, maybe older than the last war. Also Kaer Morhen. Also Vesemir."
The room narrowed.

Vesemir had been dead long enough for grief to settle into objects. A cup at Kaer Morhen no one used. A whetstone with the old man's thumb groove. A phrase in memory spoken too dryly to be comfort and too kind to be anything else. Hearing his name in Mara's room made the past step forward with mud on its boots.
"Do not say that name again unless you know why," I said.
Mara did not flinch. "I know enough to see it hurt."
"That is not knowledge."
"No. It's warning."
I stood too fast. The room tilted. Mara reached for me and stopped before touching. Good. She was learning where care became permission and where permission had to be asked.
"Tell me what Rian found," I said.
"Sit."

Mara turned. "Do not make gratitude sound like farewell."
I failed to answer quickly enough.
Her face closed by one careful inch. Not anger. Worse. Understanding.
Before Rian left, he had given me one more scrap of trouble. "There is a name in the older index," he had said. "Not just Morningstar. Faithel. It may be a place, a people, or a copying error."
"Everything useful starts as one of those."
"And Geralt," he had added, quieter. "A note says he signed nothing. That was considered unusual."

I almost laughed. Geralt refusing to sign a document was less clue than weather report. Still, the note mattered. Men had wanted a signature. Geralt had not given one. Vesemir had hidden me, but Geralt had helped keep the paper hungry.
At the door, she caught my sleeve.
"They will ask me," she said.
"Yes."
"They will ask Rian."
"Yes."
"They will make the right answer expensive."
"Usually."
She nodded. Her face did not break. I respected that more than tears. "Go to Geralt. If the name on that sheet means what Rian thinks it means, you need someone who remembers the first lie."
"You speak as if I am good at accepting help."
"I speak as if your flaws have become boring beside the scale of the threat."
That made me smile despite myself.
She saw it. Her own mouth softened, then sharpened again before it could become farewell. "Come back alive. That is not a request."
"Medical order?"

She stepped close enough to take the answer from my face before I could arrange it into something less breakable. The bag waited by the table. The map waited on the chair. Her whole life, such as war and work had left it, had been reduced to things a woman could carry quickly if men with polite warrants came before sunrise.
"Personal," she said.

The word should have warmed me. It did, and that was the problem. Warmth makes a man stupid enough to believe the road may someday forgive him. I touched her cheek with the hand that did not burn. She leaned into it once, only once, then straightened before either of us could pretend the gesture had not happened.
"Personal."
I left before she could apologize for that and before I could want her to.

On the stairs, I stopped once. Not for pain. Pain had become familiar enough to be poor company. I stopped because the room above me had gone quiet in the particular way rooms do after someone chooses not to follow. Leaving is easiest when no one has made a place for you to return to. Mara had made one by accident or worse, by intent. That made the door heavier than it had any right to be.
By noon, Devenford had produced three rumors.

Rumors are fast because they carry less than truth. Truth has to drag weather, timing, names, guilt, and consequence. Rumor only needs a mouth and a road. By noon, I had become three different men and one possible plague in a town where I had spent most of the morning trying not to bleed on clean linen.

In the first, the crimson-eyed witcher had seduced a district medic and stolen her secrets, which was nearly flattering and therefore unlikely to survive official interest. In the second, the medic had poisoned him and he had ridden away dead, which comforted several men until contradicted by hoofprints. In the third, the witcher carried a star that burned cold and made official ink run backward.

Rian Wedeck heard all three while hiding in the back room of a chandlery. He wrote none of them down. That, he thought, might be the bravest thing he had ever done, which was not comforting because bravery felt much like nausea.
At dusk, two polite auditors came to the door.

Rian had three choices then. He could run through the alley and be caught by men who had expected the alley. He could burn the papers and choke on smoke while they thanked him for destroying evidence they had already copied. Or he could sit at the table, put one harmless requisition on top of everything fatal, and look like a man too frightened to be clever. He chose the third because cowardice, when properly managed, can resemble strategy from a polite distance.
He also swallowed one scrap before opening the door. It lodged halfway down and spent the next hour reminding him that heroism is mostly uncomfortable textures.

chapters.chapter_title: THE MAN WITH TOO MANY PAPERS
paragraphs: I did not see the auditors enter the chandlery. That matters because men like Sorel Veyrane build power in the spaces a sword cannot reach. A witcher can smell rot under floorboards, hear a heartbeat behind a wall, and still fail to stop a kind-eyed man with clean cuffs asking a frightened copyist whether he remembers the order of pages in a packet he should never have touched.

I learned some of it later: from Rian, who survived because fear made him slippery; from Mara, who remembered every question because doctors know wounds by shape; from a stolen memorandum folded into a loaf of bread by a baker with revolutionary sympathies and poor judgment. The rest I guessed. Teeth differ. Hunger repeats.

Rian had prepared for torture by expecting shouting. This was because he possessed an honest man's imagination, which is to say a limited one. Shouting belongs to soldiers, drunks, cheated husbands, and market inspectors who have discovered three pigs declared as two. Real pressure arrived with warmed wine, apology, and a man named Merrow who never raised his voice because he had papers to do it for him.

Before they came, Rian had spread his stolen copies across the chandlery table in four piles: true, dangerous, already known, and possibly edible. The last pile was small but emotionally important. Candle stubs surrounded him like mourners. His landlady had knocked twice to ask whether he was praying, because no honest renter used that much light after midnight. Rian had told her yes. It was not entirely a lie. Fear is a religion if you kneel long enough.

Merrow entered first. He had kind eyes and hands that had never pulled a body from a ditch. Behind him stood a woman in a grey travel cloak, broad-cheeked, silent, and bored by the thought of resistance. Her name was Halbreck. She carried no visible weapon. That meant either she needed none or wished others to wonder. The third man remained by the door with a ledger under one arm. He was there to make silence feel witnessed.
"You are not accused of misconduct," Merrow said.
Rian nodded. He had worked with paper long enough to know that not accused meant not yet named in the correct column.
"We are clarifying a chain of custody."
"I copied notices," Rian said. "Many notices."
"Of course. Valuable work. Exhausting, I imagine. Especially after the war, with so many claims, so much displacement, so many local distortions entering official memory."
Local distortions. That was how a burned farm becomes an error, how a missing husband becomes transport loss, how a child's testimony becomes hysteria if it interrupts a clean report.
"Do you know Jack Morningstar?" Merrow asked.
Rian's first useful thought was that a brave man would deny too quickly. His second was that brave men were often dead before lunch. "I have met a witcher using that name."
Merrow smiled. "Using. Good. You understand identity may be provisional."
Rian looked at the pile marked possibly edible and wondered if paper could choke a man before words did.

They asked him when he first saw the repeated phrase. They asked whether I had displayed coercive charisma, which made Rian laugh once from terror before he could stop himself. They asked if Mara had expressed attachment. They asked whether my wound response seemed beyond ordinary witcher parameters. They asked if my horse reacted to environmental instability. Rian, to his credit, said Buck reacted to everyone and everything with principled hostility.
Merrow wrote that down.

Rian saw the sentence forming before the pen finished it. Equine hostility under environmental stress. Possible resonance sensitivity. He nearly objected, then imagined Buck being led away with a label tied to his reins and kept his mouth shut. Cowardice and wisdom often share a coat. The fit is uncomfortable, but warm.
That is one horror of clerks. They can make even jokes into doors.

Mara's questioning took place in a room that had once stored apples. The smell lingered in the wood, too sweet under damp, as if autumn had rotted politely. She sat in a chair too low for comfort and refused the tea. Halbreck conducted this interview herself.

They had taken her notes first. Not all of them. Just enough to make the absence visible. A missing page is sometimes louder than a confession. The salve record was gone. The temperature record remained. The sketch she had made of the red branching in my palm had been removed with a knife, leaving a clean rectangle in the book. Mara looked at that hole longer than she looked at Halbreck.
Care had become evidence in less than a day. That is fast even by the standards of men who ruin things for wages.
"You provided medical care to the subject."
"I treated a patient."
"The distinction matters to you."
"It should matter to everyone."
Halbreck's pen moved. "Did the subject display abnormal regenerative response?"
"Witchers heal quickly."
"Did this one heal within expected range?"

Mara thought of my side closing under her hands, my palm smoking faintly, the red lines under skin. She also thought of me saying decide before you touch me like that, and of how little the file would understand the difference between restraint and threat.
"Expected by whom?" she asked.
"Medical standard."
"Which one? Before the war, after the war, or the one invented by men who need a patient's body to fit a policy?"
Halbreck looked up. "You object to the inquiry."
"No. I object to your vocabulary. The inquiry is only the knife."

There are ways to win in rooms like that. Mara did not choose any of them. She chose a worse and better thing: she made each useful answer expensive. Yes, she had treated me. No, she would not surrender patient notes without district warrant. Yes, my presentation was unusual. No, unusual did not mean ownerless. Yes, I carried a medallion. No, she did not examine the other necklace. Yes, she knew Rian. No, she would not describe his moral state as instability just because the word had recently become fashionable.
Halbreck wrote for a long time.
"You are protecting him," she said.
"I am protecting the meaning of care. He happens to be standing near it."
"Romantic attachment?"
Mara's face revealed nothing. I would have liked to see that. Not because I doubted the answer, but because it is a rare pleasure to watch a good blade remain sheathed.
"You may record that I found the subject stubborn, injured, under-rested, professionally competent, and less dangerous than the men attempting to define him."
"That is not an answer."
"It is the only one you earned."

Miro's statement was taken in Willenford under the apple tree because Edda refused to let the boy enter Odrik's house. The interviewer disliked the damp bench, the chicken droppings near his boot, and the old woman watching him as if deciding where best to bury a man with spectacles. He began by asking whether the witcher had frightened Miro.

Before he answered, Miro looked at the axe scar on the signpost. Someone had not repaired it. Rain had darkened the pale cut. The village still did not use its name, but now children touched the hacked place when they passed, the way people touch a bruise to prove it belongs to them.
The interviewer did not notice. Men collecting statements often miss the statement made by the room.
"Yes," Miro said.
The interviewer brightened.
"Everything did," Miro added. "The mill did. The dark did. Alderman Odrik did when he lied. The witcher was frightening after everyone else had already started."
Edda smiled into her shawl.
"Did the witcher command the ground?" the interviewer asked.
Miro held his wooden horse against his chest. "He told it no."
"Did it obey?"
The boy considered. "Not at first."
Children are better witnesses than adults until adults train them out of it.

Nessa's statement went worse for the officials. She sat in a barn that smelled of sheep and smoke while her uncle leaned on a staff with both hands and glared at anyone who thought literacy was armor. The clerk asked whether she observed a dangerous uncontrolled manifestation.
"I observed a witcher saving me because your man tried to feed me to a hill," Nessa said.
"No one attempted to feed you."
"Then he was stupid by accident. That isn't better."
The shepherd said nothing. He did not need to. His beard had gathered rain and judgment in equal measure.

All these little resistances mattered and did not matter. A file does not need truth to move, only enough truth to pass scrutiny and enough error to serve its master. By the time the reports reached Sorel Veyrane, each witness had become a resource problem: Rian compromised but useful, Mara obstructive but medically valuable, Miro suggestible, Nessa contaminated by trauma, Edda local interference, the shepherd unreliable by age, superstition, and actionable hostility toward authorized personnel.

What made the file dangerous was not that it lied. Lies can be found, cornered, and sometimes embarrassed in public. This file kept enough truth to pass for memory. It knew Miro had been afraid. It knew Nessa had held a stone. It knew Mara had treated my wound and Rian had copied a packet he should not have touched. Then it moved each fact half an inch until the road led where Sorel wanted it. That was how cages learned to look like summaries.

By the end of the week, the old file had stopped being a ghost story. Before Willenford, before the garkain, before the Broken Crown, it had fragments: a child not recovered, a barbed-star object retained, a Wolf School concealment, a dead mentor's refusal to sign. After those contracts, it had public crimson pressure, wound heat, corrected witnesses, medical phrasing, a name spoken in rain, and a route that could be followed.
I would have enjoyed the shepherd.

Sorel read the file in a clean office two districts away. I imagine it clean because men like that cultivate clean rooms the way priests cultivate altars. A dirty desk admits the world exists; clean desks suggest suffering can be arranged by category. Sorel was not cruel in the simple way. Simple cruelty can be bought, trapped, shamed, or killed. He was worse: exact.

He reserved personal annoyance for poor wine, sloppy handwriting, and officials who used emergency powers as a substitute for thought. The shepherd annoyed the structure. Mara annoyed the vocabulary. Rian annoyed the chain of custody. I annoyed several categories at once.
"Do not call him a monster," Sorel said, according to the memorandum I later stole. "That word gives villages permission to think they understand him."
Halbreck objected. "Public fear is already forming. Monster language would simplify containment."
"Simplify does not mean strengthen. Occupational identity may be retained in preliminary approach if it eases voluntary cooperation. It must not control classification."
"He is a witcher."
"He was trained as one. That is not the same thing."
"The distinction is obscene."
"Many accurate things are."
There is a special kind of danger in a man who can say that and sleep.

They discussed Geralt of Rivia next. My name had finally done what names do: opened other doors. Vesemir's dead hand reached from old notes. Kaer Morhen appeared as an irregular training site. Wolf School derivative became a phrase in the margin. Geralt's name sat underlined twice because even clerks know some men should not be approached accidentally.
"Do not touch him directly," Sorel said.
"Because of his associations?" Halbreck asked.
"Because men like Geralt of Rivia are most dangerous when offered a simple enemy. Give him one villain and he becomes useful to everyone except the villain."
"Then how do we proceed?"
"With invitations, compensation language, safety concerns, medical necessity, witness protection, and enough delay for the subject to walk toward people we need mapped."
Halbreck was silent long enough for someone to notice.
"You object," Sorel said.
"No."
"That was almost convincing."
"The phrase host suitability appears in the older index. I dislike it."
"So do I."
"You use it anyway."
"Dislike is not policy."
According to the memorandum, no one answered him. Men like Sorel enjoy silence after a sentence like that. It lets the words settle over the room and pretend to be furniture.
That sentence will excuse anything if placed in the right mouth.

I knew none of this while I rode south. I knew only the road, the weight of Mara's packets in my saddlebag, the stolen notice folded inside my coat, the burn in my palm, and the old ache that came with Vesemir's name. That was enough. Men imagine ignorance as emptiness, but it has texture. Mine felt like paper sliding under doors.

The first tail found me before the last northern toll. He was a cooper's apprentice, paid two crowns and told he was serving district safety. He followed at a distance for three miles, pretending to mend a hoop whenever I looked back. A woman selling onions stood at the next crossroads with no onions worth selling and shoes too good for mud. At the toll, a thin man with bad shaving cuts asked whether I carried undeclared medical goods.
"Only declared wounds," I said.
He did not laugh. Men doing work they do not understand rarely do.

I let the first two see me. I let the third lose me. By dusk I had doubled back through a hazel stand, crossed a flooded field, and slept three hours in an abandoned charcoal burner's hut that smelled of ash and mouse arguments. Buck stood outside under a leaning roof and glared into the rain. Once near midnight, he stamped. I woke with silver half-drawn. Nothing came. That did not comfort me.
At dawn, I found a notice nailed to a milestone.

The milestone stood where three roads disagreed. One led south toward better weather and worse wine prices. One led east toward farms where every dog thinks ancestry began with its bark. One led back north, which even Buck knew was foolish and therefore likely to attract men with banners. The notice faced all three roads. Careful placement. It did not accuse me of flight. It invited everyone else to become helpful.
Not a contract. An advisement.

WANTED FOR VOLUNTARY STATEMENT AND MEDICAL REVIEW: JACK MORNINGSTAR, WITCHER, WOLF SCHOOL ASSOCIATION. NOT TO BE APPROACHED BY CIVILIAN PARTIES WITHOUT AUTHORIZED SUPERVISION. COMPENSATION AVAILABLE FOR INFORMATION LEADING TO SAFE CONTACT. SUBJECT MAY BE INJURED. SUBJECT MAY BE CONFUSED. SUBJECT MAY PRESENT PUBLIC RISK UNDER STRESS.
No accusation. No crime. No monster. Clever.
A bounty makes enemies. Concern makes citizens.
I took the notice down and read it twice. The paper was treated against rain. The ink did not smear when I spat on it. That felt personal.

I folded it instead of burning it. That was new. Until then I had destroyed every paper that tried to hold me, as if ash could win an argument with bureaucracy. Mara had been right. Rian too. Paper outlived knives. Sometimes the only way to fight a page was to carry it until someone more dangerous knew how to read the margins.
Buck nosed my shoulder.
"Yes," I said. "Confused. That's the insulting part."
He tried to bite the edge of the paper. I let him have the corner. He chewed it, considered, and spat it out.
"Agreed. Poor finish."

The next village had already heard three songs. In the first, I had saved a girl from a hill that ate lambs and kissed lightning afterward, which was inaccurate but had rhythm. In the second, I had burned a mill full of righteous dead and taken payment in children's names, which was also inaccurate and likely to spread faster. In the third, sung badly by a man with clean boots and a lute too new for his talent, I was a public burden carrying plague heat under a wolf medallion.
Buck disliked the third. He tried to bite the singer.

I should have let him. The song had the stink of a planted thing, clean boots and all. Instead I caught the reins and gave the singer a coin to stop. He stopped because coin does what taste cannot. Then he smiled at my burned glove and I understood too late that stopping had never been his purpose. He had wanted my face turned toward the room while three men decided whether the advisement matched my scars.
I paid for the broken stool, refused to apologize for the horse, and left before dawn.

Outside, in the rain barrel by the stable, someone had left a folded scrap of paper weighed down with a nail. Not official paper. Too cheap. Rian's hand, rushed and blotted. M. questioned. I am leaving Devenford badly. Do not use north ferry. S.V. prefers invitations. That means traps with chairs. I burned it after reading and hated the small ash more than I should have.

At the last northern toll road before the long way south, the gatekeeper recognized me from the advisement. I saw the moment happen in his face: eyes to hair, hair to scar, scar to medallion, medallion to my hand where the glove hid the burn. Then calculation. Then fear wearing a civic hat.
"Name?" he asked.
"Buck."
The horse lifted his head.
"Yours, master witcher."
"You asked for a name. I gave you the better one."
He swallowed. "There is a notice."
"There are always notices."
"It says you may be injured."
"Most people are, given time."
"And confused."
"Less than the notice."
His eyes flicked to the road behind me. No armed men. No clean cloak. Only rain, fields, and the distant line of trees hiding the turn I would take if this became unprofitable.
"Toll is two crowns," he said.
"How much for stealing government paper?"
The tollman looked at Buck. Buck showed him his teeth with professional timing.
"Waived today," the tollman said.
"Generous."
"War's over," he said weakly. "We're all trying to be generous."
I rode on with the notice folded against my chest. Behind me, the tollman lowered the gate for an empty road and looked relieved when nothing ancient happened.

By the time I crossed the last wet mile before the southern road widened, three truths had settled into me. First, Black Ink, or whatever clean name it used for itself, did not want me dead yet. Second, it wanted every person who had seen the crimson pressure become a page it could turn. Third, Vesemir had hidden more than a child at Kaer Morhen. He had hidden a question old enough to have teeth.

They had not found me because the world suddenly became clever. The first public field effect, the witness statements, Mara's medical phrasing, Rian's copied notices, and my own name had given an old unresolved file a living address. A life can become legible by doing honest work in front of frightened eyes.

There was a fourth truth, less useful because it had Mara's voice under it. I had hurt her by leaving cleanly. Or trying to. Clean departures are a vanity of men who want the wound without the mess. She would be questioned because of me, watched because of me, perhaps charged because she had chosen to say patient when subject would have saved trouble. The road did not make that lighter. It only gave me space to fail at naming it.
I had told Miro names were sometimes unhelpful. That was true. It was also cowardice. Some things become sharper when named. Debt. Fear. Want. Home.

Geralt of Rivia waited at the far end of the next road, though he did not know it yet. That was the trouble with fathers, even the ones who had never used the word. They stood at the end of roads they had helped build and looked surprised when the past arrived wearing boots.

I thought of Mara's hand around my wrist. Rian's shaking courage. Nessa with her stone. Miro asking whether I had a name. Edda's sausage threatening my teeth from the saddlebag. Buck's ears turning south, toward warmth and vineyards and men who retired from the Path only in songs told by people who had never met a witcher.
"Toussaint," I told him.
Buck's left ear moved backward.
"Yes, I know. Too many nobles. Too much wine. People who call monsters inconveniences until the inconvenience eats a cousin."
His right ear twitched.
"Geralt is there."
Buck sighed, long and theatrical.
"I didn't say it would be pleasant. I said it was necessary."

The road bent downhill. Rain thinned into mist. Somewhere ahead, past tolls, vineyards, old lies, and whatever clean hands were already preparing the next paper, Geralt of Rivia had a house with white walls and old swords within reach. Vesemir's name lay folded against my heart. My palm burned around the reins. The barbed star stayed cold and silent.
The road had already begun writing me down.
I rode anyway.

part_subtitle: Peace is a house with old swords still within reach.

paragraphs: Buck disliked Toussaint before I saw the first vineyard.

He made his opinion known at the border post by stopping under a whitewashed arch, lowering his head, and breathing suspiciously at a painted cherub nailed above the toll window. The cherub smiled down through peeling gold leaf with the cheerful emptiness of objects made by people who had never had to sleep in rain. After weeks of wet northern roads, corrected witnesses, clipped coins, and songs arriving before I did, plaster saints and polished officials felt less like peace than a trap that had learned manners.

Toussaint smelled wrong for a hunted man. Lavender grew beside the road. Grape vines ran in disciplined rows over hills that did not look as if armies had recently used them as butcher tables. Stone walls kept sun even after rain, and every small bridge seemed built by someone who expected admiration as a civic duty. Beauty was not innocence; it was only a well-lit surface, useful for hiding blades, debts, and witnesses told to remember the wrong thing.
In my inner coat, Mara Veyr's copied requisition sat folded around Vesemir's name. The paper had softened against my chest during the ride, changing from evidence into summons.

The tollman read my travel papers with one eye on me and one eye on Buck's teeth. He had been given a notice: pale hair, crimson eyes, Wolf medallion, possible public risk. Observation requests were always written politely. Men who wanted to own your road knew better than to sound greedy before breakfast.
"Name?" he asked.
"On the paper."
"It says unnamed witcher, probable Wolf School derivative."
"That is not a name. That is someone being paid by the adjective."

He looked at Buck again. Buck showed him one yellow tooth with excellent timing. The tollman swallowed, stamped the paper too quickly, and decided the border could survive without further conversation. "For the road," he said, waving me through. "Everyone pays for the road. Knights, merchants, wandering saints, dwarven caravans, poets if we catch them sober enough to identify. Special circumstances may be reviewed by the ducal office."
"Today?"
"Today special circumstances are waived."
"Generous country."
"Refined," he said, not sounding convinced. "Very refined."
I took the notice from under his ledger before he decided whether it belonged to him. His hand twitched and stopped. Paper has rank only when the hand holding it believes.

The road south lifted into dry hills and did not immediately try to drown us. Buck distrusted that. Toussaint gave him clean stones, flower boxes, and children who pointed at my swords with delight rather than fear. He took it as a personal attack.
By the third hill, the songs had caught us again.

Two boys in a cart were singing the red wolf verse while delivering empty bottles to an inn. They had the tune wrong, which improved it, and half the words wrong, which made it dangerous. In their version, the red wolf had eaten a fort, kissed a medic, and promised to surrender his chain to wiser hands if the countryside behaved itself. One boy made the chain noise with his tongue. The other saw me, struck the first boy in the ribs, and both discovered a sudden interest in the road behind them.
I rode past without comment. Comment fed songs. Silence fed them too, but at least silence did not pay for its own rope.

Corvo Bianco announced itself with cypresses, white walls, and a view so carefully arranged it might have been evidence in a case against grief. Late sun broke through cloud and touched the vineyard slopes in gold. The manor house stood pale against the green, neither castle nor inn, with windows open to the air and rows of vines drawn in patient order below it. A working place. A pretty place. A place that had learned to be both and did not apologize for the trick.

A man in rolled sleeves stood in the yard arguing with a vineyard worker about a wedge under a wagon wheel. Silver hair, two swords nowhere visible and somehow present in every line of him, scars in his face made softer by age and no less useful. Geralt of Rivia looked retired in the way a sword looked retired when hung above a hearth within easy reach.
He looked up when Buck's first hoof struck the courtyard stones.

No shout. No hand to blade. Geralt looked first at the horse's gait, then at my seat, then at the way I kept my left hand away from the reins. Only after that did he look at my face. Recognition moved through him and left almost nothing for strangers to see.

Then his gaze went past me: the road I had used, the upper windows, the vineyard track where a patient rider could disappear behind cypresses and still know which door opened first. He did not reach for a sword. He did not need to. Alarm sat in the stillness of his hand before he spoke again.
"Your left stirrup is too long," he said.
I let Buck walk into the courtyard. "You look older."
"I am older. Your stirrup still looks stupid."

The vineyard worker looked from one witcher to the other and decided this was either affection or a dispute about saddlery beyond civilian understanding. Geralt stepped closer. The sun caught the yellow of his eyes and the old weariness around them.
"You rode hard," he said.
"Road was soft."
"Hand?"
"Attached."
"That used to be your standard for acceptable gear too. It was bad then."

I almost smiled. Almost. The old shape tried to return and found a different mouth. Geralt saw that too. He had once taught boys to keep their shoulders loose while a ghoul tried to remove their faces. He could read pain in a saddle from across a courtyard.
"Stable first," he said. "Questions after the horse drinks."
"I came for answers."
"So did the horse, probably. His are simpler."

Buck approved this order with a long exhale that smelled of road and judgment. Geralt took the reins without asking and led him toward the stable. I followed because my left palm burned, my ribs ached where the culvert thing had opened them days ago, and arguing in front of a horse is a fine way to lose dignity in two languages.

A woman with iron-gray hair and a housekeeper's apron intercepted us at the stable door. She carried a basket of folded cloths and wore the expression of someone who had survived nobility, witchers, harvests, and the sort of guests who bled on good floors.
"You are the new trouble," she said.
"Old trouble, traveling."
"Old trouble knows where the basin is. New trouble drips in corridors. I am Malva. Do not die in the courtyard. It stains unevenly and upsets the household."
She left before I could answer, which proved she had survived Geralt's retirement by learning speed.
Triss Merigold came after Buck drank.

I heard her before I saw her: light steps on stone, a pause at the stable door, the small intake of breath of someone told only enough to make fear stand upright. She wore dark green, sleeves rolled back, hair bright as banked fire under the stable's shadow. Her face held warmth first, then intelligence, then calculation. The calculation did not replace the warmth. It stood beside it, armed.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Triss Merigold."
"Geralt said you were trouble."
"He says that about weather."
"Only accurate weather." She stepped inside and held out both hands, empty and visible. A mage announcing care without threat. Better than most. "May I see the hand?"
I turned to Geralt. He was busy pretending to inspect Buck's hoof while listening with his whole spine.
"You told her?" I asked.
"I told her someone I should have warned sooner was riding south with official trouble behind him."
"Efficient version."
"Left out the worst parts. I assumed you brought them."
I unwrapped the palm.

Triss did not reach immediately. She looked first. The red lines under the skin had darkened with the ride, five thin strokes radiating from the center of the palm in a shape too close to the hidden star at my throat. The skin was not raw. It was changed. Wounds healed. Changes kept opinions.
"Does it hurt?" she asked.
"Yes."
"That was almost refreshing. Most witchers lie first."
"I am tired."
"Good. Fatigue can be useful. It leaves fewer lies standing." She touched the edge of the mark with two fingers and stopped when the stable lantern bent toward us. "Geralt."
"I saw."
"No fever. No ordinary burn. No Sign strain." Triss's voice stayed calm. Her eyes did not. "This is not a stronger Sign. It is a response pattern. Something answered through him and left a path."

"Provisional only," she added. "Cold at the barbed star means recognition or an external pull. Heat in the palm means your body is preparing to answer or brace. A crimson field means active release, or containment failing. Useful pattern. Incomplete pattern. Dangerous to trust too far."

She lowered her hand too carefully and wiped her fingers on a cloth that had not touched blood. The gesture was small enough to deny. Professional calm had arrived first because Triss knew how to make it useful. Personal fear stood behind it, white-knuckled and quiet.
"Not him," Geralt said.
Triss looked at him.
"Through him," Geralt repeated, softer and meaner to himself than to her. "You said through. Keep that."
I looked between them and disliked the relief I felt. Men being precise about your personhood should not feel like kindness. It should be standard equipment. The world had made standards rare.

Malva appeared again with a basin, bread, and a look that suggested if any of us used the word response while she served food, she would make us eat in the stable with less polite livestock. "Kitchen," she said. "Now. Horses before men, yes. But men eventually, if we must."
Corvo Bianco fed people before it interrogated them.

That might have been Triss's influence, or Malva's, or Geralt's late discovery that questions landed better in a room with bread. I found myself at a long kitchen table rather than a council chamber. There was stew with white beans, coarse bread, goat cheese, olives, and a red wine that tasted of sun and old stone. The room smelled of rosemary, woodsmoke, hot iron from the stove, and paper because Triss had spread the requisitions beside the food despite Malva's objections that documents had no table manners.

Geralt sat opposite me. Triss sat at the table's end with the papers arranged into three piles: field reports, official language, and things she had not yet sworn at because Malva was present. Malva moved between stove and table, refilling bowls and pretending not to hear words like containment and seizure. Her pretending was unconvincing. It was also merciful.
"Start with Willenford," Geralt said.
I did.

I kept it short at first, because short was safer. A village that had hacked away its own name. Warm ground under frost. A mill rebuilt over buried dead. A child returned by something that had learned him. The creature drawn into the marsh. The mill dropped because some buildings deserved no gentler ending. Geralt listened with both hands around his cup. Triss interrupted only to ask about the warmth under the ground, the medallion response, and whether the child had touched the barbed-star necklace.
"No," I said.
Geralt's eyes moved to the chain at my throat, hidden again under the shirt. He did not ask to see it. He had known me before the world had begun to call the necklace evidence.
At the Broken Crown, my voice flattened. I heard it and could not fix it.

I told them about the staged witnesses, the chained draconid, the girl called by a dead grandmother's name, the anchor notches, the chains under the hill, the red pressure, and the heartbeat that was not mine. Triss stopped writing halfway through. Geralt put down his cup.
"Say the last part again," Triss said.
"It held," I said. "Whatever was under the hill wanted to pull. The blood answered by holding."
"Not opening?"
"No."
"Are you certain?"
I met her eyes. "No."
Honesty made the room colder than certainty would have. Malva muttered something in Toussaintois from the stove that sounded religious and insulting. No one asked for translation.
I set my spoon down. The small sound of wood against the table cut through maps, stew, wine, and every careful way they had been moving around the middle of the room.
"Why are they hunting me?" I asked.
Triss did not answer at once. Her quill stopped above the page. That frightened me more than a quick lie would have.
"Because they almost know enough," she said.
"That is not an answer."
"It is the most honest shape of one."
I looked at Geralt. He had not drunk from his cup. The wine sat untouched between both hands as if drinking would make the room too ordinary. "Why now?"

Geralt looked at the table instead of me. "They looked for a child once. Vesemir and I made sure they lost him. For years you were rumor: red-eyed Wolf, no clean registry, contracts paid in coin, gone before clerks arrived. Willenford gave them witnesses. The culvert gave them medical language. Broken Crown gave them a public event, your name, and fear with a seal on it."
"And what do they think I am?"

Triss folded one corner of the requisition under her thumb until the paper creased. "Possibility. If they knew exactly, they might choose one word and build law around it: weapon, prisoner, corpse, cure. Right now you are possibility. Possibility makes institutions greedy."
That should have clarified the room. Instead it made me feel more named, not less. Not known. Named. There is a difference, and the wrong one has teeth.
Geralt leaned back. The chair creaked. "Vesemir knew the necklace was trouble. He didn't know this."
My attention sharpened. "You knew to hide me."
"Yes."
"From mages. From courts. From Ciri."
Triss's hand stilled over the page.
Geralt did not reach for wine. "Yes."

The word stood without defense. That gave it weight. I had expected evasion, perhaps anger, perhaps the kind of explanation that began with you have to understand and ended with a man excusing younger cowardice in older grammar. Geralt gave me one word. It was worse.
"Why?"

"Because after Vesemir found you, two men came looking for a child with a black star and red eyes. Not mages. Not soldiers. Men with no banners and too-clean boots. Vesemir killed one. The other burned before he could talk. Burned from inside."
The stew cooled in front of me.
"You never told me."
"No."
"That another one of your clean yeses?"
His jaw tightened. There he was. Not the retired man. Not the legend. The wolf under the vineyard clothes. "It is not clean."
"Then say it dirty."
Triss looked from him to me and did not save either of us.

Geralt's voice dropped. "We hid you because we were afraid. We hid Ciri because everyone who knew her became a path to her. We kept you apart because Vesemir thought two hunted children would become one easier trail. I agreed. Later, I kept agreeing because not changing a silence is easier than admitting it became a wall."
That hurt more than the palm. The body is honest with pain. It sends heat, pressure, warning. The heart is worse. It disguises a cut as a question and waits for you to touch it.
"I was not a child forever," I said.
"I know."
"No," I said. "You noticed. That is different."
Malva set down a bowl harder than the bowl deserved. "Eat before you both become too proud to digest."
It should have broken the tension. It did not. But it gave us something to do with our hands, and sometimes survival begins there.
Geralt did not show me the house that night. He showed me where the house could be entered.

His action told me he was frightened. A comfortable man gives tours by rooms. A witcher gives tours by failure points: west door with a hinge that answered badly in damp weather, gallery above the yard narrow enough to hold with one sword and a chair, cellar stairs that could be barred from below, and Malva's pantry hatch, useful for flour and children but poor for broad-shouldered men unless desperation taught the ribs flexibility.
"You built a house with defensive depth," I said.
"Toussaint has vampires, knights, auditors, and guests." Geralt stopped near the lower gallery and listened to the yard without looking as if he listened. "A man plans."
"In that order?"
"Depends on the guest."

Triss followed us with one lamp and three papers, pretending she was there because the house was dark. She corrected him twice: once about the north-facing window, and once about the cellar door Malva kept difficult on purpose because a door everyone struggled with became a warning bell. Geralt accepted both corrections without pride. That told me more about their life than any speech would have.

In the study, I paused before a shelf where two of Triss's books sat beside an old whetstone, a half-repaired glove, and a vineyard ledger with Geralt's handwriting in the margins. The objects did not match. That was why they looked true. Lives rarely arranged themselves by theme unless someone had died and a curator arrived.
"You stayed," I said.
Geralt stood near the doorway. "Looks that way."
"Hard habit to start."
"Harder to believe after starting."
I touched none of the objects. The old instinct told me to leave no prints where belonging might be inferred. "Does it work?"
Geralt looked past me toward the vineyard dark. "Some days. Other days I wait for the road to call me a coward."
"Does it?"
"No. Roads don't care. That's mostly our vanity."
I almost mistook it for wisdom. I disliked it for arriving in a room with curtains.

When we returned to the kitchen, Triss had put my papers away from the food and Malva had put the food where no paper could pretend it mattered more than hunger. The warm part of the house had narrowed again around words that wanted to be cold, but for a small hour before that, Corvo Bianco had shown me its ordinary machinery: bread, ledgers, insults, boiled water, horses, and people who disagreed without drawing steel.
I did not trust it.
I remembered it.

I found the left stirrup corrected when I went back for my saddlebag. Not adjusted in front of me, not explained, not offered as kindness with a man's hand waiting to be thanked. Corrected. The worn keeper had been replaced with a darker strip of leather, old but sound, cut from something that had known rain and survived it. Geralt was nowhere near the stable when I noticed. Buck was. He turned one eye toward the strap, then toward me, with the expression of a horse who believed all human affection should be handled by tack-makers and kept away from poetry. I checked the buckle twice. It held. That was the difficulty with Geralt's care. It arrived as a fact one discovered after deciding he had said too little.

That night Corvo Bianco gave me a clean bed, a basin of hot water, and shutters that did not rattle in the wind. I distrusted all three. The room had been prepared before I arrived. Someone had thought I might come hurt. Someone had aired sheets, laid kindling, set salve on the table, and left a folded towel within reach of the basin. The care had no witness. That made it harder to refuse.
I slept badly anyway.

Near midnight the mark in my palm warmed. Not enough to burn. Enough to wake me with a gasp I would not have admitted if Buck had not answered from the stable with a hard stamp. I sat up with silver half-drawn, heart steady and wrong, listening to a house that breathed like a house and not like a trap.
In the dark, Mara's voice returned. Decide before you touch me like that.
She had decided. Then I had left. The fact had followed me into a bed with clean sheets and made the room feel smaller.

I lasted another hour in bed after that. Pride called it caution. Caution called it an inspection. The truth was less flattering: I did not know how to sleep inside a room prepared by people who knew my name.
The latch on the window had a hairline of frost along its brass tongue.

I sat up slowly. The basin water was dark. Not black, not ink, only night in a shallow bowl, but the surface had gone still in a way water disliked when wind pressed under the shutters. My palm heated under the bandage. Not enough to burn. Enough to make the red lines remember themselves.
Buck struck the stable door once.

I put on boots without lighting the lamp, crossed the hall, and reached the gallery before Geralt stepped out from the dark beside the stair. He had a shirt half-fastened, a sword in one hand, and the expression of a man who had not slept deeply since before most ballads about him began to lie.
"Window?" he asked.
"Frost."
"Mine too."
Triss appeared behind him with her hair unpinned and a flame sitting above her open palm. It was a small flame, tidy and irritated. "Do not touch any glass."
"That was my evening plan ruined," I said.

She ignored that, which was usually wise. We went down without waking Malva, or so we thought. She was already in the kitchen with a poker, a shawl, and the offended dignity of a woman whose house had been measured without permission.

Outside, the vineyard held its breath. The moon was thin. The cypresses along the road stood black and still. Geralt opened the side door with two fingers and let the cold in. It smelled of wet stone, lavender, and clove.
There it was.

Not strong. Not close. But clove-black wax had a smell once you knew it, and I knew it now the way a dog knew blood under snow. On the road beyond the gate, a rider sat in the dark, motionless under a pale cloak. No torch. No banner. Too far for a clean shot with a knife, close enough to be seen if he wanted to be seen.
"Do we take him?" I asked.
"No," Triss said.
Geralt's answer came at the same time. "Maybe."
Malva looked between them. "Try not to decide policy in whispers while my floor gets cold."

The rider lifted one hand and tied something to the roadside cypress. White cloth, perhaps. Paper, perhaps. Then he turned his horse and rode away at a walk, not a run. Running admitted guilt. Walking implied schedule.
Geralt was already moving for the gate. I caught his sleeve. That surprised us both.
"He wants pursuit," I said.
"Yes."
"You were going anyway."
"Yes."
It should have been me saying yes that badly. The world had a taste for repetition.

Triss crossed the yard before either of us could improve the argument into stupidity. She stopped inside the gate, murmured three words, and the cloth on the cypress blackened from the center outward. Not flame. Not ash. The fibers simply gave up being separate and fell in a soft gray line onto the road.
"Marked thread," she said. "A sympathetic tag. Cheap work, but patient."
"On the house?" Geralt asked.
"On the road leading to it." Her eyes moved to me. "They are not inside yet. They want to learn who leaves, who follows, who panics."

I had almost made that easy for them. So had Geralt. We stood in Malva's kitchen afterward while she poured hot water with the violent gentleness of the competent. No one said trap. No one said fear. Words like that were too broad for the small shame of almost stepping where someone had expected your foot.
Geralt looked at my boots. I looked at his sword hand. Triss looked at both of us and sighed.
"Breakfast will be cheerful," she said.
"It often isn't," Geralt replied.
Malva set a cup in front of me. "Drink before you both start mistaking exhaustion for principle."

I drank. It tasted of bitter herbs, heat, and being kept in one place against the habits of a life that had made movement look like safety. Outside, the road lay quiet again. That did not make it empty.
By morning, Malva had written my name on a breakfast slate.
Before the slate and before breakfast, there was the matter of being examined by a household that pretended it was not examining me.

The groom who brought Buck water was called Peire. He had a missing front tooth, excellent hands, and the cautious bravery of a man who had been bitten by horses often enough to respect them properly. He did not stare at my eyes. He stared at Buck's cracked left hoof and clicked his tongue in professional disapproval.
"Roads north are all stones pretending to be roads," he said.
"You've been north?"

"No. I have seen the shoes of horses that survived it. Same as reading a priest's shoes to know whether his sermon is worth hearing." He lifted Buck's hoof. Buck allowed it. That made Peire significant. "This one trusts you and hates everyone else. Sensible beast."
"He also hates cherubs."
"Then he has taste."

There are places where welcome announces itself in speeches, banners, and formal rooms that smell of money. Corvo Bianco did the opposite. It tested whether Buck would drink, whether I would sit, whether my bandage needed changing, whether a man who had ridden too long could accept bread without turning it into a debt.

Malva watched all of it without seeming to. She corrected Peire's knot, told Geralt his shirt had no right to be worn near guests, told Triss the papers would not be allowed beside fresh butter, and told me the basin upstairs was hot but would become cold if I insisted on standing around looking tragic in the stable. Her values were simple and hard to defeat: people ate, wounds were washed, horses were watered, floors were not bled on, and sorrow could wait until after soup if it wanted a chair.
I thought then that she was only a housekeeper. Another bad assumption. Some people keep houses the way soldiers keep walls.
Guest: Jack.

That should have warmed me cleanly. It did not. A person who feeds you can become kindness. A person who feeds you can also become a handle if the wrong office learns which door they use and what name they put on a slate. Corvo Bianco gave me bread, hot water, a stable, and a word that did not reduce me. Black Ink would have called every one of those things contact points.
I ate anyway. Refusing a cage is not the same as refusing every hand that reaches before the cage arrives.
Not subject. Not asset. Not public risk. Guest.
I stared at it too long. Malva saw and said nothing. She understood the cost. I saw it before she looked away.
Triss chose the cellar because beauty lied less convincingly underground.

That was my guess. She said it was cooler, quieter, and safer for papers that disliked sunlight. Above us, servants opened shutters, dishes clinked, someone in the yard argued with a barrel, and Malva told him to stop blaming wood for human carelessness. Sun warmed the stones outside. Grapes waited in disciplined rows. The world looked almost healed from a distance, and distance was precisely where most lies preferred to live.

The cellar offered better company: stone, damp, wine dust, old oak, ink, and the smell of wax warming near a lamp. Triss set a narrow table between two racks of Beauclair White and a row of red vintages Geralt had threatened to label according to which guests made him need them. A lamp burned low. Its flame stood straight unless one of my papers came too close. Then it leaned.
"Read the phrase again," Triss said.
Geralt stood by a wine rack with his arms folded. He looked older in cellar light, less silver and more bone. "Which one? There are several trying to win prizes."
"Voluntary surrender preferred."
The word surrender made the old stone feel smaller.
Geralt's cup stopped halfway to his mouth. He had brought it as if wine might keep the room human. No one had touched enough of it to prove the theory.
Triss tapped the paper. "Preferred. Not required. That means removal without consent is already permitted. The preference is for paperwork clean enough to survive review."
"Considerate," Geralt said.

"Efficient. This is for future review boards." She turned to another copy. "Witness correction. Not witness collection. Correction. They expect statements to be modified after the event. They are not hiding that from each other, only from the witnesses."
"And public-risk anomaly?" I asked.
Triss looked at me. "A holding phrase. It keeps you out of man, out of monster, and therefore out of rules written for either. An anomaly gives them room."
"Room for what?"
"Whatever they can get signed."

Geralt set the cup down. "Mage hunters used words like that. Not the same, but cousins. Heretical influence. Public contamination. Unregistered conduit. The phrase never held the knife itself. It told the knife where to stand."

I had known that, or something near it. Knowing did not make hearing it easier. The reports from Willenford, Heddel's Ferry, Devenford, and the Broken Crown lay across the table with their clean hands folded. In each one, someone had moved me a little farther away from personhood and a little closer to procedure.

Triss had added her own notes in a red-brown ink that looked almost warm beside the black. She wrote fast and cleanly, pausing only when anger made her hand too tight. I watched her cross out field response and write bodily consequence. She saw me watching.
"Words matter," she said.
"I noticed."
"No. You endured the damage. That is different."
I had no answer ready. Most bad arguments can be improved by having no answer. I ruined this one by finding one anyway.
"You sound like Mara."
Triss's face shifted. Only a fraction. Geralt looked at me with the weary interest of a man watching a young witcher step knowingly into a snare.
"Mara is the medic?" Triss asked.
"The one whose report helped them."
"And whose copy led you here."
"Both can be true."
"Yes," Triss said. "That is why blame is too blunt for this."
"Does the Lodge teach that before or after the lesson on using people for their blood?"
The cellar went quiet.

There are bad silences and worse ones. This one had three people in it: the man I had accused, the woman I had struck with a borrowed wound, and Vesemir's shadow, which somehow stood behind us all. Triss did not step back. She did not raise her voice. That made the answer harder to meet.
"Before," she said. "And after. Clever people repeat ethical failures when vocabulary makes them feel technical."
Geralt said my name once. Not warning. Not rebuke. A hand near a blade without drawing it.
I looked at Triss's papers, at the careful red corrections, at her hands. A burn scar crossed one knuckle, pale under the lamplight. Not old enough to be forgotten. Not new enough to excuse me.
"That was badly said," I told her.
"The wound was accurate," she replied. "The aim was not."
"I am sorry."
Triss did something worse than accepting my apology. She had turned me into a function.
She placed a clean sheet before me, gave me the quill, and turned one of the copied requisitions so that its black language faced my hand. "Copy the terms exactly."
"No."
"It was not a question."
"You have hands."
"Mine already hate these words. Yours should have the opportunity."

Geralt made a small sound from the wine rack. It might have been warning. It might have been approval he did not want recognized. I took the quill because refusing would have made the room about pride, and pride had already embarrassed itself in the cellar.

The first phrase was voluntary contact pathway. The nib scratched through each letter. My burned palm tightened under the bandage. The second was containment viability. The third was host suitability, and the nib caught on host hard enough to spit ink. It made the word darker than the rest. There are accidents that tell too much truth.
"There," Triss said.
"What?"
"That is what a report does when it succeeds. It makes the body carry the insult in its own hand."
I put the quill down before I broke it. "Is this a lesson?"
"Yes."
"Do you give all lessons by injury?"
"When students insist on bleeding into the ink." She took the page, dusted it, and placed it beside the original. "Look."

I looked. The official copy was clean enough to be inhuman. Mine leaned where pain had touched the wrist. Same words. Different crime. In my hand, the terms had become personal. That should have made them weaker. It did not. It made them harder to deny.
"Mara wrote like this," I said before I meant to.
Triss did not move too quickly toward the name. That was another kindness I disliked needing. "Medical language?"
"Care turned sideways."
"She wrote what she knew how to write."
"And they used it."
"Yes."
"That absolves her?"
"No." Triss folded her hands on the table. "It distinguishes her. Slower. Less satisfying. More accurate."
I hated how often accuracy arrived cold. "You sound like her."
"Then she is more competent than your anger finds convenient."
Geralt looked at me over the cup he still had not drunk from. "She helped you."
"She filed me."
"Both," Triss said. "That is why this hurts."

The cellar lamp leaned. Not toward the papers this time. Toward the candle box where Triss had hidden nothing important because she had known I would remember it. She noticed. Triss noticed rooms in layers: danger, argument, temperature, grief, and whether Geralt had eaten enough to be stubborn efficiently.
"I considered writing to her," Triss said.
My hand closed. "No."
"I did not say I would."
"Do not make her easier to find."
"She is already findable. Everyone who touched your blood has become a road on their map."
"Then why tell me?"
"Because not telling you would be another kind of management, and you are already surrounded by people who loved you badly by managing danger around you."
Geralt's face changed. Not much. Enough.

Triss saw it and did not soften the sentence for him. That, too, told me something about their life. Love in that house did not always lower its voice. Sometimes it loved by keeping the knife pointed at the right truth.
"What would you write?" I asked.

Triss took another sheet and did not dip the quill. "That she should burn duplicate notes, mislabel any retained copies under river fever, and stop using the word host in any context except parasites visible to the naked eye. That if brown-coated auditors come again, she should ask them which office pays for their horse feed before answering any medical question. That fear is not proof of guilt. That competence is not consent."
The last sentence changed the air.
I looked away first. "Do not send it."
"I know."
"Then why write it?"
"Because sometimes the letter you do not send teaches you what you are refusing to lose."

No one spoke for a while. Above us, Malva dropped a pan and blamed the pan loudly enough for the whole house to understand she had not been listening. It was a generous lie. The house was full of them. Small lies that made truth survivable.
