Triss folded the blank page and tucked it under the copied terms instead of sealing it. "Later, perhaps. Through a channel that does not smell of clove."
"That your professional judgment?"
"That is my human one. It is less tidy. I am trying to use it more often."
She accepted the apology by returning to work. That was not forgiveness. It was discipline, and perhaps more useful.

The letters took form by noon. Triss wrote to Yennefer first, not because she expected comfort, but because Yennefer knew old magic, royal appetite, and the difference between a curse, a lock, and a political opportunity dressed as both. Geralt did not object. He only watched Triss address the letter with the expression of a man respecting a knife he had once held too carelessly.

The second letter went to Dandelion. Triss drafted the facts. Geralt removed the parts that sounded like a lecture. I removed the parts that made me sound tragic. Triss put half of them back, saying bards required emotional bait if one wanted them to read beyond the first page. Geralt muttered that Dandelion would read anything with a seal if it smelled like scandal.
The third went to Zoltan Chivay. This one was shorter and uglier.

Find who paid for the songs. Follow wax, paper, courier fees, and tavern stipends. Assume Black Ink uses charitable accounts, war relief, medical freight, or public reassurance channels. Dandelion will be dramatic. Use that only where helpful.
"He will enjoy that," Geralt said.
"The task?" I asked.
"The warning."
Triss hesitated over the fourth letter. A blank sheet waited near her hand. It had no address, but all three of us knew where the silence pointed.
"No," Geralt said.
"I have not written a word," Triss replied.
"You were about to write to Ciri."
Her mouth tightened. "I was about to consider whether not warning her makes her safer or merely easier to surprise."
I stood because sitting had become impossible. The chair legs scraped stone. "Don't."
Both looked at me.

There are moments when a man realizes he has asked for something before understanding the cost. I had spent years resenting a hidden name, a hidden childhood, the secret road Vesemir and Geralt had built around me. Now I was asking them to hide another truth from Ciri because I could not bear the thought of my name arriving at her court in a line of danger.
"Don't send her my problem," I said.
Geralt's face hardened. "She is not a court."
"She is becoming one. That is the point."
"She is Ciri."
"To you. To them she is succession, Elder Blood, imperial leverage, and a door with guards. Do not make me the hand knocking."
Triss folded the blank page without writing on it. "Not yet, then."
Not yes. Not no. Not yet. The phrase joined the others and waited.
After the couriers left, Triss made one more copy by hand and did not send it. The candle flame leaned toward the page until she slid a saucer between them.
Geralt noticed. "For whom?"
"For the room that survives us if we are stupid."
"Cheerful."

"Practical." She folded the page, sealed it without address, and wrote one word on the outside: IF. "If I vanish, if you do, if Yennefer arrives and finds this house quiet in the wrong way, if Jack rides before the rest of us can catch up, someone should know which words came first."
I studied the small sealed letter. The word looked too light for what it carried. "Where will you keep it?"
Triss smiled without humor. "Somewhere no man will look because the object seems domestic."
Geralt looked at me. "Candles."
"I would have checked candles," I said.
Triss slid the letter into a plain wooden candle box between two bundles of wicks. "You would now. That is why I will move it later."

She did. I saw her return after dinner and hide it elsewhere while pretending to look for sealing wax. A person who cared about papers that way understood what papers could become. I remembered the first hiding place anyway. Habit. Sometimes protection is only another word for remembering exits that belong to other people.

That evening, I found Geralt in the stable sharpening a hoof knife that did not need sharpening. Buck stood with his head over the stall door, watching him with the professional skepticism of a horse appraising a rival. The tack board behind them held the notice from the Broken Crown, pinned crooked under an old brush and a cracked buckle. Geralt had put it there on purpose.
"Paper looks smaller near useful tools," he said without turning.
"That Vesemir's lesson?"
"Mine. Learned late."
Buck reached for the corner of the notice. Geralt lifted it out of reach. "No. Bad for the stomach."
"His or the paper's?"
Geralt narrowed his eyes. "You do make jokes."
"Under duress."
"Most good ones are."

For a while the stable held only the sound of blade on stone, horse breath, and vineyard night insects beginning their work outside. It was easier to speak in stables. Horses cared about tone, not history. They also forgave poorly, which made them honest company.

"Vesemir found you in a keep north of the Pontar," Geralt said. "Collapsed tower. Dead men in three rooms. Not killed by blade. Not magic I knew. You were alive in the chapel with that necklace in your fist. White hair already. Eyes red. No memory."
"I know the story."
"No. You know the version made for a boy who woke screaming if someone said castle after dark."
The knife stopped moving.

"There was writing on the floor around you," Geralt said. "Vesemir washed it before you woke properly. He said boys deserved one clean surface. I told him evidence mattered. He told me if I ever confused evidence and a child again, he would throw me from the wall and call it instruction."
I looked at the notice on the tack board. The paper did look smaller there. It did not feel smaller.
"What did it say?"

"He never told me all of it. Only one phrase. Last warden." Geralt placed the knife down. "I thought it was old nonsense. Family motto, maybe. Cult title. There were many cults after the war and before it, and all of them thought dying near a child made their vocabulary important."
"And now?"
"Now I think we were underpaid by the nonsense."

Geralt reached toward the tack shelf, stopped, then took down a strip of oiled leather folded around nothing. It smelled of cedar, old paper, and the kind of damp Kaer Morhen never truly surrendered. For a heartbeat I thought he might apologize. Instead he placed the empty wrap on the stall rail between us. 'Vesemir used these for papers he wanted rats and boys to leave alone,' he said. 'Cedar oil. Bitter on the tongue. You chewed one once because Lambert dared you.' He looked at the leather, not at me. 'If old notes survived, they'll smell like this.'

That was the apology, or as close as Geralt could drag one into daylight without killing it from exposure. A smell. A method. A fact withheld until usefulness made confession less naked. I wanted to tell him it was not enough. It was not. I also knew he had just given me the first practical way to recognize Vesemir's hidden hand when we reached the keep. Some men say sorry by opening a wound. Geralt had handed me the instrument and shown where the scar might continue.
"What did you know?" I asked. "Exactly. Not what you regret. What you knew."

Geralt rested the hoof knife across his knee. "That you were found alive where no child should have been. That the necklace could not be removed without hurting you. That two men searched for you afterward. That Vesemir hid your registry. That old stones sometimes answered when you stood too close. That mage glass made you sick for three days after the first and only time Vesemir allowed it near you."
"What did Vesemir hide from you?"
"More of the floor writing. Older notes. Where he sent the dead man's effects. Names he did not trust me to chase while Ciri was still being hunted."
"What did you guess wrong?"

His thumb moved once along the dull edge of the hoof knife. "That whoever searched for you died with the search. That keeping you off paper was enough. That when you left at nineteen, distance would make you safer instead of merely harder to find."
"And what do you still not know?"

He looked at the Broken Crown notice pinned among brushes, straps, and hoof picks. "What the barbed star was made to hold. Who Veyrane answers to. Why the hill called you last warden. Whether hiding you saved you, or taught the trap patience."
I almost laughed. It came out wrong.

Geralt looked at me then. The stable shadows did not soften him. He was not good at softness when guilt had both hands around his throat. "I don't know what you are, Jack. I know who I trained. I know who Vesemir fed broth to when you refused to eat after the third mutation fever. I know you tried to hide bread for Lambert because you thought he was too proud to ask, and he ate it while insulting your knife work. I know Buck hates everyone in a way that suggests he trusts you. Start there before you let a report start elsewhere."
That should have helped.
It did, which frightened me more.
"You should have told me," I said.
"Yes."
"You should have told Ciri."
"Maybe."
"That is not as clean."
"Nothing about Ciri is clean. Not when people still think her blood is a road they can pave."

The stable seemed to breathe around the name. Ciri. I had grown up under her absence like a second roof. The girl everyone protected. The woman no one wanted to endanger by admitting I existed. She had been made myth to me by omission. That was an ugly thing to realize about someone living.
"I hate that I understand," I said.
Geralt picked up the hoof knife again. "Good. Hate is less dangerous when it has to share a room with understanding."
At the stall door, Buck snorted.
"Yes," Geralt told him. "That was too wise. I'll try to do worse."

The horse tried for the notice again. This time Geralt let him tear off a damp corner. Buck chewed once, spat it out, and sneezed with such offense that I felt, for the first time since crossing into Toussaint, properly represented.
Near midnight, the cellar lamp went out by itself.

Triss felt it first. Yennefer's reply had not arrived. No courier had reached the gate. No portal opened. Yet the candle box where the IF letter was no longer hidden grew cold enough to frost the lid. The mark in my palm answered with heat. In the stable, Buck kicked the door once, hard, and Geralt was on his feet with his sword drawn before the echo faded.
Nothing came through.

That was worse. Things that attack can be killed, delayed, redirected, or at least insulted before death. Things that only measure leave the room unchanged and a man less certain of where his skin ends.
By morning, Triss had moved all letters again. This time she did not tell any of us where.
The lesson stayed with me, which annoyed me because good lessons often arrive from people you have recently insulted.

Later, while Triss sorted another copy into her neat columns of damage, I saw containment viability again in a margin note and my fingers closed before I chose it. The copied word had weight in the tendons. Host had done that. Suitability had done it worse. Triss noticed the movement and did not soften her face into comfort, which was wise. Comfort in a cellar full of seized language would have sounded like pity. She only turned the page so the next line faced away from my hand. Geralt saw her do it. He looked at my fingers, then at the candle box, then back to the wine rack, pretending furniture deserved surveillance.
This time she did not tell any of us where.
Yennefer of Vengerberg arrived at Corvo Bianco through a portal that made every candle in the house reconsider its career.

I was in the courtyard with Geralt, failing to convince Buck that a brush was not a weapon, when the temperature changed. Not cold, not heat. Precision. The air tightened into a line. The roses along the wall bent away from nothing. Somewhere inside, Malva shouted that if anyone ruined the kitchen tiles with sorcery again, the Duchess herself could scrub them on her knees.
Geralt looked toward the house. "Yen."
He said it like a man naming weather he knew would not turn aside because he had noticed it.

Triss appeared at the upper door a moment before the portal opened. She had already braided her hair and put on the calm face of a woman who had expected the impossible and resented it for being punctual. The portal tore the air above the courtyard stones, violet-black at the edges, bright at the center. Lilac and gooseberries arrived first. Then black dress, white collar, raven hair, and eyes that made every explanation in the world stand straighter or flee.
Yennefer stepped out carrying a leather satchel, a sealed tube, and the expression of someone who had been forced to hurry by other people's stupidity.
The portal closed behind her. Three rose petals continued to fall upward for half a breath before remembering themselves.
"Geralt," she said.
"Yen."
"Triss."
"Yennefer."
Their names touched like blades acknowledging old maintenance. Not hostile. Not safe. Geralt stood between them and did not look as if he enjoyed history having two pairs of eyes.

Triss did not step toward him. Yennefer did not look away from her. That was the first honest thing between them. Lesser people would have made a theater of old wounds, sharpened smiles, claimed rooms through posture, or forced Geralt to stand trial by eyebrow. They did none of that. Their history remained present, but disciplined, like a blade laid on a table with the edge turned from guests and the hilt still within reach. Triss held the sealed tube in both hands, healer's steadiness over mage's caution. Yennefer's gaze moved once to the red-brown ink on Triss's fingers and approved nothing aloud. Approval would have been too generous. Disapproval would have wasted time.

Ciri's absence stood behind them more heavily than romance did. Not the girl from stories, not the imperial problem, but the daughter neither woman would let language reduce without blood on the floor. I saw it in the way Triss checked the seals before asking about the road, and in the way Yennefer's mouth tightened whenever a document avoided the word person. Old love had made the room complicated. Ciri made it dangerous. The distinction mattered, and everyone inside that courtyard knew it except perhaps Buck, who judged portals by smell and found this one offensive.
Then Yennefer looked at me.

Most people stopped at the eyes. She did not. She took in the scar, the posture, the wrapped palm, the hidden weight under my shirt, the way Buck had shifted half a step to stand between me and the portal residue. Her gaze was not cold. Cold suggests absence. Yennefer's attention had weight, heat, judgment, and the kind of intelligence that makes a man feel briefly like a table full of disassembled parts.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Yennefer of Vengerberg."
"I know who I am."
"Useful habit."
Her mouth did not smile, but a small decision near it spared me for later. "Geralt raised you badly enough to answer back. That is evidence, at least."
"He mostly taught me not to die."
"Low ambition. Typical."
Geralt grunted. It might have been protest. It might have been agreement he disliked finding in daylight.
Yennefer held out the sealed tube to Triss. "Your letter reached me. It was followed. Badly. I removed the following part."
"Killed?" Geralt asked.
"Discouraged. One may still write, though probably not with the same hand."
Malva crossed herself from the doorway, then remembered herself and frowned. "Everyone inside. If mages must frighten flowers, they can do it where soup is not cooling."
Yennefer gave her a look.
Malva returned it with the strength of a woman who had known dukes, drought, and Geralt before breakfast.
"I like her," Yennefer said.
"She likes no one," Geralt replied.
"Even better."

We took the discussion to the study because the cellar had too many papers and not enough windows. Yennefer disliked rooms with only one exit unless she had made the exit herself. That was the first thing I respected about her. The second was that she did not pretend the study's comfort changed the subject. She placed the satchel on the table, removed three objects, and let them speak before she did.
A dead beetle split down the spine. A sprig of rosemary blackened from the inside. A shard of stone that smoked faintly where it touched the wood.

"North of Brugge," she said. "Two shrines, one chapel, one abandoned tollhouse. In each place, small heat events. Insects dying from internal pressure. Plants carbonized without flame. Stone retaining warmth after rain. All within two days of your Broken Crown incident."
"Coincidence?" Dignity required the question. Intelligence hated it.
Yennefer looked at me. "No."
"You could soften it."
"You have Geralt for softness. I came to be useful."
Geralt muttered, "I am standing here."
"Yes," she said. "You often do. It is one of your safer methods."
Triss had opened the tube and was reading the copies inside. Her face changed at the signature line. "S. Veyrane."

"Senior examiner," Yennefer said. "Old administrative parasite. Survived Redanian purges, Nilfgaardian restructuring, and his own competence, which is harder than it sounds. He favors words that make cruelty sound like maintenance."
"You know him?" I asked.
"I know his kind. I met him once. He mistook lack of shouting for permission to continue speaking."
"Did he recover?"
"Physically."
I almost liked her. That was dangerous. Yennefer seemed designed to make liking feel like another test.
She turned to me. "May I examine the necklace?"
The room tightened. Geralt did not move. Triss watched my hand. Malva, who had entered with more coffee than a meeting this grim deserved, set the tray down very carefully.
"You ask?" I said.

"I prefer my subjects alive, informed, and annoyed rather than unconscious, ignorant, and leaking on good carpets. Also, Triss wrote in red ink that treating you as an object would make her personally intolerable. I value efficiency."
Triss did not look embarrassed. She looked correct.
I drew the barbed star from under my shirt.
The room went colder. Not by much. Enough. The dead beetle on the table clicked once and opened another fraction. The shard of stone smoked harder. Yennefer's eyes narrowed.

The necklace looked almost plain in daylight, dark metal, five points, red center dull as old garnet. I had worn it so long it had become less object than omission. A thing present in every room and named in none.
Yennefer lifted her hand. Stopped before touching. "Permission?"
"Yes."
She touched the edge of the star.
The study windows rattled.

I tasted ash, snow, and something like copper under the tongue. The mark in my palm heated. Geralt stepped forward. Triss raised one hand, not casting yet, only ready. Yennefer did not flinch. Her fingers remained on the star while the lamp flames bent toward her wrist.
"This is not a charm," she said.
"I had guessed."

"Nor a curse. Nor exactly a relic. It is an anchor fragment with identity tied into it. No, not identity. Custody. Something was made to answer a bloodline, a body, or a role, and then someone forced all three to occupy the same man."
The words entered cleanly and left dirt behind.
"Say that again with fewer knives," Geralt said.

"No. He needs the knives." Yennefer released the necklace. The room warmed reluctantly. "This thing does not make him powerful. Power is the word idiots use when they see a result and ignore the mechanism. It makes him available."
I put the star back under my shirt too quickly.
Yennefer saw. Of course she did.
"Self-pity later," she said. "Fear now. Fear has practical uses."
"I did not say anything."

"You became quieter in the manner of men who think silence is dignity rather than blood loss." She sat, finally, and opened the satchel again. "The hill did not awaken something inside you. It tested whether you were still in place. That distinction matters."
"Still in place for what?"
"A lock. A prison. A seal. A bad decision made by someone with enough magic to make descendants pay interest." She looked at Geralt. "Which brings us to Vesemir."
Geralt's face closed. "He's dead."
"Yes. Death is not an argument against his handwriting."

She withdrew a copied scrap, old and damaged, wrapped in transparent wax paper. It was not from my recent reports. The script was rougher, older, written by a hand that pressed too hard when worried. I recognized Vesemir's economy of line before I recognized a word.

Subject found alive. Necklace non-removable without distress. Child responds to Wolf decoction beyond expected fatal range. Do not send to court. Do not send to mages. If Rivia argues, remind him some doors close only because someone stands in them.
I read it once. Then again.
"Where did you get this?" My voice was not loud. That was how I knew it was dangerous.

Yennefer did not pretend not to hear the edge. "An archive outside Oxenfurt. Misfiled under veterinary quarantine after the Kaer Morhen material was consolidated. I suspect Vesemir encouraged the mistake."
Geralt looked at the scrap as if the dead had opened a door and refused to step through.
I pushed the paper back across the table. "He wrote subject too."
Triss inhaled softly.
Geralt said, "Jack."
"No. Don't clean it for him. He wrote subject."

Yennefer's expression changed, not softening exactly, but choosing a different blade. "He wrote subject on an outer note because outer notes are read by thieves. The next line calls you child. Then argues to keep you out of court. If you intend to resent the dead, do it accurately. Inaccuracy gives them advantages they do not deserve."
I hated her then. Briefly, brightly, and with gratitude under it like a second wound.
"You enjoy being right," I said.
"No. I enjoy being useful. Being right is often the toll."
That ended the matter badly enough to be honest.

Yennefer spent the afternoon drawing circles that were not circles over a map of the Continent. She marked Willenford, Heddel's Ferry, the Broken Crown, Devenford, Corvo Bianco, the Brugge shrines, and three places I had never seen. The lines between them did not form a path. They formed a pressure pattern, or so she said. I did not understand all of it. That helped. Men who understand everything in a room are usually about to make a large mistake.
"These are not random contracts," Triss said. "They are sampling events."

"And performance events," Yennefer added. "Witnesses staged where reaction could be observed. Songs seeded where public interpretation could be guided. Medical notes harvested where bodily changes could be described as procedure."
"So the Broken Crown was a test," I said.
"Yes."
"And I passed."
Yennefer looked up. "No. You survived. Tests are written by the examiner. Survival belongs to the person being used. Do not grant them authorship over your lungs."
That was the third thing I respected about her.
By dusk, she had written three letters and burned two. The one she kept unsealed had no name at the top, but the first line told us enough.
My dear daughter,
Geralt saw it from across the room. His face did not move. Triss's hand stilled over a map pin. I looked away because some forms of tenderness were private even when weaponized by politics.
"Are you sending it?" Geralt asked.
"No."
"Yen."

"Do not use that tone. I invented better ones before you learned to brood at women with proper posture." She folded the page. "Ciri has imperial watchers, court tutors, Nilfgaardian scribes, Temerian sympathizers, mage remnants, and enough destiny around her to choke a dragon. If I warn her now, I may give Veyrane proof of precisely the connection he wants to map."
"And if you don't warn her?" I asked.
Yennefer's eyes came to me. "Then I may protect her from one danger by leaving her blind to another. Yes. That is the problem. Welcome to family."
The word struck the room and found every crack.
Family. Geralt looked at the window. Triss looked at him, then at Yennefer. I looked at the map, because maps lie openly and are therefore easier company.

That night, Yennefer took the room beside mine, not because she trusted the house but because she trusted the wall between us to tell her if my mark heated again. Triss worked in the cellar until Malva threatened to pour soup into her ink. Geralt walked the perimeter with his swords belted under a loose coat. Corvo Bianco did not sleep. It performed domesticity with old weapons within reach.
I lay in bed and listened to the room breathe.
Before dawn, I heard Yennefer's pen moving through the wall. Slow, then fast, then stopped.
She opened my door without knocking at first light.

I had slept with a knife under the pillow and my boots near the bed. She noticed both, stepped over the boots, and placed a steaming cup on the table. The steam smelled of bitter root, black tea, and a faint spell meant to keep the cup hot without admitting it was magic.
"Drink," she said.
"Does everyone in this house command before breakfast?"

"Only those with judgment. Drink. Your hands shook in the courtyard yesterday after I touched the necklace. Geralt noticed and pretended not to. Triss noticed and worried politely. I noticed and made tea. We all have our failings."
I sat up. The room tilted, not from sorcery but from a body using pride as scaffolding. The tea helped. That irritated me.
She also noticed the mud on my boots.
Yennefer said nothing about it until after I had swallowed half the tea. That was good tactics. Bitter root and warmth had already entered the blood, making sudden departure less elegant.
"You went to the stable after midnight," she said.
"I inspect horses I own."
"At midnight, with a packed saddlebag, without waking Geralt, while your hand was hot enough to steam through linen." She looked out the window. "Buck refused."

I said nothing. Buck had refused. He had planted all four hooves, looked at me with the flat moral contempt of a beast who had carried me through wars, swamps, and bad decisions, and declined to participate in this one. I had nearly cursed him. Then the mark in my palm had pulsed, the road had seemed to lean open beyond the gate, and I had realized the horse had been wiser than me by the usual insulting margin.
"He is not fond of being used as an accomplice to stupidity," Yennefer said.
"Did he tell you that?"
"He has expressive ears."
"So does Geralt. Usually less useful."
A small decision moved near her mouth and became almost amusement. "You distrust being helped."
"Sensible."
"You distrust tenderness."
"Also sensible."
"Less. Understandable, but less." She turned from the window. "You distrust rooms where people know your name. That will become impractical by noon."
"This your bedside manner?"
"I reserve bedside manner for beds. This is strategic discourtesy. It includes fewer lies."

The tea was beginning to work. Not magic, or not only magic. My fingers had stopped shaking. I disliked that she had seen them shake. I disliked more that she had done something useful instead of making the seeing into a triumph.

Yennefer studied me. Not like Halbreck. Not like Mara with fever instruments. Not like Triss with documents. Her attention moved as if it could cut the strings tied to a subject by naming who held them.
"Do not mistake my interest for ownership," she said.
"People usually do not warn before owning."

"Better people do when they fear the habit." She looked toward the courtyard, still gray before sunrise. "I have watched the world try to make Ciri into blood, gate, heir, weapon, bargaining chip, prophecy, and daughter when daughterhood suited someone's speech. I will not assist the same crime with a different body and better stationery."
The words entered the room and settled hard.
I looked at the cup because cups rarely required answers. "I don't know Ciri."
"No. But your enemies are already borrowing her vocabulary. That will make her know you before she meets you."
"Is that good?"
"No. It is useful. Try not to confuse the two."
I looked back. "Geralt teach you that?"
"Geralt has taught me many things. Usually by accident, rarely in the order he intended."
A faint sound came from below, some servant beginning morning fires. Dawn pressed pale light against the shutters.
"Stay until we have a plan that is not simply a road with panic wearing boots," Yennefer said. "Then go north if north remains necessary."
"And if I choose otherwise?"
"Then I will call you an idiot with accuracy and decide whether stopping you would make me useful or merely another person taking your choice. I dislike that calculation, so avoid forcing it."
There was no kindness in her tone. That made the respect easier to bear.
She picked up the empty cup. At the door, she paused without turning. "If you run again, leave a note for the horse. He deserves better procedure."
After she left, I sat in the clean room and listened to the house wake around me. Someone below laughed once. Malva corrected them. Buck stamped in the stable, still offended by the night.
"Traitor," I said, though he could not hear me.
He probably heard me.
Yennefer stood by the window and looked out at the vineyards. In morning light, she seemed less like a storm and more like the thought that came before one. "I was unfair yesterday."
"Should I fetch witnesses?"

"Do not spoil a rare event." She turned. "I said self-pity when you were closer to grief. I dislike grief in armed men. It makes them either sentimental or destructive, and I have little patience for either. But dislike is not accuracy."
The apology had arrived wrapped in wire, but it had arrived. I accepted it the same way.
"I was deciding whether to hate Vesemir," I said.
"And?"
"I have postponed it."
"Good. The dead are patient and cannot defend themselves. That makes hatred of them too easy. Save some for the living. They can use the exercise."

She took from her sleeve a folded paper, not the letter to Ciri. A different one. "If I am forced to warn her before I choose to, this version removes your name. It describes office language, Veyrane, and the risk of host terminology without tying it to a man she may feel honor-bound to find."
"Why show me?"
"Because you are one of the people endangered by whether I send it. Agency is not a sweet given to children after they behave. It is information with consequences."
That, more than any softness, made me trust her a little. Not comfortably. Trust should not always be comfortable. Sometimes it is only the right person holding the wrong knife in plain view.
She was writing to Ciri and not sending it.
I understood the cruelty of that restraint too well. That was why I disliked it.

Dandelion arrived with bad news, a lute, two bags, a dramatic cloak unsuitable for travel, and Zoltan Chivay, who looked as if he had been included by the gods to prevent the cloak from becoming policy.

Priscilla rode beside them on a bay mare and appeared to be the only member of the party who had understood that roads contained mud. Her cloak was plain, her hair tied back, her eyes sharp in the way of performers who learned to read a room before the room decided whether to love or stone them. Dandelion waved from the saddle as if entering court. Zoltan glared at a grapevine as if it owed him money.
Geralt met them in the yard. He had put on his mild face, which frightened no one who knew him and comforted too many who did not.
"You came fast," he said.

"Art moves at speed when friendship harnesses it," Dandelion declared, then dismounted badly enough that Zoltan caught his elbow without appearing to do so. "Also your letter said public narrative contamination, and I will not have prose that ugly roaming Novigrad unchallenged."
Zoltan snorted. "He came because Triss wrote songs are being paid for. A bard can ignore famine, plague, tax law, and his own creditors, but not funded bad verse."
"Untrue," Dandelion said. "I ignore creditors with distinction."
Priscilla looked past them to me. "You are Jack."
"That depends what song you heard."
"Three. In one you are a wolf. In one you are a door. In the third you are a burden wiser hands must carry."
"Useful range."
"Dangerous range," she said. "They are not trying to make people hate you. Hate is unstable. They are teaching people to feel responsible for letting you remain free."
I liked her less safely than I had expected.

Dandelion approached with both hands open and only a little flourish, which I appreciated because I was tired and did not want to kill punctuation before noon. He was older than the songs made him, handsome in the way of men who had survived their own legend by revising it often, with eyes too quick to belong only to vanity.

"My dear fellow," he said, "if even half of what is sung about you is true, you are either a miracle, a calamity, or a public relations disaster. Having met Geralt, I assure you these conditions can coexist."
"You always talk this much?"
"Not always. I sleep sometimes. Poorly, since Zoltan snores like a mill arguing with geology."
"You wound me," Zoltan said. "And my millwork."
Geralt rubbed his brow. "Inside. Before someone hears him and invents a chorus."

Malva fed them before allowing evidence onto the table. Dandelion called the stew rustic, heartfelt, and almost Provencal, then ate three bowls when Malva threatened to define rustic with a ladle. Zoltan produced receipts wrapped in oilcloth, wax scrapings in small packets, and a ledger page copied in a hand so square it might have been carved. Priscilla laid out song variants, tavern locations, audience reactions, and three lines underlined in red.
"You came prepared," Triss said.
"Dandelion came loud," Zoltan replied. "Priscilla came prepared. I came because someone had to count."
Yennefer entered with coffee and a face suggesting she had already judged every document and found it lacking in posture. "Proceed."
Dandelion stood.
"Sit," Geralt said.
"But presentation requires,"
"Sit."
Dandelion sat. Priscilla did not hide her smile. Zoltan grinned into his beard.
The first sheet was a song paid for in Novigrad. The title had changed by tavern. The refrain had not.

Red wolf, red wolf, bright in the rain,
Who will hold your silver chain?
Not the child and not the bride,
Give the key to hands that guide.
I read it twice. The first time as insult. The second as instruction.
"Not surrender," Priscilla said. "Guidance. Care. Civic safety. It turns taking into help before anyone touches a shackle."
Dandelion tapped the page. "Also the meter is lazy. Which may be part of its evil. Bad songs travel faster because common throats can carry them without injury."
"Six crowns," Zoltan said.
"What?" I asked.

"First payment I traced. Six crowns to a tavern singer with clean boots and worse conscience. Another twelve for copying fees. Three for a printer near St. Gregory's Bridge. Courier wax from a South Quay account that also pays for medical freight. All routed through a war-widow relief designation because men object less to charity than surveillance."
"You're certain?" Triss asked.
Zoltan looked offended. "I am a dwarf, a merchant, a gambler, and an old friend of this peacock. If I were not certain about money, I'd have died of embarrassment years ago."
Dandelion placed a hand over his heart. "I choose to hear affection."
"You often do. Saves time."
The room almost breathed. Humor did that. It did not save anyone, but it kept the walls from closing while the blade was measured.

Zoltan's trail had not begun with a grand informant or a dramatic confession. It had begun with wax on a receipt, because money liked small doors. A dock clerk remembered a bundle of broadsheets marked as lamp oil. A tavern girl near St. Gregory's Bridge remembered the first altered verse because the man who taught it had paid in clean copper and asked which lines made drinkers laugh. Dandelion had traced the wording from throat to throat, insulted by each damage to meter as if bad scansion were a prosecutable offense. Zoltan traced the coin behind him, finding that the same charitable account paid for a singer's winter boots, a printer's extra hour, and a courier who took the long road after being told the short one was watched.

Between them, rumor stopped looking like weather and began looking like plumbing. Pipes, valves, leaks, pressure. A joke in a market became a verse at a bridge inn. A verse at a bridge inn became a warning at a ferry. A warning at a ferry became a route map for anyone asking which road the red-eyed witcher had taken. Dandelion called it vulgar. Zoltan called it cheap. Priscilla called it effective. They were all right, which made the matter worse.

Zoltan turned the ledger page. "Name tied to three payments: Valden Rue. Not high rank. Middle rat. Good coat, nervous habits, enjoys private rooms above lamp-oil shops. Rue moved south two nights ago. Left debt behind. Men expecting death sometimes settle debts. Men expecting protection often don't."
"Who protects him?" Geralt asked.
"S. Veyrane discretionary channel," Priscilla said, pointing to the notation. "Public reassurance layer."
Yennefer's mouth became a line. "There he is."
"There his money is," Zoltan corrected. "Men are harder to find than their payments only when they are poor. Rich men leave tracks because they believe paying others makes the floor clean."
Dandelion produced another paper and smoothed it with theatrical care. "There is more. Rue burned letters. Badly. Zoltan recovered fragments because he believes ash owes him answers."
"Ash is honest when handled with patience," Zoltan said.
Priscilla read the first scrap.
Retain wolf terminology in public layer.
The second.
Avoid dragon-blooded designation pending senior review.
The third.
Vineyard probability increasing. Do not engage Rivia directly.
The study lost its ordinary sounds. Outside, the vineyard wind moved through leaves. Inside, the words sat in the middle of the table and waited for us to understand how long they had been ahead.
Zoltan gave the rest because he distrusted summaries that let men avoid smelling the room.

Rue's rented room, he told us, had stood above a lamp-oil shop in a lane too narrow for honest carts. The bed had been slept in badly. The washbasin held black grit under the water. The window latch had been repaired from inside after forced entry, which meant either Rue had locked himself in after being visited or staged the visit with carpentry worse than his morals. On the table lay bread, goose fat, and three grains of red sealing wax that did not match the clove-black.
"He ate before leaving," Dandelion said, repeating his own conclusion with theatrical displeasure. "Confidence, or hunger."
"Hunger," Zoltan said. "Never build philosophy on goose fat."

Priscilla had found mud on the windowsill. Narrow boot. City make. Not dock work, not soldier. She said it without pride, which made me believe it more. Pride is useful in a fight and dangerous in a witness.

The important evidence had been in the stove. Rue had burned letters and trusted flame too much. Men in haste do that. Flame has a reputation for finality it does not always earn. Zoltan sifted the ash with a knife and recovered the three scraps now lying before us. He had wrapped them with the care of a man holding cheap paper that had become expensive by surviving the wrong fire.
"There was a boy," Priscilla added. "Sent up with cold tea. Paid to say Rue went east if anyone asked. He was frightened enough to tell the truth and hungry enough to remember the coin."
"What happened to him?" I asked.
"Fed," Zoltan said. "Then told to forget us specifically and remember the man with gray gloves generally. Cheapest witness protection available."
Dandelion winced. "We also gave him my autograph."
"That may count as endangerment," Yennefer said.

The room almost laughed. Almost. Then Triss turned the ash scraps with a needle and the words returned, dragon-blooded designation, vineyard probability, do not engage Rivia directly. Laughter retreated in good order.

The bread. The wax. The boy with tea. Rue's unfinished meal. They kept the enemy from becoming a fog named conspiracy. Fog cannot be stabbed, followed, embarrassed, or billed. A man with goose fat on his table could.
Geralt's face went still.
"They wanted me here," I said.
"Expected," Triss said. "Possibly wanted. Difference matters."
"Not enough."
"Enough to keep us from stepping where they painted a circle and calling it our own road," Yennefer replied.
I stood. The chair scraped.
Geralt looked up. "Where?"
"Road."
"No."
"That was fast."
"So was the stupidity."

There was a time, not long before, when I would have left anyway. I almost did. My hand went to the table edge. My burned palm hurt. Mara's report lived somewhere in this pattern. Rian's stolen copies. Nessa's corrected witness statement. Miro's story. Every person who had seen me becoming a page someone else could turn. The road called because roads lie simply: move, and the last place loses you.
Geralt did not block the door. That made staying harder.
Priscilla spoke before pride won. "If you leave now, they get the better song."
I looked at her.

She held my gaze with the calm of a woman used to men thinking beauty made her decorative and learning late that listeners own knives too. "A dangerous witcher arrives at a peaceful vineyard, brings officials, disrupts Geralt of Rivia's retirement, endangers household, flees rather than answer. That is the song. It will scan."
Dandelion made a pained sound. "Unfortunately, it will."
"What is the alternative?" I asked.
Zoltan leaned forward. "We write the bill first."
That was how the afternoon became less mystical and more useful.

Dandelion and Priscilla worked on counter-lines, not lies, which surprised me. I had expected public defense, hero nonsense, a red wolf reframed as noble. Dandelion rejected it before I wasted contempt.

"Never call a frightened public wrong for being frightened," he said. "It makes them defend their fear as virtue. You give them a better fear. Not of you. Of men who call neighbors unstable after saving their children."
Priscilla added, "And you give them a phrase they can carry."
Zoltan grunted. "Useful is not owned."
The words landed without flourish. Dandelion stared at him.
"What?" Zoltan asked.
"Say it again."
"Useful is not owned."
Priscilla nodded. "That is the line."
"Of course it is," Zoltan said. "Took me all morning not to dress it like a goose."

I disliked the line because it was good. Good lines travel. They also invite hands to claim them. But this one had a stubborn shape. It did not make me harmless. It did not make me noble. It named the theft before the thieves arrived with softer language.

That evening, a vineyard boy sang the red wolf refrain near the press house while carrying buckets. He had learned only half of it and changed chain to rain because he had misheard, which made the song less useful and more survivable. I was halfway across the yard before I knew I had moved. The boy saw me and froze.
Dandelion caught up with me, breathing too hard for a man who claimed theatrical stamina. "Do not frighten him."
"He is singing their words."
"He is carrying them. Different disease. Different cure."
The boy's bucket shook. He was twelve, perhaps. Thirteen if hunger had done its usual work of making childhood look shorter.
I crouched so my eyes were lower than his, the way I had with Miro. "Where did you hear it?"
"Market, master witcher. Man with a little drum. Said it was about you. Said you saved a girl from a hill."
"Did he say I should be chained?"
The boy swallowed. "Said guided."
"And what do you think?"

He looked at the buckets, the yard, Geralt watching from the porch, Triss beside him, Yennefer black as a judgment near the roses, Zoltan and Priscilla listening, Dandelion trying not to perform concern.
"I think if someone saved my sister from a hill, I would not let the hill's friends write the song."
Dandelion closed his eyes. "Oh, excellent. Terribly phrased. Excellent."
Zoltan called from the steps, "Pay the lad before the bard steals him."
The boy took a coin, received stern instructions from Malva to carry water rather than revolution, and left with the solemn dignity of a messenger who had nearly become art.

That night Dandelion began drafting in the kitchen because he claimed kitchens understood rhythm better than studies. Priscilla corrected his first four lines, Zoltan corrected the invoice, Triss corrected the legal risk, and Yennefer corrected everyone by silence alone. Geralt listened at the window. I stood in the yard with Buck and watched warm light move behind white walls.
The first counter-song failed immediately.
Dandelion found me later by the press house, where I had gone to stand with Buck and the smell of crushed grapes because the kitchen had become too full of strategy.

He did not approach like a fool. That disappointed some part of me that wanted him easy to dislike. He stopped beside the water trough, placed both hands where I could see them, and looked toward the vineyard boy rather than at me.
"You frightened him only a little," he said.
"Encouraging."
"For a witcher, practically saintly."
"I have killed saints. Most were poorly managed."
"Naturally. Saints require editors."

Buck lowered his head and breathed into Dandelion's hair. The bard held still with admirable discipline, though fear made one of his decorative feathers tremble. I respected that. Courage was not the absence of fear. It was refusing to give a horse the satisfaction.
"You think a song can help," I said.
"I think a song can harm. That is the same profession facing the other way."
"Not enough."

"No." His voice lost ornament. "Not against chains, writs, and men with carriage vents. But songs decide who looks away when the carriage passes. They decide whether the woman at the window thinks, poor dangerous creature, or, why does a safe man need to be taken in a box?"
I watched a line of ants working along a crack in the stone. They had found sugar near the press. Entire civilizations had risen on weaker motives.
"That is your craft?" I asked. "Teaching strangers which question to ask?"
"On good days. On bad days, I rhyme bosom with blossom and consider leaving the continent."
"Do you have many good days?"

"Fewer than my reputation suggests. More than my enemies deserve." He leaned one elbow on the trough, thought better of it when Buck looked at him, and straightened. "Priscilla is better at listening. Zoltan is better at counting. Geralt is better at glowering until walls confess. Triss and Yennefer are better at... well, nearly everything inconvenient. I am good at making a thing portable."
"Portable."
"Fear already is. That is why it spreads. If truth cannot travel in a pocket, fear arrives first and rents the room."

I wanted to dismiss him. I almost did. Then I thought of Miro with his wooden horse, Nessa with her stone, the boy in the yard with his bucket, all of them carrying what adults had placed in their mouths. Dandelion had not made that weakness. He had simply made a life listening to it.
"What do you need from me?" I asked.
"Specifics. Ugly ones. The price of rope in Willenford. The alderman's attempt to subtract a mill from payment. Branka's goose, if the goose mattered."
"It bit a boot."
"Excellent. Very human."
"It was a goose."
"Exactly. No symbol survives a goose intact."
I nearly smiled. Bad sign.
Dandelion's face gentled, which I trusted less than his jokes. "I also need permission not to make you handsome."
"Too late."
"True, but I meant morally. Audiences love clean victims and clean monsters because neither asks them to wash their hands. You are inconvenient. I need you to remain so."
"I can manage that."
"Splendid. It may save your life."
"Or make the report longer."
"Both are possible. Art is rarely efficient."
He left before he became sentimental. That was kind of him. Buck waited until he was out of hearing, then sneezed into the trough.
"Yes," I told him. "Too many feathers."

The horse looked at the road. I followed his gaze. Beyond the cypresses, fear was already moving with better shoes than ours. It had paper, couriers, coin, and songs that asked to be sung while pretending they asked nothing at all.
Behind me, Dandelion began again from Priscilla's line.
Useful lives are not tools made.
The words did not save anyone.
Not yet.

It began with noble wolf, which made Geralt leave the room. The second used crimson twice in three lines, which made Dandelion leave the room on his own to recover from shame. The third avoided wolf entirely and became so legal that Zoltan suggested it be nailed to a tax office door where joy went to die. Priscilla listened to all of them with a composure that made cruelty unnecessary.
"You are defending him too directly," she said at last.
"He is in the room," Dandelion replied. "One tries to be polite to endangered men with swords."
"Politeness is killing the verse. The state is not saying he is evil. It is saying he is valuable and unsafe. Answering with virtue misses the wound."
Zoltan pointed his pipe stem at her. "There. That's why she should write it."
"I am writing it," Dandelion said.
"You're decorating it."
Priscilla took the quill. Her hand was smaller than his, steadier, and less interested in being admired. She wrote four lines.

When hands that heal are made to bind,
When fear buys songs and calls them kind,
Ask who profits, ask who paid,
Useful lives are not tools made.
No one spoke for a moment.
Dandelion read it once, then twice. "The second line needs lift. But the bones are good. Infuriatingly good."
Priscilla handed the quill back. "Then give it lungs."

I had thought bards were men who made noise near danger and called it history. That night I learned history often began in rooms with bad coffee, stubborn friends, and arguments over whether a line could be sung by a drunk before the third cup. Dandelion cared about applause, yes. He also cared about what applause trained people to forgive. Priscilla cared about the listener no one else saw. Zoltan cared about the cost of moving words from mouth to mouth. Between them, the song stopped being ornament and became a road of its own.
I distrusted it anyway. Roads could be ambushes. But this one, at least, was being laid by people who knew where the stones came from.
A house could not save a man from being made public.
But it could make the first public lie less lonely.
Zoltan's evidence arrived in small packets because money, unlike prophecy, preferred being counted.

He spread them across the study table after breakfast: slivers of clove-black wax, red sealing crumbs, three receipt copies, two tavern tallies, an account mark drawn on scrap paper, and one piece of ribbon so black it seemed to drink the light from the window. Dandelion watched the display with the melancholy of a poet forced to admit ledgers had dramatic structure. Priscilla brought a stool closer. Triss fetched another lamp. Yennefer did not fetch anything. She simply occupied the room in a way that made objects consider behaving.
Geralt stood beside me, arms folded. He had barely slept. I knew because he moved better when tired, as if exhaustion stripped him back to the necessary parts. That was not healthy. It was familiar.
"Wax first," Zoltan said. "People lie. Wax only lies if heated, and even then it leaves a smell."
"You have a philosophy for everything," I said.

"No. I have survived enough fools to distrust mystery before breakfast. This here, this is South Quay wax. Good grade. Clove and lampblack. Used by medical freight offices and high-value correspondence that expects weather. Same wax on Rue's routing slips, same wax on two field packets delivered near Devenford, same wax on the notice copy your tollman had stuffed in his ledger."
"Tollman?" Geralt asked.
"Border post," I said. "He had a copy. Pale hair, crimson eyes, public risk. Buck waived the fee."
Zoltan nodded at Buck through the window. The horse stood in the yard biting leaves from a shrub Malva had threatened to defend with a broom. "That animal has a future in negotiation."
"He already thinks so."
Triss picked up the ribbon with tweezers. "This matches the strip from the culvert creature?"

"Not the same batch," Zoltan said. "Same supplier. Narrow punch holes. Used to bind packets, not animals. If it ended up on the creature, someone repurposed office material or wanted office material found."
"Wanted," Yennefer said. "Too neat otherwise."

I looked at the ribbon. My ribs remembered the culvert before I did. Black water in my mouth. Aard thrown badly. Branka's pitchfork buying me one ugly second. I had told that story quickly in the kitchen. Too quickly. The ribbon had mattered more than I had wanted to admit because it meant the net had started before I understood there was one.
"I missed that," I said.
The room turned to me.
"The ribbon. I saw it. Took it. Did not chase it hard enough. I was tired and bleeding. Branka helped, widow cried, Rian warned me. I moved to the next threat because the next threat was louder."
Geralt did not offer comfort. Good. "You followed what you had."
"I followed what hurt."
Triss set the ribbon down. "That is usually what people do. Institutions know this. They put small clues where pain makes them look secondary."
"Then I was handled."
Yennefer's eyes narrowed. "You were injured. Do not donate your agency to the first person who exploited your bleeding."
Her tone made comfort sound like reprimand. It worked better than it should have.

Zoltan continued, perhaps from mercy, perhaps because he disliked emotional interruptions that did not produce figures. "The cracked-hinge mark appears in three places. Courier receipt. Medical chest order. Tavern stipend. It is not a crest. Trade sign. Doors and repairs. Could be a shell. Could be someone's idea of humor."
"Doors," Geralt said.
The word had weight in the room. Door. Lock. Warden. Anchor. Corvo Bianco's own doors stood open to sun and still felt briefly like a test.
Dandelion leaned over a receipt. "Public reassurance layer. Is there any chance that means exactly what it says?"
"There is always a chance," Yennefer said. "Civilization is built on small chances and large disappointments."
Priscilla touched the receipt edge. "The payment amounts are small. Six crowns. Twelve. Three. Too small for a conspiracy people imagine in songs."

"That's why it works," Zoltan said. "You don't buy a kingdom by paying one lord. You buy the boy with a drum, the clerk who folds the letter, the widow's fund that moves without questions, the singer who needs winter shoes. Six crowns is not nothing when the stomach has opinions."
I thought of Branka arguing over fingers, of Edda's sausage, of Rian's mother in Devenford, of Mara filing notes because useful work had once existed. Small amounts. Small decisions. Large nets.
Malva entered with more coffee and a folded paper in her apron. She had the look of someone carrying trouble and resenting it for having no tray manners.
"This was left with the herb seller," she said. "For the white-haired guest. The herb seller brought it because I buy mint from her and she values continued breathing."

Geralt took the paper first. Not because I could not. Because he saw my palm heat before I did. The gesture irritated me, then helped, then irritated me more because help should not arrive before permission and sometimes does anyway.
He opened it. Read once. Handed it to me.
Rian's handwriting had lost its careful margins.

M. questioned. Notes seized. She delayed them and kept one page back. I am leaving Devenford badly. Do not use north ferry. S.V. prefers invitations. That means traps with chairs. If you reach Rivia, tell him the old Kaer Morhen fragments are being pulled from three archives. Tell the medic she was right about the word host.
The last line had been added later, cramped.
Auditors asked whether touch produced compliance.

The paper blurred at the edges. Not from tears. Anger can change vision without needing sentiment. I saw Mara at the cooper's room, hair loose after the night we had refused to make clean, her hands on my burned palm, her report in another man's file. I had wanted betrayal to be simple. It had not obliged. Now the system had taken the most human part of that night and filed it as a question.
Touch produced compliance.
Geralt said my name.
I had crossed half the room before I understood I had moved. The door stood open. The yard beyond it shone with innocent morning. Buck lifted his head and went still.
"Jack," Geralt said again.
"Move."
He did not. That was one of the old wolf's talents, making refusal look like poor furniture placement.
"If you ride now," Triss said, "you confirm route prediction."
"They have Mara."
"They questioned Mara," Yennefer said. "Different immediate problem."
"Do not spend grammar on me."
"Then stop offering yourself to their grammar by acting like a predictable wound."

I turned on her. The mark in my palm burned hard enough to make the air waver. The lamp flames bent. Priscilla stepped back. Dandelion went quiet, which made the room more frightening than any shout. Zoltan lowered one hand toward the axe at his belt, not drawing, only admitting the day had become that kind.
Geralt moved before the heat climbed higher. Not toward his sword. Toward me.
He caught my wrist.

The contact should have been nothing. Leather, hand, pressure. Instead the red lines in my palm flared and the study window cracked from corner to corner. Geralt's jaw tightened, but he did not let go. I saw pain enter his hand. I saw him choose to keep it.
"Enough," he said.

I could have broken his grip. Maybe. I thought so in the hot, stupid part of my blood. Then I saw his eyes. Not command. Not fear. The old guilt was there, yes, but underneath it a steadier thing. He was not stopping a weapon. He was holding a son neither of us had agreed to name.
That made the rage lose its shape.
I pulled free too hard. He let me. The red heat faded. The cracked window held together in its frame, pretending usefulness.
"I am not a child," I said.
Geralt flexed his burned fingers once. "No. Children are easier to stop."
No one laughed. Good. It was not a joke.
The knock at the front gate came five minutes later.
It was not loud. Polite knocks rarely are. Loud men expect resistance. Polite men expect walls to remember who owns them. Malva reached the window first and looked down. Her mouth hardened.
"Brown coats," she said. "Three riders. One carriage. One woman with a tube. Nobody useful."
Yennefer stood. "Do not open immediately."
"I wasn't born yesterday," Malva said. "Or under a table."
Geralt looked at me. "Stay behind me."
"No."
"That was not a request."
"I noticed."

Triss stepped between us before the argument could become a second threat. "Both of you are adorable in the least productive way available. Jack stands where he can be seen but not reached. Geralt stands where he can be blamed if steel appears. Yennefer terrifies them politely. Dandelion talks only if talking creates witnesses."
Dandelion pressed a hand to his chest. "I am wounded."
"Not yet," Zoltan said.
"Priscilla," Triss continued, "you listen. Zoltan, money."
Zoltan grinned. "Always."
We went to the front yard with the shape of a household deciding, briefly, to become a fortress by manners.

The riders waited beyond the gate. Their coats were dark brown, without local colors. The carriage behind them had iron-rimmed wheels, clean canvas, and small vents under the side shutters. That detail moved through me like a blade drawn slowly. One woman sat beside the driver with a black tube on her lap. The man at the gate held a folded writ in gloved hands.
"Geralt of Rivia," he said. "By cross-border safety memorandum, we request voluntary cooperation regarding an anomalous public-risk person believed to be on your estate."
Geralt leaned on the closed gate. "No."
The man paused. He had expected difficulty. Not brevity.
"Master Rivia, refusal may complicate your standing with,"
"No."
Dandelion murmured behind me, "Elegant. Limited rhyme, but excellent repetition."

The man's eyes flicked past Geralt and found me. He did not call my name. Better trained than the ferry officer. "The person in question may be injured, confused, or subject to influence. Medical assessment is strongly advised."
Triss smiled. It was not warm. "I am a licensed healer in three jurisdictions and unwelcome in four more, which proves experience. He has been assessed."
"Independent review is required."
"Independence funded by whom?" Zoltan asked.
The man looked at him. "I beg your pardon."
"Funds. Office. Account code. Who pays for the carriage, the gloves, the tube, and the little holes in the shutters? If you ask to remove a man for care, I ask who bought the box."
The woman with the tube shifted. Priscilla saw it. So did I.

Yennefer came forward then. Not far. Enough. "Tell Sorel Veyrane that if he wishes to address this household, he may write in his own hand and use nouns that survive scrutiny. If he sends another carriage with ventilation slits to a private estate under ducal protection, I will assume he is requesting a lesson in public embarrassment."
The man in brown recovered. "This estate is not exempt from public safety law."
Malva opened the side hatch in the gate, threw a bucket of wash water onto the road between his boots, and closed it.
Everyone looked at her.
"Mud," she said. "Public safety begins with clean thresholds."
Dandelion whispered, "I love her."
"Everyone does eventually," Geralt said. "Quietly."

The riders withdrew after leaving a paper nailed to the gate. They had not come to win. That was clear once they left. They had come to put a mark on the house, to make the servants see, to let the road know a carriage had arrived and been refused. Witness correction could happen later. First came witness creation.
I stood in the yard until the wheels vanished below the cypresses.
Geralt tore the paper from the gate and handed it to Triss without reading it aloud. The nail hole remained in the white wood.
That small black dot bothered me more than the writ.
They had not come to take me. They had come to prove the house could be touched.
They also came close to taking Peire.

I saw it only because Buck saw it first. The horse's ears flattened toward the carriage while the brown-coated man at the gate spoke. Peire had been standing near the side wall, half-hidden by a trellis, holding a brush and watching the proceedings with the hungry fear of young servants near official danger. The woman with the black tube looked past Geralt, past me, past Yennefer, and fixed on the groom. Not long. Long enough.

When the riders withdrew, the last one let his horse drift too close to the side wall. A folded slip fell from his glove into the mud near Peire's boot. The boy bent for it because boys bend for fallen things before suspicion has grown old enough to stiffen their knees.
Buck screamed.

The sound cut through the yard. Peire froze. The rider turned. I was already moving, not fast enough to be elegant, fast enough to be seen. The slip had a wax crumb on it. Clove-black. A hook with paper bait.
"Leave it," I said.
Peire looked at me, then at the rider. The rider smiled like a man who had only dropped litter. That was his mistake. People who smile before the joke is explained are usually the joke.
Geralt's hand closed on the gate latch. Yennefer lifted one finger. Triss said, very softly, "Do not."
I did not know whether she meant me, Geralt, Yennefer, or the entire yard. The word held us all for one breath.
Zoltan solved the matter by walking through the side wicket, picking up the slip with two fingers, and dropping it into his empty coffee tin. "Evidence," he said. "Costs extra when retrieved in mud."
The rider's smile failed.

Later, in the study, Triss opened the slip under a glass charm. It contained no message, only Peire's name written three times, each in a different hand, as if someone were testing which version looked most official.
Peire tried to apologize for bending toward the slip.

He did it in the stable because boys prefer to confess where horses can interrupt. His hands worked a brush over Buck's flank with more force than grooming required and less force than panic wanted. Buck tolerated it for two strokes, then shifted his weight and pinned one ear. Peire stopped at once. Smart boy.
"I thought it was dropped," he said.
"It was."
"Then I thought I should return it."
"That is what they counted on."
His face went pale in the clean southern light coming through the stable door. "I made myself a fool."
"No. You made yourself available. Different problem."
"That better?"
"Usually worse."

He swallowed. Outside, Malva was telling someone that the gate did not need sympathy, it needed a better nail. Her voice carried through the yard with enough force to keep Peire's shame from filling the whole stable.
"I was not thinking," he said.
"You were thinking like a decent person."
He looked at me then, startled.
"Decency is easy to bait," I said. "So is pride. So is hunger. So is fear. No shortage of hooks."
"How do I stop it?"
"You don't. You learn to check the line before you bite."
Buck snorted. The teaching method had received equine review.
Peire reached for the brush again, hesitated, then continued more gently. "Will they come for me?"
"Maybe."
That was not the answer a kind man would give. It was the answer he needed. His shoulders tightened but did not fold.
"What do I do if they ask questions?"
"Say you know horses."
"I do."

"Then say only true things that are useless. Buck eats too much. Geralt's gray gelding dislikes wet oats. The north stall latch sticks. If they ask about me, say I bleed on floors and offend housekeepers."
"You do."
"Good. Accuracy improves lies by making them unnecessary."
Malva entered carrying folded linen and anger she had sorted into practical shapes. "He will not answer questions alone."
"No," I said.
Her eyes moved to me. "That was not a request for permission."
"I noticed."
Peire looked between us, then at Buck. "Master Jack says I should say true useless things."
Malva considered me with the suspicion of someone discovering a thief had shelved a book properly. "That is not terrible."
"High praise."
"Do not get used to it."

She set the linen on a shelf and took from her apron a small wooden whistle on a cord. Plain, cracked at the edge, polished by use. "My brother used that in the vineyards before he learned wine pays worse than funerals in bad years. One blow means loose horse. Two means fire. Three means men at the gate who should not be there."
Peire took it with both hands. That made the gift heavier.
"I am not a child," he said, because boys are made to say the least useful truth available.
"No," Malva replied. "Children are often better at screaming. Practice anyway."
She left before gratitude could embarrass any of us.
Peire stared at the whistle. I recognized the look. An object had become responsibility. Happens to swords, medallions, letters, rings, horse tack, and sometimes names.
"You should wear it under your shirt," I said.
"Why?"
"Visible warnings get stolen first."
He nodded and put it on. Buck lowered his head and pushed his nose against the boy's shoulder, hard enough to make him step back. Peire laughed once before fear remembered itself.
The laugh mattered. Not because it healed the moment. It did not. But it put a small, living sound into the place where Black Ink had tried to place a hook.

That was when Corvo Bianco stopped being shelter in theory and became shelter in practice. Not because it kept danger out. It did not. Because when danger reached for the smallest hand in the yard, the house closed around him before anyone asked whose problem he was.
The council began badly because no one touched the wine.

I knew this offended Geralt before he said anything. Wine had once been a luxury he distrusted on grounds of price, taste, and the kinds of people who described it with words better saved for weather or lovers. Owning a vineyard had complicated the matter. He had learned that good wine could be work, bad wine could be useful, and certain conversations required a bottle on the table if only to prove civilization had not fully surrendered. Now a fine red from his own cellar sat breathing in the middle of the study while six people stared at paper, wounds, and one another's failures.

The room had been built for estate business and had become, by force, a war room pretending to remain domestic. Ledgers shared space with Black Ink copies. A vineyard map lay under Zoltan's payment trail. Dandelion's notes rested beside Priscilla's song variants, each line marked with audience effect. Triss's letters were stacked in order of danger. Yennefer's map held pins that made the Continent look diseased. Geralt stood by the hearth. I stood by the window because leaving needed to remain visible, even if I did not take it.
Malva brought food and did not ask whether she should stay. She stayed. Anyone who had thrown wash water at a state carriage had earned the right to hear what the carriage meant.
"Where first?" Zoltan asked.
"Kaer Morhen," Yennefer said.
Geralt's eyes moved to her. "Not Ciri?"
"Not yet. You hate that. Good. Hatred may keep you from being sentimental and stupid."
"Yen."
"Do not Yen me while every road toward her is likely watched. Veyrane wants connection. We do not hand him the brightest one because fear feels parental."

Triss nodded once, reluctantly. "Kaer Morhen holds older fragments. Vesemir's notes. Trial records. Whatever he hid from later copies. If the archive requests are already being pulled, we need the source before the source becomes another corrected statement."
"Winter roads," Geralt said.
"It is spring," Dandelion offered.
"Kaer Morhen does not care."
Zoltan leaned over the map. "North roads are watched if Rian's note is good. Main passes worse. If I were setting the net, I'd expect Jack to run alone or Geralt to run with him."
"I am sitting here," I said.
"Aye," Zoltan replied. "And the net is probably disappointed. Let it wait. Builds character."

Priscilla traced one finger along the southern route. "If the public song starts in Novigrad and the state paper follows from district offices, then keeping Dandelion there matters. Songs can outrun riders if given the right shoes."
Dandelion put a hand over his heart. "At last, a military doctrine worthy of me."
"You will not be alone," Triss said. "Priscilla knows the audience better than you do. Zoltan knows coin better than both of you."
"I know coin better than most gods," Zoltan said. "Gods rarely itemize."
The room almost became manageable.
The route discussion grew ugly because every sensible road required an unsensible trust.

Yennefer wanted false starts, decoy letters, a northbound rumor of Geralt leaving without me, and two southbound couriers carrying enough noise to attract men who preferred their targets named. Triss wanted medical language turned back against the offices, quarantine seals prepared for every town likely to receive questions, and a list of phrases that would tell her which Black Ink desk had touched a notice. Zoltan wanted account codes. Dandelion wanted taverns. Priscilla wanted names of ordinary witnesses before they vanished into phrases like unreliable, hysterical, provincial, and grateful.
Geralt wanted Kaer Morhen.
He did not say it like nostalgia. He said it like a man naming a place where a knife had been left in a wound because removing it required two hands and a winter no one had.
"And if the keep is watched?" I asked.
"It will be."
"If the records are gone?"
"Some will be."
"If Vesemir burned the useful ones?"
"Then he was himself until the end."
That earned a silence with old snow in it.

Triss broke it by pouring wine into Geralt's untouched cup. "We are not going to Kaer Morhen because it is safe. We are going because it is the only place where the lie began before the current liars learned the shape of it."
"Beautiful," Dandelion said. "Terrible. Almost singable."
"No," everyone said.
He looked wounded and wrote something anyway.
Yennefer placed one finger on the map where the roads tightened toward the mountains. "You will not take the direct pass. They will expect old men to take old roads."
Geralt looked at her. "Old?"
"Experienced. Weathered. Emotionally repetitive."
"Better."

"Not much." She slid a pin to the east. "You ride toward the wrong crossing first. Let the first observer believe you are taking the river road. Then cut through the charcoal track near Upper Sodden. It is miserable, steep, and smells of wet goat."
"Safe?" I asked.
"No. Less literary. Ambushes prefer roads with witnesses."
Zoltan nodded. "And wagons. You cannot overcharge an ambush if no wagon survives to complain."

Priscilla had been quiet, writing small names beside each town where rumor had touched. Miro. Nessa. Branka. Peire. Mara. Rian. She wrote like a singer, careful of breath even on paper. "Someone needs to reach Devenford again."
"No," I said.
She looked up. "I did not say you."
That embarrassed me more than being wrong should have. "Who, then?"

"Not Dandelion. He is recognized even by people who pretend good taste. Not Zoltan. Anyone watching medical freight will know to watch dwarven carriers now. I can send a singer through the hospice route. Women with sick songs are invisible to men who think intelligence wears boots."
Dandelion's face tightened. Not jealousy. Fear. "Priscilla."
"I said send. Not go." Her hand moved back to the list. "Though I may, if the safer plan proves stupid."
"All safer plans become stupid under pressure," Yennefer said. "Prepare two."

That was how the room worked when panic had been forced to sit down. Each person took a portion of the net and named its knots. No one made the danger smaller by liking me. No one made it cleaner by caring. Care became work, and work became routes, copies, burns, warnings, false songs, saddle straps, witness lists, and Malva instructing Peire how to blow a whistle without fainting.

No one simply agreed. Geralt chose the road because the oldest lie wore Vesemir's fingerprints and he would rather put his body between that lie and me than let another letter arrive first. Triss chose healer channels because vocabulary was already cutting and she knew where medical knives were kept clean. Yennefer chose delay around Ciri because a warning sent too early could become a leash tied by another hand. Dandelion and Priscilla chose the song because silence had already been bought. Zoltan chose money because money rarely remembered to disguise its boots. Malva chose the house, the servants, the gate, and Peire, because strategy that forgets kitchens deserves to starve.
I chose not to run alone. It felt less heroic than songs prefer and more difficult than courage usually admits.
It should have comforted me.
It did. That was the problem.

Comfort entered like a thief and began moving things I had nailed down years ago. It made Mara's absence sharper, Geralt's guilt less useful as armor, Triss's steadiness difficult to resent, and Yennefer's precision almost merciful. It made Dandelion less ridiculous, which I considered the day's gravest structural damage.
Then Malva placed a sealed packet on the table.
"This came with the last vegetable cart," she said. "The boy thought it was a recipe. I told him no recipe ever arrived with wax that smelled of cloves unless the meal was for enemies."
The wax was black. The mark pressed into it was the cracked hinge.
Geralt reached first. This time I let him. Help, accepted before pride could make speeches, saved time. He opened it and read. His face changed the way stone changes under frost.
"Read it," I said.
He looked at Triss.
"Read it," I repeated.
He did.

Field Medical Addendum, copied through Devenford channel. Subject: Jack Morningstar, probable unregistered Wolf School derivative. Wound response exceeds expected witcher range. Eye coloration anomalous but stable. Contact episode recorded by attending medic. Touch did not produce visible coercion, but subject displayed measurable reduction in resistance after private interaction. Recommend host suitability vocabulary remain restricted until senior review.
The room went quiet in a way even Dandelion respected.

I had thought the line in Rian's note had already done its work. Auditors asked whether touch produced compliance. I had been wrong. A question wounds differently from an answer. The answer had taken Mara's hands on my wound, her private care, the salve after, and translated all of it into measurable reduction in resistance.
It made betrayal uglier because it was not only betrayal. It was translation. Mara had cared. Black Ink had taken the shape of that care once it entered paper and made it serve the wrong master.
I picked up the wine bottle and threw it into the hearth.

The glass shattered. Red wine hit flame and hissed into steam. Geralt stepped toward me. Triss raised a hand, then lowered it. Yennefer did not move. Zoltan said a dwarven word that sounded expensive. Dandelion whispered, "That was an excellent vintage," and Priscilla stepped on his foot.
The hearth smoked red for a moment. Not crimson power. Only wine, heat, and the ordinary violence of a man too late to protect the meaning of a night that had already happened.
"Satisfied?" Yennefer asked.
I turned on her.
She met it without blinking. "The bottle is dead. The report remains."
"Do not teach me restraint right now."
"Then learn aim."

Geralt moved between us before I did something we would all regret and several officials would enjoy. He did not touch me this time. His burned fingers from the earlier flare were wrapped. The bandage made him look older and more alive.
"They did that," he said. "Not Mara."
"You know that?"
"No. I know the difference between a hand and a machine that uses the handprint."
I laughed once. It had no humor. "Convenient distinction for men who hid children."
That struck. I saw it. I wanted to take it back and did not, because anger is proud of bad work if the cut is deep enough.
Geralt's face emptied. "Yes."
The word had followed us from the kitchen, from the cellar, from every room where he refused to decorate guilt. It landed now with less defense than before.

"Yes," he said again. "I know something about hands becoming machines. Mine did. Vesemir's did. We told ourselves hiding you was protection. It was. We told ourselves keeping Ciri separate was protection. It was. We also built walls and called them roads because roads sound kinder."

No one saved us. That was the mercy of the people in the room. Triss did not soften it. Yennefer did not sharpen it. Malva stood by the door with her hands folded, a witness who would not let the house pretend family business was above servants. Dandelion looked at his own hands as if remembering every song that had made a man larger or smaller than truth. Zoltan watched the window. Priscilla watched me.
"What am I to her?" I asked.
Geralt's eyes came up. "Ciri?"
"Yes."
"I don't know."
"That is your answer?"
"It is the honest one."
"Honest because you are out of useful lies?"
His mouth tightened. "Maybe."

That almost broke me. Not because it was cruel. Because it was not. We were standing in a room full of powerful people, old lovers, loyal friends, papers, maps, and a dead man's choices, and the truth at the center was a hole shaped like a woman I had never met.

Yennefer spoke quietly. That made everyone listen harder. "Ciri does not need another man arriving as prophecy. She has endured enough of that to fill several mausoleums. If you meet her, you meet her as a person first or not at all. That is not courtesy. It is survival."
"For her?"
"For both of you."
