Triss went to the hearth and picked a shard of glass from the edge with a cloth. "The report about Mara changes our timing. Veyrane is willing to convert care into evidence. Anyone near Jack becomes usable: Rian, Mara, Nessa, Miro, Branka, the tollman, this house. All of us."
"Especially this house," Priscilla said. "Because it gives them a better song if they can make warmth look like influence."

Dandelion straightened, offended into usefulness. "Then we make the counter-song about the theft of warmth. Not that he is harmless. Not that he is noble beyond need. That he is a man, and men are not seized because care reached them first."
"Too long," Zoltan said.
"I was drafting."
"Draft shorter."
"Useful is not owned," Priscilla said.
The line returned to the table. This time it did not sound clever. It sounded like work.

Plans took shape because plans are what people make when fear cannot be killed immediately. Dandelion, Priscilla, and Zoltan would return toward Novigrad by separate roads, carrying copies with enough truth to be dangerous and enough gaps to avoid handing Veyrane the whole map. Triss would send quiet letters through healers and mage contacts, warning them against host vocabulary and false medical custody. Yennefer would shadow the archive routes and decide, with visible irritation, when Ciri had to be told. Malva would keep Corvo Bianco running, which everyone except Malva understood as a strategic necessity. Geralt and I would ride north to Kaer Morhen for Vesemir's source notes.
The old loves in the room did not behave the way songs would have preferred.

There was no duel of glances over Geralt's shoulders, no elegant cruelty, no woman reduced to yesterday so another could stand brighter in today. Triss corrected Geralt's assumptions with the ease of someone who had earned the right to be impatient with him. Yennefer argued with Triss as if respect were a blade they both kept sharp. Geralt listened badly at times and better at others. Their history did not leave the room. It simply stopped demanding the largest chair.

I noticed because I had expected something simpler. Men raised on roads expect lovers to become claims, rivals, debts, or wounds. Here, affection had survived by becoming work. Triss passed Yennefer a page before being asked. Yennefer warmed Triss's cooling tea with a negligent finger movement and insulted the blend in the same breath. Geralt watched them both, guilty and grateful in a way he did not know how to divide.

It made Mara harder to file inside me. Not easier. Harder. If old love could remain present without becoming ownership, then leaving her behind could not be excused as mercy by distance alone. It was also fear. Mine. I disliked that discovery and had no one convenient to stab for it.
"I can go alone," I said.
Six people answered no in six different tones. Buck stamped outside, making it seven.
"You are all becoming tiresome."
Before sleep, Triss found me in the corridor outside the guest room. She had a sealed packet in one hand and no patience in the other.
"For Mara," she said.
I did not take it. "You said not yet."

"This one is not sent unless Devenford is already compromised. It contains no names she does not know, no location she can be punished for receiving, and three pieces of advice rude enough to sound like me if intercepted." Triss lifted the packet. "Take it anyway."
"I am not going to Devenford."
"No. You are going north with Geralt. That is why you need to practice carrying a thing you cannot use immediately."

The corridor lamp hummed softly. Her red hair looked darker at night, less fire and more wine. I took the packet because refusing would not save Mara and would only make Triss right in a more annoying way.
"Why help her?" I asked.
"Because she helped you and hurt you, which makes her inconvenient enough to deserve accuracy."
"That a moral principle?"

"A political one when morals are tired." Triss leaned her shoulder against the wall. "Also because I know what it is to be named useful by frightened powers. I know what it is to sign something and realize later whose door it opened."
I looked at the packet. "You think she can be saved."
"I think saving people is rarely clean enough to deserve the word. Sometimes you only make the next question harder for the men asking it."
"That sounds like failure wearing perfume."
"It is. Most decent work smells worse by morning."
I almost smiled. "Geralt know you talk like this?"
"Geralt knows very little in an organized manner."
From somewhere below, he muttered something. Witcher hearing had disadvantages in houses with clever women.
Triss's expression softened by half a degree. "Do not let what happened with Mara become permission to trust no one. That is what they want, Jack. Isolation makes clean handling."
"They want me surrounded too. Witnesses. Roads. Contact pathways."
"Then the answer is not alone or owned. The answer is chosen company, chosen risk, and enough witnesses who know how to say no in public."
That sentence stayed with me longer than the packet did. It was the sort of thought a man could spend years learning too late.
"Thank you," I said.
"Try not to sound as if it wounded you."
"It did a little."
"Good. Progress."

She left me with the packet in my hand and the door behind me open. In the room, the bed was still clean. The shutters still held. The basin had been filled again. Corvo Bianco kept offering ordinary mercies as if ordinary mercies did not change the arithmetic of leaving.
I put Mara's packet beside the powder from Yennefer and sat on the edge of the bed until the lamp burned low.
"Good," Zoltan said. "Tiresome friends live longer than agreeable corpses."
That evening, Geralt found me in the vineyard.

Rows of vines ran toward the darkening hills. The house glowed behind us, windows gold, voices moving inside. It looked peaceful from a distance. Nearer, one could see the nail hole in the gate, the cracked study window, the scorch in the hearth, the way Malva had set two brooms by the door as if household tools might be called to war. Peace was not the absence of weapons. It was choosing where to keep them.
Geralt carried a second bottle of wine.
He also carried two practice swords.
"No," I said before he offered one.
"Good. Reflex still works. Take it."
"My hand is burned."
"That's why."

The vineyard rows were damp from evening mist. Fireflies worked above the grass in brief green mistakes. From the house came Dandelion's voice, then Zoltan's correction, then Malva shouting that if art required another pot of coffee, art could wash the cups itself. It should have been impossible to fight beside so much ordinary life. Geralt proved otherwise by throwing me the wooden sword when I was looking toward the window.
I caught it badly. Pain flashed up my palm.
"Again," he said.
"We are not boys in the keep."
"No. Boys complain less creatively. Guard."

He attacked without the kindness of warning. Wooden blade to shoulder, step inside, turn of wrist toward my burned hand. I blocked the first, missed the second, and nearly dropped the sword. He struck my thigh where the old Willenford cut still pulled when the weather changed. My leg buckled.
Anger answered faster than thought. I came at him hard, too hard, driving for the gap under his arm. He turned with me, let my momentum spend itself, and put the flat of his blade across my throat.
"Dead," he said.
"You cheated."
"You overcommitted. Cheating was unnecessary. Again."

We went again. I lost again. Not cleanly. Worse. I lost in useful ways. My burned hand made me compensate with shoulder strength. My shoulder made me late. My anger made me obvious. The red mark in my palm heated when I pushed too hard, and Geralt hit the wrist each time before the heat became more than heat. No speeches. No lesson named aloud. Only impact, breath, failure, correction.
On the fifth pass I caught him under the ribs and almost smiled. That was when he hooked my ankle and put me on my back in damp grass, wooden sword against my chest.
"Dead with a smile," he said. "Bards would love it."
I lay there staring at the darkening sky. My ribs hurt. My palm burned. My pride had taken worse wounds and deserved most of them. Geralt stood over me, breathing harder than he would admit.
"Your power makes you lazy in the wrong half-second," he said.
"I did not use it."
"You waited for it. Different rot."

I wanted to deny it. The denial arrived late and badly dressed. At the Broken Crown, in the study, at the gate, something in me had begun to expect the red pressure to answer before my body finished choosing. That expectation was a door. Veyrane did not need to open me if I learned to reach for the handle myself.
Geralt offered a hand.
I took it.

He pulled me up and did not let go at once. "Tomorrow, you ride hurt. Angry. Watched. If you reach for the old thing inside you every time fear knocks, they will not need iron. You will build the cage from habit."
The words were too accurate to forgive quickly. I nodded anyway.
From the house, Triss called that if we were done demonstrating masculinity to the grapes, there was food.
Geralt let go. "She means me."
"Obviously."
He almost smiled. "Again after supper."
"No."
"Good. Reflex still works."
"Replacement?" I asked.
"Inferior year. Good for throwing."
I took it and did not throw it. That seemed to satisfy him.
For a while we stood between the vines and said nothing. Geralt was good at silence. I was better at using it badly.
"Did Vesemir love me?" I asked.
Geralt looked at the house. "Yes."
"You answer too fast."
"Some answers waited long enough."
The anger in me had cooled enough to show what it had been protecting. That was the problem with anger. It kept the small animal alive, then left you alone with it when the fire dropped.
"I don't know what to do with that," I said.
"You don't have to do anything tonight."
"That advice from retirement?"
"From being wrong often enough to recognize when action is just fear with boots."

I looked at him then. The white-haired witcher of stories stood beside me in a vineyard he had somehow failed to ruin by existing. Geralt of Rivia had spent his life being dragged through other people's prophecies and had still learned to plant something. That should have made me hopeful. It made me suspicious first. Hope requires more courage than battle. Battle at least tells you where to point the sword.
"I may bring this to your door again," I said. "Worse than today."
"Probably."
"That doesn't trouble you?"
"Troubles me plenty."
"You still ride with me?"
He opened the bottle, drank, and handed it over. "Beside, if you let me. Behind, if you don't. Ahead, if you're being particularly stupid."
I drank. The wine tasted of dark fruit, oak, and a household that refused to surrender its table manners to dread.
"Beside, then," I said.
Geralt's face did not change much. It did not need to.
We left at dawn.
Before dawn, I went to the cellar alone.

Triss's maps had been cleared from the table, but ink ghosts remained where the lamp had warmed the wood. I found the candle box, the first one, empty except for wicks. Of course it was empty. Triss had warned me she would move the IF letter. I opened it anyway because some men press bruises to check whether pain has become memory.
Geralt found me there.
"Looking for wine?" he asked.
"Evidence."
"In a candle box?"
"Your house has strange storage customs."
He leaned in the doorway. "Triss moved it."
"I know."
"Still checked."
"Yes."

He nodded, as if that answered something he had not asked aloud. "I checked Vesemir's old saddle once after he died. Nothing in it. I had checked it three times before the funeral. Still did it again."
The cellar smelled of oak, dust, cold wax, and old bottles breathing through cork. It was a good place for shame, which prefers stone rooms and no audience.
"Did it help?" I asked.
"No."
"Useful."
"Honest."

We stood there until the house above began to wake. A pan moved in the kitchen. Someone coughed. Buck stamped once in the stable, impatient with whatever grief humans had decided to practice before travel.
Geralt looked at the racks. "When we reach Kaer Morhen, some things may not be there. Vesemir hid well. Others may have found enough."
"And if there is nothing?"
"Then we learn which nothing frightened them."
I closed the candle box. "That is almost optimistic."
"Don't tell anyone."

Corvo Bianco made departure harder than any battlefield had. Malva packed food as if feeding an army and then pretended it was nothing. Triss gave Geralt a letter, then gave me two packets of powder and instructions precise enough to be threats. Yennefer handed me a folded charm that looked like paper and felt like a command.
"Do not open unless the necklace heats without nearby source," she said.
"What happens if I open it early?"
"You disappoint me."
"Tragic."
"For you."
Dandelion embraced Geralt, attempted to embrace me, reconsidered after looking at Buck, and settled for a bow that included too much elbow. "If you hear a song improving, assume I survived."
"And if it worsens?" I asked.
"Assume I was kidnapped by amateurs."

Priscilla took my hand, the unburned one, and held it with stage grace and private seriousness. "They will try to make you only symbol. Resist by being inconveniently specific. Names. Places. People. Receipts. Bad stew. Horses with opinions. Specificity saves what slogans eat."
"You always talk like that?"
"Only when men are about to become legends against their will."
Zoltan clasped my forearm. "Don't die before I finish tracing the freight account. It is rude to creditors."
"I owe you?"
"Everyone owes me eventually. I am patient."

Malva came last. She tucked a packet of dried rosemary into my saddlebag and slapped Buck's neck when he tried to inspect it. "Come back if you need a room. Do not ask permission. Rooms are for using."
That almost did what the Black Ink report had failed to do. It almost stopped me.
Geralt saw. Triss saw. Yennefer saw. Malva, mercifully, turned to tell a groom to stop gawking at family business.

Geralt stepped to the tack board outside the stable. The Broken Crown notice was still pinned there, wrinkled and ridiculous among brushes, straps, and hoof picks. He tore it down. The paper ripped around the nail, leaving four small holes in the board.
He held the notice a moment, then threw it into the manure bucket.
Buck sniffed the bucket and sneezed. It was the most honest review the document would ever receive.
We rode out under a sky scrubbed pale by rain.

At the first ridge, Geralt stopped and looked back. I let him. The road bent below us, pale between vineyards, then vanished behind cypresses and stone walls. Corvo Bianco itself was hidden by distance, but the hills still carried its shape: tended rows, morning smoke, the promise of a roof that did not ask a man to justify sleeping under it. Geralt had spent most of his life distrusting places that promised return. Now one waited behind him, which made leaving an act of trust rather than habit.
"You can stay," I said.
"No."
"Triss is there."
"Yes."
"Yennefer."
"She is not there for me."
"The vineyard."
"It will survive me. Malva will see to that. Possibly by frightening the vines into obedience."
Buck shifted under me, eager for road, irritated by sentiment, correct as usual.
Geralt turned north. "You said beside."
I drew level with him.
Together, we entered the trees.
Preliminary Routing Note, restricted circulation.

Subject departed Corvo Bianco in company of Geralt of Rivia. Voluntary contact pathway confirmed. Household resistance significant but non-escalatory. Public seizure not advised while vineyard witnesses remain uncontrolled. Narrative layer requires adjustment: emphasize influence risk, mutual danger, and possible contamination of known associates.
Priority action: retrieve Kaer Morhen fragments before subjects do.

part_subtitle: The past is not buried if someone kept the key.

paragraphs: The watcher in the trees had good boots and poor discipline.

I noticed the boots first because mud takes impressions before men take credit. Narrow iron shoes, southern make, expensive, and then scuffed on purpose to look poorer than they were. The half-moon nick in the right heel had followed us out of Toussaint, vanishing when stone took the road and returning whenever rain softened the edges. A careful man would have changed shoes. A clever man would have walked where cart wheels ate the ground first. This one had done neither, which meant he was nervous, arrogant, or an office creature wearing courage badly.

Geralt noticed two miles later and said nothing for another mile. Old habits respected useful silence. Roach kept to the left of the track, Buck to the right, the two horses sharing the road with the narrow dislike of professionals forced into partnership. The smell of Toussaint had died behind us. No lavender. No warm stone. No grapes pretending civilization had worked. Pines thickened around the road, wet and black at the roots. The air tasted of cold bark, leaf rot, iron water, and the northern weather that waits behind every season with its arms folded.
"One close," Geralt said.
"One meant to be found," I said. "Another farther back."
"Counting?"
"Likely."
"Could let them count trees."
"Too generous."
"Retirement softened me."
Buck snorted. Roach flicked one ear. Both horses had opinions about men who declared improvement aloud.

We did not stop. Stopping tells watchers which moment matters. Geralt led us onto a logging track abandoned since thaw, then down a wash where water had cut through the soil and left stone bare. I dismounted before the wash bent west and handed Buck's reins to Geralt. He took them without asking. That was not forgiveness. It was worse. It was trust built before the argument and still working after it.
The watcher entered the wash seven minutes later.

He wore a brown cloak, a short sword, and a crossbow wrapped against damp. His face had the dull forgettable look of a man paid to be background, but fear had begun to sharpen him. He crouched where our tracks vanished and stared at the stones as if the road had committed fraud.
I stepped from behind a black pine and put my steel point against his kidney.
"Quiet."
He became quiet with impressive speed.

Geralt appeared on the far side of the wash with the horses. He had not drawn a sword. That frightened the watcher more than mine did. Men understood violence when it announced itself. They became very nervous when it remained optional.
"Name," Geralt said.
"I carry road advisories."
"Bad name."
"Calver." His throat moved. "Calver Drem. Courier. Freelance."
"Freelance means paid by cowards who want handwriting without fingerprints," I said.
He tried to look offended. The sword at his kidney damaged the performance. "I was told to observe movement only."
"By whom?"
"No names."
I pressed just enough for cloth to part. "Try one."
Calver shut his eyes. "Merrow."
Geralt's gaze moved to me.

I knew the name only as a shape from the reports: clean cuffs, clean phrases, the sort of man who could put a cage inside a sentence and call it safety. We had not met. That had not stopped him from learning my road.
"Second watcher?" Geralt asked.
Calver hesitated.

I should have waited. A good interrogator lets silence do half the work and fear do the rest. I knew that. Vesemir had taught it after he caught me threatening a stable boy at thirteen for stealing my knife. Start too hard, he had said, and men give you pain-noise instead of truth.
I started too hard anyway.

The word I used was not a Sign, not exactly. It came with my hand around Calver's collar and the mark in my palm heating under the bandage. The air tightened. Frost jumped along the edge of his cloak. His eyes went wide and empty. Behind me, Buck stamped once. Geralt said my name, and the single word cut through the pressure better than any blade.
I let Calver go.
He fell to his knees and vomited into the wash.
The second watcher bolted.

Geralt moved first, because old wolves do not need speeches to begin running. I went after him, boots slipping on wet stone. A shape broke between the pines above the wash: gray hood, small pack, no weapon drawn. Not a spy holding position. A messenger escaping with what we had just given him.
My mistake reached the trees before I did.

The messenger’s escape had probably been designed around me. Calver had not needed to give a full answer. He had only needed to shake, vomit, stare at my hand, and let the second watcher carry the shape of it away. A blade could be denied in a report. Fear in a man's eyes traveled better. Black Ink had not asked me to speak. It had asked me to demonstrate. I had obliged before I understood the question.

Geralt caught a glimpse of him and threw a knife. The blade struck a pine handspan from the man's head. The messenger dropped, rolled, and disappeared into a drainage cut too narrow for either of us to take at speed without losing bones. I reached the cut in time to see him slide down a wet slope toward a waiting horse. He did not look back. People carrying useful news rarely did.
"Could have had both," Geralt said.
It was not accusation. That made it harder.
Calver was still shaking when we returned. His hands had gone stiff from whatever my palm had done to him. I crouched in front of him. He flinched so badly the movement became ugly.
Good.
Then not good.
I had frightened men before. I had been paid for it. This felt different. Fear attached to a blade at least knows the shape of its danger. What had passed through me had not cared about shapes.
"Look at me," I said.
Calver did not.
I softened my voice, which sounded wrong in my mouth. "Look at me."
He managed it.
"Who was the second?"
"No name. Woman. Red scarf. Missing two fingers." He swallowed. "She carried the tube. I only walked close enough to make you notice."
"And if we killed you?"
"Then she would have written that too."
The efficiency of it annoyed me more than the cruelty. Cruelty wastes itself. Efficiency saves strength for the next person.
Geralt took the packet from Calver's inner coat. No crest. No signature. One black oval. Inside, the instruction was short.

Observe voluntary contact pathway. Record emotional interference from Geralt of Rivia. Do not engage target directly unless contact creates public necessity. Northern archive retrieval likely. Secondary team to move if subjects proceed to wolf-site.
"They know Kaer Morhen," I said.
"They know enough," Geralt answered.
Calver stared at the ground. "They said you would go there because dead men keep the best keys."
I stood too quickly. The wash leaned a little. Geralt saw. Buck saw. Calver, gods help him, saw too.
I wanted to kick him for seeing.

The wanting passed quickly. The shame stayed longer. It settled in the hand that had tightened on his collar, in the sour taste at the back of my throat, in the way Calver watched my fingers instead of my sword. A blade had edges a man could understand. Whatever I had pushed through him did not. That made his fear uglier because some part of me had enjoyed how efficiently it worked.
Geralt saw that part too. He did not call it monster. He did not call it necessary. He only looked at my bandaged palm and said, "Do not let them make you demonstrate the word they want."
It gave the shame a job.
Instead I cut the laces on his boots and threw one into the trees.
He blinked at it. "What are you doing?"
"Making your second report slower."
Geralt took the other boot and tossed it into the stream. "And wetter."
Calver looked between us with the expression of a man discovering witchers had discovered pettiness before civilization and had refined it.
We left him with his life, one loaf from Geralt's pack, and a message.
"Tell Merrow," I said, "that if he wants my route, he can walk it with better shoes."
Geralt waited until we had ridden half a mile before speaking. "You scared yourself."
"No."
"Good lie. Needs work."
I kept my eyes on the road. Pines closed around us. "He was bait."
"Yes."
"I still took him wrong."
"Yes."
We rode in the kind of silence men use when anger and shame have both lost authority. It lasted until dusk.

Dusk put us in a charcoal burner's hut with one wall missing and a roof that considered rain an intellectual problem. Geralt chose it because the chimney drew, the rear slope broke sight from the road, and Buck did not try to bite the air around it.

I watered Buck before tending my hand. That was not virtue. Horses complain louder than wounds and negotiate worse. The mark under the bandage had faded to a dull red forked through the palm, but the flesh around it felt too tight, as if someone had stitched heat under my skin and tied the thread around my wrist.
Geralt watched me fail to retie the linen twice before he took the strip from my fingers.
"I can do it."
"I know."
He tied it anyway.

Geralt checked the bandage instead of arguing. His hands were rough, exact, and gentler than either of us wanted named. He checked the knot, tested whether I could close the fist, and then looked at the fire as if the fire had been the one showing concern.
"You used the pressure on Calver," he said.
"Pressure used me."
"That true?"
I flexed the fingers until pain found each line. "It felt true for a moment. Then it felt convenient."
Geralt's mouth moved once. Not a smile. Something older and less amused. "Convenient lies are the ones that live longest."
Outside, the road clicked under a single loose stone.

Geralt's hand went to his sword. Mine went to mine. Buck lifted his head and listened without fear, which meant the sound belonged to something small. A boy stepped from the pines with both hands raised and a face too thin for his age. He wore a courier's scrap-bag over one shoulder and a string of saints around his neck, all cheap, all desperate.
"Message," he said.
"For whom?" Geralt asked.
The boy looked at me and swallowed. "The red one."
I almost laughed. The sound would not have been kind. "Try again."

"Master Morningstar," he said quickly. "A woman paid me to say the road north is watched at the stone bridge and the west pass has fresh men with dry tents. She said if I used wolf or chain she would take back the second coin."
"What woman?"
"Red scarf. Missing fingers." He lifted his own hand, folded two fingers down, and watched my face to see what the information bought.
Calver's second watcher.

Geralt gave the boy bread before he answered any more questions. It made the boy less likely to lie from hunger and more likely to lie from fear, which was at least easier to smell. He had been paid in honest coin and followed only to the old mile marker, where the woman vanished into fir shade and left him with instructions not to take the main road home.
"Smart," Geralt said.
"The woman?"
"The boy. He listened."

The boy did not smile. Children who carry messages between armed men rarely waste energy on reward expressions. He ate, took one of Calver's discarded bootlaces because his own had snapped, and left toward the stream track after Geralt told him which stones would keep his feet dry. Practical mercy. Geralt's oldest language.

When the trees swallowed him, I looked north again. The route to Kaer Morhen had become less road than question. Black Ink expected us. The woman with the missing fingers expected Black Ink. Vesemir's dead hand waited in the keep.
"Still north," Geralt said.
"You asking?"
"No. Checking whether you planned to run ahead and call it strategy."
"I considered it."
"Progress. Usually you do it first."
"Everyone is becoming difficult," I said.
Geralt fed the fire one wet branch and watched it smoke. "Family does that."

We slept in turns. Geralt took first watch because he did not trust my hand. I took second because I did not trust his guilt. Near dawn, the mark cooled, not from healing but from recognition. Kaer Morhen was still hours away, and it already felt awake.

Kaer Morhen came by degrees: broken road, old wolf stones, towers bitten by weather, walls repaired by too few hands and too many ghosts. Snow clung in the shaded cuts above the valley. Meltwater ran black under ice skins. The gate stood open.
That was the first bad sign.
The second was Lambert's bolt passing close enough to my ear to comb one strand of white hair.
"Still ugly," Lambert called from the wall.
Geralt sighed like a man watching weather return. "He missed on purpose."
"Comforting."
"He used to miss less politely."

Lambert stood above the gate with a crossbow in hand and the expression of a man who had found a reason to be angry and did not intend to waste it. He looked leaner than I remembered, sharper around the cheekbones, but the eyes were the same: quick, hot, and looking for the place a room wanted him to strike. A second figure stood below the arch, broad-shouldered, scarred, steady as old stone. Eskel. He had one hand near his sword and the other open at his side, because he had always understood that peace should arrive armed but not shouting.

Behind Eskel, Keira Metz leaned against the inner wall in a cloak too fine for Kaer Morhen and boots too practical to mock. Fair hair braided over one shoulder, mouth curved as if she had already read three secrets and found two poorly written. She looked at me the way mages look at locked boxes they have not decided whether to open with a key or a hammer.
"Geralt," Eskel said.
"Eskel."
"Jack."
I nodded. "Still alive."
"Lambert lost a wager."
"To whom?"
"Me."
Lambert came down from the wall two steps at a time. "I wagered he'd arrive with more trouble. Turns out I underestimated both of you."
Buck bared his teeth.
Lambert looked at him, then back at Geralt. "Even the horse knows when a room is lying."
The first exchange had enough edge to stand on, but Lambert's anger had chosen a deeper target.
Then Lambert looked at the bandage around my palm, the stiffness in my left shoulder, the way Geralt watched him watching me. His face changed. The jokes remained, but the thing under them moved.
"Another hidden child," he said.
No one answered.
Lambert turned on Geralt. "You sent for us because Vesemir buried another child in the walls."
"Because Black Ink is moving toward the records," Geralt said.
"No. That's why you sent now. The old crime is you called it protection again."
I had expected anger. I had not expected it to be on my side. That made me slow.
Keira noticed. Of course she did. "Crude phrasing," she said, "but his diagnosis is sound. He is reacting to recurrence, not novelty."
"Careful," Lambert said.
"I am. Repetition is the only method you've survived."
Eskel stepped between them without quite moving. "Inside. Wind carries."

Lambert kept his shoulders forward, anger first and body after, the way he had always entered rooms he expected to betray him. Eskel did the opposite. He angled himself where a quarrel would have to pass through him to become damage. Quiet men can be mistaken for gentle by people who have never watched them decide where violence should stop.
"The wind already knows," Lambert said.
"The wind charges less for silence," Eskel replied.

The courtyard felt smaller than I remembered. Training posts leaned under old scars. The trough was cracked. Near the wall, rusted practice swords waited in a barrel like boys left for a lesson that would not resume. I saw myself at twelve there, hands blistered, teeth clenched, Lambert calling my footwork tragic, Geralt pretending not to smile, Vesemir watching from the steps with a cup of something hot and judgmental.

Past the kitchen arch, the western corridor still narrowed before the guest rooms. I remembered being turned away from that passage when southern riders visited, Geralt's hand on my shoulder, a training excuse too clumsy to fool even a child. The keep had hidden more than papers. It had hidden footsteps.
The keep had taught hiding to sound like duty, which was a harder lesson to forgive.
No wound involving the dead does anything cleanly.
Inside, Kaer Morhen smelled of cold stone, dust, old smoke, mouse droppings, rust, and the faint sour trace of alchemical work that never truly leaves a place. Keira wrinkled her nose.

The smell found old rooms before thought could arrange them: the kitchen where broth tasted of onions, marrow, and Vesemir pretending it was medicine; the narrow stair where I had learned to fall without putting a hand out; the hall where Lambert had thrown a wooden sword at my head because, he said, reflexes preferred encouragement. Every stone seemed to know which boy had bled on it and which man had survived badly enough to return. Vesemir's absence did not sit in one chair. It occupied the gaps between tasks. No cup by the hearth. No muttered correction. No old hand reaching for a ledger before anyone admitted the ledger mattered.
"I had forgotten how this castle combines abandonment and infection."
"You missed it," Lambert said.
"I missed you. The castle was collateral."
Eskel set packs on the long table. "Records first."
"No supper?" Lambert asked.
"You cooked last."
"That's an argument for supper somewhere else, not against it."

Geralt unfolded Black Ink's road note and laid it down. The black oval looked smaller on the scarred table, but not less hateful. Lambert read it once and swore with technical care. Keira read it twice and smiled.
"High curiosity risk," she said.
"That line isn't there," I said.
She glanced up. "Not in this one. It was in the raven they sent ahead."
Geralt's head lifted.
Eskel pointed toward the broken tower. "Arrived before noon. Copper tube. No full seal. Keira bribed the raven with Lambert's meat."
"That was mine," Lambert said.
"You were slow," Keira said.
She produced the page from her sleeve.

Northern ruin inquiry: possible archive retrieval at wolf-site. Monitor for relational interference. Avoid direct engagement with Lambert unless provoked. Subject profile suggests provocation likely and unproductive. Keira Metz present by association. High curiosity risk. Consider false alchemical lead if containment review requires delay.
Keira looked delighted for exactly the wrong reason. "At last, an institution recognizes my gifts."
Lambert snatched the page. "They think I am likely to be provoked."
"They think correctly," Eskel said.
"By cowards using grammar, yes."
The keep groaned as wind moved through a broken upper corridor. No one looked toward it. That was how I knew they had all heard the second sound under the wind.
Metal. Soft. Wrong.
Geralt's hand went to his sword.
"Archives," I said.
"Old lab first," Eskel said. "Vesemir sealed the lower cabinet after the winter before he died. Didn't say why."
"He did that often?" I asked.
Eskel looked at me. Kindness and discomfort wrestled across his face. "More than we wanted."
Lambert took a lantern, then hesitated and threw me a second. "Try not to set the castle humming. The stones are nostalgic enough."

The old lab waited under the eastern stair, behind a door that had swollen from damp and pride. Keira opened it with a gesture. The lock clicked, then the door stuck anyway. Lambert kicked it. Magic had dignity. Boots had results.
The room beyond was colder than the corridor.

Dust lay over benches, jars, trays, cracked alembics, straps gone stiff with age, notes in Vesemir's cramped hand, and the old iron chair no one had ever called by its proper name if there was a boy within hearing. I stopped at the threshold.
I had stood in that room before.

Not often. Vesemir had kept me out of the worst of it after the fevers. Still, the body keeps certain rooms without asking permission: bitter decoction under the tongue, leather at the wrists, iron under the spine, Geralt's voice somewhere behind the shaking, telling me to breathe as if breathing remained part of the agreement.
"Jack," Geralt said.
I realized I had not moved.
"Door's not going to get less ugly," Lambert said, but his voice had softened by half an inch.
I stepped in.

The room did not need sorcery to remember me. My jaw tightened before I chose it. The old scar under my ribs pulled as if a strap had found its buckle again. The iron chair stood at the edge of sight, smaller than memory and therefore worse. Childhood had enlarged it. Pain had preserved the larger version for private use.

The medallion twitched once. The mark in my palm warmed. Keira's eyes sharpened. She lifted a hand before touching me, a small question. Mages did not always remember that bodies were not public instruments. Keira did, at least in that moment.
"May I?" she asked.
I gave a short nod.

She took my wrist with cool fingers and turned my palm toward the lantern. The lines under the bandage answered her nearness by heating. Her pupils narrowed with curiosity, not tenderness: the dangerous intimacy of a mind meeting a wound and wanting to know what law it obeyed.
"Interesting," she said.
"Try another word."
"Unstable."
"Better?"

"Less charming." Her thumb hovered near the center of the mark. "This is not a Sign scar, curse burn, or mutation response. It behaves like a seal recognizing a pressure route and borrowing the nearest living structure to reinforce it."
"Living architecture," Lambert said. "Wonderful. Can we stop letting people call him house parts?"
Keira did not look away from my palm. "I said borrowed, Lambert. Not owned. Precision is what keeps clever people from killing patients."
"It matters to whom?"
"To anyone trying to keep him alive without mistaking him for the mechanism."
That put a decent silence in the room.
I should have thanked her. Instead I pulled my hand back too fast.
"Try not to enjoy it before asking whether it hurts," I said.
Keira's expression cooled. "It hurts?"
"Yes."
"There. Asked."
Lambert made a low sound. Eskel looked at the shelves as if hoping a bottle might offer mediation. Geralt watched me without helping. He had done too much helping by hiding things.

Keira folded her hands. "For the record, I enjoy difficult knowledge because ignorance is lethal and common. If I forget pain while naming mechanism, remind me. Do not call mechanism vanity because pain has made you lonely."
That landed exactly where she aimed it.
"Fine," I said.
"Poor apology," she replied.
"It wasn't one."
"I know. That is why I criticized it."
Lambert laughed once despite himself. The laugh freed the room enough to work.

The lower cabinet sat behind two shelves of old monster parts and one skull Lambert claimed had belonged to a tax collector until Eskel pointed out the horns. Vesemir had sealed it with three locks and a plate of old witcher script scratched backward. Keira read the surface, frowned, and stepped aside without theatrics.
"This one is not for me."
"For who?" I asked.
Geralt looked at the plate. His face changed.
"For a boy with a Wolf medallion and another name hidden under his shirt," he said.
The barbed star at my throat cooled.
I touched the plate.
The locks opened.
So did the wall behind us.

Stone split with a hard dry crack. A man in a gray hood came through the hidden service gap with a knife blackened against reflection. Not alone. Two more followed, then something low and pale between them, leather muzzled, long forelimbs scraping the floor, an alchemical hound built for scent and impact rather than mercy.
Immediate threat leaves no room for wisdom. Good. I had been choking on wisdom.

The first man threw a glass bulb. Geralt cut it in the air. The liquid burst green and hissed against the floor. Keira snapped a barrier up too late to save the edge of her sleeve. Lambert shoved her back and took a knife across the ribs for the trouble. Eskel met the hound with silver and got driven into a table hard enough to crack the wood.
I went for the cabinet.
Wrong choice.
The hound ignored Eskel and came for my hand.

It moved fast. Too fast for its starving shape. It struck low, shoulder first, and took my knees out from under me. My back hit stone. Air left. Teeth snapped at my bandaged palm. I jammed my forearm into the muzzle and felt leather straps strain. The thing's filmed eyes did not know me. Its nose knew the mark.
"Jack!" Geralt shouted.

I tried Igni. Nothing clean formed. Pain stole the shape before the Sign could become fire. I kicked, hit ribs, felt bone shift, no effect. The hound drove harder. Its teeth cut through bandage and into the red lines.
My palm leapt awake.
Not bright. Hot.

The hound screamed through the muzzle. The lab answered with every glass vessel singing at once. Shelves rattled. The iron chair scraped backward across the floor as if pulled by an invisible hand. My vision reddened and narrowed around the creature's mouth, the cabinet, the open locks, the black oval on the knife one man dropped when Lambert cut him from shoulder to hip.

That was the honest part. Not only to save myself. To make the room stop touching what belonged to me, even if I did not know what that was. To burn the hound, the men, the cabinet, and the old chair until memory had nothing left to bite with.
Geralt's hand closed around my wrist.
"Hold," he said.
Not stop. Not control. Hold.
The word fit the Broken Crown. It fit the mark. It fit the shape of a chamber holding pressure instead of becoming it. I hated that it helped.
Keira drove a pin of white light into the hound's eye. Eskel cut the neck when it reared. Lambert kicked the corpse off me and kept kicking after it stopped moving until Eskel caught his shoulder.
"Enough."
Lambert's breath came hard. "Didn't ask."
"Still enough."
The third intruder tried to run with a leather tube from the cabinet. Buck solved that problem from the corridor.

No one had invited Buck into the keep. Buck had disagreed with invitation as a legal concept. He came through the door like weather with hooves, struck the runner in the chest, and sent him backward over a stool. The tube rolled across the floor. Roach, standing in the corridor with the offended dignity of a mare who had not chosen this family, blocked the man's second escape route by existing.
Geralt stared at the horses.
"Stable latch," Eskel said.
"Bad latch," Lambert said.
"Buck improved it," I said, because speech was easier than admitting my hand was shaking.

The lab stank of acid, blood, wet leather, old dust, and hound breath. Keira pressed cloth to Lambert's ribs while insulting his stitching prospects. Eskel tied the surviving intruder with enough calm to make the man regret having wrists. Geralt picked up the leather tube and gave it to me.
For seven breaths after the hound died, the room had no leader. Songs pretend battle ends when the last enemy falls. Bodies know better.

The first bulb's acid had reached a shelf of empty vials. Keira froze it into green crust before it found anything worth exploding. Lambert bled through his shirt and insisted he was not bleeding badly. Eskel kept one knee between the prisoner's shoulder blades.
The alchemical hound twitched once.
I moved to cut it again and nearly fell.
Lambert caught my elbow. Not gently. That helped. Gentle would have made the room tilt worse.
My hand shook against his sleeve. He felt it. He looked at it. For once, Lambert said nothing. That mercy was so abrupt I nearly disliked him for it.

Geralt crouched by the hound. The muzzle straps had Black Ink's ribbon threaded under the buckles, not decorative, not accidental. A small copper tag had been hammered flat and riveted into the leather. No crest. One number. Seventeen.
"They made more," Eskel said.
"Or counted failures," Keira replied.
The intruder beneath Eskel's knee laughed once into the floor. It was a wet sound, either courage or a loose tooth. Eskel increased pressure by half an inch. The laugh became a gasp.
"Where did the hound come from?" Geralt asked.
The man said nothing.

I took one step toward him. Everyone saw it. That was the problem. My anger had become a room event, no longer private enough to pretend discipline. The mark under the torn bandage warmed. The bound man flinched before I touched him. He knew what Calver had learned. Or he had been told to hope I would prove it.
Keira moved first. She put herself beside the prisoner, not between us exactly, which meant she respected the sword and insulted the impulse. "No."
"You don't command me."
"Correct. I diagnose patterns. You are about to provide evidence for men who brought a witness with a pulse."
The prisoner's eyes flicked toward her.
There. Not fear. Relief.
I stopped.
Lambert saw it too and spat on the floor near the man's face. "They wanted him frightened, not dead. Wanted him to watch you become the story."
"Useful prisoner," Eskel said.
"Ugly phrase," Geralt answered.
"Still useful."
I stepped back. It cost more than stepping forward would have. That made it the better choice and the less satisfying one, which is often how better choices identify themselves.
Only then did Geralt pick up the leather tube. Only then did he give it to me.
The room watched my hand.
"Yours to open."
My hand left blood on the seal.
Inside were three pages, a black disk, and a strip of cloth that had once been blue.
The first page was Vesemir's hand.
Not a copy. Not a report. His cramped, practical script, slanted hard to the right as if even letters had work to finish.
If this opens for Jack, I failed to burn it. That means either I am dead, sentimental, or both. Geralt, do not argue with the page. You will lose.
Lambert read over my shoulder and went very still.
I did not read the rest aloud.
Not then.
Outside, the wind moved through Kaer Morhen's broken teeth. Inside, the keep had been entered, the dead had been robbed, and the people still breathing had all learned the same thing.
We were late.
Recovered fragment, black oval courier routing, intercepted at wolf-site perimeter after failed archive retrieval:

Subject responded to origin-contact stimulus. Crimson pressure contained but not absent. Geralt of Rivia exerted verbal control phrase: "hold." Note relevance to future restraint models. Lambert interference severe. Keira Metz exceeded curiosity profile and applied protective action. Eskel present, stabilizing. Animal interference unexpected. Update field assumptions: horse may require classification.
Vesemir's page waited until morning because the living needed bandages and the dead had already practiced patience.

Lambert argued that bandages could wait if answers were bleeding in front of us. Keira told him his ribs were also bleeding and had the advantage of not being written by a dead man who enjoyed making instructions difficult. Eskel boiled water. Geralt cleaned the old lab floor in silence, which looked practical until I noticed him washing the same patch twice.
I did not help.

That was not pride. My hand had swollen around the red mark, and every flex pulled like hot wire. Keira had cleaned the hound bite with a tincture that smelled of pepper, grave soil, and punishment. She said it might reduce sympathetic resonance. Lambert asked whether she had any for stupidity. Keira said she rationed it around him.
Kaer Morhen made room for us the way abandoned places do: badly, with drafts.

We gathered in the old hall after noon. A fire burned low because the chimney drew poorly and because nobody trusted comfort too close to Vesemir's hidden words. Geralt sat on the bench across from me. Eskel stood near the hearth. Lambert paced. Keira occupied Vesemir's old chair, not out of disrespect, but because she had looked at it, looked at the rest of us, and decided someone needed to be brave about furniture.

The black disk sat on the table beside the pages. Palm-sized, matte, heavier than iron, cold at the edge and warm at the center. It had no symbol until the lantern shifted. Then a five-point impression appeared and vanished.
My necklace did not like it.
Neither did I.
"Read," Lambert said.
Geralt reached for the first page.
"No," I said.
He stopped.
I took it with my bandaged hand and paid for the choice in heat.
Vesemir's handwriting put him in the room more cruelly than any ghost could have done. His words had no drama.
If this opens for Jack, I failed to burn it. That means either I am dead, sentimental, or both. Geralt, do not argue with the page. You will lose.

We found the boy in a ruined keep north of the Pontar, in the lower chapel, alive inside a circle of ash and heat. White hair already. Eyes red. No memory. Necklace clenched in his fist. The dead around him were not cut. They were emptied. No rot. No fever. No ordinary curse trace. Writing on the floor used eastern hands, damaged by fire. I removed what I could before he woke. I do not know whether that was mercy or arrogance.
The boy answered to no name for three days. On the fourth, he took bread from Geralt and bit Lambert for laughing. Good teeth. Strong will. Possible survival.
Lambert stopped pacing.
I kept reading.

The signet mark appears in two damaged sources: one Nilfgaardian confiscation sketch from a Zerrikanian caravan raid and one older Redanian church catalog of "non-human prison emblems." Both are unreliable. Both agree on one phrase: Last Warden. Do not assume title means king, priest, savior, or weapon. Men who assume too quickly build altars and prisons with the same hands.
I did not tell Geralt everything. I should have. That sentence is easy to write and was apparently difficult to live.
My throat tightened. I hated the body for that. A page should not have hands.
Geralt looked down.
"Go on," Eskel said softly.
I did.

The child should be hidden from courts, mages, cult collectors, and any office that uses safety as a door into ownership. He should also be hidden from Ciri until we know whether two hunted bloodlines near each other make a beacon. I dislike this decision. I dislike more that fear can look like wisdom when one is old enough.

There are references to Faithel, perhaps a people, perhaps a role. Eastern survivor unknown. Burned woman seen asking for a child with white hair after mage seizures in Novigrad. Record likely connected. If I do not follow, it is because winter took three boys that year and I chose the one breathing in front of me. That does not make the choice clean.

Addendum, winter after second fever. If the boy lives, he must learn ordinary things before he learns the shape of the cage around him. Spoon first. Blade second. Roof before lineage. Bread before title. Let him know which boards creak near the kitchen, which horse bites, which stairs ice over, and how to mend a sleeve before anyone teaches him why men with seals might want his blood. This is not softness. It is order. A child who knows only danger becomes easy for dangerous men to define. If I have contained him, I have also fed him. If that sounds like absolution, burn this page and curse me properly.
Keira exhaled once.
Lambert rounded on Geralt. "You knew."
"Not all."
"You knew enough."
Geralt nodded. "Yes."
The word sounded like a door closing because there was no better defense behind it.

Eskel set both hands on the table. "I knew Vesemir kept you off the outer ledgers. I knew men came once and did not leave with answers. I knew the necklace hurt you if anyone pulled at it. I did not know Faithel. I did not know Last Warden meant anything alive."

Lambert laughed without humor. "I knew there was a boy everyone pretended was just another bad winter decision. I knew we were told not to ask why Ciri and Jack never shared the same hall. I knew fear gets called protection when old men want to sleep."
Geralt did not defend himself. That was the nearest thing to honesty left on the table.
Lambert looked at me then. "And you?"
"What?"
"You going to sit there like a corpse someone taught to read?"
"Lambert," Eskel warned.
"No. He gets to be angry. Or not. Something. We don't need another shrine in this miserable stone heap."
"I don't know what I am," I said.
The words came out sharper than I meant. Then quieter. The second part cost more. "I don't know what anger would hit first."
Lambert's mouth closed.
Keira leaned forward. "Then conserve it. Rage is data until you spend it. After that, it is only damage."
"No. I prefer you alive for the footnotes."
I almost laughed. It would have been a bad sound, but it might have counted.
The second page held sketches. Barbed star. A ring of chained points. A line of eastern script Vesemir had copied three times, each worse than the last. Keira winced.
"This is not writing," she said. "This is an assault on language with witnesses."
"Vesemir knew six tongues," Geralt said.
"And apparently met the seventh in an alley and lost."

She drew the phrase properly on a clean scrap. Her letters curved like heated wire. "Zerrikanterment. Or something close. Not a person-name. More like office, rite, perhaps custodial force. The next line is damaged, but this word here is cinder. This one seal. This one... no, not blood. Vessel, perhaps. No. Warden."
The black disk clicked.
Nobody moved.
The click was small. A cup settling might have made it. A nail in old wood might have answered weather that way. But the room heard intention.
Keira's face lost all humor. "Do not touch the disk."
I had not meant to.
Geralt caught my wrist again. "Hold."
This time the word made me angry.
"Stop using that like a leash."
His hand opened at once.
Too quickly. Too guilty.
The disk clicked again.
I reached for it because I wanted to prove the reach was mine.
That was my second mistake, if anyone was counting. Someone always was.
The moment my fingers touched the black surface, Kaer Morhen disappeared.

Not vanished. Folded behind pressure. I stood in a room of heat and smoke, low walls, eastern voices, a woman screaming orders in a language I did not know and understood in the bones. A man with blood in his beard shoved a bundle into another woman's arms. The barbed star was not cold there. It was white-hot. Something enormous pressed against the sky without wings, without body, all authority and grief. Under it, a black hunger laughed through human throats.
Then a baby's cry.
Then stone.
Then Geralt's hand on my shoulder and Lambert yelling my name with an anger that sounded almost afraid.
I was on the floor.

The disk lay three feet away. Eskel had one boot on it, pinning it as if old witchers had been trained to step on impossible things until they behaved. Keira held both hands above my chest, light gathered between her fingers. Geralt's face hovered over me, pale under scars. Lambert had a knife in his hand and no target.
"How long?" I asked.
"Three breaths," Eskel said.
"Felt longer."
"Usually does," Lambert snapped. "When you grab cursed heirlooms like a toddler with a stove."
I looked at the disk. "Not cursed."
Keira's eyes sharpened. "What, then?"
"Memory with teeth."
The humor was thin, but it got me sitting upright. Geralt helped. I let him for half a second too long, then pulled away. He noticed. Did not comment. That was either wisdom or exhaustion.
The third page was a letter never sent.
Not to me.
To Ciri.
Geralt saw the name before I opened it. The room changed around him.
"Read it," I said.
"Jack."
"Read it."
He took the page. His hand did not tremble. The rest of him did.
Cirilla,

There is a boy in the keep I have not told you about. That is a poor beginning. I keep rewriting it, which proves it will not improve. His name is Jack Morningstar because the necklace gives him one piece and the rest he earned by refusing every bad name boys tried to hang on him.
You would like him. That is one reason I have not let you meet.
The page bent in Geralt's hand. He kept reading.

You were hunted by blood, prophecy, empire, hunger, and affection sharpened into ownership. He is hunted by something we do not yet understand. I told myself keeping two dangers apart was protection. It may be. It may also be cowardice with better boots.
If I live long enough to know the difference, I will tell you.
If I do not, Geralt must.
The room had no sound after that except fire and old stone.
Geralt folded the page carefully. Too carefully. "He never gave it to me."
"Convenient," I said.
That was cruel. I knew before it finished leaving my mouth. I said it anyway because pain likes company and will invite guilt if no one better is nearby.
Geralt took it.
Lambert did not. "Dead men hide letters, live men bleed for it, and we all stand around pretending silence is a family heirloom."
Eskel looked at him. "Not all silence is pretending."
"No. Some is just failure dressed warm."
Keira held up the raven message between two fingers. "Before the room eats itself, may I point out the living enemy?"
"Please," Eskel said.

"The message says consider false alchemical lead. They expected us to chase the wrong note if we opened the cabinet. The intruders moved for the tube, not the shelves. That means they either knew Vesemir's real cache or guessed which object would wake."
"Who told them?" Lambert asked.
"No one needed to tell them if they had copies from Novigrad," Geralt said.
Zoltan's thread. Dandelion's songs. The road bent west while the dead still stood in the hall.
I looked at Vesemir's letter to Ciri. It had become heavy without gaining weight. "We go to Novigrad."
"After we burn what cannot travel," Eskel said.
"No," Keira said. "We copy before we burn."
"You're proving the curiosity risk."
"Good. If institutions are going to profile me, I expect accuracy."
We worked until night.

We worked until night through the keep's colder pieces: the fever room with the crooked shutter, the sword gallery with hooks shaped by missing blades, and the narrow stair behind the library where I had once hidden after hearing Ciri spoken of like weather no one could afford to meet.

No note held the smell of decoction boiled too long, Lambert sharpening a blade to avoid admitting worry, or Geralt waiting outside a door while a boy learned his body could become a question adults feared. Black Ink wanted papers. The keep gave me rooms that remembered why the papers existed.
Work meant cold fingers, bad lamps, mouse nests in old correspondence, Lambert cursing Vesemir's decoy locks, and Keira informing us that witcher filing systems explained several unsolved monsters.
"This is not an archive," she said, holding up a bundle of cracked papers tied with fishing line. "This is a cultural hostility to retrieval."
Eskel looked over. "The line held."
"So did several plagues. Endurance is not design."

Lambert found two false bottoms in the mutation stores and one bottle of preserved kikimore venom that had eaten through its cork and the shelf beneath it. Geralt found a ledger page in Vesemir's hand with my name written once, crossed out, written again, and then replaced with boy for three lines. He did not show it to me immediately. I saw it anyway. Witchers are poor at hiding things from other witchers when the thing weighs on the hand.
"Show me," I said.
Geralt gave me the page.

The ink was old, browned at the edge, but the correction still had force. Jack Morningstar. Boy. Boy. Boy. Subject appeared nowhere on that page. I hated how much relief that gave me. Hated more that relief could be purchased so cheaply by a dead man's inconsistent grammar.
"He tried," Eskel said.
Lambert slammed a drawer shut. "Trying is what people call failure when they want the dead forgiven before supper."
"Sometimes," Eskel replied. "Sometimes it is the only thing a man can leave that proves he knew he was failing."
The room did not like that. Rooms in Kaer Morhen had never liked tenderness unless someone disguised it as criticism.

Later, after Keira wrapped the black disk in silver thread and argued with it as if difficult objects could be shamed into cooperation, Eskel took me to the wall walk. He did not announce purpose. He simply nodded toward the stairs and began climbing. That was his way. Eskel could make invitation feel like weather without Geralt's talent for guilt.

The wind above the keep smelled of snow and wet stone. Below, the courtyard lay in broken shapes: training posts, trough, collapsed arch, old blade marks in packed dirt where boys had learned to become less breakable or failed to finish trying. In the far corner, half-covered by frost, stood three small stones without names.
"Trial dead?" I asked.
"Some. Not all. Vesemir moved a few after the Hunt. Said the courtyard had heard enough screaming without being asked to keep graves too."
"But these stayed."
"These had no one left to move them."
I looked at the stones. No names. No dates. Just three pauses in the snow.
"Was there one for me?" I asked.
Eskel leaned his forearms on the wall. The scar on his face turned pale in the cold. "After the third fever, Lambert put a stone there. Vesemir threw it at him."
That surprised a laugh from me. Not pretty. Real enough.
"Hit him?"
"Shoulder. Lambert claimed it was proof Vesemir valued accuracy. Said a grave before death was poor record keeping."
The laugh left and took warmth with it. "I don't remember that fever."
"Good. It was ugly."
"Most things here were."

Eskel looked over the valley. "Not all. That's why the ugly ones have teeth. If it were only pain, we'd leave and be done. But then you remember soup after training, a dry cloak, Lambert accusing mathematics after losing at cards, Geralt pretending not to worry, Vesemir cutting bread too thick because he thought boys healed faster with something to chew. You cannot hate a place cleanly after it has fed you."
The line should have been too soft for him. It was not. It had scars in it.
I placed my bandaged hand on the cold stone and felt nothing answer for once. No crimson. No seal. No buried pressure. Only cold rock under wounded skin.
"You think I should forgive them?"
"No." Eskel did not hesitate. "Forgiveness is expensive and people keep trying to spend it for others. I think you should know what you are refusing before you refuse it."

We read, copied, sorted, argued, burned three decoy pages, kept four originals, and wrapped the black disk in silver thread and wolf-hide. Geralt held the letter to Ciri for an hour before giving it back to me.
"Yours," he said.
"It was addressed to her."
"Yes."
"Then why give it to me?"
"Because I do not get to decide what part of your silence becomes hers."
That was almost the right answer. Almost.
I put the letter inside my coat beside Mara's copy and Vesemir's notes. The past had begun traveling with me in layers.
At dawn, a raven landed on the broken tower with another tube.
Lambert reached for his crossbow.
Keira caught his sleeve. "Shoot every messenger and the next message arrives with legs and teeth."
"Better target."
The message bore a black oval and one new line.
Archive event confirmed. Relational interference exceeded forecast. Wolf-site no longer passive. Move rumor operation to Novigrad. Initiate public chain language.
Geralt read it twice.
"Public chain," Eskel said.
Lambert looked toward the road. "Dandelion."
"And Zoltan," Geralt said.
"And Triss," I said.
Keira looked at me. "And you."
I did not like that she was right.

By the time we rode from Kaer Morhen, the keep looked no more empty than before. That was the insult of old places. They could be robbed, wounded, entered, and still appear unchanged to anyone who did not know which shelf had lost its dust.
At the first bend, I looked back. Lambert stood at the gate with Eskel beside him and Keira between them, all three small against the stones and larger than most armies I had seen.
Lambert cupped his hands around his mouth. "Try not to become infrastructure before I get to insult you properly."
"Try not to miss me," I called.
"I'll aim near you."
Keira lifted two fingers in a farewell that was either blessing or diagnostic interest. Eskel raised one hand, steady as ever.
Geralt rode beside me down the mountain.
He did not say he was sorry. Good. The word had grown too small for the road.
Novigrad smelled of fish, smoke, old money, wet rope, horse dung, fry grease, fear, and ambition wearing perfume.

Buck hated it before we reached the gate. Roach endured it with the patience of a mare who had survived Geralt's life and considered most cities a temporary failure of open ground. The guards examined our papers three times because correct documents in Novigrad looked more suspicious than forged ones. One guard stopped at my eyes, then at Geralt, then at the papers again.
"Reason for entry?"
"Business," Geralt said.
"What kind?"
"Witcher."
"Both of you?"
"He's apprenticing in charm," I said.
Geralt did not look at me. "Needs work."
The younger guard looked ready to ask whether charm required two swords. The older one had lived longer and waved us through.

The Chameleon had survived Dandelion by learning flexibility. Its front room was tavern, theater, office, refuge, rumor mill, debt collector, and restaurant when the cook remembered edible as a category. That afternoon, Dandelion stood on a table in burgundy velvet with one sleeve rolled up because ink had attacked it.

"A bridge cannot be sued," he declared to three patrons arguing with professional intensity. "It lacks property, personhood, and the capacity to look ashamed. A bridge keeper may be sued. A city may be sued if one has coin, patience, and a death wish. A troll may be negotiated with. A poet should be paid in advance because civilization is fragile."
"Get down," Priscilla said from the corner.
"I am conducting public education."
"You are avoiding the ledger."
"The ledger is hostile to art."
Zoltan Chivay sat beneath the table with an account book open before him and a knife holding one page flat. He did not look up. "The ledger says art spent twelve crowns on feather maintenance."
"A moral investment."
"A structural failure," Zoltan said.
The room noticed Geralt first. Then me. Noise thinned but did not stop. Novigrad never stopped. It only lowered its voice to earn more from listening.
Dandelion stepped down without crushing any pamphlets. His performance fell away in one breath. People who thought the bard shallow had likely mistaken brightness for lack of depth.
"Geralt," he said.
"The feather got worse," Geralt said.
Dandelion embraced him anyway. Geralt endured it like a man submitting to sudden weather.

Then the bard looked at me. White hair, crimson eyes, scar, Wolf medallion, posture, hands, the way Geralt had entered half a step beside and not ahead. He took all of it in and did not immediately make it into verse. That alone earned him more respect than I wanted to give.
"Jack Morningstar," he said. "My apologies. The city has described you with less accuracy than it describes its bridges, and one of those tried to kill a cart last spring."
"Did the bridge win?"
"Against the cart, yes. In court, pending."

Priscilla joined us with a stack of notes and a face that made careless words stand straighter. Plain cloak, hair pinned back, eyes trained by stages and streets. She read rooms before rooms decided whether to love or stone her.
"Before introductions become decorative," she said, "the city is rehearsing you."
"That sounds uncomfortable."

"It is meant to." She laid scraps of paper on Zoltan's table. Children had written some in chalk. Dock men had written some in charcoal. Clerks had written others in formal hands pretending not to be propaganda. Phrases repeated.
Wise hands hold dangerous locks.
No chain is cruel if it saves the town.
The red wolf yields because he is wise.
Useful blood deserves useful keeping.
Better kept than loose.
I touched none of them.
A child had written one phrase badly in blue chalk: wise hands like other men's locks.
"That last one is ours," Priscilla said. "Not because we wrote it. Because the city answered back."
"Children should not be in this."
Geralt gave me an old look. "Children are always in it. Adults just file them under consequences."
That should have been too carved. It was not. It was too tired.

Dandelion's feather trembled in a draft and, for once, seemed embarrassed by itself. "Black Ink wants the crowd to practice agreeing before the cart arrives. We cannot win by saying Jack is harmless. Fear knows when comfort lies."
"Then what do we say?" I asked.
Priscilla answered. "Ask who benefits from calling another person's body public property."
Dandelion winced. "It does not scan."
"Then shorten it."
He looked at the scraps, then at me. The professional mask settled over something deeply human. "Wise hands like other men's locks."
Zoltan pointed at him. "That one."
"Of course that one," Dandelion said. "Moral clarity, vulgar aftertaste, excellent street life."
People laughed. Not because it was funny enough. Because dread had sat down without paying rent and the room needed proof it could still be made uncomfortable.
Zoltan jabbed a thick finger into his ledger. "Wax first. Clove-black. Bought under medical freight by South Quay Counting House through three accounts and a charity for war widows."
"The charity real?" Geralt asked.

"Very. Which makes the lie better and the bastards worse. Paper came from a printer who handles indulgence blanks and pest notices. Paid in clipped Redanian silver through a barge owner's debt. Witnesses bought with favors, not coin: rent settled, tax forgiven, permit returned."
He spoke accounting like a man disassembling a trap by insult.
"Who is the printer?" I asked.
"Pavo Lutt," Zoltan said. "Four ledgers, three names, two consciences if you count the dead one. Lives above his shop. Likes satin. Owes Dandelion money."
"Everyone owes Dandelion money?" I asked.
"Spiritually, yes," Dandelion said.
"Financially, tragically not."

We spent the next hour turning fear into errands. Dandelion gave rumor a door. Priscilla gave it discipline. Zoltan gave it weight. Geralt gave it a blade. I stood near the wall and tried not to become the room's reason for existing.

The errands had names, routes, and prices: barges carrying medical freight without medical cargo, witnesses who needed bread before questions, and counter-lines short enough for drunk throats and market stalls. None of it looked heroic. That was why it might work.

It failed first in the doorway, where a dock woman with eels asked whether witchers paid full price for fish if they were already half-cat. It failed again near the hearth, where two Oxenfurt students rehearsed public custody doctrine until Priscilla made them repeat the sentence slowly enough to hear its cowardice.

Dandelion's rumor room sat behind the stage curtain, between a broken harp, costume crates, and a painted moon from a comedy Zoltan called financially treasonous. The table held street rhymes, market jokes, priest warnings, tally marks, unpaid names, and paid names pretending conviction.
Priscilla had made a map of mouths. Dandelion hated the phrase because he had not invented it. Zoltan loved it because maps could be charged for.

"Here," Priscilla said, tapping a square near the fish market. "Custody language becomes religion near the north bridge, property near the docks, and civic mercy where war widows need rent relief. Same message. Different hunger."

A boy came in with chalk on his sleeves and three new lines from the alley behind the bathhouse. He gave them to Priscilla, received bread from Zoltan, and ran before anyone could make gratitude slow him. The lines were crude, dirty, and better than Dandelion liked.
Dandelion read the last one and winced. "The city has no respect for meter."
"The city has rent," Priscilla replied. "Meter arrives after food."
She turned to me. "Say the line."
"No."
"Say it as if you heard it in a tavern and disliked it."
"That narrows little."
"Good. Use that."
I looked at the chalk scrap. Better kept than loose. It had the dull sturdiness of a thing meant to be shouted by people who did not want to examine it.
"Better kept than loose," I said.
The room listened. Not to the words. To how they fit in my mouth. They fit badly. That helped.
Priscilla shook her head. "Too official when you say it. Fear loses its neighborly shape. Dandelion?"

Dandelion performed it with three different accents. In a dock voice, it sounded like advice from a man who had seen cargo break loose and kill someone. In a priest's voice, it sounded like mercy with a lock. In a merchant's voice, it became insurance.
"There," Priscilla said. "That is the problem. It survives because it is not one lie. It is a lie that lets every listener choose their own virtue."
I disliked the respect I felt. Killing a monster that had claws was easier. This had grammar, hunger, and civic rhythm.
"How do you kill it?" I asked.
"You don't," Dandelion said. "You make it unfashionable first, then expensive, then embarrassing. After that, it dies of loneliness."
"That takes time."
Zoltan closed one ledger and opened another. "Everything worth doing takes time or a larger axe than I brought."

Below us, someone began chanting wise hands like other men's locks. Another voice answered with useful is not owned. A third voice changed it into something obscene involving aldermen and keys. Dandelion looked pained. Priscilla looked pleased.
"See?" she said. "Human breath. Once the crowd dirties a phrase, offices cannot hold it clean."

I looked through the cracked curtain at the common room: drinkers, actors, fugitives, debtors, clerks, whores, students, one dwarf with a knife, one bard pretending he could afford all this, one city teaching itself how not to become a document.
It was not safety.
It was resistance with bad chairs.

A stable boy came in through the kitchen and whispered that men were asking after a white-haired witcher. Dandelion told him every white-haired witcher in Novigrad had gone to confession and would not return until the priest learned better questions. The boy accepted this with the solemnity children reserve for adult nonsense and left through the back.
"You brought Buck?" Zoltan asked.
"He's in the yard."
"You left that horse in a Novigrad yard?"
"With Roach."
"That's not security. That's an incident waiting for witnesses."

We found Buck with one stable thief pinned against the wall by teeth in the man's coat and another lying in straw after Roach had introduced him to a hoof. The thieves were young, frightened, and very clear that they had meant only to inspect tack quality. Zoltan took their names, their fence, and the location of a pawn stall that had been moving stolen courier straps. Priscilla gave them bread. Dandelion gave them advice. Geralt gave them a look. I took the knife from the boot of the one Buck held.
"Bad knife," I said.
The boy, still suspended by his coat, swallowed. "It was my uncle's."
"Bad uncle."
Buck let him drop only after Zoltan promised to charge the fence double.

Ordinary inconvenience helped. For ten minutes the world was horse theft, bad knives, hungry boys, and Zoltan muttering that prophecy rarely survived stable management. Then we went to Pavo Lutt and the room became paper again.

Pavo lived above a printer's shop and had decorated his room with unpaid confidence. Velvet cushions, two cheap icons, three locked boxes, a mirror too large for the room, and a desk built to impress people who did not understand desks. He wore a satin waistcoat the color of overripe plum and smelled of ink, cardamom, and panic.
"Dandelion," he said. "What an unexpected honor."
Zoltan closed the door behind us. "Lock it."
Pavo locked it.
That was promising.
"We need your ledgers," Priscilla said.
"My accounts are private."
Zoltan placed a small pouch on the desk. It clinked. "This is what you are owed."
Pavo looked hopeful.
Zoltan placed a larger folded paper beside it. "This is what you owe."
Hope left.

Geralt stood near the window. Dandelion examined a shelf of playbills with theatrical grief. I looked at Pavo's hands. Clean nails. Ink at the edges. A small burn on the thumb from hot wax. No callus from blades. A man who would sell a dangerous thing, then call the danger commerce until it returned with teeth.
"South Quay Counting House," Zoltan said. "Clove-black wax. Pest notices. Monster contracts. Songs."
Pavo laughed badly. "Novigrad prints many things."
"So do presses. Yet here I am talking to the man, not the machine."
Pavo looked at me then. His eyes caught on mine and stayed. Something shifted in him. Not fear only. Recognition taught by paper before the person arrived.
"You are the asset," he said.
The room cooled.
He knew at once he had used the wrong noun. His mouth opened.
I moved before judgment did.

One step, then another, hand on his desk, face close enough that he smelled my breath and remembered all the songs at once. The mark in my palm heated against the wood. The desk groaned. Ink in the nearest pot climbed the side of the glass.
"Say it again," I told him.
"Jack," Geralt said.
Not hard. Not loud. Enough.
I stopped.

That was what stayed with me later: I had wanted him to say it again so I could punish the word through the nearest throat. Pavo was guilty, yes. But the word had passed through too many hands before his mouth.

Priscilla stepped beside me, not between us. Brave and clever. "Master Lutt," she said, "what you meant was that you have seen a description. You now understand why descriptions should be handled carefully."
Pavo nodded too fast.
"Ledgers," Zoltan said.
They were under the bed.
Of course they were.

Zoltan broke the first layer in three minutes and the second by asking where Pavo stored his real ink. The answer produced a smaller book bound in cracked red leather with no title. The moment it came into the lamplight, the barbed star at my throat cooled.
Geralt saw my hand move. "This one?"
"Yes."

Pavo began talking quickly. "It was part of a lot. Confiscated materials from the witch-hunt years. Mage notes, church seizures, private collections. I sold originals to Vander Rogh and Sons. Kept extracts for scholarly value. Commerce. Civic preservation. History."
"You are making me miss silence," I said.
He shut up.

The red book contained copies of copies. Relic sketches. Patient notes. A diagram of a barbed star labeled eastern non-human containment emblem. Three witness extracts from the purge years mentioning a burned woman with desert scars asking about a child with white hair. A tally of payments to a field doctor attached to irregularities. One marginal name: S. Veyrane, junior review.
"Bastards have childhoods," Zoltan said.

Priscilla read one witness line aloud. "Woman asks for child with white hair and red sickness. Burn scars. Speaks Northern poorly. Carries bone knots. Refuses payment. Threatens clerk with knife after phrase state custody. Escaped before questioning."
"Asha," Geralt said.
"Seems so," Zoltan replied. "She was looking before the songs. Before Broken Crown. Before your office rats had better titles."
Need had become crowded. The burned woman had been looking for me while I was learning to parry in a keep full of men who thought silence was safer than grief.
"Easier to betray in a crowded room," I said.
Zoltan looked up. "True. So we pick useful bastards and watch their hands. Welcome to friendship."
Pavo made a small sound.
Zoltan turned to him. "Not you."

We took the red book, three ledger leaves, and a list of payments. Dandelion also took a playbill from The Sorrowful Duchess and claimed it was evidence of aesthetic persecution. Priscilla told him it was evidence of mercy if the production remained unperformed.
Outside, fresh sheets dried on lines in the printer's lower shop. Sermons, prices, notices. A city could become a hunting dog if ink taught it which scent mattered.
From somewhere near the market, a child chanted wise hands like other men's locks in a skipping rhythm.
Dandelion stopped at the sound.
"That one is not ours anymore," he said.
"Good."

That night, we slept in rooms above the Chameleon. Slept is generous. Geralt slept like a man conserving violence. Dandelion snored in wounded meter. Zoltan counted coin past midnight. I lay with Vesemir's letter under my coat and the red book on the table beside the bed.
