The red book did not let the room rest. Not by magic. Worse. By implication.

Every creak below became a press beginning work. The page with Asha's description lay under my dagger because steel on paper is a childish form of control and therefore exactly the kind a tired man uses. Burned woman. Desert scars. Bone knots. Refuses payment. Threatens clerk after state custody.
She had looked for me before I had known there was anything to be found.

A knock came after midnight. Two soft taps, one harder. Geralt's hand appeared at his door across the hall before the second tap died. Mine had already taken the knife. We opened together and found Priscilla holding a candle, her hair unpinned, her face too awake.
"Not an attack," she said. "A correction."
That word had learned too many ways to bruise.
She handed me a scrap still damp from the street. Someone had pasted it under our counter-line near the bathhouse.
THE RED WOLF'S FRIENDS PROFIT FROM HIS FREEDOM.
Below it, in a different hand: ASK THE BARD WHAT HE WAS PAID.
Dandelion, woken by the word bard as if summoned by vanity's darker cousin, appeared in the hall with a robe over one shoulder and a lute in his hand. "I heard slander. It had poor rhythm."
"It will work," Priscilla said.
The room changed. Dandelion's face lost its performance so quickly it seemed younger without it.
"Yes," he said. "It will."
We gathered in the narrow hallway because no one trusted the common room and because urgency is rarely considerate about furniture. Zoltan arrived last with a cudgel, a ledger, and no shoes.
"Who paid?" Geralt asked.
"No one yet," Priscilla said. "That's why it matters. They don't need to prove Dandelion took coin. Only that defending Jack looks profitable. Once doubt starts, every song becomes business."
Dandelion leaned against the wall. For once, he looked like a man who understood his own usefulness as danger. "Then I stop singing."
"No," I said.
Everyone looked at me.
I hated being correct in public. It encourages people.
"If you stop, they prove pressure works," I said. "If you sing harder, they call it payment. So don't sing about me. Sing about who paid everyone else. Make the coin louder than the wolf."
Zoltan's eyebrows rose. "That is almost a plan. Unsettling."
Priscilla was already nodding. "Follow the money as chorus. Names where we have them. Questions where we do not. Rue. South Quay. Wax. War-widow relief. Permit returns."
"A fiscal ballad," Dandelion said, horrified and inspired. "Dear gods, I have aged into civic verse."
"You have aged into usefulness," Zoltan said. "It happens to the lucky."
Dandelion touched the damp smear on the scrap and looked at the ink on his fingertip. "They are making the room around Jack expensive."
"Yes," Geralt said.
"Then we make the expense visible."

The night became work again: Dandelion and Priscilla over dirty paper, Zoltan naming accounts, Geralt at the window, me holding a red book and learning that reputation could be cut without touching skin.
Near dawn, the mark in my palm warmed.
Not warning. Recognition.
Below, someone nailed four new notices to the contract board in the square.
The contract board had acquired an audience before sunrise.

That was how I knew Sorel Veyrane had manners. A cruder hunter would have sent men with nets, blades, and a cart with air holes. Sorel sent a crowd first. Bakers' apprentices. Former witch hunters pretending to be concerned citizens. Dock laborers paid through forgiven debts. Two priests with different gods and the same fear. Three clerks. A widow who had been given back her confiscated permit. A boy selling hot chestnuts who kept glancing at the wrong men for instruction.
Violence arrives cleaner when people believe they gathered by accident.

The square woke around them. Shops opened shutters. Carts complained over stones. A beggar with one leg cursed at a pigeon for professional reasons. The statue of St. Luthar looked down with chipped mercy and a fresh stain on his sainted brow. Above the contract board, four notices hung in a perfect row. The paper was dry despite morning mist.
Geralt stood beside me at the square's edge. Not behind. Not ahead. Beside. That posture had begun doing work neither of us named.
"Crowd's wrong," he said.
"Too many eyes. Too few errands."
"The chestnut boy is real."
"Yes."
"Hungry."
"Yes."
"Don't use Igni near the cart."
I turned to him. "That your strategy?"
"I like chestnuts."
The humor helped because it was too small to lie.

Dandelion had placed three singers in nearby alleys, none singing about wolves. Priscilla watched from a linen merchant's upper window with two students beside her, copying crowd phrases. Zoltan's people moved where practical people always move: behind stalls, near carts, under awnings, beside exits, next to anything that could become a barricade. Dandelion had drawn the map badly. Zoltan had redrawn it with insulting accuracy.

Yennefer stood beneath a church arch in black and white, one gloved hand resting on the head of a cane she did not need. She looked at the notices, then the crowd, then the drain cover near the saint's statue.
Triss was not visible.
That meant she was somewhere useful.

A city clerk mounted the steps beside the contract board. He wore municipal blue over a breastplate polished too carefully for a man expecting paperwork. Two clerks followed with tablets. Three former witch hunters stood nearby, each pretending history had given him a new profession. The chestnut boy pushed his cart half a pace closer to the board and looked at a man in brown for approval.
I should have moved then.
I did not because I was watching the notices. That is the kind of mistake that sounds intelligent in a report.

The clerk unrolled a paper. "Citizens of Novigrad, in light of recent disturbances involving anomalous field phenomena, public safety requires calm cooperation, accurate witness practice, and temporary custody protocols where necessary."
The crowd shifted around custody.
Dandelion's first singer began in a nearby alley, light and mocking.
Wise hands like other men's locks.
A few people laughed. Not enough.
The clerk raised his voice. "A dangerous body may be best preserved by lawful restraint."
The chestnut boy's cart began to smoke.

Geralt moved first. He crossed the square in a straight line that made people step aside before understanding why. I followed too late. The boy looked down at the cart, confused. Smoke leaked from under the coal pan, white at first, then green. His eyes watered. He coughed and gripped the handle instead of running because poverty teaches children not to abandon property, even when property has begun trying to kill them.
"Let go," I shouted.
He did not.
The drain cover exploded upward.

Something came through under the smoke, pale and scaled, all starved forelimbs and a jaw too broad for its skull. A small draconid, sick with alchemical heat, eyes filmed white like the hound at Kaer Morhen. Chains had been cut from it recently. The stubs still dragged from its neck and shoulders, clinking over stone. It struck the nearest man, not to feed. To clear space.
The square became noise.

People ran badly. They always do. Fear gives every body the same bright idea in different directions. A woman fell under a cart. The chestnut boy froze. The clerk with the tablets kept writing, which told me everything I needed to know and nothing that would save anyone.
I went for the boy.
The draconid went for the board.
Geralt saw it. "Jack!"
I heard him and kept moving.

That was not nobility. It was panic choosing a child-shaped excuse. I reached the cart, cut the handle with one stroke, and shoved the boy away hard enough to send him rolling under a fishmonger's awning. He lived. Good.
Then the draconid hit me from the side.

Stone met my shoulder. Air left in a grunt. Claws skidded over my breastplate and caught under the edge, tearing through leather into ribs. I tasted blood. The creature snapped at my face. I jammed my left forearm under the jaw, felt teeth lock into the bracer, and drove my knee up. It weighed less than a full-grown draconid and moved like a wounded animal taught to hate direction. Sick things do not fight cleanly. They spend everything.
"Down!" Geralt shouted.
I dropped.
His silver cut over me and opened the creature's neck. Hot blood sprayed across the stones, steaming where it hit the notices. The four papers darkened. The words on them curled, then brightened.
Response event.
Necessary custody.
Voluntary preservation.
Public chain.
The paper was the bait. The creature was the hammer.

The trap was not built to win the fight. Winning the fight was mine to do and theirs to record. They wanted a public sequence: dangerous body near official language, civilian terror, crimson pressure, lawful hands arriving late enough to look necessary. It was not a hunt. It was a jurisdictional rehearsal with teeth.
The draconid screamed. The sound struck the square and came back wrong from the walls. The mark in my palm answered. The barbed star went cold.
"No," I said.

The creature lunged toward the board again. I went after it. Geralt grabbed my shoulder and missed when blood made his hand slip. The draconid tore through the first line of stalls. Chestnuts scattered. People trampled them. Someone shouted that I had called it. Someone else shouted that I had saved the boy. Both truths reached the crowd at the same time and began fighting for ownership.
Yennefer lifted one hand.

The space between the creature and the largest group of civilians hardened. Three men hit the invisible wall and bounced back with the offended confusion of drunks meeting architecture. Yennefer did not look at them. Her attention stayed on the drain.
"Left," Geralt said.
I moved left.
The creature did not follow. It went right, toward the notices.

Triss appeared from behind the board with a wet cloth over her mouth and one hand full of torn paper. She had used the smoke and panic to get what the trap wanted protected. The clerk saw her and shouted. Zoltan's nearest man tripped him with a cabbage crate. Civic resistance has many forms. Cabbage is underrated.
The creature changed course toward Triss.

I threw Axii because it was the wrong Sign and the only one my hand remembered clearly through pain. The Sign touched the creature's sick mind and found nothing to hold. Not wild hunger. Not trained obedience. A pain-loop. It did not know why it had been cut, drugged, chained, released. It only knew heat, paper, and the scent of the red mark.
It came for me.
This time I was ready for the direction and wrong about the speed.

It struck low. My boots left stone. My back hit the contract board hard enough to crack the frame. One notice slapped against my chest and stuck there, not from damp. From heat. Words pressed through leather for a heartbeat: subject proximity, necessary custody, public-risk event. Then the paper blackened.
The crowd saw it.
Of course they did.

The draconid's jaw opened over my throat. Geralt's sword took one forelimb. The creature screamed into my face. I had my dagger in my right hand but no angle. My left palm was against its chest, the red mark under bandage touching scales where old chain wounds crossed.
The crimson pressure rose.

Not outward. Inward first. It filled my hand, then arm, then ribs, looking for a route. The square narrowed into heat, smoke, blood, stone, and every eye that would become a statement by supper. I heard the child under the awning crying. I heard Dandelion's second singer falter. I heard Yennefer swear in Elder Speech, low and sharp. I heard Geralt breathing like he had been stabbed. Later I learned he had not been. Not yet.
"Hold," Geralt said.
I hated the word.
I used it anyway.

The heat stopped rising and became weight. I drove my palm into the draconid's chest, not burning through, not opening, holding. The creature convulsed. The chain stubs went rigid. For one breath I saw not the square but a line from the drain to the board to the papers to me. A staged route. A bell rope with my blood as the hand.
"Triss!" I shouted.
She understood. She always understood too quickly for comfort.
She threw the torn writ into Yennefer's barrier. Yennefer snapped the barrier inward, crushing paper, smoke, and spell residue into a hard knot of black ash. The route broke.
The draconid sagged. Geralt cut the throat. I shoved it aside and rolled clear as it hit the stones.
Then the drain opened again.
Not another creature. Men.
Three of them in dark coats, half masks over their faces, crossbows drawn. They had waited for the crowd to look at the beast. Efficient. I had been wrong to think the draconid was the whole knife.
The first bolt hit Geralt.

It struck his upper arm and spun him half around. He did not fall. Geralt rarely granted enemies that kind of satisfaction. The second bolt came for me. I raised Quen too late. It clipped my neck guard and opened skin under the jaw. The third went toward Triss.
Yennefer killed the shooter.
No drama. One flick of her hand. The man folded as if his strings had been cut and struck the stones with a sound no song would improve.

Zoltan's people surged from the stalls. Not soldiers. Better in close quarters. A fishmonger hooked one masked man behind the knee. A laundress threw scalding water at another. Zoltan himself took the nearest by the belt and beard and drove him headfirst into St. Luthar's pedestal.
Priscilla's students kept writing.
That, more than anything, may have saved us.

The crowd had seen too much to correct easily and too many versions to own at once. A woman shouted that the creature came from the drain before I touched anything. The chestnut boy screamed that I had thrown him clear. A former witch hunter shouted contamination until the widow with the restored permit struck him in the face with her document.
Dandelion's third singer found his voice.
Wise hands like other men's locks.
This time the crowd answered.
Not all of them. Enough.
The municipal officer arrived too late and too polished. He wore blue over mail and carried authority like a lantern he had never had to refill. Two clerks followed him. Behind them came Merrow.

I knew him before anyone named him. Clean cuffs. Kind eyes. The man from Calver's mouth. He did not look at the dead draconid first. He looked at me, then Geralt's wounded arm, then the crowd, then Triss's ash knot cooling under Yennefer's barrier.
"Master witcher," Merrow said. "For public safety, remain where you are."
The chestnut boy, still crying, shouted, "He saved me!"
Merrow did not look at him. "All statements will be received in order."
Priscilla stepped down from the linen merchant's doorway with two pages already filled. "They already have been."
Merrow smiled at her. It was a well-made smile. "Unofficially."
"Accurately," she said.
Yennefer came to stand beside Triss. "You released a sick draconid under a public board to create a custody event."
The municipal officer stiffened. "Madam, accusations of that nature require proof."
Triss held up the ash-blackened writ with one gloved hand. The paper had not fully burned. Good paper resists fire when purchased by bad men.
"Then how fortunate," she said, "that your colleagues brought proof with them."
Merrow's eyes moved to the writ. So did everyone else's.
Yennefer smiled very slightly. "Literacy survives."
I tried to stand and failed the first time.

That mattered. The crowd saw. Geralt saw. The chestnut boy saw. I hated it, then stopped hating because the boy looked less afraid when I looked breakable. People trust pain more than perfection. They should not have to, but they do.
Geralt offered me his unwounded hand.
I took it.
Beside us, Dandelion looked at the ruined board, the corpse, the crowd, and the ash in Triss's hand. "I will need three verses and a better rhyme for custody."
Zoltan spat on the stones. "Rhyme it with bastardry."
"Too many syllables."
"Work harder."
Triss cleaned my neck in a rented room above the Chameleon while Geralt complained downstairs because someone else was cleaning his arm.
"He complains like it won't heal," I said.
"He complains because it will," Triss replied. "Men who think they may die become quiet or poetic. Men who will heal become tyrants about thread."
She unwrapped my palm.
The red lines had branched. Not much. Enough that her mouth went still.
"Keira should see this."
"You sound unhappy."
"Keira enjoys interesting things before asking whether interesting things are suffering. She asks eventually."
"You ask first."
"Not always." She dipped cloth into warm water. Steam rose though the water had cooled. "I have been young, ambitious, frightened, and useful to the wrong rooms. I try to ask sooner now."
Honesty sat between us without asking to be comforted. That made it easier to respect.
"Today becomes a file," I said.
"Yes."
"Everything does."
"No." She tied the bandage carefully. "Some things become people first if we are fast enough."

Downstairs, the crowd's answer had already reached the tavern. Wise hands like other men's locks. The line had become uglier, smaller, stronger. Black Ink had wanted a chain. Novigrad had found teeth in it.
That should have felt like victory.
It did not.
The boy's scream kept finding my ear.
The scream found other people too. That was the part Black Ink had not priced correctly.

By noon, the chestnut boy had a name in four versions. Jarek, Jarko, Little Jarek, and Chestnut, because cities are generous with names when they intend to avoid responsibility. His mother came to the Chameleon with flour on her sleeves and fury sharpened by terror. She slapped me before anyone could decide whether to stop her.
Good aim. Open hand. No ring. I had been struck by worse for less honest reasons.
Geralt took one step and stopped when I lifted my hand.
"He is alive," she said.
"Yes."
"He has not stopped shaking."
"No."

"They told him to stand near the cart. A man in brown said the best place to sell was by the board. Gave him a coin for the spot. One coin. One." Her voice broke on the number, not from weakness but from the insult of arithmetic. "My son nearly died for one coin and a better angle."
I had no answer that would not make her grief carry my guilt. So I gave her the only useful thing I had.
"Name him."
Her eyes narrowed. "What?"

"The man in brown. Describe him to Zoltan. To Priscilla. To Dandelion's people. Not to the municipal clerks. Not first. If they get his description first, they will polish it until he becomes weather."
The anger in her face shifted. It did not soften. Good. Softness would have been dangerous to her. "You want me to become witness."
"No. You already are one. I want you to choose whose hands touch the words first."

That landed. I knew because she looked at my bandaged palm, then at the door behind which Triss had hidden the ash-black writ. The city had taught her paperwork could steal. Now she was being asked to use it before it used her child.
"Jarek," she said. "His name is Jarek. If the bard calls him Chestnut, I will put his feather in a pie."
Dandelion, listening from the stairs, placed one protective hand over his hat. "A clear and reasonable boundary."
She did not smile. "The man had a soft beard and a scar under the chin. Brown coat. Good gloves. Bad boots. One heel cut."
Calver's kind. Maybe Calver's report had already bred replacements. Maybe the city had always been full of men with good gloves and bad boots. Either answer was ugly.

Priscilla took the statement at the kitchen table with Triss beside her. Not a formal deposition. Better. A living record, rough where memory shook, exact where fear had branded itself. Yennefer watched from the doorway and did not interrupt. Geralt stood outside with Jarek and showed him how to hold Roach's rein flat across his palm so a horse could not pull the skin open.
I should have stayed inside.

Instead I watched the boy touch Roach's neck with two fingers, careful as prayer. He glanced once at me, then away. Not fear exactly. The body remembering impact. I had shoved him hard enough to bruise. Saved is not the same as unharmed. That distinction matters when adults start congratulating themselves.
"You did what you could," Triss said behind me.
"That sentence has murdered plenty of improvement."
"Yes. But today it is also true."
I looked at the boy's hands. "Truth is getting crowded."
"Then let it stand in line."
She handed me a folded strip from Mara.
It had arrived through Rian, then Zoltan, then a pastry seller who apparently owed half the city and trusted none of it. Mara's hand was clean, fast, and more tired than ink should be able to look.

If the branching continues after crimson restraint, do not let them call restraint proof of controllability. A restrained wound is still a wound. Also, tell whoever is bandaging you that if the linen sticks, use warm water, not pride.
No signature. Sensible woman.
I folded it twice and kept it. Triss saw that too and pretended not to. That was care, in its less irritating form.

Downstairs, Zoltan was already buying the hour before Black Ink could buy it first. A baker signed one statement for rent forgiven and another for truth. Priscilla kept both, because contradiction recorded honestly was better than agreement corrected clean. Dandelion sent two singers to repeat Jarek's name until Chestnut began to sound like cowardice. The city did not become righteous. It became harder to edit quickly, which was the only victory available before supper.
Preliminary Public Incident Summary, Novigrad irregular board event, restricted circulation:

Public chain language achieved partial uptake before hostile song interference. Subject engaged staged draconid and civilians under high witness density. Crimson pressure manifested in contained form, apparently responsive to verbal restraint from Geralt of Rivia. Public perception unstable. Counter-narrative active: "wise hands like other men's locks." Recommend adjustment. Direct seizure in Novigrad not advised while witness field remains contested. Pursue origin pressure and imperial association channels.

chapters.chapter_title: THE WOMAN WHO SURVIVED THE FIRE
paragraphs: Asha had watched me kill the draconid and decided not to trust me.

It was personal. It was also evidence. Black Ink's route had pointed east, Vesemir's cache had used custodial language no northern archive could read cleanly, and the red book named a burned woman with bone knots before any song learned my road. Asha was not a mystery arriving for atmosphere. She was a surviving witness who had been looking longer than we had known there was a search.
Good horse. Annoying horse.
I stopped beneath a clothesline heavy with damp shirts. "Come out or stay useful."
She stepped from the shadow.

Asha was not old, but the fire had tried to make her ageless and failed rudely. Her skin was brown under burn-scars that ran from collar to jaw in branching pale lines. Her hair was black, streaked once with ash-white near the temple and braided tight against the nape. She wore a travel coat patched at the shoulders, a curved knife at the hip, and a bone charm wrapped around one wrist. Her eyes did not widen at mine. They narrowed as if comparing me against a debt.
"You named me in the room," I said.
"Others have named you worse."
"That does not answer why."
"No. It refuses to hurry."
Buck stepped between us by half a pace. I put a hand on his neck. The animal settled, but not kindly.
"You followed from the roof," I said.
"Yes."
"Black Ink?"
Her face changed so little that I missed the answer and saw only the knife.
I moved.
That was the misread. Mine. Ugly and fast.

Steel cleared half the sheath before Buck slammed his head into my shoulder hard enough to move me. Asha's knife was already in her hand, but pointed down, not at me. The alley held one breath. Above us, someone cursed a leaking roof. Somewhere near the square, a drunk tried the wise hands line and was told where to put his wisdom.
Asha looked at the horse, then at me. "Your animal has better judgment."
"He has more practice."
"You reach for steel when afraid."
I should have denied it. The denial was ready. The alley did not deserve that much stupidity.
"Sometimes."
"Good. A liar would be useless."
She sheathed the knife first.
I sheathed mine second, which was not trust. It was arithmetic.
Asha reached into her coat and brought out a small cup sealed with wax. "Drink."
"No."
"It steadies the heat."
"Poison does many things."
"Then give it to me first."

I took the cup, smelled it, and offered it to her. Her eyes changed. Approval, perhaps. Or disappointment that the test had not been easier. She broke the wax and drank one swallow without grimacing. Discipline. Then she gave it back.
I drank.

The taste was bitter enough to have legal standing. For a moment nothing happened. Then warmth settled low in my chest. Not crimson heat. Human heat. The kind that reminded lungs they had work besides surviving.
"A Zerrikanian draught," she said. "For seal-sickness."
"You are far from Zerrikania."
"So are your bones."

"Why now?" I asked. "If you knew enough to carry seal medicine in Novigrad, why not before Willenford? Before Broken Crown? Before four years of me being strange on the Path and pretending that counted as normal?"

Asha closed the empty cup with her thumb. "Because your trail was cut well enough to bleed inward. Vesemir broke the first search. Geralt kept the second from finding shape. For years you were rumor with horse tracks: red eyes, Wolf steel, no registry, gone before names settled. Then Broken Crown rang an old route scar. Novigrad taught the crowd chain-words. Your name moved through too many mouths at once. A cut trail became a shouted one."
She said it without apology. That did not make it gentler. It made it harder to dismiss.
That line tried to become too large. I let it pass.

We took the alley behind the Chameleon because Asha refused the common room and Yennefer, naturally, appeared anyway. She did not step from shadow. She simply became a fact near the rain barrel. Triss arrived from the other end with a lamp. Geralt came last, because Buck let him and no one else.
"Asha," Geralt said.
She looked at him a long time. "You are the one who did not look east."
"I looked badly," Geralt said.

"You looked north," Asha replied. "You looked at courts, mages, hunters, Ciri, winter, walls. I looked east first, then west, then into graves that had been emptied before I arrived. I found burned ledgers, false names, a mule seller who remembered a child he never saw, and one dead man with Wolf tracks near his last fire. I did not find Jack. I found absence with your hand on it."
Geralt accepted that like a man accepting a wound he had known existed under armor. "Yes."
Dandelion would have made that into a line. Zoltan would have asked whether the line had expenses. Neither was there. Good. Some meetings need fewer witnesses.
Asha opened her collar.

The burn pattern continued below the jaw, over the shoulder, and down under her shirt in branching lines. Not random damage. A symbol interrupted by pain and survival. My necklace cooled against my chest.
"Faithel," I said.
Asha's eyes sharpened. "You know the word?"
"Vesemir wrote it badly. Keira pronounced it worse."
"Mages do that to most things east of their vanity."
The word sat between us, too old for the alley and too practical to become myth. Asha watched my face until she was satisfied I had not turned it into a crown.

Asha tied her collar again. "Faithel were custodians. Not priests. Not kings. Not the sort of people Northern scholars flatten into cult when they lack patience. We maintained routes, seals, witness-lines. We remembered which water should not be drunk, which ruins should not be rebuilt, which songs were maps and which names were handles."
"Handles for what?" Triss asked.
"For things that should not be pulled."
The alley seemed to grow narrower.

Asha took a ring from inside her sleeve. Dark metal, red stone, one edge warped by heat. Not the same as my necklace. Kin to it. Or witness to it. The barbed star under my shirt went cold enough to hurt.

"Helena Morningstar wore this through three disguises," Asha said. "Handmaid, widow, trader's sister. She hated bad lies, which made survival tiresome. Jacob Morningstar carried the seal-key. They were your parents."
Names arrived badly.
Not with thunder. Not with a vision. No proper drama. Just two names placed in an alley that smelled of fish guts while my horse breathed against my shoulder.
Jacob.
Helena.
The body has no training for names it should have grown around.

Geralt went very still. Triss's eyes softened and sharpened at once, already arranging where grief might need support if I allowed it. Yennefer watched Asha more than me, perhaps because she knew stories can be knives even when held by survivors.
"Key," I said.
Asha nodded. "Not ruler. Not chosen savior. A living custody key. Last Warden after the line narrowed. The seal recognized breath, not worth."
"Comforting."
"It was never meant to comfort you."
Good. I could believe that.

She told us enough to make the room necessary, then refused to tell the rest in the alley. We moved upstairs, not to the common room but to Zoltan's back chamber, where the table had stains honest enough for grief.

Dandelion and Priscilla joined us. Zoltan brought bread, watered beer, and a knife he used only to cut sausage after making certain everyone saw it could do more. That was his version of hospitality. I appreciated it more than comfort.
Asha did not sit until Geralt did. Not deference. Calculation. She distrusted men who stayed ready to rise.
Yennefer began badly.

Dates. Route markers. Rite components. Whether Zerrikanterment was title, force, person, or office. Whether Vharakthul's contamination could be separated from the Cinder-Seal. Whether my mutations worsened or stabilized the original architecture.
Asha answered the first three, refused the fourth, and let the fifth die in the air.
Yennefer's patience thinned. "You came to give half a truth."
"I came to see if he had become a door."
"He is sitting in front of you."
"So do doors, in your towers."
The temperature changed.
Geralt lifted one hand without looking at either woman. "Enough."
Asha looked at him. "You do not command me."
"No," Geralt said. "But if you and Yen start measuring pride, the table will suffer first."
Zoltan put his hand flat on the scarred wood. "The table has done nothing to deserve mage politics."
That helped. Not enough.
Triss leaned forward. "Asha, tell it as it happened to people first. We can survive terms after."
Asha looked at her, then at the bread, then at me. "People first," she said. "That is a northern idea you forget often enough."
Yennefer did not answer. Good. Silence can be an apology if no one insists on making it clean.
Asha told the story of the fire.
Not beautifully. That saved it. Beauty would have made the dead too arranged.

There had been a sanctuary route under a dry ridge. Three families, two wounded custodians, one child, false merchant papers, a kitchen wall hiding a door, and a night wind that smelled wrong. The enemy did not come as monsters first. They came as men with paid guides, black oils, powdered bone, silver dust, and prayer hooks. They knew where to set heat so the seal would answer before the guardians were ready.
"Vharakthul?" I asked.
"His contamination. His hunger. His priests were ash by then, mostly. Hunger survives better than priesthood."
"Usually does," Zoltan muttered.
Asha continued. "Helena held the child route. Jacob held the lower gate. I was sent with the second group. Then the wall fell and the cradle was gone."
The table seemed to lean toward her.
"We found it under stone. Empty. Blood on the cloth. Not enough to prove death. Enough to ruin everyone."
Geralt closed his eyes.

"Then Zerrikanterment came down through the smoke," Asha said. "Not as songs say dragons come. No wings breaking clouds. No sermon in gold. Heat, light, pressure. Every liar in the courtyard screamed. He knew the line had narrowed to one breathing child. He knew the enemy had touched the key. He chose compression over purity. He saved what could be saved."
"And trapped the contamination," Yennefer said.
"Yes."
I looked at the ring. "Did he know what it would make?"
Asha held my gaze. "I think he understood the choice and hated it."
"That is not an answer."
"It is the only honest one left."
The room took that badly because it was true.
Asha did not continue immediately. She reached for the bread, tore off a piece, and did not eat it. Her hand held the crust as if the body remembered hunger but the mind had misplaced appetite.

"There was a woman named Sihra," she said. "She carried water for the route. No title. No bloodline. No song. She knew which wells turned bitter after midsummer and which muleteer would sell children for debt if allowed near them. Helena trusted her more than any sworn guardian. When the wall fell, Sihra took two children into a grain pit and held the lid down while men searched above. They lived because she did not cough."
No one moved.
"Why tell that part?" I asked.

Asha looked at me. "Because if I tell you only Jacob, Helena, Zerrikanterment, Vharakthul, seal, warden, you will think history is made by large names and then hate only large names when it wounds you. The road that saved you was made of small people. The road that lost you too. Do not let courts and cults teach you the same bad scale."
Zoltan grunted. "I like her."
"You like anyone who insults aristocratic accounting," Dandelion said.
"Good category."
Yennefer sat down at last. That was not surrender. It was strategy changing clothes. "Names, then. Small ones too. Give us all you remember."
Asha considered her. "You will write them?"
"Yes."
"Correctly?"
"If you spell them."
"You will not turn them into components?"
The question had teeth for every mage in the room and several who were absent.
Yennefer's face stilled. "No."

Asha watched her long enough to make pride uncomfortable. "Then write. Sihra of the Dry Ridge. Parel who walked with a cracked hip. Navo who lied badly but cooked well. Letha who hated Helena and died keeping her child quiet. Two brothers called Hesh and Hesh because their father was unimaginative. A mule named Bitter. Write the mule. He bit a priest and deserves record."
Dandelion inhaled with visible pain. "A mule with a better entrance than most nobles."
"Write it," Asha said.
Yennefer wrote it.

Seeing those names enter Yennefer's hand did more damage than another prophecy would have. Prophecy arrives dressed for importance. Small names arrive carrying buckets, bad soup, broken hips, duplicated family names, and one mule with better theology than several priests. They gave the past weight in places a man could not dodge with contempt. A title could be refused. A woman who held a grain-pit lid while children breathed under it had to be carried.

The absurdity did not break the grief. It gave the grief handles. I understood then why Asha had refused the alley. A truth told only in myth becomes a blade with no grip. This truth needed bad cooks, bitter wells, children hidden in grain, and a mule who had bitten clergy. It needed enough ordinary weight to resist becoming prophecy.

Triss glanced at me across the table. Not pity. Warning, perhaps. She knew what this was doing. Every name added a person between me and the clean emptiness I had used for years where parents should have stood.
"Helena sang when frightened," Asha said.
My hand closed around the ring.
"Badly?" Geralt asked.
Asha looked at him, and for the first time something like mercy crossed her burned face. "Very. Jacob said enemies would flee if the seal failed."
That almost broke me.

Not the death. Not the words Last Warden or living custody key. A woman I could not remember singing badly in fear while carrying me through a route built by people whose names had nearly vanished. Grief does not always arrive through the gate. Sometimes it slips through a kitchen door with a detail too human to defend against.
I stood.
I stood.

No one stopped me. That was either wisdom or exhaustion. I went to the stable because horses do not ask what you feel when standing near them already answers enough. Buck was awake. Of course he was. He lifted his head, considered me, then returned to hay.
"Don't overdo the concern," I said.
He chewed.

The stable smelled of straw, leather, horse, rain, and the mercy of animals who did not care whether my mother had worn disguises. I pressed my forehead against Buck's neck. The warmth there was plain. No doctrine. No Obsidian Crown. No Last Warden. Only breath, muscle, hay, and the slow patience of a beast deciding movement could wait.

Asha looked at me. "Because if I tell you only Jacob, Helena, Zerrikanterment, Vharakthul, seal, warden, you will learn the scale your enemies prefer. History is also bad cooks, bitter wells, grain pits, and a mule who bit clergy. Remember the small names before the large ones ask to own you."
Geralt came after a while.
He stopped outside the stall and waited for Buck's permission. That took two breaths and one skeptical ear.
"Asha is still at the table," he said.
"Good for the table."
"Yen is interrogating less like a sorceress."
"Progress."
"Triss is making notes."
"Of course."
"Dandelion is pretending not to cry by revising a rhyme."
"Sounds fatal."
"Zoltan is feeding everyone."
"Most useful man in Novigrad."
Geralt leaned against the stall. The lantern in his hand made the straw gold and the shadows softer than they deserved.
"I am sorry," he said.
I kept my face against Buck's neck. "That word is tired."
"Yes."
"Don't make it carry more than it can."
"I won't."
The silence was not comfortable. It had never promised to be.
"Jacob and Helena," I said.
"Good names."
"You knew them?"
"No."
"Then don't."
Geralt accepted the cut. "All right."
I hated that too. I hated that he did not argue when arguing would have given me somewhere to put my hands.
After a while he said, "Vesemir would have liked Helena."
"You don't know that."
"She hated bad lies."
That almost made me laugh. It came out as breath against horsehair.
I took the ring from my pocket. Asha had placed it in my hand before I left the room. It weighed less than history. That felt wrong. It also felt survivable.
When I returned, Asha had placed a bone charm beside my cup.
"I do not ask you to accept duty tonight," she said. "I do not ask you to trust me. I do not ask you to mourn people you cannot remember on command."
"What do you ask?"

"Do not let the North's fragments convince you they are the whole truth. Do not let Black Ink's hunger convince you your body is public infrastructure. Do not let our dead make you their obedient monument."
"And if Zerrikania does?"
"Then I have brought you to another cage," she said, "and I must help you break it."
Yennefer studied her for a long second. "That, at last, sounded like an answer."
"It was expensive," Asha said.
"Good answers usually are."
Dandelion wiped his eye and claimed smoke. There was no smoke. Priscilla said nothing, which was kinder. Zoltan cut more bread with unnecessary force.
I picked up the bone charm. It did not burn. It smelled faintly of oil, ash, and a spice I did not know.
"Come north, come east," Asha said.
The phrase cooled the ring in my palm.
"What does that mean?"
"Old maintenance verse. A route for truth when maps were forbidden. North for witness. East for water. Home only after the fire names you."
"Old songs are cheerful."
"Old songs were tools," she said. "Cheer was optional."
For the first time since she stepped from the alley, I believed her without having to decide whether I trusted her.
That was not the same thing.
It was enough for the night.
We laid the evidence on Zoltan's table because the table was already scarred.

Fine tables encourage lies. Polished surfaces ask people to behave as if history can be arranged symmetrically, with clean papers on one side and ugly ones on the other. Zoltan's table had knife marks, beer rings, wax scars, two gouges from an argument involving a halfling and a cheese invoice, and a burned corner Dandelion claimed was artistic. It accepted ugly things without pretending they were guests.

Kaer Morhen records went north on the left. Novigrad ledgers went below them. Triss's notes formed a precise line in the center. Yennefer's sketches of magical dead zones sat above everything, black ink over fine paper, each mark sharp enough to look like a threat. Dandelion's song map covered the right side in hooks, phrases, arrows, and one sketch of a chain that Priscilla had crossed out because it looked too heroic. Zoltan's wax and coin trails anchored the bottom. Asha placed her bone charm beside the black disk from Vesemir's cache and made no attempt to explain why every candle leaned away from it.
I stood with my back to the wall.
Geralt stood beside me.
Everyone noticed. No one named it.
"Say it plainly," Zoltan said. "If I stare at one more decorative line on a mage map, I will begin taxing elegance."

Triss touched the middle page. "Black Ink is not only following Jack. They are testing which public and legal phrases create resonance. Host suitability. Hereditary infrastructure. Bloodline custody. Voluntary cooperation. Public-risk anomaly. Public chain. Each phrase appears near a physical event, planned event, or witness cluster."
"Words as bells," I said.
Yennefer nodded. "And your name as the clapper."
Dandelion winced. "Effective and unpleasant."
"Then remember it," Yennefer said.

Asha pointed to Yennefer's sketches. "These are anchor sickness. Not full breaches. Old sites with wounded pressure. The North built over more than graves. Broken Crown was an old route scar. St. Luthar's drain was made into a bell. Willenford was an echo made louder by human rot."
"How much does the distinction matter?" Zoltan asked.
"Enough that people die if we misread it."
"Helpful scale."

Triss added one more note, delivered through a spice merchant who thought he carried pepper and a small resentment against tariffs. The note had been opened, resealed, and then opened again by Yennefer because trust, she said, did not survive laziness.
Geralt read it aloud.

The dossier has moved from advisory summary into restricted imperial circulation. It does not name Jack directly in the first paragraph. It names a crimson-eyed witcher, Geralt of Rivia, Kaer Morhen omissions, potential bloodline custody, and destabilizing association with Her Highness's private history. Your window to speak as family narrows. If you delay, the state will teach her the shape before you give her the facts.
No one moved when he finished.
Ciri's absence became the largest person in the room.

Yennefer took the note back with fingers that did not tremble because she would not permit them the vanity. "Emhyr's people will see risk. Northern enemies will see leverage. Black Ink will see opportunity. Ciri will see betrayal if she learns everyone moved around her again."
Geralt looked down at the table. "Then I write."
"You write badly," Dandelion said, too gently to be joking.
"Good. She'll know it is mine."
Triss shook her head. "Too little. Ilyra said the room matters."
"What room?" I asked.
"Not court," Yennefer said. "Not Corvo Bianco if roads are watched. Not the Chameleon if Black Ink knows we use it. Somewhere she can arrive as Ciri before anyone makes her arrive as title."
Asha touched the bone charm. "North first. East after."
"Meaning?"

Asha tapped the bone charm once against the black disk. The sound was small and dry. "North first means witness before origin. East after means water before fire. If you go east without the northern witness, your enemies will say you fled proof. If you stay north too long, the old road closes and the dead keep speaking through bad translators."
"Convenient phrasing," Dandelion said.
"Then remember it," Yennefer said.
"Old songs usually are. People confuse age with quality."
Dandelion looked offended. "On behalf of songs, I object selectively."
I picked up Ilyra's note. Destabilizing association with Her Highness's private history. The words sat there with clean boots. "They are already using her around me."
"Yes," Yennefer said.
"Then I should not meet her."
Geralt's head came up.
That was the wrong thing to say, perhaps. It was also what fear had written under my ribs.
"If I stay away, they have less to connect."
Yennefer looked at me as if I had just failed an examination in a subject she considered basic. "They already connected you. Absence will not unwrite the page."
"It may slow the next one."
"It may let the next one speak first."
Triss softened it. "Jack, this is not you bringing danger to Ciri. This is danger using your absence as another silence."
I looked at Geralt. "You agree?"
He did not answer quickly. Good. Quick answers near old guilt are usually dressed for a funeral.

"I hid you from her once because I thought distance made fewer trails," he said. "It made a different trail. I don't know the clean answer. I know I don't want the first words she sees to be bloodline custody."
The room waited.
I hated that too many people were right.
"Then north," I said.
Dandelion exhaled. "Splendid. Terrifying, but splendid. I will pack three cloaks and four excuses."
"No," Yennefer said.
Dandelion placed one hand over his heart. "Madam, I have followed Geralt into worse with less preparation and better boots."
"You stay in Novigrad."
His theatrical injury faded into real anger. "Songs move with me."
"Songs move faster when you stay where they can multiply," Priscilla said.
He turned to her. "You too?"
"I especially. If you leave, the city gets only Black Ink's verses and whatever your vanity can shout from a horse. If you stay, we can keep cutting the chain in public before it locks."
Zoltan nodded. "And I need the bard's debts. They open doors my axe would only close permanently."
"My debts have become strategic assets," Dandelion said. "I feel seen and insulted."
"Good," Zoltan said. "Efficient feelings."

The splitting took shape because it had to. Geralt and I would ride north with Yennefer's route and Asha's verse. Yennefer would move ahead and sideways, because she had safer ways to arrive dangerously. Triss would hold the courier lines until Ilyra's answer came. Zoltan and Dandelion would keep the songs ugly enough to resist holiness. Priscilla would collect witness language before it cooled into official memory. Asha would come partway, then east when the northern meeting was arranged.
I disliked every part of the plan.
Plans that do not offend anyone usually belong to the enemy.
Geralt wrote to Ciri in the back room while the Chameleon made noise below.

I did not read over his shoulder. Not at first. I stood by the window and watched rain turn the alley black. Buck was below under the awning, harassing a barrel with his teeth because no one had provided a better enemy. Dandelion's singers practiced the chain line two streets away. A child corrected the meter. Novigrad was becoming involved despite itself.
"Read it," Geralt said.
I turned.
The letter was short.
Ciri,

I should have told you about Jack years ago. Vesemir meant to. I did not. We believed two hunted children near each other would draw every predator with a map. We were not entirely wrong. We were not right.

There is more. Too much for courier paper and too dangerous for court hands. Black Ink, or people using that language, are turning him into public risk, bloodline custody, and useful infrastructure. They have begun to use your name around his. That is why I am writing now instead of waiting for courage to improve.
Come as yourself if you can. Come north if you cannot. Trust Ilyra's dullest packet. It will be the real one.
Geralt.
He had not written love. He did not need to. The places men omit words tell you which ones they fear mishandling.
"Add one thing," I said.
He gave me the quill.
I did not take it. "Tell her I am not asking anything of her."
Geralt's mouth tightened. "That is asking."
"No. It is refusing."
"Same family."
I hated him for being right. Not much. Enough.
"Then write that I don't want to become another burden placed in her hands by people who love her."
Geralt's expression changed with the pain of an accurate cut. "Then don't be. Be a man with his own trouble. She respects that more than burdens."
"That advice?"
"Maybe."
"Needs work."
"I know."
He wrote one line.
Jack comes with trouble of his own and no claim on yours.
That was not perfect. Perfect would have been suspicious. I let it stand.
Yennefer read the line and made no correction. That was how I knew it had weight. She corrected breathing if it threatened strategy.
"Ilyra will carry the outer packet," she said.
The name meant nothing to me. It meant something to Geralt. His shoulders changed by half a thought.
"She is in Ciri's circle?" I asked.
"Near it," Yennefer said. "Not close enough to invite poetry. Close enough to know which dull papers survive court inspection."
"A spy."
"An intelligent woman with employment," Yennefer replied. "Try not to flatten people only because they are useful. You dislike the courtesy when it is done to you."
Fair hit. I let it stand.

Triss spread three copies on the table, each safer and duller than the last. The first told too much and would be burned. The second hid my name under description. The third was so boring that even danger seemed to yawn. That one would travel farthest.
"Court hands love dullness," Triss said. "They think it proves loyalty."
"And if Ilyra is turned?" Geralt asked.

Yennefer's eyes did not move from the page. "Then the first two routes poison each other and the third becomes a laundry account until Ciri asks why a laundress near Novigrad is billing for wolf-hide thread."
Dandelion leaned in. "That is either genius or a cry for help from the art of correspondence."
"Both," Zoltan said. "Most useful things are."

Asha listened without admiring any of it. That made her valuable. Northerners around paper sometimes began to worship cleverness after surviving stupidity. Asha looked at the copies and saw only routes where hands might close.
"Does Ciri choose after reading?" she asked.
Yennefer looked up. "Yes."
"Not Geralt? Not you? Not empire?"
The room sharpened.
"Ciri chooses," Geralt said.
Asha held his gaze. "You said distance protected her once."
"I did."
"You were not entirely wrong. You were not right."
The words were his letter thrown back without cruelty. He accepted them because there was nothing else to do with truth when it returned wearing another voice.
"She chooses," he said again.
No one called it an oath, but it held.

By dusk, Zoltan had corrected documents, Yennefer had frightened couriers into competence, Triss had hidden copies in places no sensible search would begin, Priscilla had gathered statements, and Asha had bought dried fruit, lamp oil, and a knife from a woman who tried to overcharge her until Asha smiled without warmth.
I went to the stable alone before leaving.

Mara's memory found me there because leaving had become its own scent: leather oil, wet wool, packed food, horse sweat, rain on stone. She had told me I could leave because I put the horse, the exits, the coin, the wound, and the road in order before the thing that mattered. I had thought that unfair then. Accurate things often are.
Buck nudged my shoulder.
"I know," I said.
He did not. He knew oats, weather, nerves, and the difference between a safe hand and a false one. That was enough.
Asha found me at the stall.
"You are afraid of Ciri," she said.
"That your gift? Making rooms worse?"
"No. Making doors visible."
"I am not afraid of her."
Asha waited.
I sighed. "Fine. I am afraid of what people will do with both of us in the same sentence."
"Better."
"Still not your business."
"It is if your fear sends you east before the north is warned."

That angered me because it touched the plan I had not admitted making: leave before the meeting, take the road east alone, find the origin before Ciri's name came close, and make distance do the work again.
A familiar cowardice. Inherited, perhaps.
"You would stop me?" I asked.
"No."
That surprised me.

Asha looked at Buck. "I would follow until the first river. Geralt would follow longer. Yennefer would appear ahead and call you foolish in three languages. Triss would send the letter anyway. Zoltan would complain about wasted permits. Dandelion would write something unbearable. You would discover distance does not make you free of love or danger, only late."
Buck chewed hay as if this were obvious.
"I dislike your list."
"It dislikes you too."
At the gate, farewells kept trying to become scenes. Dandelion tried to embrace me, reconsidered after looking at Buck, and settled for a bow that used too much elbow.
"If you hear a song improving," he said, "assume I survived."
"And if it worsens?"
"Assume I was kidnapped by amateurs."

Priscilla took my unburned hand with stage grace and private seriousness. "They will try to make you only symbol. Resist by being inconveniently specific. Names. Places. People. Receipts. Bad stew. Horses with opinions. Specificity saves what slogans eat."
"You always talk like that?"
"Only when men are about to become legends against their will."
Zoltan clasped my forearm. "Do not die before I finish tracing the freight account. It is rude to creditors."
"I owe you?"
"Everyone owes me eventually. I am patient."
Triss came last among those staying. She checked my bandage because useful tasks could carry what words could not. "The branching has slowed."
"Good."
"That is not the same as safe."
"Nothing good is."
"Too neat," she said.
"Sorry."

"No, you are not." She tied the bandage tighter. "Better. Now listen. If the mark heats near running water, stop. If the necklace cools without visible pressure, make Geralt stop too. If Asha says a song is a map, assume she means that literally enough to be annoying. And if Yennefer says she is only going ahead to observe, she is lying in the helpful direction."
Yennefer, already mounted near the far side of the yard, did not turn. "I heard that."
"I know," Triss said.
Geralt looked between them and found something in the exchange too old to touch.

We rode out under rain that had stopped pretending to be dramatic and settled into irritation. It turned the road into brown paste and made the guards at the gate unpleasant because discomfort loves company. Zoltan's permits worked. The youngest guard read them three times because correct papers offended his instincts. Yennefer solved the delay by asking him to spell his superior's name for a complaint. His literacy failed him at once.
Outside the city, the road opened north.

Open is a generous word for a road that began with mud, a broken shrine, and three separate places where men had stood recently pretending not to wait. Zoltan's permits got us through the first gate. Yennefer's absence got us through the second, because the guard who might have objected had spent the previous quarter hour trying to remember whether he had always intended to inspect a hay wagon facing the wrong direction. Magic, used tastefully, resembles bureaucracy done faster.
At the third mile marker, we found the first Black Ink correction nailed to a tree.
Not a notice. A correction. Someone had taken one of Dandelion's fresh street sheets and amended it in red pencil.
WISE HANDS LIKE OTHER MEN'S LOCKS had become WISE HANDS GUARD DANGEROUS LOCKS.
Below it, in a rougher hand, someone else had written, THEN SHOW YOUR HANDS.
Dandelion was not with us to admire the reply. I tore the sheet down and handed it to Geralt. He read both lines, then folded it instead of burning it.
"Evidence?" I asked.
"Morale."
"Yours?"
"Maybe."

Asha rode behind us on a narrow gray mare that looked as if it had once survived a siege by judging everyone involved. She studied the tree, the road, the distant line of hills. "The correction came from ahead. The answer came from behind."
"Meaning?"
"The city is following. Not with feet. With breath."

That should have sounded like another old-song sentence. Instead it felt practical. Behind us, Novigrad was chewing on the language Black Ink had tried to feed it. Ahead, Ciri waited. East, if Asha's verse told true, water and names waited under a hotter sky.
I had wanted a clean road once.
The wish seemed childish now. Clean roads are swept by people who decide what dirt must vanish. Mud, at least, remembers who stepped where.
Geralt rode beside me. Asha behind. Yennefer was gone before the first bend, which meant either she had taken a side road or the world had wisely given her room.
"About Ciri," Geralt said.
"No."
"I hadn't asked."
"You were about to."
"Was I?"
"Yes."
"Annoying."
"You taught me."
He looked almost pleased and almost sorry. Geralt's face had poor manners that way.
The rain stopped near dark. Trees dripped. A nightjar called once and fell silent. Buck lifted his head, listening. The ring in my pocket cooled, not warning exactly. Recognition. Distance closing.
North for witness.
East for water.

The words did not come from me alone. They came from Asha's verse, Vesemir's page, Black Ink's files, Ciri's approaching letter, the dead who had waited too long for names, and the living who had become inconvenient enough to matter.
I rode beside Geralt until darkness took the road's edges.
Extract from a sealed memorandum carried under the name Ilyra Sarn, copied in a cipher Triss Merigold considered serviceable and Yennefer of Vengerberg considered optimistic:
To my principal,

The language is familiar enough that I dislike writing it down. A hidden Wolf School witcher, name withheld in outer channels but recoverable through Geralt of Rivia's recent movement, has become the center of overlapping administrative, magical, and rumor operations. Current hostile descriptors include host suitability, bloodline custody, hereditary infrastructure, voluntary cooperation preferred, public-risk anomaly, and public chain. I know you will notice the shape of the crime before I describe it.

He is not reported to have attacked civilians. Repeated accounts, including hostile ones, show him moving toward civilian danger even when that danger appears staged to produce a record against him. This does not make him harmless. It makes the people writing harmlessness and danger into legal costumes more dangerous.

Geralt is involved. Yennefer is involved. Triss Merigold is involved. The bard is involved, which means the songs are already either a problem or a weapon, depending on the hour. A Zerrikanian survivor has entered the matter and has spoken names I will not commit to open paper.
You once told me that the first sign of a cage is not iron, but people lowering their voices and calling it necessary.
They are lowering their voices now.
I await your decision.
Signed: I.S.

The memorandum traveled under three wrong names, through a courier who thought he carried theater gossip, a priest who believed he carried a list of orphan stipends, and a laundress who knew perfectly well she carried trouble and charged accordingly. By the time it neared Ciri's hands, the outer papers had become boring, which let them survive inspection. That was Triss's gift, Yennefer's suspicion, and Zoltan's contempt for official curiosity working in one narrow packet.
It did not make the facts safe.
It only made them arrive before the lie could sit down first.

part_subtitle: Blood is only destiny when someone else needs a leash.

paragraphs: Extract from an unsigned transitional memorandum delivered to the imperial apartments at dawn:

Her Highness is not to be burdened with technical irregularities unless such irregularities threaten succession optics, mage safety, or the stability of northern settlement language. Her Highness is, however, to be reassured that all matters touching anomalous bloodlines are being handled with appropriate discretion.
Ciri read the word reassured twice and decided the writer had never survived being reassured by powerful men.

She told me that story later, after the rain, the dead mill, the draconids, the dragon, and the night everyone pretended not to understand what had changed. She told it flat. That meant fear had been folded and kept.

She had been in Vizima at a black lacquered table that probably cost more than three villages and fed fewer people. Ilyra Sarn stood across from her with a leather case, sober dress, still hands, and the sharp calm of a woman who arrived before lies became official.

Ciri had been given twelve documents. Seven were meant to reassure. Three were meant to delay. One was meant to confuse the difference between safety and custody. The last was Geralt's letter, written in a hand that still looked as if it distrusted paper for not being a whetstone.
I did not see the letter until much later. I did not need to. Geralt writes like he fights when someone he loves is watching: short, direct, and more frightened than he permits the words to admit.
Ciri,
This is political. It is also personal. Continue if it remains political. If it becomes both, remember that the world will use whichever answer costs you more.
G.
"He is improving," Ilyra had said, or so Ciri claimed.
"No," Ciri had answered. "He is becoming harder to hate efficiently. There is a difference."
I liked that line when she told me. I disliked how much.

Ilyra did not smile after that. Ciri remembered that too. The woman had the kind of face court functionaries called severe when they meant inconvenient. She opened the leather case and arranged the documents into four piles with such neatness that the table seemed to develop rank under her hands.
"This pile delays you," Ilyra said. "This pile frightens you. This pile flatters your sense of duty. This one insults your intelligence while wearing the other three as gloves."
Ciri looked at the smallest pile. "You have been busy."
"Your enemies have been generous. They mistake volume for persuasion. It is a common imperial illness."

Outside the windows, Vizima moved in polished layers: boots on marble, wheels over wet stone, servants carrying trays no one looked at, officers lowering voices as they passed doors they wanted to own. Palaces have their own weather. It smells of wax, wine, clean linen, and people waiting for permission to become knives.

Ciri took up the document with the phrase technical irregularities. She read the first page, then the second, then stopped at a line advising that royal attention should be conserved for matters of direct dynastic impact.
"Conserved," she said.
Ilyra waited.
"Like grain," Ciri said. "Or candle wax. Or soldiers."
"A generous reading."
"No. I am done being generous with men who ration my own knowledge back to me and call it protection." She placed the page down. "Who has seen these?"

"The outer summaries passed through two imperial clerks, one Nilfgaardian liaison, one northern settlement office, and a scribe attached to Veyrane's review chain. Geralt's letter came through the theater route, which means it passed by a singer, a laundress, two barrels of salted herring, and a boy who believed he was delivering stage gossip."
"Safer company."
"Infinitely. Herring rarely informs on principle."
Ciri looked at Geralt's letter again. Political. Personal. The words had the weight of a man who had spent his life mistrusting both and was now asking her to carry them without dropping either.
"Does Emhyr know?"

Ilyra's answer arrived too late to be simple. "He knows there is a matter. He does not yet know there is a man at its center, unless someone has decided the man is useful enough to mention upward. The memorandum language is careful. Too careful. It keeps Your Highness removed while preserving the right to claim you were protected."
"Protected from a choice."
"Yes."

Ciri stood and went to the window. Rain made the palace courtyard shine like black lacquer. Two guards below moved aside for a courtier with a red portfolio. One of them glanced up and then away too quickly.
"They are watching whether I react," she said.
"Yes."
"Then we give them a reaction worth keeping."
"Define worth."

"Boring. Official. Irritating." Ciri returned to the table and pulled a blank sheet from the case. "Draft an order for an inspection of grain restitution along the northern route. Put my seal on the version that takes three attendants, two clerks, and enough noise to make every observer sleepy. Then draft a second order sending me to a chapel review west of the city. Make that one leak."
Ilyra took out a pen. "And the true route?"
"Not on paper."
"Good. I dislike writing useful things down."
"You write everything down."
"I write what I want the next thief to misunderstand." Ilyra's pen paused above the page. "Your Highness, there is one more matter."
"There usually is."

"If you go, you go as yourself. Not as courier, not as message, not as emergency daughter sent to steady Geralt, not as imperial witness. If the witcher has become the place where the crime gathers, your presence will be interpreted before you speak."

Ciri did not answer at once. She set Geralt's letter down with the edges aligned too precisely, then ruined the precision by pressing one thumb over the old scar near her wrist. She had told me later that no one in Vizima needed to say Elder Blood for the room to remember it. Courts had a way of leaving certain words unsaid and still making every chair face them.

For three breaths she only watched the rain on the glass. Her breathing stayed even because Ciri had learned young that panic became more expensive when witnesses could itemize it. The first men who wanted her blood had used prophecy. Later ones used empire, succession, treaty, safety, and maternal concern borrowed without permission. Different gloves. Same reaching hand.

When she turned back from the window, Ilyra had already noticed the scar, the letter, the controlled breath, and the fact that Ciri had not asked whether this crimson witcher deserved help. She asked the better question: what the room would do to him if she arrived too late.
Ciri almost laughed. "That has been true since I was ten."
"Yes. But this time the interpretation may be used to trap him as well as you."
That was the line that stayed with her. She told me later she hated it because it gave fear good grammar. Fear with good grammar has always been harder to dismiss.
She took Geralt's letter and folded it once, then again, along the original crease. "Then I speak before interpretation settles."
"To whom?"
"To him first. To the rest if they forget."
Ilyra inclined her head. "A dangerous order."
"No. A private one. People keep confusing those because privacy gives them fewer handles."

By the time Ciri left Vizima, three false routes had become tedious enough to survive scrutiny, two officials had congratulated themselves for delaying a matter already riding away, and one guard below the courtyard window had reported that Her Highness appeared calm.
The report was accurate enough to fail.

By the time Ciri reached us, we had chosen a dead mill because living houses had owners, neighbors, and witnesses who learned faster than facts. It stood two miles east of the road in a hollow where the stream had forgotten its direction and the wheel had rotted into a circle of bad ideas. Rain worried the roof. Wind moved through the boards. Buck approved only after biting a beam and finding it sufficiently unimpressed.

Geralt had gone outside to check the slope for tracks. Asha sat by the hearth with her bone charm in one hand and her knife within reach of the other. Yennefer had burned one listening charm from the rafters and was hunting for a second with personal contempt. I stood near the door because doors tell better truths than tables.
The necklace at my throat cooled before the horses arrived.

Not the sharp cold of danger. Not the dragging weight that pulled east. This was recognition, or the nearest thing metal can perform without deserving to be called alive. I put a hand over it. The barbed star lay still beneath my shirt, patient as a debt.
"Company," I said.
Asha looked up. "Title or person?"
"Both, probably."

Geralt returned first from the rain, mud on one knee and water in his hair, wearing the careful face of a man trying to stand between his past and the door without appearing to block either. Behind him came Yennefer, because emotional danger offended her only when she was too far away to strike it. Then a rider in a dark cloak dismounted under the dead willow.

Ciri did not arrive like a princess. That would have been easier. Princesses announce themselves with banners, escorts, and enough perfume to warn honest animals. Ciri arrived wet, tired, mud-spattered, and too still in the saddle. Her hair had been pinned beneath the hood and was escaping at the temples in pale strands. A sword hung at her side. Another weapon, harder to see and less forgiving, sat in the way she looked at the mill before looking at any of us.
Buck saw her and did not bare his teeth.
That was either a compliment or a lapse in security. With Buck, the distinction usually charged by the hour.
I opened the door before anyone could turn the moment into ceremony.
"Jack Morningstar," she said.
"Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon."
Geralt's face tightened at the full name. Yennefer's eyes sharpened. Ciri almost smiled.
"That is a great deal of name to use in a wet mill," she said.
"I wanted to see which one made you angry."
"All of them, depending on mouth and hour."
"Useful."
Her expression changed. The word had been mine too often and too carelessly. "No," she said. "Not that word. Not with me."

I felt the rebuke before I understood it. Not because it was loud. Because it was clean. Ciri had been described by everyone around me as a risk, a crown, a daughter, a bloodline, a sovereign-in-waiting, an old danger wearing a living face. One careless word from me had reached for the same shelf.

The word sat between us like a tool I had taken from the wrong table. I had meant it as respect. That made it worse, not better. Courts made people useful before they made them obedient. Mages made blood useful before calling the body optional. Black Ink had done it with cleaner ink and worse manners. I had reached for the same shelf because it was near, familiar, and sharpened by habit.

A proper man might have apologized beautifully. I distrusted proper men and beautiful apologies in equal measure. I moved my hand from the doorframe instead, giving her the room by inches rather than sentence. Ciri saw the correction. She did not reward it. That helped. Rewards make men think basic decency has become an achievement.
"Fair," I said.
The answer did not earn warmth. It earned permission to continue breathing in her presence. Considering the house she came from, that was probably generous.

We found the second listening charm under the threshold after everyone stepped inside. I should have seen it sooner. The wire ran beneath the plank and into a clay tube packed with powdered glass and something that smelled like boiled nettles. A rude little device. Not clever enough to kill, clever enough to blind whoever opened the door wrongly and make the witnesses describe panic as aggression.
Ciri noticed it a breath after I did.
"You missed that," she said.
I cut the wire. "Yes."
She watched me for the lie that did not come. "Good."
"Missing traps improves me?"
"Admitting it does."

Yennefer looked between us and made a small sound that might have been amusement if anyone else had owned the mouth. Geralt pretended to be busy with the latch. Asha, who distrusted every northern silence on principle, did not bother pretending.

We sat around a table that had lost one leg and gained three stones as compensation. Yennefer laid out copies. Asha placed Helena's ring beside them. Geralt set Vesemir's page down last, as if putting the dead man in the room required more care than drawing steel. Ciri read everything once without speaking. Then again. On the second pass she stopped at hereditary infrastructure and touched the paper with one fingertip, very lightly, as if filth could pass through ink.
"Who wrote this?"
"Black Ink's language," Yennefer said. "The hand varies. The appetite does not."
"Names."
"Sorel Veyrane appears in senior review. Merrow in field movement. Halbreck in medical advisories. Others."
"Emhyr?"
The room changed around the name. Not because anyone was surprised. Because saying a ruler's name aloud always reminds the walls they are weaker than documents.
"He knows a public-risk matter may intersect succession optics," Yennefer said. "He does not know enough to own it cleanly. Yet."
Ciri nodded once. "Then he will try to own the uncertainty first."
"Likely."
"And the North?"
Geralt answered. "Some will want you far from it. Some will want you near enough to make a claim. Some will want Jack dead because a corpse can't ask what category it belonged to."
"Some will want him alive," Ciri said, eyes on me, "because living keys are more useful than dead warnings."
The necklace cooled again.
I did not move. Moving would have made everyone look at my chest. Everyone already knew what hung there. Knowledge and looking are not the same. Looking has hands.
"Asha says my parents carried a seal route," I said. "Vesemir says Last Warden. Black Ink says host suitability. Every new word improves the cage and worsens the man."
Ciri looked at me then, not at my eyes first, which surprised me. She looked at my hands. The left was bandaged. The right rested near the table edge, not quite a fist.
"And what do you say?"
I had answers ready. Working answers. Witcher answers. Coin, road, contract, survival, no one's property, no one's holy fool. They crowded my mouth and became worthless there.
"I don't know," I said.
No one spoke. It was a fine silence. Uncomfortable, expensive, and too honest for the furniture.
Ciri accepted it with a small nod. "Then we begin there, before everyone else improves it."

She did not let uncertainty become fog. Ciri asked who had known, and the room answered in pieces: Vesemir had hidden me, Geralt had maintained the wall, Triss and Yennefer had learned late from sharpened documents, and Asha had searched for a child without knowing what man the child had become.

Ciri listened to all of it without forgiving anyone for the convenience of the meeting. Her face stayed calm. Her hand folded Geralt's letter once along the old crease, then once again, making a smaller square of his fear. "So everyone had reasons," she said. "Good. Reasons are not absolution. Continue."
So the first council began with Ciri choosing uncertainty before cleaner hands could name it for her.

The plan itself was less noble. Plans usually are. Ciri would not return to the imperial apartments immediately. Ilyra would make her absence appear official, then dull, which is the best disguise for dangerous movement. Yennefer would keep one path visible and take another. Geralt and I would ride with Asha and Ciri until the eastern pull became clearer. Triss would remain in the courier mesh long enough to spoil the next clean version of events. Dandelion and Zoltan, gods preserve us from useful friends, would keep the songs vulgar, contradictory, and too popular to correct quickly.
"Vulgarity as public defense," Ciri said.
"Dandelion has been training for this all his life," Geralt replied.
The almost-smile came easier then. It lasted only a moment, but the room needed it. Even Yennefer let it live.
Ciri did not let the smile become policy. The room behaved differently around her after that.

She pulled the rough map toward herself and weighted its corners with a knife, a cup, Helena's ring, and one of Geralt's stones from the hearth. A poor parliament, but honest in its materials. The roads across the vellum looked certain only because ink has always been arrogant. In truth the land between the mill and the eastern hills was full of failed bridges, bribed ferrymen, leftover patrols, hungry settlements, and people who would remember a white-haired man with crimson eyes better than they remembered their own taxes.
"We do not travel as a secret," Ciri said.
Geralt looked up. "Bad idea."
"No. Traveling as a secret is what lets everyone else own the explanation. We travel as something dull enough to pass and specific enough to resist correction."
Yennefer's eyes narrowed in reluctant approval. "Which is?"

"Inspection. Agricultural restitution, bridge repairs, and plague-road review. Ilyra already built the outer noise. A minor imperial matter with too much paperwork and too little glory. No one wants to volunteer for that unless paid."
"Ciri," Geralt said.
"No," she answered without looking at him. "If you are about to say this endangers me, begin again with the part where I was not already endangered."
His mouth closed.
That was the difference between recklessness and being finished with false shelter. Ciri did not look excited. She looked like someone who had counted the exits and found all of them watched.
Triss was not at the mill, but her influence arrived through folded notes and coded inventory lines. Yennefer read one, made a sound of approval she would deny under oath, and slid it to Ciri.
"Triss suggests the safest cover is a sanitation review," Yennefer said.
"Of course she does," Geralt muttered. "No one questions sewage."
"No one wise," I said.

Asha studied the map upside down and tapped the old road with one scarred finger. "Your sanitation lie crosses two places where the old route breathes close to the surface. That will not remain dull."
"Then dull gets us to the first breath," Ciri said. "After that we become honest quickly."
Ciri looked at me. "Can you ride in an inspection cloak without biting anyone?"
"Depends who calls me infrastructure."
"If someone calls you infrastructure, I will answer first."
"That sounds expensive."
"Most useful things are."
The word useful came back between us. This time she corrected it before it could grow hands: expensive to the people trying to buy us, not to us.
"Better," I said.
"Do not grade me."
"I was grading the sentence."
"It has my protection."

Geralt inspected the rain through a hole in the wall with suspicious urgency. Yennefer watched him with the expression of a woman hearing silent fatherhood from across a room. Asha placed Helena's ring back in the center of the map.
"Then decide who carries what," Asha said. "A route is not a promise until the hands are named."

That made the room practical again. Practical was mercy. Geralt took the forward scout rhythm and hated that Ciri noticed. Yennefer took counter-listening and false temperature marks. Asha took old-road signs and the duty of telling us when northern certainty became stupid near eastern ground. I took the visible risk because hiding me would turn every hedge into a witness.
Ciri took decisions because she refused to let anyone else take them from her while pretending rank was the reason.
Before we slept, she wrote one line for Ilyra and sealed it with a plain wax mark rather than a royal one.
Do not protect me from the facts by making yourself their owner.
She sanded the ink, folded the note, and looked at me when she caught me reading upside down.
"Witcher training?"
"Bad habit."
"Keep it. But do not pretend you did not read."
"I read."
"Good. Then understand it applies broadly."
I did not ask whether broadly included me. The answer had already found a chair.

Later, when rain thickened and the mill settled into the creaks of a place that had outlived profit, Ciri came outside while I checked Buck's tack for the third time. Checking tack is a respectable way to avoid emotion. Horses understand. People interfere.
