"He likes you," I said when Buck lowered his head toward her sleeve.
"He has excellent political instincts."
"He bit a taxman once."
"I said excellent."
Buck huffed into her glove. She did not flinch. The horse remembered that.

For a while we listened to the stream. Inside the mill, Geralt and Yennefer argued quietly, which meant neither had yet decided to be cruel. Asha sang under her breath in a language full of small stones. Ciri stood beside me with her hood down and rain silvering her hair.
"Geralt wrote that this was political and personal," she said.
"It is."
"He also wrote that if it became both, the world would use whichever answer cost me more."
"Sounds like him. Short enough to pretend it isn't fear."
She glanced at me. "You know him well enough to be unfair."
"He raised unfairness in me."
"He hid you from me."
The words had been waiting. I had heard them in every small pause since her arrival.
"Yes."
"Did you know?"
"No."
Ciri looked toward the mill door, where Geralt had left mud on the threshold like an apology he could not speak. "And who decided I should not know?"
"Vesemir first. Geralt after. Fear after that. Fear is good at forging signatures when no one wants to admit the hand moved."
She nodded once, too carefully. "Then do not say they protected me. Say they managed me. I may understand the first word later. I know the second now."
"Would you have wanted to?"
There. A trap without malice. The worst kind. Malicious traps at least tell you who set them.

"At twelve? I would have been furious that a girl with a famous destiny existed while I was still being told to hold a sword correctly. At sixteen? I would have resented you for being protected by the same silence that made me invisible. At twenty?"
"Yes?"
"I might have left before meeting you."
Her face did not change much. It did not need to. I had hit something and felt no victory in it.
"Because I was dangerous?" she asked.
"Because needing answers from someone who did not owe me any would have made me worse company than usual."
"You are not skilled at comfort."
"No."
"Good. I get enough practiced comfort from men who want me managed."

She looked back at the lit cracks in the mill door. For a moment I saw not title, not Elder Blood, not political hazard, but a woman tired of every love in her life arriving with a reason attached. I should have said something kind. I had several poor options and chose none fast enough.
"I don't know what I am to you," I said instead.
Ciri gave a short breath that was almost laughter and almost not. "That may be why it has not yet been ruined by certainty."
Inside, Geralt moved near the window and pretended not to watch the door.
Ciri saw him too. "He is impossible."
"Yes."
"He is also trying."
"Yes."
"Those two truths are not a defense."
"No. But they are a beginning."
She looked at me again. Rain slipped down her cheek and gathered at her jaw. "Careful, Jack Morningstar. You sound almost hopeful."
"I was aiming for exhausted."
"You missed."
That was the first time she smiled at me properly. Not kindly. Not safely. Properly.
I knew then, with the same dull certainty that tells a man a bridge will fall only after he has stepped onto it, that leaving would be harder now.
That did not make staying wise.
It only made wisdom less persuasive.
Private note, Ilyra Sarn to retained courier network, cipher-class low enough to be intercepted by the right enemies:

The principal has moved under self-command. Do not describe this as flight. Flight implies fear in charge. Fear is present, but not governing. Distribute two false routes, one imperial, one northern. Preserve the mill reference only in oral chain. If asked whether she rides for the witcher, answer that Her Highness rides for state necessity.

We left the dead mill before dawn, which is the hour chosen by fugitives, farmers, and people who dislike honest farewells. The road had softened overnight. Mud swallowed hoofprints and then reconsidered, leaving just enough trace to tempt a bad tracker into confidence. Geralt rode ahead until the mist took him. Yennefer vanished sideways. Asha moved beside me with her scarf high, watching the ditch instead of the horizon. Ciri rode under an inspection cloak so plain it became expensive by implication.
Buck hated the cloak.
"He knows I outrank it," Ciri said when the horse tried to bite the hem.
"He dislikes textiles with ambition."
"Then he will enjoy court."
"Buck would start a succession crisis before lunch."
"Good. Lunch is often dull."

We reached the first checkpoint near a broken bridge where two militia men, one clerk, and an old woman selling boiled turnips had established what they called civic review. Civic review meant a rope across the road, a table with one leg shorter than the others, and a list of names copied from three different offices by someone who had lost a fight with spelling.
The clerk looked at Ciri's papers. Then at Geralt returning from the fog. Then at my eyes.
Men rarely know which fear to serve first. It makes them slow.
"Inspection party," Ciri said.
"Yes, my lady, only there is a notice regarding unusual persons."
"Everyone is unusual before breakfast. Be specific."
The clerk's finger moved down the list and stopped at a description that had learned me badly: pale witcher, probable hazard, red ocular abnormality, relational contamination risk.
Ciri read it upside down. I watched the exact moment her patience died and became policy.
"Your rope is tied to a bridge support that will fail within a week," she said.
The clerk blinked. "My lady?"

"Your table lists three dead men as liable for road tax, your militia are standing downwind of a fever ditch, and that woman has been overcharged for turnip license twice because the office cannot distinguish cart from stall. Yet your concern is ocular abnormality."
The old turnip woman looked at Ciri as if witnessing a saint develop practical skills.
"I have instructions," the clerk said weakly.
"So do I." Ciri took the list, turned it over, and wrote across the back. "Temporary override. Inspection priority. Road structure, fever drainage, and unlawful duplicate market levy. Name of clerk?"
"Berrit, my lady."
"Berrit. If the bridge falls after I leave, I will remember you as the man who preferred eyes to engineering."
Geralt made a small sound behind me. It might have been pride choking on fear.
The rope came down.

As we rode through, the turnip woman handed Ciri one boiled turnip wrapped in cloth. Ciri accepted it with solemn dignity. The woman looked at me next and said, "You don't look so hazardous. Mostly tired."
"Common mistake."
"Tired people are dangerous. They stop caring which rules were written by fools."
Ciri looked back at her. "You should run the checkpoint."
"I do," the old woman said. "They simply have not noticed."
We rode on before affection could become another witness.
Half a mile past the bridge, Yennefer appeared from the trees and fell in beside us.
"Well?" Ciri asked.
"One watcher in the ditch. He left when you began auditing the turnips."
"Good."
"You turned a checkpoint into a complaint office."
"Better than turning it into a tribunal."
Yennefer considered that and did not disagree. Coming from her, silence could be a signed medal.

By noon, the false inspection had become real in three villages. That was Ciri's trick. She did not wear power as ornament. She used it like a knife to cut ropes everyone else had learned to step over. A bridge got marked unsafe. A fever ditch was ordered filled. Two children were removed from a toll clerk's debt list because Ciri asked why a six-year-old owed arrears to a crown that had changed twice since she was born.
I watched all of it and understood something late.

Ciri's political agency was not separate from danger. It was one of the ways she fought. And every time she used it near me, the world gained another line it could twist into motive, influence, impropriety, contamination, attachment, leverage.
The realization made me want distance.
Ciri caught the want on my face before I found a useful lie to cover it.
"Later," she said. "Do not leave over a thought. At least wait until it becomes a plan I can insult properly."
I almost smiled.
That was dangerous too.
I let the next village fall behind us, then nudged Buck ahead under the excuse of checking the road bend.

It was not a bad excuse. That annoyed me. A narrow lane ran between two fever ditches and a stand of alder thick enough to hide a patient man with a crossbow. Geralt had already checked it, which made my version of strategy thin in the middle, but pride has worn worse disguises.
Ciri caught up before the bend.
"Your horse walks like a confession," she said.
Buck flattened one ear. I chose not to translate.
"Forward scout," I said.
"Geralt is forward scout."
"Second opinion."
"No. Distance."
The word landed too cleanly. I kept my eyes on the road. "Every time you use authority near me, someone gets another line. Influence. Impropriety. Contamination. If I ride ahead, the line weakens."
"How considerate of the line."
"Ciri."
She drew her gelding level with Buck and made the road narrower by existing in it. "You do not get to call abandonment prudence because men with ledgers might describe my choices badly."
The sentence was not loud. It did not need volume. It had been forged somewhere older than this road, in rooms where people lowered their voices and called it protection.
"I am trying to keep you from becoming evidence," I said.

"I have been evidence since I was a child. Blood evidence. Succession evidence. Prophecy evidence. Geralt's failure, Yennefer's daughter, Emhyr's heir, the North's excuse. Silence did not protect me from being used. It only made the first explanation belong to someone else."
That should have given me an answer. It removed several.

Behind us, Asha slowed her mare. Not close enough to interfere. Close enough to witness. Yennefer had vanished again, which meant she was probably hearing all of it and would deny enjoying the accuracy later. Geralt remained ahead, too far to rescue either of us from the conversation, which was perhaps his most useful action of the day.
"If they connect us," I said, "they will use it."
"They already have. That is not permission for you to manage me by absence."
"Absence is sometimes safer."
"For whom?"
I did not answer quickly enough.
Ciri nodded once, as if the silence had signed its name. "There. Not for me. For your fear. You would rather leave me with a cleaner report than stand beside me while I choose an ugly one."
The road bent through alder shade. Wet leaves brushed my shoulder. Buck, traitor that he was, slowed without command.

"I am not asking you to be careless," she said. "I am telling you I will not be protected into ignorance, distance, or obedience because someone else may miswrite the page. If danger comes from my choice, then I carry the choice. Not you. Not Geralt. Not the report."
"And if my presence costs you?"
"Then I will know the price before I pay it."
She turned her horse ahead of mine and took the bend first. Not recklessly. Deliberately, sword hand loose, cloak plain, posture steady as a verdict.
I did not win the argument.
That was becoming a pattern.
Worse, it was improving me.

chapters.chapter_title: THE WOMAN WHO WATCHES TOO STILL
paragraphs: The country had begun misbehaving before it offered us a corpse polite enough to examine.

Crows left the ridge in a black rope at dawn and did not settle again. A fox crossed the road ahead of us, stopped at a rain-filled rut, and backed away from its own reflection with its teeth showing. The stream below the pines ran clear over stone, but every frog along it had gone silent at once, as if a hand had closed around the throat of the morning. Geralt noticed the silence. Ciri noticed Geralt noticing. Yennefer noticed both and looked angrier at nature for becoming legible without her permission.

The wolf medallion gave only small complaints, the ordinary shiver of monster residue somewhere near and wrong. The barbed star under my shirt did something colder. It did not warn. It recognized. My palm stayed quiet until the road bent east, and then heat gathered under the bandage like a muscle preparing before I had agreed to lift anything.
The first draconid lay in the road with its throat closed from the inside.

I found it after dawn where the lane rose toward a ridge of bare stones and pine roots. It had been a forktail once, young enough to be stupid and old enough to make stupidity expensive. Gray-green scales. Torn wing membranes. Claws dug four trenches into the mud, each trench pointing south, as if the body had tried to flee after the throat had already refused air.
Buck stopped ten paces away and gave me an opinion with both ears.
"Noted," I said.

Roach came closer because Roach considered fear something to be endured privately. Ciri's gelding trembled but obeyed. Asha's mare ignored the corpse and watched the trees. That was the horse I trusted most in that moment. Dead things rarely kill a man twice. Living watchers try harder.
Geralt crouched by the head. "Poison?"
"No bait smell," I said. "No wolfsbane. No alder resin. No rot sweetener."
Yennefer knelt without letting her skirt touch the mud, a skill I respected against my will. "Heat pulled inward. Tissue cooked where it should have cooled."
"Disease?" Ciri asked.
"Not one that respects nature."

Asha stood behind us with her scarf pulled over the burn scars along her jaw. Wind moved through the pines and carried a scent like hot stone under old rain. Her eyes had narrowed before the rest of us finished being clever.
"Scales feel pressure first," she said. "People write about it after the bodies make a road for them."
"From where?" Geralt asked.
Asha pointed east.

The road had been telling us before the corpses learned to speak. A trough in the last village had shown every horse a different moon at noon. Two goats had refused their own shadows and broken their necks against a fence rather than cross the yard. A woman selling eggs told Geralt, without knowing why she whispered, that her youngest had dreamed the same black word three nights running and woken with the taste of hot stone in his mouth. None of it was proof. Proof is usually what danger becomes after it has finished being useful.
Of course she did.

The necklace at my throat had been pulling that way since before dawn, lighter when I faced the line of hills, heavier when I turned away. It was not dramatic. Dramatic artifacts are made for bards and fools. This one preferred the practical cruelty of being right.
Ciri watched my hand move toward my collar and then stop.
"You don't have to hide it," she said.
"Habit."
"Habits can be trained badly."
"So can princesses."
Her mouth tightened. "Careful."
"I said can."
"Better. Not good."
Geralt made a noise that would have become advice if Yennefer had not looked at him. The noise died with dignity.

I examined the forktail's tongue. It had split along a line too straight for sickness. Black saliva dried between the teeth. The wolf medallion trembled, stopped, trembled again. My left palm warmed beneath the bandage, not much. Enough to remind me my body had opinions it did not ask me to approve.

That was the pattern beginning to separate. The medallion disliked the corpse because monster residue had been taught bad habits. The barbed star answered the crescent burn because something older than the corpse had touched it. My palm warmed only when the two began pointing at me. Recognition was not command. Not yet.
The throat had not been crushed. It had obeyed something else.

I should have stepped back then. That is easy to say later. Later is full of men who would have done everything better while dry and unbitten. I leaned closer because the corpse had a crescent burn at the back of the jaw, and because pattern is a hook for men trained to survive by noticing too much.
The corpse inhaled.

Not properly. No lungs, no life, no magic bright enough to name. The throat opened with a wet click and black air rushed inward from the road, pulling leaves, grit, and the loose end of my bandage toward the mouth. My medallion jerked against my chest. Buck screamed. Geralt shouted my name. I moved too late.
The forktail's head snapped upward.

Dead jaws do not need strength if something else is using them. Teeth closed on my sleeve. Pain flashed up my forearm. I drove my knife under the hinge and hit bone that should not have held. Ciri moved before Geralt did, because she was closer and because she had not yet learned the bad habit of waiting for someone older to be first. Her boot came down on the snout with enough force to drive the teeth apart. I pulled free and rolled back through mud as the corpse convulsed.
Yennefer's spell cut the air into a white line. The head froze. Asha flung ash from her bone charm into the mouth and spoke three hard words. The black inward pull broke.
The corpse sagged into the road.
My arm bled through the sleeve. Not badly. Badly would have been simpler. This was narrow, shallow, humiliating.
Ciri looked at the blood. "You moved toward it."
"I noticed."
"After I noticed."
I stood, too fast. "Do you want thanks?"
Her eyes hardened. "I want you to stop acting as if being helped is an insult."
The road went very quiet. Even the horses seemed to reconsider their involvement.
She was right. Worse, she was right in public.
"It bit me," I said.
"And yet your mouth works fine."
Asha laughed once. It sounded like a stone falling into a well.

Geralt found something to inspect on his sword. Yennefer watched Ciri with an expression too complex to survive naming. I cleaned my knife, because a man needs occupation when he has lost a small battle and everyone has seen the corpse.
"Thank you," I said.
Ciri inclined her head as if accepting tribute from a defeated province. "You are welcome."
"Don't enjoy it too much."
"Too late."

We burned the head separately. Yennefer insisted. The rest of the corpse would not catch properly until Asha cut three scales from the chest and laid them on stone away from the smoke. Each scale had a red thread beneath it, thin as a vein, pulsing once every seven breaths. Not blood. Not spell. Something between a memory and an instruction.
"Scale-sickness," Asha said.
Yennefer's eyes narrowed. "That is not a common classification."
"Because common people have the sense to run before naming it."
"Try being useful without making me dislike translation."

Asha gave her a look. "Old draconid pressure can be taught to lesser bodies. It makes them flee wrong directions, breathe wrong air, obey wrong hunger. If an anchor is nearby, the sick scale becomes a bell."
"Calling what?" Ciri asked.
Asha looked at me.
I hated the answer before she gave it.
"Keys," she said.
My palm warmed again.

The second corpse waited two miles farther east, in a slate hollow where rainwater gathered black in shallow pools. Basilisk. Larger than the forktail, older, and frightened enough before death to have dragged itself into water and held its own head under until something inside gave up. No creature does that unless pain has become a country with no roads out.
I crouched at the pool edge. My arm ached. The bite was already closing too quickly. Triss would have hated it if she had been there. The thought almost comforted me. I disliked that.
"It drowned itself," I said.
"Chose water," Asha corrected. "Not death."
"Important distinction to the basilisk?"
"To us. It means pressure came through air first."
Ciri stood beside me, close enough that I felt the shift of her cloak. Not touching. Not far. She had learned the exact cruelty of distance quickly.
"Can it spread to people?" she asked.
Yennefer answered before Asha could. "Not like fever. But resonance can be trained. Repeated exposure, blood contact, panic, old sites, wrong witnesses."
"Reports," I said.
She looked at me. "Yes. Reports. If someone knows what pressure events produce which symptoms, they can build occasions that teach the seal to respond."
"To me."
"Through you," Ciri said.
Geralt looked at her. The correction had come fast, almost angry. She did not look away.
"Through me," I said.
The basilisk's eye moved beneath the cloudy film.
I saw it too late again.
Not the eye. The pool.

Black water rose in a ring around the corpse, each drop lifting from the surface and hanging there, trembling. The red thread under the cut scales brightened. My medallion snapped hard against my chest. Buck tried to rear behind me. The necklace went cold enough to make the breath leave my lungs.

This time the order arrived clean enough to hate: medallion for residue, barbed star for old recognition, palm for the answer my body was preparing to give. The crimson pressure had not risen yet. It waited behind the ribs like a held breath, and the waiting frightened me more than fire would have.
The basilisk's dead mouth opened.
Something under the water spoke without sound.

My knees bent. Not by choice. The road, the pool, the dead throat, the scar at my palm, all of it lined up inside me. I reached for Aard and found no shape. Not fear exactly. Panic. The low animal kind that does not ask what a man believes about courage.

Geralt caught my shoulder from behind and hauled me back as Yennefer threw a ward over the pool. It shattered before it finished forming. Ciri drew steel and stepped between me and the corpse as if steel could cut pressure. Foolish. Brave. Often the same movement seen by different survivors.
"Move," I said.
"Stand first."
"Ciri."
"Stand."
I hated her then for half a heartbeat. Not for command. For witnessing the part of me that had obeyed the pull before I could make a clever sentence out of it.
I stood.

Asha cut her own thumb, spat blood into her palm, and flung it into the water. The drops fell all at once. The pool cracked white with cold. The basilisk collapsed into itself, not burned, not slain, simply emptied of whatever had borrowed it.
Silence returned with rain in it.
No one spoke until Buck shoved his head into my chest hard enough to hurt.
"I'm upright," I told him.
He pushed harder.
"Yes. Poorly."
Ciri wiped her sword, though it had touched nothing. Her hands were steady. Her face was not.
"You were going down," she said.
"Yes."
The word cost more than the wound.
"Do you know why?"
"No."
"Good."
I looked at her.
"Not good that you don't know," she said. "Good that you said no."
That almost made me smile. It failed on the way and became something else.
A voice came from the stones above us.
"He chose not to call fear obedience. First useful sign."
Every blade in the hollow came halfway out.

The woman stood on a fallen marker stone where no one had heard her arrive. Tall, dark-haired, plain cloak the color of dry bark, face too calm to belong to weather, hunger, or ordinary age. Her eyes were human if one looked quickly. If one did not, they held a depth like old gold kept under water.
Geralt lowered his sword first, but not all the way.
"Saesenthessis," he said.
Ciri's head turned. Yennefer's hand remained full of violet light. Asha bowed her head a fraction, not submission. Recognition between old injuries.

I had heard the name in stories. Dragons make poor rumors because men prefer wings and fire to intelligence. They leave out the stillness. They leave out how the world seems to wait for permission to continue when one looks at you properly.
"You are watching us," Yennefer said.
"Yes."
"For whom?"
"Myself. That is the only answer anyone should trust from a dragon."

"I followed pressure," Saesenthessis added, before Yennefer could cut another question out of the air. "Not prophecy. Not certainty. Forktail, basilisk, water that dislikes faces, children dreaming words too old for their mouths. I know old draconic sickness when it chooses a road. I did not know you."
"Comforting," I said.
Saesenthessis looked at me. "You are not owed comfort."
"Good. I would spend it badly."
Something almost amused moved behind her face. "Perhaps not entirely useless."
Ciri stepped beside me, not in front. I noticed. So did Geralt. So did Yennefer. There are many ways to draw a sword.

Saesenthessis looked at the dead basilisk, the frozen pool, my bandaged hand, then Ciri. "Hunger is the mouth that wants flesh. The lock is the old pressure around the seal. The call is the thread pulled through sick scale and witness. Invitation is the first tug. Training is what happens when fear teaches the lock to expect your answer. Black Ink has learned to arrange the tug."
"Name what is calling," Yennefer said.
"No."
"Because names have power?"
"Because humans use names like hooks. You catch a thing with them, then complain when it drags you into water."
I was tired, bleeding, embarrassed, and cold. This made me less diplomatic than usual, which was already a narrow road.
"If you know so much, why arrive after the corpse tries to drink my spine?"
Geralt closed his eyes briefly.
Saesenthessis regarded me with no visible offense, "Because I needed to know whether you would reach for power before help."

"Do not mistake the test for omniscience," she said. "I can read pressure. I can read old hunger. I cannot read a man until he chooses in front of me, and even then I may be wrong. Dragons are ancient, not excused from error."
"And if I had?"
"Then your friends would need a different plan."
"Do I get to know the plan?"
"When you stop thinking knowledge is the same as control."
Ciri made a small sound. It might have been sympathy. It might have been agreement. I resolved to resent both later.
Saesenthessis came down from the stone. The horses lowered their heads. Even Buck did, though he looked offended by his own body for recognizing royalty older than crowns.
The dragon in human shape stopped before me.

"You are not what Black Ink calls you. You are not what frightened songs call you. You are also not what the grieving wish to make of you. The difference will become important when someone asks you to die politely."
"Someone already has. In better paper."
"They will improve the phrasing. Humans always improve cruelty before abandoning it."
Asha spat into the moss. "She is not wrong."
"Then what do you want?" I asked.
Saesenthessis looked east. The hills there were gray under rain, patient and badly named on maps. "To test whether the last living lock is a man, a weapon, or a door pretending to be either."
My hand closed before I chose it.
Ciri saw. "And if he refuses your test?"
Saesenthessis turned her gaze to Ciri. "Then I will respect him more and trust the continent less."
That was not an answer. It was good enough to survive until supper.

We camped in a ruined shepherd house above the hollow. Saesenthessis sat on a wall and watched the fire dislike her. Asha set charms under the door. Geralt and Yennefer argued outside in low voices. Ciri sharpened her sword with strokes too even to be about the blade.
I took first watch because pride is a disease that learns new excuses every morning.
Saesenthessis came to the threshold after midnight.
"You are watching the wrong dark," she said.
"It was the only one available."
"No. You watch the road because enemies are easier than hunger."
I did not look at her. "Dragons speak too much for creatures famous for hoarding."
"Wisdom is easier to carry than gold. Less useful in taverns."

Inside, Ciri slept near the wall with one hand close to her sword. Sleep did not soften her so much as remove the court from her face. She looked younger. Not young. Younger. There was a difference men around her forgot whenever forgetting helped them decide for her.
Saesenthessis followed my glance.
"You are already turning affection into distance," she said.
"You confuse observation with confession."
"No. I distinguish badly concealed cowardice from strategy."
I looked at her then.

She did not smile. "The world will test whether you can be used. It will test whether she can be used through you. It will test whether Geralt's guilt can be used through both of you. You cannot prevent that by leaving. Distance is only a slower chain when the people holding it know your names."
"You sound like Asha."
"Asha survived me. Some of my sentences stuck."
"If you know so much about not owning people," I said, "why test me like property?"
For the first time, she paused.
The courtesy of that pause did more than any apology could have.

"Because the world is already testing whether you can be used," she said. "I need to know whether you will use yourself first. There is a difference between a man choosing sacrifice and a man addicted to being the tool that makes everyone else safe. The first may save. The second becomes an argument for anyone with a handle."
I looked at Ciri again. Her brow had tightened in a dream. Her hand moved once, searching for a sword that was already within reach.
"And if I cannot tell the difference?"
"Then pray someone who loves you can."
"I don't pray."
"Then make better friends."
She returned to the dark before I could find an answer good enough to insult her with.
I kept watch until dawn. When Ciri woke, I was looking away before she caught me looking.
Not fast enough.
Ciri caught me looking before breakfast and said nothing until the fire had been bullied back to life.
That restraint should have warned me. People who speak immediately usually want victory. People who wait until bread is warm often want accuracy.

Geralt had taken a strip of dried meat and was pretending not to monitor my bandage. Yennefer cleaned mud from one glove with the expression of a woman considering whether the glove had failed morally. Asha crushed bitter herbs into a cup for my arm. Saesenthessis sat outside the shepherd house on a broken stone, close enough to hear everything and far enough to claim patience as a species trait.
Ciri handed me the cup.
"Drink."
"Does everyone plan to command me before noon?"
"Only until you begin preserving yourself without supervision."
The herbs tasted like bark, metal, and someone's old grudge. I drank because refusing would have given the cup too much importance.
"You looked away," she said.
"Habit."
"No. That was not habit. That was you seeing me asleep and deciding tenderness had become evidence against me."
The cup stopped halfway down.
Asha looked into the fire. Geralt became very interested in dried meat. Yennefer's glove paused. Saesenthessis, outside, had the courtesy not to turn her head.
"You prefer accuracy early," I said.
"I prefer not having to chase your noble cowardice through three counties."
"It was a glance."
"It was a route beginning."
That landed because it was true enough to hurt.
Geralt spoke without looking up. "He's good at routes. Bad at reasons."
"You trained him," Ciri said.
"Didn't say I was proud of every result."
I should have been irritated. I was. Unfortunately, I was also warmed by it, which made irritation less clean.
Asha pushed the cup toward me again. "Finish. Then fight. Your northern arguments go stale when interrupted by medicine."
"Your medicine tastes like a failed forest," I said.
"It survived you. Show respect."
I finished the cup.

Only then did Saesenthessis speak from the threshold. "This is why affection matters to the test. Not because it makes you weak. Because you keep trying to solve its danger by making yourself absent. Absence is a crude form of control. Humans admire crude control when it wears self-denial."
"Do dragons ever say things people can thank them for?" I asked.
"Rarely. Gratitude makes humans inattentive."

Asha set her cup down. "The old sickness in draconids uses three hungers. Body hunger, territory hunger, and command hunger. Lesser beasts die when command hunger has no proper body to sit in. Greater beasts learn to speak through it. People like Black Ink have found the dead middle: make sick scales ring near an anchor, then watch who answers."
Yennefer's gaze sharpened. "You knew this before the basilisk."
"I suspected."
"And told us half."
Asha met her eyes. "I told you what would keep you moving without making the witcher decide he was the problem to be removed. You are not the only woman here who has learned management badly."
The room went still.

That was perhaps the first time Asha looked tired instead of hard. The difference mattered. Hardness is a shape made against pressure. Tiredness is what remains when pressure has been winning for years.
Saesenthessis looked at her, and for a moment the dragon's stillness did not seem proud. It seemed old.
"Asha carried names out of fire," she said. "Not all of them survived being carried. That makes truth arrive from her in portions. It is not kindness. It is damage trained to serve."
Asha's jaw tightened. "Do not make poetry of me."
"I was making a correction."
"Make it shorter."
"Very well. She is afraid you will become what her dead became: necessary after no one admitted they had choices left."
No one improved that sentence. Some truths arrive already armed.
Ciri sat beside me, close enough for her sleeve to brush mine. "Then we keep choices visible. All of them. Even the ugly ones. Especially those."
Saesenthessis inclined her head, once. "Better."
"Do not grade me before I have boots on."
"Then wear boots sooner."

For one breath, the shepherd house became almost ordinary: bad breakfast, wet gear, old arguments, people who cared enough to be unpleasant in useful directions. Then the eastern pull returned under my ribs, gentle as a hook placed by someone patient.
I stood.
Ciri stood with me.
This time I did not look away fast enough.
This time I did not try.
Dandelion's discarded lyric fragment, recovered later from a wine-stained notebook:

A wolf may wear the chain, or bite the hand, or run. But what of the wolf who lowers his teeth because the room is full of frightened children, and every man with a chain calls that proof he should be leashed?
Saesenthessis chose a place already ruined by people, which proved she understood the continent better than she admitted.

The old tannery stood at the edge of a village stripped after the last war: doors gone, wells fouled, roof beams stolen, the saint in the shrine carved up by knife practice. Behind the main building, flooded pits held rainwater, lime, rot, and blue-green scum that bubbled whenever the wind remembered it had somewhere else to be.
Buck stopped at the lane and refused to enter.
"He is wiser than the rest of you," Saesenthessis said.
"He knows," I replied.
"Good. Stay with him."
Buck gave me a look that suggested he would have preferred to be consulted before being assigned to dragon philosophy.
The rest of us walked in: Geralt, Yennefer, Ciri, Asha, Saesenthessis, and me. Enough dangerous people to frighten a small country, not enough to make an old tannery feel safe.
"This is the test?" Geralt asked.
"This is the bowl," Saesenthessis said. "The test is what enters it."
"I liked it better when dragons demanded riddles."
"You were younger and had better knees."
Yennefer walked the edge of the largest pit. "Draconid musk. Distilled."
Asha crouched near a cracked vial half-buried in ash. "Lured."
"Weaponized," Yennefer said.
Saesenthessis looked at her. "Weapon is a human compliment for fear with a handle. Lured is sufficient."
The dragon removed a clay vial from her sleeve and broke it on the threshold.

Scent moved before magic: musk, iron, hot stone, old blood, fruit left too long in a sealed room. It entered the back of my throat. My palm warmed. The necklace went light, then heavy. The dead pits answered with bubbles.
Ciri's hand went to her sword. Geralt's to his. Yennefer had a spell already forming between two fingers. Asha drew a curved knife and cut a line in the dirt with her heel.
"No Signs unless necessary," Saesenthessis said.
"Define necessary," I said.
"When not using one kills someone who did not choose the risk."
"Generous."
"Accurate."
The first thing that came was not a draconid.
It was a child.

A boy, perhaps nine, thin as a broom handle, barefoot in mud, holding a dead hen by the legs. He came from behind the broken dye shed and stopped when he saw us. His face had the empty look of children who have survived long enough to understand adults bring weather. Behind him, three more children crouched under the shed wall. One had a cough. One held a rusted pot. One had a knife made from a table hinge.
I looked at Saesenthessis.
She did not look surprised.
"Bowl," she had said.
"You knew they were here," Ciri said, and her voice went cold enough to cut water.
"I knew someone had used the tannery for shelter. I did not know if they remained."
"That is a distinction for scholars."
"No," Asha said. "For scouts. Scholars arrive after the bodies."
The boy lifted the dead hen as if it were proof of citizenship.
"We didn't take anything," he said.
I lowered my hands. "You took a hen."
"It was dead."
"Then it complained less than most owners."
"Where are your people?" Ciri asked.
The boy looked at her cloak, the sword, the white hair, the posture that belonged nowhere near a ruined tannery. He answered me instead. "Gone."
"Dead gone or road gone?" I asked.
His eyes flicked to the pits.
I took the answer.
The scent thickened.
Every bubble in the tannery pits stopped at once.
Geralt turned toward the far wall. "Move the children."
We were late by one breath.

Something hit the roof from above. Tiles exploded inward, wet and sharp. The first forktail dropped through the broken rafters and landed between the pits, wings half-spread, jaws wet with black saliva. Not dead. Sick. Its scales carried red threads beneath the surface, pulsing too fast. One eye rolled toward the children, the other toward me.
The second came through the yard wall low and fast.

Panic removed decoration. Ciri ran for the children. Geralt met the second forktail with silver. Yennefer threw a shield against roof tiles, rain, and buckling pressure. Asha dragged one child behind a broken vat. Saesenthessis stood very still.
Too still.
The first forktail lunged at me.
I drew steel by mistake.

That is the sort of thing songs leave out. Steel, not silver. Wrong sword. Wrong hand. The scent had filled my head with heat and old stone, and my body chose the blade closest to habit rather than the one closest to survival. The forktail's jaw hit my guard. Its weight drove me back into a pit rail. Rotten wood broke. My left boot slipped. Lime water swallowed my leg to the knee, cold through leather and then burning.
Teeth snapped near my face.
I tried to shift the blade. The creature hooked one claw into my shoulder strap and pulled. Pain crossed my chest. The barbed-star necklace slipped free and struck the air.
The forktail froze.
So did the second.
So did every child in the room.
The red threads under the scales brightened.
"Jack," Geralt said, too quiet.
Not warning. Not command. Prayer, maybe. He would have hated that.

The scent rushed toward me. Not wind. Want. I felt it in my mouth, copper and heat. The pit water shivered around my boot. My palm opened. Red lines under the skin answered. The forktail lowered its head by one finger-width.
Obedience.

It sickened me. It also came with a terrible ease: children behind me, Geralt under pressure, Ciri near the second beast, and power waiting in my hand like a knife already sharpened. I could have made the sick thing kneel.
The boy with the dead hen stared at me. His lips had gone white. He had seen men use fear before. Every child who lives in ruins has.
I let the sword fall.
For one breath, everyone thought I had lost.
The forktail moved.

I went under it, not with grace, with wet panic and a bad knee. Its teeth closed on empty air. I drove my shoulder into its wounded foreleg and shoved sideways, hard enough to send both of us toward the pit. Lime water splashed. It screamed and tried to climb over me. I got my right hand on the fallen steel, used the crossguard like a hook, and jammed it into the pulsing red line below its throat.
Not command. Pain.
The creature jerked away from the children. That was enough.
Ciri reached the boy and hauled him back. The hinge-knife child stabbed the air bravely in the wrong direction. Asha grabbed him by the collar and kept him alive through insult.

Geralt cut the second forktail across the wing joint, but the beast did not retreat. Sick creatures do not respect sensible injury. It drove him into a dye vat. The vat toppled, bursting old blue stain across the floor. Geralt hit hard. His silver skittered away.
Ciri saw it.
So did I.
She had a child under one arm and a sword in the other. She could not reach him without dropping the boy. For half a second, the room held too many necessities and not enough hands.
Yennefer's shield cracked.
Saesenthessis still had not moved.
Anger cleared the scent from my head better than magic.
"Are you testing him or us?" Ciri shouted at the dragon.
Saesenthessis looked at her, and something like approval moved there.
The second forktail reared over Geralt.

I threw my steel sword. It was still the wrong blade. It did not need to kill. It struck the beast's jaw and turned the head aside. Geralt rolled, found a knife, and drove it up under the softer scales near the throat. Asha followed with her curved blade, cutting the red vein beneath the left wing. The creature convulsed. Yennefer's spell finished it in a burst of violet heat that burned the sickness out before it could jump.
The first forktail came at me again.
This time I had no sword in hand and one boot half-eaten by lime.
Ciri threw me hers.
I caught it badly. The hilt slammed my injured palm. Pain went white up my arm. The red lines flared. For one dangerous instant the sick scales answered again, the creature slowing, head lowering.
"No," I said.
I do not know whether I spoke to the beast, myself, the old seal, or every clerk who would have liked to write that moment down.
I used Ciri's sword like a sword.
The blade went under the jaw, angled through wet heat, and came out behind the skull. The forktail's weight hit me chest-first and drove us both into the pit. Lime water closed over my head.

Cold. Burn. No air. My left hand trapped beneath scaled weight. My right still on Ciri's sword. The beast kicked once, twice. The red thread under its scales burst against my wrist. Heat spread through the water like blood in reverse.
I could not tell up from down.
Something grabbed the back of my collar.

Ciri and Geralt pulled me out together. I came up choking, half-blind from lime, one boot gone, hair plastered to my face, coughing tannery water in front of a dragon, a sorceress, an imperial heir, a Faithel survivor, four terrified children, and the man who had taught me to keep my footing.
I vomited on the ground.
The hinge-knife child said, "Is he dead?"
"Not yet," Ciri said.
"He looks dead."
"He often does," Geralt said.
I tried to tell them all to go to hell. What came out was water.

Yennefer cleaned my eye with a spell that hurt more than the lime. Asha gathered the children near the broken doorway and gave them dried fruit from a pouch that should not have held enough for four. Saesenthessis finally moved, stepping over the dead forktail to examine the cut where I had refused the red pressure.
"You chose the sword," she said.
I spat water. "I chose breathing. Badly."
"You chose not to own them."
"They were sick."
"Yes."
"And frightened."
"Yes."
"Then stop making it sound noble."

For once, the dragon did not answer with old patience. She looked at the children, the dead creatures, and the pits where men had once made rot into trade. "Nobility is what humans call a difficult choice after the blood is dry. I am naming it while it is still wet."
Ciri stood beside me with her empty scabbard at her hip.
"My sword," she said.
I looked at the blade still in my hand. It was slick with black blood and tannery filth. "Your balance is too forward."
"You are welcome."
"Thank you."
"Also, you owe me a cleaning."
"For the sword?"
She looked me over: lime, mud, blood, no boot, wounded arm, disgrace fully present. "For the world, eventually. But begin with the sword."
The children began laughing.
Not because it was funny enough. Because they were alive and laughter sometimes arrives wearing the wrong coat.
That saved me more than Saesenthessis's test did.

We burned the sick bodies with Yennefer's help and Asha's ash-words. The fire burned blue at first, then white, then ordinary orange once the red threads curled and died. The children watched from the lane. Ciri gave the oldest boy a coin and the dead hen back, because one should never interfere with a child's property rights after surviving a monster.
"There is a village west," Geralt told them. "Ask for Branka at the mill road. Tell her Geralt sent you."
"Will she feed us?" the boy asked.
"She will complain first," I said. "That means yes."
He looked at me, then at Ciri, then at the sword I was cleaning with increasingly poor results. "Are you the red wolf?"
I closed my eyes.
Ciri answered before I could. "He is the man who owes me a sword cleaning."
The boy considered that. "That's not as good."
"Good," she said. "Tell it that way."
He would not. We all knew it. Still, he left with the smaller children and the hen, and for a few moments the story had not yet outrun the fact.

We followed far enough to make sure no third sick thing had learned hunger from the first two. The oldest boy limped after the first mile because pride had kept a splinter in his foot. Ciri noticed with the efficiency of rank used properly.
"Sit," she said. He sat. Rank has many crimes. Occasionally it saves time.

She pulled the splinter with a hairpin. The boy watched her hands as if care without a price were another trick. When he asked whether princesses did feet, she said, "Lazy ones do not." When he asked whether witchers did, I told him only if the contract paid extra. Ciri elbowed my knee until I improved the answer under duress.

Yennefer gave the coughing girl a draught and lied badly about the taste. Asha gave them dried apples and one instruction: if men with clean boots asked about the tannery, say the roof fell, the birds screamed, and the horse was angry. All true. None sufficient.

At the fork, Geralt tied a strip from his cloak around the boy's bundle. "Show Branka this. She'll complain. Then she'll feed you. If she asks who sent you, say the white-haired ones did." The boy nodded, committing the wrong version to memory with great seriousness.

After the children vanished down the western track, the road felt emptier in the wrong way. Black Ink had tried to make them proof: if they died, I was danger; if I commanded the beasts, I was danger; if Ciri saved them, she was compromised. Every prepared path led back to a clean sentence.
Ciri looked west until they were gone. "We need witnesses before they do."
"The children?" I asked.
"No. The truth. Children should not have to carry it alone."
Saesenthessis watched her with old gold eyes.
"Political," the dragon said.
"Human," Ciri corrected.
"Sometimes."
"Today," Ciri said.
We did not speak again until the western track swallowed the children and the ruined tannery lost their voices.

Ciri stayed at the fork longer than strategy required. The oldest boy had looked back twice, once at her sword, once at my eyes. By supper someone would improve the story. By morning, if Black Ink found him first, he would be useful in three directions and safe in none.
"They will name him witness," Ciri said.
"Or contamination," I said. "Or saved child. Or manipulated minor. Depends which office gets hungry first."

Her jaw tightened. "When I was a girl, they called me destiny when they wanted my future and daughter when they wanted my obedience. Later, empress made a tidier cage than prisoner. People think a better word makes the bars kinder."
"Bearer," I said. "Key. Risk. Host. Last Warden when someone wants the myth to do the heavy lifting."
"And Jack?"
I looked at the western road. Mud held the children's footprints for ten yards, then gave up. "Some days."

Ciri reached toward my bandaged hand, stopped before touching it, and left the space honest. "I will not comfort you by saying they cannot use me. They can. They will. But I would rather be used for a choice I made than protected into someone else's lie."
"That sounds expensive."
"It is. So is being alive without permission."

The almost-touch remained between us longer than touch might have. Then she turned back toward the broken house, cloak dark with rain, sword at her hip, and the road had one more reason to become difficult.

That evening, we took shelter in the upper room of a roofless house whose lower floor had become too ambitious about mushrooms. Geralt slept badly by the door. Yennefer sat beside the cold hearth and wrote notes with a face that promised consequences for ink itself. Asha repaired a strap. Saesenthessis watched the eastern dark through a broken wall.
Ciri found me outside with Ciri's sword across my knees and my left hand shaking too hard to oil the blade properly.
"You should have said," she said.
"About the hand?"
"About almost taking them."
I rubbed oil along the blade. Too much. A novice error. "I did not take them."
"That is not what I asked."
Rainwater dripped from the broken roof behind us. Somewhere in the dark, Buck cropped wet grass and judged civilization.
"I wanted to," I said.
The words left me like something pulled from a wound. Not enough to kill. Enough to prove the wound went deeper than the skin.
Ciri sat beside me, not touching. "Because it would save us?"
"Because it would end the room," I said.

I rubbed oil along her sword until the blade shone too wet in the broken light. My hand shook once. The oil caught on the edge, thick and badly spread, and the smell of leather, rain, old smoke, and tannery rot sat between us like evidence neither of us could throw out. Outside, Buck cropped wet grass with the moral calm of a beast who had not been asked to watch a man nearly become a command.
Ciri did not reach for the sword. She watched my hand.
"That is not what I asked."
"No."
"Then answer the question I asked."

Rainwater dripped through the roof behind us. Somewhere inside the house, Geralt shifted in his sleep, or pretended to. Yennefer wrote by the cold hearth. Asha worked a strap through her fingers. Saesenthessis watched the dark with the patience of a wall that had learned to breathe.

I set the oilcloth down because my grip had become too tight for tools. "Yes. Because it would save us. Because it would save the children. Because Geralt was on the floor and you had no sword and I could feel the sick thing bowing its head as if fear were a language my blood had always known."
Ciri listened without rescuing me from the sentence.
"And because it would have felt easy," I said.
There. The ugly part. Named badly, perhaps, but named.
Her face changed in the gray night. Not horror. Not disgust. Something sharper and more dangerous, because it had room for understanding. "Easy is not the same as desired."
"No. But there was a breath where I wanted the room to stop being a room full of choices. I wanted it to become one answer."
"And then?"
"Then the boy looked at me like men had already used fear on him."
She was quiet a long time.
"I know that look," she said.

I believed her. That was the problem. Belief made the space between us less defensive and more dangerous. A person can argue with beauty, rank, myth, or blood. It is harder to argue with someone who names the bruise you thought you had hidden by standing well.
"I should leave before this becomes another way to use you," I said.
Ciri gave me a look so flat it could have served as a table. "You are choosing the worst hour to become stupid."
"It is a flexible talent."

"No. Listen. If I stay, they will use me. If I go, they will use the absence. If you stay, they will use proximity. If you go, they will use abandonment, threat, guilt, and every silence Geralt ever built because he thought love worked better hidden. There is no road out of being used by people determined to use you. There is only deciding who gets your truth first."

I looked at her. The broken wall put gray night behind her hair. Mud marked one cheek. She had lost a glove in the tannery and not noticed. Her ungloved hand rested palm-up on her knee, empty and unguarded in a way that might have been accidental if I had been a fool.
I was a fool in many directions. Not that one.
"Ciri."
"If you say this is unwise, I will consider stabbing you with the sword you cleaned badly."
"It is unwise."
"Good. Now that we have honored truth, continue."
The word continue did something to the air between us.
It did not make permission of itself. It demanded a decision.
Ciri's ungloved hand remained open on her knee. She did not reach for me. That refusal to rescue my courage made the distance sharper than touch.
I set her sword between us first, hilt angled toward her.
She noticed. Of course she noticed.
"That is mine," she said.
"Yes."
"You are returning it before touching me?"
"I am making sure you can stop me without asking politely."
Her eyes changed. Not softened. Sharpened. "Afraid of me?"
"No. Respecting the part of you that survived people calling cages protection."

For one breath, the ruined house held still around the answer. Rain moved through the broken roof. Somewhere inside, Geralt shifted in his sleep, or pretended to. Yennefer's pen scratched, paused, and continued. No one had vanished merely because Ciri and I had found a private darkness.
"Say it," she said.
"I want you."
"That part is obvious. Say the dangerous part."

I took off my sword belt and laid it beside hers, steel within reach and not between us. The buckle struck the floorboards with a small hard sound. "I want you, and I do not want wanting you to become another reason someone decides what you are."
Her expression sharpened. "That decision is mine before it is theirs."
"I know."
"Do you?"
"I am trying."
"Poorly."
"Consistently."
The corner of her mouth moved.
"Then try from closer."
I stood.

It would have been easier if she had pulled me in. Ciri did not. She had offered the road and left me to take it like a man rather than stumble into it like a wound.
