"Consent usually precedes collection," Ciri said.
"You shed it on the chair," Yennefer replied. "Blame furniture."
"I blame mothers by habit."
"That is traditional."
The bowl clouded. The scales turned inward, points aiming toward my hand, then toward Ciri, then toward the eastern wall. Finally all three aligned like arrows.
East.
Of course.
"Scale-sickness is a messenger," Triss said. "But not one language. It carries scent, heat, fear, obedience pattern, and blood-recognition."
"Can you cut it out?" I asked.
The question was too calm. Calm is the sound a man makes when he has already imagined the knife and is measuring the table.
Ciri's chair moved back a finger-width. Geralt shut his eyes. Triss lowered the pen. Yennefer did not soften.
"No," Yennefer said. "Not without possibly opening what it contains."
"Possibly."
"Certainly too much for me to gamble with your body to improve the quality of our ignorance."
I nodded once. "Then it is not a wound."
"It is a wound," Triss said. "But not every wound can be closed by cutting. Some have grown around things we cannot yet name without making them worse."
I wanted to dislike her for that. She had the unfair habit of being kind and precise at once.

Saesenthessis leaned forward and dipped one finger near the bowl without touching the water. The scales trembled. "The sickness is looking for command. If Jack commands, it will learn him as master. If others command him, it will learn them as handles. If fear commands everyone, Black Ink wins without a cage."
"And if nobody commands?" Ciri asked.
"Then you may become interesting."
"Careful," Ciri said. "I have a sword and dislike being graded before breakfast."
"You have several swords," Saesenthessis replied. "That is why the grading continues."

Triss made notes. Yennefer read over them. Geralt repaired the fire because not every crisis gives a sword something to do, and men who have spent their lives with blades sometimes discover logs to be mercifully honest. Asha watched me across the table with the expression of a woman who had seen another family burn for trying to solve love with silence.
"The archive route cannot wait," she said. "Each site will wake other sites. Every sick scale turns the old road under the old road."
"And Black Ink knows the route?" Geralt asked.
"They know enough to arrive late with boxes," I said.
The room did not like that.

Triss unfolded the message she had brought. "They have issued a soft recommendation. Separation of known associates from subject during pressure events. Public framing: contamination prevention. Private note: relational interference may stabilize noncompliance."
Ciri stepped beside me, not behind. It was small. Deliberate. A correction to the report without ink.
"If they recommend separation," she said, "they have misunderstood proximity."
Geralt turned to her. Pride and terror looked poor together on him. "Ciri."
"No."
He stopped.
I felt the word strike him. It struck me too, though not in the same place.

Yennefer took the message from Triss and read the next line aloud. "Known emotional conflicts may be exploited to induce surrender posture. Maternal, paternal, erotic, fraternal, and civic categories all under review."
Silence entered like a knife and took the best chair.
"They are naming the handles," Asha said.
Triss placed both hands flat on the table as if she wanted to hold the wood in place before the room tilted. "Then we name them first. Not as handles. As choices."
"Explain," Ciri said.

"If Black Ink writes maternal category, erotic category, paternal category, civic category, they make relationships sound like instruments. We answer by recording consent lines, not ownership lines. Who may touch the mark. Who may give medical instruction. Who may countermand Jack during pressure events and under what condition. Who may not. Who may speak to Ciri's staff. Who may not."
"A contract," I said.
"A refusal to let them draft one for us."
Yennefer's eyes moved to Triss with a strange mixture of approval and old pain. "You intend to bureaucratize intimacy against bureaucrats."
"No. I intend to make their theft legible before they rename it care."

Geralt leaned against the mantel. "Witchers had rules for this. Bad ones. Still rules. A boy in mutation fever could be held by two instructors, never one. A panic blade got kicked away, not taken into hand. Decoctions were counted aloud so no one later improved the dose in memory."
"You never told me that," I said.
"Didn't think I'd need to."
"You trained me in a castle where needing rules meant already being too late."
He accepted that without defense. "Yes."
Ciri drew the paper toward herself. "Then we write living rules. Not secret rules. Private rules. There is a difference."
She wrote first, because no one in the room had the courage to tell her not to.

Jack Morningstar is not to be removed, restrained, examined, stabilized, hidden, transported, bled, sedated, exposed, separated, or offered to any authority under language of mercy without his informed choice unless immediate unconsciousness prevents survival decision.
"That sentence is ugly," Dandelion would have said if he had been there.
Dandelion was not there. The sentence survived.
Ciri added another.
Cirilla is not to be shielded from facts that materially concern her blood, rank, body, route, or chosen companions. Delay for operational security must be named as delay, not protection.
Yennefer read it, then took the pen.
No one uses love as substituted consent.
That one left the room very quiet.
Triss added:
Medical language must identify the person before the condition.
Asha added in a script I could not read, then translated grudgingly. "No debt on the child. No leash on the living. No silence without witness."
Geralt looked at the pen for a long time before writing.
If Jack says hold is a leash, choose another word.
That struck harder than it looked.
I took the pen last. My hand hurt. The ink line trembled once before settling.
If I try to leave to spare everyone the cost of choosing, stop me by truth first, force only if truth arrives too late.
No one liked that. Good rules often make every honest person uncomfortable.
Ciri read it twice. "Force only if truth arrives too late," she said.
"Yes."
"Who decides too late?"
I looked at the table: Ciri, Geralt, Yennefer, Triss, Asha, Saesenthessis near the window, all the people Black Ink wanted categorized neatly enough to use.
"Not one person," I said.
Triss underlined that.
The paper did not save us. Paper rarely does. But for once, the paper had been made to serve the bodies in the room instead of preparing them for custody.
That felt like a small rebellion.
Small rebellions are sometimes the only kind that fit in an inn parlor.
"Then we break the handles," Geralt said.
"No," Triss replied. "We stop pretending not having handles is possible."
Ciri looked at Geralt. "There will be a council."
"Now?"
"After food. I am furious, not stupid."
Saesenthessis inclined her head. "Promising distinction."
"Do not grade me."
"Then stop answering well."
Ciri almost laughed. It became something else before it escaped.

That evening, Triss and Yennefer took over the inn's small pantry because it had one window, one door, shelves thick enough to hide notes, and a smell of onions strong enough to discourage casual listeners. They hung charms in the corners, burned two, found a third sewn into a flour sack, and left the fourth untouched because Yennefer said an enemy deserved one bad piece of information as a treat.

The rest of us ate in the parlor of The Velvet Hart, which had no velvet and very little hart unless the stew had led a morally complex life. The innkeeper watched us with the strained expression of a man seeing too many famous people and wondering whether fame paid damages. Geralt paid in advance. The expression improved but did not heal.
Ciri sat beside me. Not touching at first. Then her knee brushed mine beneath the table and stayed. No one mentioned it. That was mercy. Or cowardice. The room contained enough of both.
After food, Yennefer found me outside under the eaves, trying to wrap the bandage one-handed because pride had no sense of proportion.
"Give it," she said.
"I can manage."
"Many disasters begin there."
I gave her the bandage.
Her hands were cool and exact. She wrapped without tenderness at first. Then slower, when the mark warmed under her fingers.
"You knew before breakfast," I said.
"Yes."
"Does Geralt?"
"He knows and does not know. A common parental arrangement."
"You are angry."
"At many people. You are not first in line."
"That should comfort me?"
"I am not offering comfort. I am preserving function. Comfort comes later, if the world behaves better than expected, which it rarely does."
She tied the knot. Her fingers remained a moment longer than necessary.
"Do you disapprove?" I asked.
"Of you and Ciri?"
"Yes."

Yennefer's eyes lifted to mine. Violet in low light looked almost black. "I disapprove of timing, danger, politics, old blood, secrecy, guilt, and every institution that will try to make your bodies into arguments. I do not disapprove of two adults choosing one another with open eyes."
"That sounded practiced."
"It had all afternoon to bleed into shape."
From inside, Ciri said something that made Triss laugh. Geralt did not laugh, but the silence after it was softer.

Yennefer looked toward the window. "If the world decides she is dangerous blood, every cage becomes protection. If the world decides you are sacrifice walking, every affection becomes a delay to be overcome. We will not help them by doing the violence in advance."
I had no answer. A good one might have looked like gratitude, and gratitude near Yennefer seemed likely to be punished for poor posture.
"Thank you," I said anyway.
Her mouth curved. Not quite a smile. "Try not to become sentimental. It slows the work."
Inside, the council waited with bad stew, worse wine, and every relationship in the room ready to become either a defense or a weapon.
We went in.
Private advisory drafted in Ilyra Sarn's cipher for later reconstruction:

The principal refuses the premise that secrecy protects her. She distinguishes privacy from concealment with unusual force. Any handler attempting to manage the distinction for her should expect dismissal, injury, or both.
The parlor at The Velvet Hart had thick walls, two exits, one painted hunting scene, and enough smoke in the beams to make every heroic argument smell like old sausage.
It would do.

Ciri arranged the room, which told me more about her than an imperial genealogy would have. Geralt by the hearth, where he could see the main door and be seen by everyone. Yennefer near the window, not because she trusted it, but because she preferred to know how the night intended to misbehave. Triss at the table with papers, ink, and the patient expression of a woman prepared to wound friends in the service of clarity. Asha by the side door. Saesenthessis in shadow, because dragons appreciate unfair advantages even when pretending otherwise.
I stood until Ciri pointed at a chair.
"Sit."
"This a council or a trial?"
"Yes."
I sat.

Geralt looked as if he wanted to object and had spent the last hour being taught how little good that would do. Triss saw him gather himself, then placed a hand over his on the table. A small touch. Not restraint. Reminder.
"Before magic," Ciri said, "before route, before Black Ink's next invitation, we name what this company is not."
"A bold beginning," Saesenthessis said. "Humans usually begin by naming things incorrectly."
"You may be quiet beautifully or be thrown out plainly," Ciri replied.
The dragon inclined her head. "Proceed."
Ciri looked at me first. "You are not a problem to be solved by disappearing."
I opened my mouth.
"Do not improve my sentence with martyrdom," she said.
I closed it.
"Geralt," she continued, turning to him. "You are not permitted to turn fear into authority and call it love."
Geralt flinched. Not visibly enough for most rooms. Enough for this one.
Triss's hand tightened over his. "She is right."
"I know," he said.
"Knowing is not the same as obeying," Ciri replied.
"Also true."
That cost him. I saw the cost and, to my annoyance, respected it.
Ciri turned to Yennefer. "You are not allowed to protect me by deciding which truths I receive after everyone else has sharpened them."
Yennefer folded her arms. "I object to the word allowed."
"Noted. Denied."
The corner of Yennefer's mouth moved. "Very well. I will endeavor not to be protective in ways that resemble statecraft."
"That is the most Yennefer apology I have ever heard," Geralt said.
"It was not addressed to you."
"Felt nearby."

Triss spoke next, before the warmth could become avoidance. "No one in this room uses secrecy to spare someone from a choice that belongs to them. Privacy, yes. Concealment, no. If we hide facts, it must be to protect routes, not to manage feelings."
Asha nodded slowly. "Your northern families argue like treaty councils."
"Treaties are easier," Geralt said. "Fewer feelings. More assassins."
Ciri looked at Triss. "And you?"

Triss did not pretend to misunderstand. "I am not neutral. I am not only a scholar here, nor only Geralt's partner, nor only Yennefer's old friend, nor only a woman who has seen institutions ruin people by naming them efficiently. If my notes begin treating any person at this table as material first and person second, burn the notes and correct me."
"With fire?" Yennefer asked.
"Preferably not first."
"A limiting framework. Disappointing but workable."
I looked at the ugly painting above the mantel. The stag in it seemed resigned to being hunted by nobles with small dogs and large hats. Lucky stag. It at least knew what room it was in.
Ciri came to me last again. "And you."
"I was hoping we had finished with me."
"No. You were hoping to survive by being useful enough that no one asked what you wanted."
I disliked how many women in my life had developed precision recently.

"You are not comfort," she said. "Not cure. Not political lever. Not proof that I am free. Not proof that Yennefer can want without betraying old history. Not proof that Geralt can repair the past by standing closer now."
The room changed around Yennefer's name. Geralt looked at her. Triss did too, but differently. Ciri did not look away from me.
"And if you begin treating yourself as sacrifice because sacrifice gives you a cleaner place to stand than desire, grief, fear, or need," she said, "I will name it."
My mouth had gone dry. "You make it sound easy to tell the difference."
"It is not easy. That is why I am saying it while we are warm, fed, and not actively being bitten."
"I was bitten this morning."
"Then you are already behind. Listen faster."
A laugh moved around the table. Small. Needed. It let the room breathe again.
Geralt rubbed both hands over his face. "Didn't expect a council to begin with emotional definitions."
"Then you failed to study the room," Yennefer said.
Triss leaned back. "Also, everyone here is terrible at waiting until danger passes. Danger never passes. It only changes clothes."
Asha pointed toward the stable. "The horse understands this."
Buck struck his hoof against something outside as if accepting appointment.
"Good," Ciri said. "Then we agree."
"We have not discussed route," Geralt said.
"Route is simple. East. The necklace pulls, the scales point, Black Ink moves, and the dragon is insufferably confident."
"Route is not simple," Yennefer said. "We need supply, false paperwork, messenger control, ward rotation, and a way to move you without every innkeeper becoming a historian by noon."
"Then route is complicated," Ciri said. "Direction is simple."
That was Ciri's talent, I began to understand. Not recklessness. Distillation. She cut until the heart of a matter had no room to pretend it was another organ.

The rest of the council turned practical. That saved us. Practical things are often the mercy after emotional accuracy. We listed supplies: salve, horse feed, salt, silver wire, wax, copy paper, false seals, two spare cloaks, dried apples because Asha insisted, and enough coin to make innkeepers philosophical. Yennefer wrote letters that did not look like letters. Triss coded routes into inventory lists. Geralt inspected the stable twice. I helped with the packs and avoided being praised for lifting things.
Ciri did not let practical become another word for being handled.

When Yennefer began assigning false names, Ciri corrected two and refused a third because it made her sound like a decorative widow in a provincial play. When Geralt suggested she ride center in the column, she told him center made sense only if every ambush came from a school exercise. When Triss proposed routing messages through Ilyra without naming Ciri's preference, Ciri took the pen and wrote the preference herself.
"Ilyra works for me," she said. "Not around me."
Yennefer's face changed. That one landed near old history.
"Good," Yennefer said.
Ciri looked at her. "You are allowed to be proud without turning it into command."
"Generous."
"Accurate."
Asha watched them and murmured something in Faithel that made Saesenthessis's mouth almost become amused.
"Translation?" I asked.
"No," Asha said.
"Insult?"
"Prayer."
"Those overlap in many faiths."

Geralt finally moved the conversation to horses, which was safer except that Buck heard his name and began striking the stall board as if objecting to proposed governance. The sound carried through the parlor wall: one hard knock, pause, another.
"He votes no," Ciri said.
"He does not know the proposal," Yennefer said.
"That has never stopped a council."

Triss laughed into her cup. Geralt tried not to and failed by half a breath. That small failure did more for the room than another oath would have. Humor did not erase the handles Black Ink had named. It reminded us the handles belonged to people with bad tea, wet boots, stubborn horses, and the ability to make each other unbearable without becoming enemies.

The final route was ugly enough to be believable. We would ride under the sanitation-inspection cover until the next town, split our messages but not our bodies, leave one visible trail for a courier chain to chew on, and keep the real map in three memories rather than one document. Ciri held one part. Asha held one. Geralt held the old road logic because his memory for bad paths had been annoying before it became useful.
"And Jack?" Triss asked.
"Jack carries the thing everyone is following," Ciri said. "He does not also carry the whole plan. That is how men become excuses to abandon plans when they fall."
I looked at her. "When?"
"If."
"You said when."
"I said what fear says when I am tired. I corrected it. Try to keep up."
The correction mattered more than the mistake. Perhaps that was the lesson for the whole room, though I would have preferred a cheaper one.
Near midnight, Yennefer and Ciri disappeared into the small upper room for a conversation no one asked to hear and everyone thought about anyway.

Geralt stood in the stable yard under thin rain. Triss found him there. I was mending Ciri's sword belt inside the tack room, which meant I heard more than I should and less than a worse man would have tried to.
"You are afraid," Triss said.
"Yes."
"Of him?"
A pause.
"Of what happens around him. Of what happens to her. Of what happens if I interfere. Of what happens if I don't."
"That is a great deal of fear to carry while pretending to check a girth strap."
"The strap needed checking."
"Of course. Several times. Heroically."
Geralt exhaled. "She is not a child."
"No."
"I know that."
"You do. Then danger stands near her with a human face and you forget."
There was a long silence.
"I hid him," Geralt said. "Now he stands in front of her because of what I hid."
"Because of what Vesemir hid. What you maintained. What fear improved. Share guilt accurately or it becomes vanity."
That was Triss, warm enough to approach and sharp enough to prevent comfort from becoming rot.
"Do you hate it?" Geralt asked.
"What?"
"Yen. Jack. Ciri. All of it."

"I hate the danger. I hate that Black Ink will try to make every tenderness evidence. I hate that Yennefer still frightens me where I am most honest and that this no longer means I want her gone. I hate that you think pain becomes less selfish if you keep it quiet."
"That's not an answer."
"Yes, it is. You just wanted one with fewer rooms."
I set the belt down. My hands had gone still.
Buck leaned his head through the tack room window and breathed on my ear.
"Do not start," I whispered.
He lipped at my hair.

In the upper room, Ciri and Yennefer spoke long enough that the candle burned halfway down. I did not hear the words. I heard the shapes. Ciri's voice first, quick and hard. Yennefer's lower, controlled, then less so. A silence. A laugh, unexpected and too short. Then Ciri saying something that made Yennefer answer with only one word.
Yes.
Not a spell word. Not a court word. A mother word, perhaps, if such things can survive women like them.
Ciri told me enough later to put bones under the shapes. Not all. Some doors in families stay private because forcing them open only proves one has learned nothing from locks.

The upper room had smelled of spent candle, damp wool, and the sour wine the innkeeper insisted was respectable. Ciri had stood by the shutter. Yennefer had remained near the table, one hand beside the lamp, close enough to extinguish it if the conversation deserved darkness.
"You are going to tell me I am too close," Ciri had said.
"No," Yennefer answered. "I am going to tell you proximity changes the attack surface."
"That is mage language for being afraid."
"It is also accurate."

Ciri had looked at her then, not as court looked at sorceress, not as child looked at mother, but as a woman who knew exactly how love could become policy if the frightened person held enough power. "If you try to protect me by moving facts out of my reach, I will call that what it is."
"Maternal terror?" Yennefer asked.
"Management."

That had wounded because it was just. Yennefer, to her credit and discomfort, had not dressed the wound in pride. "I am terrified," she said. "For you. For him. For Geralt, who will try to stand between all consequences and discover he has only one body. For Triss, who will turn pain into notes until the notes bleed. For myself, because wanting anything in this room gives the enemy another thread to pull."
Ciri had softened only after the honesty, never before it. "Then do not pull mine first."

Yennefer had reached out and corrected a loose strand of Ciri's hair with the kind of care that could steady kingdoms and still fail at one daughter. "Choose with your whole sight," she said. "Not because he mirrors your cage. Not because danger makes loneliness sound like courage."
"And you?" Ciri asked.
Yennefer had looked toward the door, toward all of us without seeing any of us. "I choose nothing simple."
"That is not an answer."
"No," Yennefer said. "But it is the truthful part before the answer."

Later, when everyone had either gone to bed or found a place to pretend not sleeping was a plan, Asha came outside and found me with the whetstone. The rain had stopped. The yard smelled of wet straw, horse, and smoke from the inn chimney.
"You listened badly," she said.
"To which conversation?"
"All of them."
"Efficient criticism."
She sat on an overturned bucket. "You think they are making ties around you."
"Aren't they?"
"Some. Also beside you. Also between each other. You are not the center of every thread just because your blood is loud."
I deserved that. I still disliked it.
"Your people have a gift for comfort."
"We trained under dragons and grieving women. Lower your expectations."
I turned the whetstone in my hand. "They will use it. Ciri. Yennefer. Geralt. You. All of you."
"Yes."
"That is not comforting."
"You keep asking for the wrong thing."
"And what should I ask for?"

Asha looked through the stable door at Buck, who had stolen a mouthful of hay from a neighboring stall and looked morally untroubled. "Ask who stays when usefulness becomes costly. Ask who corrects you when your fear sounds noble. Ask who keeps your name in their mouth when paper finds prettier nouns."

I thought of Ciri's hand on my wrist. Geralt saying hold. Yennefer refusing the knife. Triss writing bodily consequence. Asha placing Helena's ring in my palm. Buck pressing his head into my chest because horses dislike philosophical collapse.
"That seems sentimental," I said.
"Yes. Try not to die of it before morning."
I smiled despite myself. Briefly. Almost young, perhaps. Asha looked away before I could decide whether that mattered.
Inside, Saesenthessis stood by the parlor window, watching us through rain-streaked glass.
Dragons, I decided, were worse than mothers. They saw too much and apologized less.
Black Ink relational assessment, extracted from intercepted field summary:

Known associates resist separation framing. Direct coercion may convert relational network into defensive witness cluster. Recommended next instrument: voluntary supervised mercy, phrased as responsible personhood. Secondary note: target displays recurrent surrender ideation under protective stress. Exploit carefully. Excess pressure may trigger group consolidation.
The invitation arrived folded inside a prayer book borrowed from the inn's chapel and returned with no prayers improved.
I found it because Buck bit the courier.

Not badly. Buck had standards and, in this case, excellent judgment. The courier was a young man with a Temerian accent, Nilfgaardian boots, Redanian paper in his satchel, and the pale face of someone who had been told the job involved delivering a devotional volume to a disguised noblewoman. When Buck took a professional interest in his sleeve, the young man dropped the book. It opened on the stable floor between a hymn to mercy and a woodcut of a saint holding what looked either like bread or a liver.
The paper slid out.
Geralt looked at Buck. "He is getting better at intelligence work."
"He prefers direct methods," I said.
The courier clutched his sleeve. "I swear I did not know. I was paid at the south gate. I thought it was a prayer book."
Yennefer took the paper with two fingers. "Most people do not know the moment they become useful. That is why offices survive."
We brought the invitation to the parlor. Everyone read it. No one hated the same sentence first.

Under seal of provisional civic review, the office offers supervised mercy, identity stabilization, protected medical oversight, and political silence for the prevention of wider panic. Voluntary compliance will be recorded as evidence of responsible personhood.
Responsible personhood.
There are phrases so clean they leave dirt on the hand.
Triss turned the page over and examined the fold. "Three handlers."
Yennefer leaned over her shoulder. "Four."
"One not human?"
"One not careful."
Ciri looked at the phrase again. Her fingers had gone still. "They knew we would all touch it."
"Yes," Triss said. "Pressure marks along the seam. It was folded around something small. Hair, powder, wax grain, listening grit. It may react to heat or magic. Do not burn it yet."
"Pity," Yennefer said.
Geralt stood by the window. "This is not a request."
"No," Ciri said. "It is an accusation dressed as mercy. If he refuses, they call him irresponsible. If he agrees, they call him voluntary."
The page did not need Sorel Veyrane's name. It had his habits: mercy cool enough to file, threat polite enough for review, consent waiting to be harvested from fear.

I read it again. Medical oversight. Political silence. Prevention of panic. Responsible personhood. The room shifted inside me. A path opened, ugly but straight: if I went, perhaps pressure left Ciri long enough for the others to move. Not much. A week, maybe. Enough, fear said, and fear has always been fluent in arithmetic.
Ciri saw it before I finished building the lie around it.
"Do not," she said.
"Do not what?"
"Make that face. Geralt makes that face when he thinks ugly arithmetic becomes nobility if he says little enough."
Geralt looked offended, then considered the charge and lost confidence.
I placed the invitation on the table. "If I go, some pressure leaves you."
The room changed at once.
Yennefer stood. "No."
"I said if."
"And I answered the version of you that believed if made it less idiotic."

Ciri's face had gone pale with anger. Triss looked sad in the dangerous way healers do when a wound begins choosing the knife. Geralt leaned back, measuring whether command would become the ownership we had spent a night naming.
"They have public language," I said. "Witnesses. Residue reports. Draconid sickness. Ciri's name close enough to use. You think refusing does not cost everyone?"
"Of course it costs everyone," Triss said. "That is why they wrote it."
"Then what is the alternative?"
"To stop accepting their accounting," Ciri said.
"Easy sentence."
She stepped toward me. "No. Necessary sentence. Different thing."
"If their next move is public seizure, they will choose a crowd. A road. An inn. Children if they can arrange it."
"And if you walk in," Geralt said, voice low, "they learn that arranging enough fear makes you deliver yourself."
That stopped me. Enough to bleed.

Asha's voice came from the side door. "A man can choose sacrifice. But when enemies train the choice and set the room and write the witness line first, it is not sacrifice. It is compliance with better lighting."
Saesenthessis looked almost pleased. "Blunt. Good."
"I learned from survivors, not dragons," Asha said.
"Often the same classroom."
Yennefer picked up the invitation and held it near the candle. The flame leaned toward it but did not touch. "They folded something inside."
Triss used tweezers to open the seam. A bead fell into the shallow dish beneath the page. Small. Dark. Red at the center.
Every candle leaned toward it.
My necklace turned cold.

Ciri stepped beside me again. Her shoulder brushed mine. Not accident. Public correction. Private warning. The part of me that still wanted to leave disliked it. The rest of me held on without moving.
"What is it?" Geralt asked.

Yennefer's expression sharpened into professional anger. "A calling bead. Poorly made, which makes it more insulting. It was meant to wake under heat from Jack's mark or Ciri's blood. If we had burned the invitation, it would have recorded the reaction. If Jack touched it alone, it would have given them a signature."
"And if we all touched it?" Ciri asked.
Triss looked at the dish. "Then it would have mapped relational heat."
"They are not only studying my blood," I said.
"No," Yennefer said. "They are studying what makes you answer."
That was the real intelligence of the trap. It was not guessing our hearts. It was teaching paper how to follow them.
The old thought returned anyway. Surrender. Clean path. Bad math. Knowing it was wrong did not remove its shape from the room.
Ciri took the invitation, read the first line once more, then folded it with care.
"We send it back," she said.
"With what answer?" Geralt asked.
Yennefer smiled.
It was not a comforting sight.

At dusk we returned the calling bead to its own trap. Not by letter. No ink. No argument for them to quote. Yennefer built a small ward around it, Triss cut the listening grain from the fold, and Asha tied the page with red thread in the Faithel way that meant witnessed and refused without giving anyone the satisfaction of reply. Saesenthessis added nothing except a breath across the knot that made the paper remember heat without burning.
"What did you do?" I asked.
"Taught it disappointment."

"Black Ink?" Geralt asked.
"Too muddy for their preferred boots," I said.
"Hired hands, then."
Asha crouched by the rut where the riders had turned off. "One soldier. One office dog trying to smell like soldier."
"Office dogs ride now?" Ciri asked.
"Everything rides if fear pays for saddle leather," Asha said.

The route bent through a stand of birch where white bark peeled in strips like old bandages. Triss marked two trees with chalk that looked like accidental fungus and would tell any friendly courier behind us to take the southern fold. Yennefer erased one of her own footprints with a flick of two fingers, then left a false one ten steps away with more irritation than magic required. Saesenthessis watched from the slope above, human shape almost hidden among gray trunks. She moved when she chose and was absent when being seen would have made anyone think they understood the road.
Ciri noticed that too.
"She knows the cache," she said.
"Probably."
"And still makes us find it."
"Dragons call that teaching."
"Courts call it manipulation."
"Witchers call it not being paid enough."
She glanced at me. "And you?"
The necklace pulled lightly under my shirt, then heavier when I slowed. A reminder. Not command. Or I hoped not.
"I call it someone deciding the size of truth I can survive," I said.
Ciri's expression sharpened. "Then ask for the rest."
So I did. Poorly, because asking dragons for anything makes a man feel like he has brought a spoon to a siege.
"Saesenthessis," I called.
The dragon appeared on a fallen wall above us. She had probably been there for ten minutes. That was exactly the sort of arrogance that could become invisibility if old enough.
"Yes?"
"Do you know where this leads?"
"Yes."
"Are you withholding it because the knowing matters, because the asking matters, or because dragons enjoy being hated efficiently?"
Asha made a small sound that might have been approval. Yennefer looked almost proud, which was more frightening.
Saesenthessis considered me. "All three, but not equally."
"Try the largest."

"The cache is kin-marked. If I point to the door, you arrive as an object brought to a lock. If you follow the pull and still choose to ask, you arrive as a man with witnesses. The old rite will know the difference. So will you, later, when grief becomes hungry enough to pretend it was forced."
I wanted to reject the answer because it sounded too close to wisdom. Unfortunately, it also sounded useful.
Ciri looked from the dragon to me. "There. You asked."
"I dislike the reward."
"That is often how answers prove they are not flattery."

The road narrowed after that, and the ordinary problems ended. No birds. No cart tracks after the birch line. No fresh dung from deer, boar, or wolves. The eastern pull settled into the sternum, light when I trusted the path, sharp when I began looking for excuses in the wrong ditch.
By late afternoon, the day narrowed.

The road worsened quickly, which meant it was honest. Paved imperial confidence gave way to ruts, then a hunter's track, then an old quarry path swallowed by grass. The country had been passed between crowns too often to retain loyalty to any of them. Broken boundary stones lay in ditches. A shrine to a local field goddess had been repaired with a soldier's shield. Apple trees grew wild where a manor garden had burned.

Ciri rode hooded and without visible escort because Ilyra had taken the imperial riders on a false inspection route at dawn. Yennefer moved ahead and sideways, which is to say she vanished whenever the road became too simple and reappeared whenever someone began lying within a mile. Triss rode with us now, having refused to stay behind after the calling bead. Geralt did not object. Geralt had learned, in recent days, that objecting to adult women with specific plans was a good way to discover the limits of witcher endurance.
By late afternoon, the necklace stopped pulling.
It did not release. It settled.

The ruin stood in a fold between two hills, half-hidden by birch and thorn. Not a castle. Not a shrine. A way-station perhaps, once, built for people who knew which roads had to remain unnamed. The walls had collapsed inward. Rain collected in the old threshold. A lintel stone lay split across the entry, carved with lines so worn they looked natural until Asha knelt and brushed moss away with her sleeve.
She did not speak for a while.
That worried me more than her riddles.
"Faithel?" Geralt asked.
"Border house," Asha said. "Not home. Not temple. A place for changing hands without changing truth."
"A cache," Triss said.
"If no one came first."
Yennefer examined the threshold. "Someone tried. Years ago. Poorly."
Saesenthessis stood beyond the fallen wall and would not enter. Ciri noticed before I did.
"Why stay outside?" Ciri asked.
"Some grief is made smaller by old witnesses standing too close," the dragon said.
Asha's jaw tightened. Not anger. Not gratitude either.

We cleared the threshold by hand. No spells at first. Asha insisted. The work was slow, wet, and ordinary. That helped. Ordinary work gives grief somewhere to put its feet. We moved stones, cut brambles, cleared glass, swept dirt from old grooves. Geralt found a rusted hinge and kept it, for reasons known only to men who collect useful metal against the wishes of narrative. Ciri tore her sleeve on thorn and swore like a soldier. Yennefer looked proud and disapproving, a difficult facial arrangement she managed well.
At the wall behind the old hearth, Asha found the hidden cuts.
"Door acknowledged," she said.
"That one of your clean explanations?" I asked.
"No. Work." She placed her palm against the stone. "Threshold swept. Glass removed. Fire named. Water thanked. Blood kept inside the skin unless the stone asks otherwise."
"Practical religion," Triss murmured.
"The only kind that survives travel."
Asha turned to me. "If the cache is kin-marked, it may hurt less if you ask first."
"Hurt less."
"Yes."
"Comforting."
"No. Accurate."

I stood before the wall. My necklace lay cold against my chest. Helena's ring, carried in my pouch, seemed heavier than metal. I could feel everyone behind me. Geralt trying not to step closer. Ciri not trying and succeeding anyway. Yennefer's attention sharp as a hook. Triss holding a notebook closed for once. Asha watching the wall, not me. Saesenthessis outside with the rain.
I touched the stone with my bandaged palm.
Nothing happened.
For one stupid, terrible breath, I felt relief.
Then Asha said softly, "Ask."
I swallowed. The sound was small and worse than grief.
"I don't know the proper words."
"Use improper ones honestly."
The wall waited. Stones are good at that.

"I am here," I said. My voice sounded wrong. Too young in the ruin. "If this belonged to them, I will carry it. If it was meant for someone else, I will leave it. If there is debt here, do not put it on the child."

My bandage stuck to the stone. Not by magic. By damp, dirt, and blood that had dried badly under linen. I could have pulled away. I did not. For once the door was not being forced on me by a report, a dragon, a crown, or an old man's fear. I had asked, and the asking had left me nowhere to hide.
The last sentence had not been planned.
The wall opened.

Not with drama. A click. A sigh of dust. One stone shifted inward, then another. Behind them lay a narrow chamber lined in clay, dry despite the rain. Inside waited a copper tube, a broken sword hilt, a small medallion with the barbed-star mark, a cloth-wrapped packet of letters, and one blue bead.
A child's bead.
No one spoke.
I took the bead first. That surprised me. I think it surprised everyone. It was blue glass, cheap, flawed, strung once on a cord that had rotted away. It weighed almost nothing. That felt obscene.
"Your cradle cord," Asha said.
The ruin changed around me. Not magic. Meaning, which is sometimes worse.
Yennefer took the letters only after I nodded. She opened the first with a care that made her look less like a sorceress and more like a woman handling another woman's last breath.
"Helena," Asha said.
Yennefer read.
Jacob,

If the house burns, do not come back for proof. I write that knowing you will want proof because men with swords think evidence can be rescued if only they are stubborn enough. Rescue the child. Rescue Asha if the lower gate holds. Rescue your own breath if it can still carry his name. Leave the rest to people who understand hiding better than heroes.
Yennefer paused.
Geralt looked down.
The rain moved through leaves outside.
She continued.

His name is Jack because you said a child should have a name a tired man could say while smiling. His house-name is Morningstar, not because we were meant to rule, but because the morning star is seen before the sun and vanishes when the world thinks light belongs to something larger. Remember that. We were never crowns. We were warning.
My throat closed. I hated it for closing. A page should not have hands.
Ciri's hand touched my sleeve.
Not my skin. Not yet. Sleeve. A place where a man could pretend touch was incidental if pride required a chair. I did not pretend. I leaned one finger against hers.
Yennefer read the next page.

The line is narrow. That is not his fault. The seal is failing. That is not his fault. Zerrikanterment says he can fold the last cinder into the child, make him hidden enough to live, closed enough to hold, dangerous enough to be hunted if the wrong hands learn the old grammar. I asked whether the child must pay for our unfinished work. The dragon said no child must pay. Then he prepared the rite anyway.
Asha made a sound. Not sob. Not speech. Something older and less useful.
Saesenthessis remained outside.
I understood then why.
Yennefer's voice changed. Not softer. More careful.

If you live, tell him we loved him before we knew whether he would survive. If I live and you do not, I will tell him badly and often. If neither of us lives, let whoever finds this remember the only law I still trust: the child bought nothing. Do not let priests, wardens, kings, clerks, dragons, or grieving parents place debt on the child.
The room blurred.
I closed my eyes once. Opened them because darkness had begun offering me worse pictures.
"Read Jacob," I said.
Yennefer looked at me.
"Please."
The word landed badly and honestly.
She opened the second letter.
My son,

That is a ridiculous way to begin a letter to someone who may never read it, but your mother said a man should practice courage in small humiliations before attempting large ones. I am Jacob var Moorlen by birth, Jacob Morningstar by choice, shield-man by trade, and your father by astonishment. If anyone tells you fatherhood made me noble, distrust them. It made me frightened in a direction I preferred.
Geralt gave a very quiet breath through his nose. It might have been pain. It might have been recognition.
Yennefer continued.

The old seal does not choose virtue. It chooses continuity. Men will try to make that sound holy because holiness improves obedience. Do not believe them. If the seal lives in you, it is because we failed to keep danger away from a cradle and because a dragon with more grief than mercy decided survival was the least cruel answer available.

I do not ask forgiveness. That asks too much of a child. I ask only that if you stand before a door that wants blood, you remember a door is not a god. It is wood, stone, law, pressure, fear. Everything built can be refused, opened, broken, or outlived. Choose with people beside you if you can. Alone is sometimes necessary, but many fools have called it purity and died easier to use.
I had to sit then.
There was no chair. A broken stone did the work. My legs had become less interested in legend.
Ciri sat beside me. Geralt did not move. It may have been the kindest thing he could do, and the hardest.
Asha took the broken hilt from the cache. "Jacob's."

It had been a short sword once. Practical. No gems. No noble foolishness. The guard had one notch worn by a thumb. A working weapon held by a man who had probably checked doors with his shoulder and called that preparation.
Asha placed it across my knees.
I touched the worn notch.
The necklace at my throat warmed for the first time without pain.

Yennefer opened the copper tube last. Inside was a strip of cloth written with operational tags in three hands. Faithel. Nilfgaardian. A third script Asha refused to name until she had to. Triss leaned in, and for once no one told her to wait.
"It records the rite," Triss said quietly. "Compression, transfer, concealment. Last Cinder folded into living custody. Termination marker falsified. Completion tag assigned."
"Completion," I said.
The word tasted worse than blood.
Asha's face had gone old. "They marked the child as completed so no one would seek him."
"Who?"
She looked at Saesenthessis outside. The dragon did not move.
"Everyone who survived long enough to choose badly," Asha said.
The answer should have been evasive. It was not. It was worse: shared guilt without a place to stab.
Geralt finally spoke. "Vesemir found him because the tag failed."
"Or because mercy did," Yennefer said.
No one corrected her.

We buried nothing because there were no bodies, but Asha insisted on a rite, and no one in the ruin had the cruelty to argue with a woman who had carried forty years of unfinished mourning in her spine. She chose a place beneath the split threshold where rain reached but did not pool. Jacob's hilt lay on clean cloth. Helena's letter rested beside it under a flat stone so wind could not perform scholarship on grief. The blue bead sat between them.
I did not want to let the bead go.

That surprised me. It was a cheap thing. A child's thing. Mine, perhaps, but mine from a life I had not lived. I had carried swords, signs, coin, contracts, names spoken wrong by frightened people, and a necklace that had made my body into an argument. The bead was useless.
That made it harder.
Ciri stood beside me, shoulder touching mine.
"You can keep it," she said.
"Asha says rites need objects."
"Asha has carried mourning long enough to know it sometimes shares. Ask."
I looked at Asha.
She looked at the bead, then at me. "A child's proof belongs first to the child. The dead can borrow memory without taking everything."
I picked up the bead. My hand shook. Not much. Enough for Geralt to see. Enough for him not to move.
Asha sang.

The Faithel mourning verse did not try to be beautiful. It tried to be accurate. Names, minutes bought, breath carried, silence purchased by fire, no debt on the child. The words moved through the ruin and made the rain feel less like weather and more like witness. Yennefer held a candle. Triss wrote nothing. Geralt stood with his head bowed. Ciri's hand found mine, bead between our palms. Saesenthessis remained outside the threshold until the final line.
Then she bowed her head.
The song ended, but none of us moved.

Rituals do that when they work. Not because they trap anyone, but because they make leaving feel like another sentence that should be spoken carefully. Rain tapped through the split roof. Smoke bent along the floor before finding the broken wall. Somewhere beyond the threshold, Buck stamped once, then settled, as if even he had agreed not to interrupt the dead too quickly.
Asha stayed kneeling longer than her knees wanted. I saw the pain in the set of her shoulders. She ignored it. Survivors often treat pain like a creditor: recognized, disliked, not yet paid.

Geralt moved first, because he had always understood practical mercy when words became too expensive. He put two fingers under Asha's elbow and helped her stand without making rescue of it. She allowed the help.
"The verse says no debt on the child," Triss said quietly.
Asha looked at the flat stone over Helena's letter. "It also says the living will try anyway. That is why the verse has to be repeated."

Yennefer held the candle until wax touched her glove. She did not flinch. Ciri noticed and took the candle from her hand. No speech. Only transfer. Mother and daughter had languages that made silence look crowded.
I could not stop looking at the bead.

It sat between my palm and Ciri's. Blue glass. Flawed. Absurdly ordinary. A thing a child could chew, lose, love for no reason, or throw at a wall in a tantrum. I had expected proof to feel larger. Men expect origin to arrive like thunder because otherwise the years stolen from them seem too poorly compensated.
Instead I had a bead.
"That is not enough," I said.
I had not meant to speak.
No one pretended not to hear.
Ciri's fingers tightened around mine. "No."
The answer struck strangely. Not comfort. Agreement. Better.
"It should be more," I said.
"Yes."
"A grave. A voice. A memory that belongs to me because I earned it by living, not because six people bled around a cache and called it inheritance."
Geralt looked away. That might have been guilt. It might have been respect. It is hard to tell with men who make weather of remorse.
Yennefer said, "You are allowed to hate the size of what survived."
"Allowed."
"Yes. A legal word used offensively in an emotional setting. I chose it to irritate you into staying present."
Despite everything, something in my chest almost laughed and failed.
Asha stepped closer. "The dead do not always leave enough. Sometimes they leave what fire missed. Sometimes that is insulting. Insult does not make it false."
I looked at her then. Forty years of ash, bone charms, scarred jaw, old guilt, and the stubborn refusal to let my parents become clean myths for northern convenience.
"Did she sing?" I asked.
Asha understood before anyone else did. "Helena?"
I nodded once.
"Badly," Asha said.
The answer entered the ruin and changed it.

"She knew three songs. Two had the same melody because she claimed melody was an inefficient extravagance. Jacob said this was proof soldiers should not marry women who could turn music into logistics. She threw a boot at him. Missed on purpose. Probably."
Ciri's thumb moved against my hand.

Asha continued, voice low, reluctant, and more generous for the reluctance. "When you cried, she did not sing softer. She sang more angrily, as if the world had insulted you and volume was an answer. It worked, sometimes. Or you stopped crying from surprise."
There. A memory that was not mine, but close enough to warm the door.
I closed my eyes. Not to hide. To listen.
Asha sang one line.

It was not beautiful. It was better. Rough, low, uneven around smoke-damaged breath. A tune with too few notes and too much stubbornness. I did not remember it. I would not lie and say blood recognized what the mind did not. But my body went still in a way that was not fear.
When the line ended, Saesenthessis finally stepped over the threshold.
Only one step.
A dragon granting the dead their distance and the living a witness.

"She sang it at the western gate," the dragon said. "When the smoke turned black. I told her silence carried farther. She told me dragons did not understand children. I was offended. She was correct."
Asha looked at her. The two women held an old battlefield between them without raising a blade.
"You prepared the rite," Asha said.
"Yes."
"She hated you for it."
"Yes."
"So did I."
"Yes."
The bead in my palm pressed into Ciri's skin and mine.
"And now?" I asked.
Asha's answer took a long time.
"Now hatred has had forty years to learn the shape of the choices we did not have and the ones we refused to see. It is still hatred. It is less stupid."
Saesenthessis bowed her head again, lower this time.
No one forgave anyone in that room.
I trusted it for that.
A dragon's bow is a terrible thing. Not because it is grand. Because it admits the scale of what even power could not undo.

After the rite, we sat in the ruin and ate bread that had gone hard at the edges. Ordinary acts are sometimes the only bridge back from the dead. Buck stole half of mine when I failed to watch him. I let him, which should worry scholars of my judgment.
Ciri leaned against the wall beside me. "Jack because a tired man could say it while smiling."
"Apparently."
"It suits you."
"I have been told I look more like a public-risk anomaly."
"By people with no ear for names."
I turned the blue bead in my palm. "Morningstar. Warning, not crown."
"That suits you too."
"Does it?"
"You arrive before people are ready for daylight and disappear when they start worshiping the wrong thing. Yes."
"That was almost kind."
"I can be imprecise when tired."

I looked at her then. Mud on her sleeve. Hair loose from the ride. Eyes too old for any throne and too alive to let a throne become the whole of her. She had chosen to be here with proof in the dirt and danger on the road, not because I was hers, not because she was mine, but because truth had reached her before lies dressed properly.
"Thank you for staying," I said.
Her gaze softened and sharpened. "I did not stay for you only."
"I know."
"Good."
"I am still thankful."
That landed. Quietly. She did not answer at once.
"Then I accept without making it efficient," she said.
A courier found us before we reached the main road.

He came on a mule too stubborn to be frightened and too ugly to be stolen, which made it ideal for sensitive messages. Zoltan had chosen well. The courier was half drunk from fear and fully sober from money. He carried a packet wrapped in oiled cloth, tied with green thread, and smelling faintly of pipe smoke, apple brandy, and dwarven contempt for subtlety.
Geralt took it first, checked the seal, then handed it to me.
"For you."
I opened it with Helena's ring still warm in my pouch and Jacob's words still sitting badly in my chest.
Zoltan's note was short.

Found the account under three charities, two military freight ledgers, and one brothel linen contract, because apparently shame has better bookkeeping than virtue. Name you need: Sorel Veyrane. Not only senior examiner. Keeper of Eastern Continuity Custody shelf, old Barbed-Star materials. Archive room moved after war. Current route points to civic review house near Vengerberg. Dandelion says this needs a rhyme. I told him to rhyme it with axe.
Attached: freight mark, clerk initials, one receipt for ventilation crates. Do not die before I charge you for this.
Z.
No one spoke for a long moment.
The road had done what roads do. It had delivered us from a ruin containing grief to a room containing proof of the next cruelty.
Vengerberg.
Yennefer's face went still in a way that made the air reconsider movement.
"Of course," she said.
Geralt looked at her. "You don't have to go."
She gave him a look that would have killed a more perishable man. "Try that sentence again after removing the stupidity."
"We're going to Vengerberg," he said.
"Better."
Triss unfolded the receipt. "Ventilation crates. Same design as the carts at Broken Crown."
Ciri's hand closed around the hilt of her sword. "Then the invitation was not mercy. It was logistics."
Asha looked east, then north-east. "The shelf will not only hold your origin. It will hold their version of ending."
Saesenthessis finally stepped onto the road. The horses shifted. Buck did not lower his head this time. He stood beside me, ugly, wet, and magnificently unimpressed.
"Now," the dragon said, "you have proof. Beware. Proof makes men think they are done listening."

I touched the bead through my glove and thought of Helena refusing to let me become a debt, Jacob warning me not to mistake doors for gods, Vesemir hiding a living child because secrecy had looked kinder than exposure, and Geralt now standing near enough to be family without asking the word to forgive him quickly.
I was not strengthened in any heroic sense. I was a man with proof in his pocket, a name under his ribs, a bead in his hand, and too many people close enough for enemies to count.
I did not trust it.
I carried it anyway.
The next road did not lead toward origin.
It led toward the office that had filed origin as completion.
Outside the ruin, the rain stopped. Water dripped from birch leaves onto old stones. Buck nudged my shoulder, then bit at the edge of Zoltan's packet. I pulled it away.
"No. Bad for the stomach."
He snorted.
"Yes," I said, looking toward the road to Vengerberg. "Mine too."
Operational note, restricted shelf request, Eastern Continuity Custody:

Subject has obtained family proof. This confirms previous concealment chain and increases likelihood of hostile inquiry. Retrieve or destroy remaining Morningstar materials before arrival. If retrieval impossible, prepare correction file: Jacob var Moorlen, Helena Morningstar, Faithel continuity rite, Zerrikanterment compression, child termination tag. Preferred public language remains: completed event, no living claimant.
Margin, hand unknown:
The claimant is riding.
Extract from a Black Ink transfer ledger, lower edge burned before seizure:

BARBED-STAR CONTINUITY, closed action inventory. Bearer-class adult female, terminated. Military protector, compromised by sentiment, terminated. Infant continuity risk, unresolved. Servant-witness category, unresolved. Golden draconic containment anomaly, status uncertain. Recommendation: recover or erase secondary cache before eastern custodial groups can contest custody doctrine.

The line was old. It had not been written after Willenford, Devenford, Broken Crown, or the songs that learned my road. Black Ink had kept a failure warm under other names: infant continuity risk, servant-witness unresolved, golden draconic anomaly uncertain. Part I had given the old failure a living address.
The archive stood under a tannery because the living preferred bad smells above old crimes.

We reached it by four roads that disliked being named: dye-house gutters, a cooper's yard, a fishwives' passage, and a gap between leaning walls where I had to turn my shoulders and Dandelion sacrificed a feather to masonry.
"A noble death," he whispered, looking at the torn plume.
"It was blue," Zoltan said. "Death improved it."

I noticed the choice before I noticed the door. Banks used money to guard secrets. Temples used guilt. Tanneries used rot. No patrol wanted to search a cellar where lime, urine, wet hide, old hair, and boiled fat punished every breath.

Zoltan had found the place through wax, debt, and an eel seller who stopped believing in secrets after the third mug. Dandelion had found the door by insulting a municipal clerk until the man produced a key only to make the argument end. Triss had found the false inventory number by comparing three ledgers and muttering at them until the ink looked guilty. Yennefer found the ward on the threshold and removed it with two fingers, one cold glance, and a phrase in Elder Speech that made the ward reconsider its career.
Geralt studied the tannery steps, then me. "Smells worse than Kaer Morhen's west drain."
"No," I said. "This has ambition."

"You two compare filth like vintners compare grapes," Dandelion said from the alley. He wore a butcher's apron, a cap too small for him, and the expression of a man forced to murder art in public. "It is one of your least marketable talents."
Zoltan looked him over. "You look respectable. It is disgusting."
"I feel morally diminished."
"Good. You blend in."

Ciri stood beneath the overhanging upper floor, hood low, boots deliberately muddy. She had argued against coming for thirteen minutes and then won by refusing to continue. She had left her two quiet riders at the far lane because imperial protection entered rooms before fact, and she wanted the evidence to trip over fewer banners.

Asha waited near the stair with one hand by the bone knots at her belt. Saesenthessis had not entered the city. She had said stone that remembered gold behaved badly under too many roofs, which sounded like an answer until one noticed it was also refusal. She watched from somewhere outside the walls. Dragons made absence feel intentional.
We had spent the hour before entry becoming ordinary in pieces.

Dandelion became a butcher's assistant and looked betrayed by pork. Zoltan became a delivery man with invoices and debts. Geralt became a man who did not want attention, which was unfortunately close to impossible. Triss carried lamp oil as if it were medicine. Yennefer carried nothing and made that a threat. Asha wrapped her scars and became a widow from too far east for polite ignorance to question.
Ciri became the hardest thing to counterfeit: someone no one thought worth remembering.

The cloak helped. Mud helped more. She rubbed ash along one cheekbone, tucked her hair, and accepted a cracked market token from Ilyra's courier. In alleys, power vanishes only when it understands what poor cloth does to the eyes of men who believe rank announces itself.
I did not like it.
Ciri saw that before I found somewhere to put my face. "Do not start."
"I have not started."
"You arranged your jaw into a lecture."
"That is an old injury."
"Then limp elsewhere."

A boy carrying fish heads came through the passage then, bare feet red with cold, shoulders sharp under his coat. He stopped when he saw our group and decided instantly that whatever we were, we were not his problem unless paid. Zoltan gave him a copper and asked whether brown coats had passed that morning.
"Three," the boy said. "One with boots too clean. One with cough. One woman who paid for silence and got directions instead."
"Directions to where?" Triss asked.
The boy pointed past the tannery. "Old lime cellars. But she asked wrong. Everyone knows the upper door is for idiots."
"Useful child," Dandelion said.
The boy looked offended. "Expensive child."
Ciri gave him another copper. "Be more expensive elsewhere for the next hour."
He bit the coin to test it, nodded once, and vanished between hanging hides.
That was the first cost before the archive opened: a child learning danger had a market price. It was low.
At the corner, an old woman with blue-stained fingers washed skins in a barrel and sang a market tune built to keep hands moving through stink. She stopped on one word when I passed.
Red.
Only that. A color becoming address.
Ciri heard. So did Yennefer. Neither looked at me.
The city already had a mouthful of me before I touched the archive door.
That was why we went in. Waiting had become another way to be written.

The cellar door opened on hinges recently greased by a hand that respected silence more than law. Below, the air grew wet and chemical. I went first because the signet at my throat had cooled with recognition. Geralt followed close enough to intervene and far enough not to make intervention the point.

The archive was not grand. That was the obscenity of it. Brick walls, three tables, eight shelves, a warped cabinet, two stools, lime dust on the floor, and boxes arranged by region, date, and category. Some were scorched. Some sealed. Several bore the same clean hand that had called dead people inventory.
"Ordinary," Triss said.
"Yes."
Her mouth tightened. She had meant it as accusation. I had heard it as fact.
A dead rat lay beneath the cabinet, dried into a comma. Zoltan nudged it with his boot. "Even the vermin gave up. That is how you know it is official."
Yennefer touched the nearest box without opening it. "Post-purge relic lots. Non-human custodial cults. Eastern continuity."
Asha's face went still at custodial cults. "That is not our name."
"It is never the victim's name on the label," Ciri said.

The first bundle held a brass daylight clasp bent at the hinge. Asha made a sound so small I almost missed it. That frightened me more than a cry would have. Cries leave the body. Small sounds stay and teach the ribs.
"Helena," she said.

My mother had become a word in other people's mouths before I knew how to answer it. Helena Morningstar. Not bearer-class adult female. Letter-writer. Bead-giver. Woman who had bought a child minutes and received a file instead.

Asha did not give the clasp to me immediately. She turned it in her fingers first, very carefully, as if metal could bruise if memory handled it badly. The hinge had been worn smooth on one side. Not broken in battle. Worn. Opened and closed by thumb, by habit, by a woman doing ordinary work while danger learned her address. There was a pale groove near the catch where cloth had rubbed for years.
"She used it to pin back her sleeve," Asha said. "When she cooked. When she wrote. When she carried you and needed one hand free."

The archive lost some of its power then. Not enough. Never enough. But the label bearer-class adult female had to stand beside a sleeve pinned out of flour, ink, and a child's reach. My mother had existed in repeated gestures before she became their category. That made the category smaller and the loss harder to hold.
Triss opened the folded sheet beside the clasp. Her hands were steady, which was not the same as calm.

"Operational closure," she read. "Subject Helena Morningstar prevented extraction by use of Faithel closure rite. Military protector Jacob var Moorlen delayed entry team beyond allowable threshold. Protector terminated. Infant not recovered. Servant-witness Asha unconfirmed. Golden draconic interference prevented complete burn accounting."
The words behaved themselves. That was the insult. A page describing the ruin of my first life should have done something except sit there with administrative patience.

No one reached for the next page. Asha stood with both hands closed around nothing. Geralt looked at the floor as if the right apology might have been written there twenty years too late. Triss set the report down carefully, because my mother deserved more care than the page did.
Infant not recovered. Asha unconfirmed. Golden draconic interference. The old file had not known enough to find us. It had known enough to wait.
Geralt reached for the edge of the table and missed it by half an inch before correcting the movement. I saw. So did Yennefer. Triss did not look away from the page, which was her kindness.
"There are later margin notes," she said. "Different hand. S. Veyrane. Junior review. He disagrees with the original failure category. He calls it incomplete custody event."
Zoltan spat on the floor. "That sentence deserves a shovel."
"Several," Yennefer said.

I took the page. Jacob's broken hilt lay in my pack. The blue bead lay in my inner pouch. Helena's letter was folded twice and wrapped in oilcloth. The dead had given me a name. The living had given me a category.
I chose the name.
"Next," I said.
"Jack," Ciri said.
"Next."
She knew I was asking for more pain because the pain already given had nowhere to go. Worse, she let me do it.

Geralt's hand moved, not toward the page, toward me. A stop half-born. A father trying to become a door before remembering I had spent the last months refusing doors with kind hinges. He lowered the hand and put it on the table instead. The wood took the apology badly.

Yennefer saw the movement and did not help him finish it. Her face had the severe mercy of someone understanding that interruption could become another form of ownership. Triss waited with the second report unopened. Ciri stayed looking at me, not soft, not safe, but present enough that the next pain would not arrive alone even if I had asked for it badly.
Triss opened the second report.

This one held diagrams: five outer barbs, inner anchor marks, and a central chamber drawn as a circle, then crossed out in red. Three translations fought over the same horror: vessel-prison, blood chamber, living hinge.
LIVING CHAMBER POSSIBILITY: REJECTED.
The sentence made the archive seem underbuilt. Someone had considered making a person into a room, then rejected the method for reasons that had nothing to do with mercy.
I did not breathe properly until Ciri moved. Not toward me. Toward the page. She touched the table beside it, not the ink, as if even contact needed consent in that moment.
Yennefer took the sheet before anyone could ask. Manners had been insulted too deeply and were waiting outside.
"Rejected," she said. "Not because it was cruel. Cruelty is marked tolerable under emergency doctrine. Rejected because a living chamber might refuse."
"Sensible fear," Asha said.
Her voice was dry. Not empty. Dry things burn well when flame finally reaches them.
"Veyrane kept the idea," Triss said. "The later notes cross-reference Broken Crown, Willenford, and Kaer Morhen. He believed refusal could be trained until surrender felt like mercy."
Yennefer read the next paragraph and went colder than anger. "This is policy. They are asking how to make a body governable after it has been turned into infrastructure."
Triss took the page from her without pulling. "Cruelty was too crude. They looked for review language, witness language, consent language. They wanted the cage to survive a committee."
They had not only imagined using me. They had imagined me agreeing if the room around me held enough people I loved.

The notes had no interest in heroism. Their lack of interest in heroism made the notes colder. They studied lamps, witnesses, medical language, public panic, a child's cry, Geralt's guilt, Ciri's authority, Yennefer's refusal, Triss's ethics, Asha's dead. Not as people. As room conditions. As temperatures around a body they hoped would decide a cage was mercy because everyone else looked cold.

Black Ink had not simply searched for a way to kill me or bind me. Killing was crude. Binding left bruises visible enough to embarrass committees. They were building the weather in which I might walk into the chamber myself and let them call the storm consent.
The mark in my palm warmed. I closed my fingers until the bandage pulled.
"Do not," Ciri said softly.
I looked at her. "Do not what?"
"Become useful to the wrong sentence."
For once, I had no good reply. A man can spend years sharpening his tongue and still discover it makes a poor shield against someone who has begun to know him.

The cabinet yielded more, but the anchors mattered most: the blue bead reduced to decorative residue, Helena's cloth tagged as bearer garment, Jacob's hilt as compromised military material, and the Living Chamber page waiting among names written as if grief had inventory value.
Dandelion, for once, stopped making noise.
Zoltan looked at the objects and said, "I have stolen from kings, generals, moneylenders, and men with fewer morals than fleas. None of them ever made me want to apologize to a drawer."
"Then do not apologize," Yennefer said. "Steal well."
The next box should have been easier because it held maps.

Maps came next. Red threads crossed the North beside fever sheds, war-widows' kitchens, patrol huts, tollhouses, charity granaries, and chapels where new priests inherited cupboards without opening them.
Zoltan leaned over it and made a sound from somewhere deep in the beard. "That is not a route. That is a habit."
"A habit of what?" Dandelion asked.
"Moving things no one wants to admit are things."

Triss copied while Yennefer read the marginal numbers. Geralt stood close enough to see and far enough not to crowd me. Ciri took the left edge of the map, where three marks converged near Marna's Bend, then looked at Asha.
"These old marks," Ciri said. "Do they mean anything to you?"
Asha did not answer quickly. She touched one circle, then another. Her finger stopped over a jagged symbol drawn near a dry riverbed east of the Yaruga.

"Not as they drew it," she said. "They copied without knowing warning from welcome. This one means water is not owed to liars. This one means children sleep inside the middle ring. This one means a messenger died and the road should be fed salt before anyone passes."
Dandelion swallowed. "And they used it for transport scheduling."
"They used graves as milestones," Asha said.
That quieted even Zoltan.

The cabinet's lower drawer stuck. I pulled once. It did not move. I pulled again, harder than necessary, and the mark in my palm heated as if old metal had spoken through the handle. Ciri's hand landed on my wrist.
Not stopping. Present.
"Let someone else," she said.
The words should have irritated me. They did. But under the irritation sat relief. My hand opened before I could make pride into policy.
Ves used a knife and two thin picks. "Drawers lie. They lie less under women who have opened pay chests in occupied towns."
Roche had trained her well, or she had survived him well. The drawer came free with a dry click and a smell of cedar, smoke, and hair.
Inside lay seven envelopes tied with white thread.

White thread. Not black. That was the insult. Black Ink used black for transfer, risk, correction, and field custody. White thread was for family memoranda, personal assurance, mercy language, anything an office wanted to smell less like theft.
The top envelope read HELENA M., charitable extraction irregularity.
My body made no dramatic movement. No growl. No crimson flare. No blade half-drawn. That would have been easier to bear. Instead my breathing became careful. Too careful. The room heard it.
Triss reached for the envelope, then stopped. "Jack?"
"Open it."
She did.

It contained no new secret. Two receipts for bandages. A list of kitchen stores seized after the raid. A note from a quartermaster complaining that the military protector had damaged three doors and one officer before termination. A child's blanket described as contaminated textile, retained pending identification. A hair ribbon marked female domestic article, not strategically relevant.
Asha took the ribbon from the sheet of protective paper.
Her fingers shook once.

I had seen Asha through fire stories, Jacob's proof, and every northern word that made her people smaller. I had not seen this. The ribbon was narrow, smoke-darkened, and frayed where someone had cut it with a knife too dull to deserve the dead.
"She wore it when she baked," Asha said.

Four words. The archive became smaller because of them: a woman in a kitchen, flour on her hands, heat behind her, a baby close enough to smell bread. Not bearer-class adult female. A woman who baked.

I stepped back from the table. My heel struck a box. It toppled. Papers slid across lime dust. Geralt moved and stopped himself. That was the kindest thing he could have done, and I hated that I knew it.

Yennefer picked up the fallen sheets. Her face had gone white in the old cold way. "This set cross-references a later inventory. Someone reviewed household objects after the raid and separated them by emotional utility."
"Emotional utility," Ciri said.
There was no royal voice in her then. Only witness.
"Objects useful for inducing compliance," Yennefer read. "Objects useful for witness destabilization. Objects suitable for false kinship reconstruction."
False kinship.
The phrase entered the room and found Geralt.
He flinched so little a human would have missed it. I did not. His eyes went to the papers, then to me, and all the years between us seemed suddenly made of the same white thread.
"Do not," I said.
"I wasn't."
"You were."
"Yes."
He had learned that from me, perhaps. Or I from him. A clean yes in a filthy room.
Ciri tied the envelope again with fingers too steady to be calm. "We take this."
"Evidence," Triss said.
"No," Ciri answered. "Witness. Evidence is what they call it when they think the dead belong to the room that labels them."
Triss looked at the ribbon, then at me. "Yes. Witness."
The archive gave us one more drawer before it tried to kill us.
That drawer contained only a list of names.

Not long. Eleven entries. Three crossed out. Four marked unconfirmed. One beside Asha's old service name. One beside a woman called Ilde of the Southern Gate. One beside a boy who had been paid for silence in sugared figs.

The last entry read: S. Veyrane, junior review, present but not active during field closure. Recommendation: retain for future doctrine development. Displays unusual calm during infant-continuity discussion.
There he was.
Not yet the monster behind the desk. A young man in a room where my mother had been reduced to inventory, marked for promotion because he had not looked away.

That was the true age of the hunt. The office had failed to recover an infant, failed to identify Asha, failed to understand the golden interruption, then preserved the failure as method. Years later, my contracts, wounds, witnesses, field effects, and name had taught the old method where to point.
I had not become interesting in Part I. I had become locatable.
We stole well for nearly six minutes.
Then the ceiling creaked.
Not old wood. Weight.

Geralt moved first because old wolves begin before speeches. Ves, who had arrived without ceremony at the same time as the threat above, came through the stair with a knife in one hand and the expression of a woman about to improve a room by reducing its occupants. She looked from Geralt to Roche's countermark on the stolen permits.
"Roche says your bard makes too much noise."
Dandelion straightened. "Roche wounds from afar. Cowardly and efficient."

The first watcher dropped from the trap in the ceiling with a hand crossbow and sincere confidence. Confidence is useful right until it meets people who have survived longer than the plan. Ves struck my shoulder with the flat of her hand, not asking, not warning, just moving the most important target out of a quarrel with mathematics. The bolt struck the brick where my throat had been and broke with a small sound that changed the room.

I was too slow. I knew it as my boots slid in lime dust and my left hand went for a Sign that my body refused to shape. The mark in my palm heated, eager in the ugly way of wounds that think they are doors.
"No," I said, to my hand more than the man.

The second intruder came through the stair. Geralt took him into the wall. Zoltan threw a stool with such professional hatred that the stool became briefly heroic. Yennefer raised a ward over the table. Triss snatched the copy packet to her chest and ducked as a second bolt cracked against the ward and fell smoking to the floor.
Ciri was already moving.

She did not save me cleanly. Nothing about it was graceful enough for song. She kicked the first man's knee sideways, took a cut across her sleeve for the trouble, and caught his wrist before the blade meant for my bandaged hand found it. I saw the blade too late. Again. There are humiliations that repeat because they have learned your address.
Ciri drove the man's hand into the table edge. Bone made a noise paper should not hear.
"You missed that," she said.
"Yes."
"Good answer. Bad habit."

Geralt looked at my face once and went back to violence. That was kindness. The third intruder tried to burn the cabinet. Asha caught the thrown bottle in the edge of her scarf, twisted, and sent it into a bucket of lime water. The hiss filled the room with a stink sharp enough to make even the tannery seem polite.

When the last man fell, the archive did not look more dramatic. That irritated me. Blood on lime dust, split shelves, a dead rat still refusing involvement, papers scattered under boots. Crimes rarely choose stages worth the pain they caused.

The tied clerk behind the cabinet was alive, gagged, and terrified enough to smell of vinegar and cheap wool. His name was Ossen Birt. He had soft hands, a bald crown, and the exhausted morality of a man who had chosen paper because swords were too honest.
"I only indexed transfers," he said after Ves cut the gag.
"That sentence begins many hangings," Zoltan told him.
Ossen swallowed. "I can identify the courier distortion. It is not only Temerian. It is old royal resistance work, used to move fugitives through hostile inspection. Someone repurposed it."
Ves went colder. "How many?"
"Nine this month. Medical chests. Legal cases. Relic lots. One livestock certificate, though I suspect there was no livestock."
Geralt looked at me. We were all thinking of ventilation crates at Broken Crown.
"What did the livestock certificate carry?" I asked.
Ossen looked at the floor. "Manacles. Padded. Sized for wrists. Built for panic."
The room did not change temperature. It only felt as if it had.
Ciri stood. "Roche. Now."
