"At dawn," Ves said. "The road is watched, the bridge is bought, and the patrol captain believes his own honesty, which makes him dangerous after dark."
Ciri's eyes sharpened. "You give orders well."
"I survived men who gave worse."
That ended the argument because it was not argument. It was credential.
Ves did not take us to Roche by the direct road.

She took us through a country that had learned to survive by looking less alive than it was. A field left fallow because planted grain attracted tax riders. A shrine with no icon inside, only a chipped cup and three folded scraps of paper that men kissed before pretending not to. A ruined toll gate where someone had carved the Temerian lily under the crossbeam so low only a child or a wounded man would notice.

Roche's people moved through such places like mice with knives. Not glamorous. Not clean. Effective. A woman selling turnips gave Ves a sack with two real turnips and one sealed tube. A boy with a lame dog counted our horses, looked at Buck, and adjusted the count downward on the principle that no sane officer would list that animal as transport. At a burned cider press, an old man spat into the road after hearing Ciri's cover name and then gave us directions he claimed were worthless.
"He knows who I am," Ciri said when we had passed.
"Likely," Ves replied.
"And still helped."
"He hates Nilfgaard, Redania, taxes, rheumatism, and whoever last stole his ladder. The order changes by weather. Today Black Ink is high enough to be useful."
Ciri looked back once. "That is not loyalty."
"No. Loyalty is expensive. Resentment is common coin. Spend what the road offers."

Roche had trained a country to be practical after losing the right to be proud in public. That made the meeting harder. I had little patience for patriot speeches. I had more trouble with widows who hid messages in turnips because the alternative was letting men with clean boots decide who counted as cargo.
At a creek crossing, Ves stopped and crouched by a boot mark half-filled with water. Geralt saw it a breath later. I saw it third and disliked that ranking.
"Pilgrim," Ves said.
"Too much heel," Geralt answered. "Soldier pretending."
I knelt beside the print. Mud had taken the sole pattern clearly: repaired outer edge, stitched arch, one nail newer than the rest. "Same as the archive second stair."
"Yes," Ves said.
Ciri's gaze moved to the road ahead. "We are being pulled."
"Everything is a pull if someone wants you impatient," Ves said.
The answer should have slowed me. It did not slow me enough.

A mile later we found the first sign of the transport: not a cart, not manacles, only a child's mitten pressed into mud beside the old road. Brown wool, patched twice, one thumb torn. Small enough to fit inside a fist and heavy enough to steer mine.
I picked it up before anyone could tell me not to.
The mark in my palm warmed through the wool.
Geralt said my name.
"Do not start," I said.
Ves looked at the mitten, then at me. Her voice did not soften, "Objects are bait when placed cleanly in dirty roads."
"It could be real."
"Good bait often is."
I knew that. I knew it with every road scar I owned. But knowing a child's mitten can be bait does not make leaving it in mud feel like wisdom. It makes wisdom smell cowardly for three breaths.
Ciri took the mitten from my hand.
I let her.
Again, the letting cost more than the taking.
"We carry it," she said. "We do not let it carry us."
Ves watched the exchange and gave a short nod. Not approval. Adjustment. She had moved me, in whatever inner map she kept, from liability to liability with handles.
"Now you are ready to meet Roche," she said.
"That was a test?"
"No. Tests are for instructors and fools. That was road behavior."
The mitten went into Ciri's pouch. I did not ask for it back.
That was, irritatingly, progress.

By midnight, Triss had made three sets of copies. Yennefer had burned the discarded scrap in a blue flame that left no ash. Geralt repaired two straps, a torn glove, and Buck's bridle buckle after I told him twice the buckle was fine. Buck bit no one, which either meant discipline or contempt too deep for expression.
I slept for one hour in a chair by the door with Jacob's hilt under my coat and the living chamber page sealed in Triss's copy packet, not mine.
Ciri noticed.
Good, I thought before sleep took me.
Let the page have witnesses.
Sleep did not keep me long.

The archive followed me into sleep as shelving. I dreamed of Helena's ribbon filed beside compliance, Jacob's hilt under compromised military material, Asha crossed out as if survival were an accounting error. Each box had my name on it. When I opened them, the labels changed to other names: Ciri, Geralt, Triss, Yennefer, Tavin, Mara, Rian, Miro, Peire, Calver. Everyone near me had become easier to store.
I woke with my hand around the hilt of my knife and Ciri sitting across from me in the dark.
"Bad dream?" she asked.
"Boring one. Shelves."
"That sounds worse."
"It was."

The room above the cooper's yard had three pallets, two stools, and a roof that translated rain into arguments. Zoltan slept with one axe under his hand and one boot on stolen papers. Geralt watched the window. Yennefer was absent in the way only she could make structural. Triss slept with ink on two fingers. Asha did not sleep at all.
Ciri had Helena's ribbon in her lap.
I noticed before I could decide whether noticing hurt. "Why?"
"Because you looked at it as if it might vanish if no one else held it."
"It is not yours to hold."
"No. That is why I am holding it carefully."
I put the knife down.

"When I was young," she said, "people preserved things from places I lost. Dresses, toys, pieces of courts, letters, names. They meant kindness. Often it felt like being asked to thank them for making a museum of a room I could no longer enter."
"Then why hold it?"
"Because not everything preserved is theft. Sometimes someone keeps watch until the owner decides whether memory is object, wound, or firewood."
The rain worked on the roof. The words worked elsewhere.
"What would you do with it?" I asked.
"With this? Nothing. It is not mine. With the men who labeled it? Several things Yennefer would call imprecise."
"Yennefer would not complain about imprecision if the pain was educational."
Ciri looked toward the shadow where Yennefer was not and almost smiled. "True."
Geralt spoke from the window. "Street below. Two men. One pretending to piss, one watching the pretending."
Asha stood. Ves was already awake. I had not heard her wake because I had not heard her sleep. That was the sort of thing that should have disturbed me more than it did.

The two men below did not attack. They changed the room around the choice. One nailed a notice to the cooper's door, then limped away with the careful speed of someone paid by distance. Ves brought the paper up with tongs, because Roche's people had survived long enough to respect petty poison.
No seal. No signature. Only a line written in a narrow hand.
Return stolen family effects for preservation under neutral care.
Neutral care.
Asha made a sound like cloth tearing.
Triss took the notice, looked once, and burned only the edges until the center remained. "They know which objects moved."
"Ossen?" Zoltan asked.
"Maybe," Ves said. "Or the archive was never blind."
Yennefer came back through the wall that was apparently a door if one was arrogant enough. "It was not blind. It was baited to measure what we valued."
Geralt looked at me. He did not say calm. He had learned.
The notice in Triss's hand curled slowly inward.
I wanted to go back to the tannery and burn every box until the city coughed my family into the sky. The want was clean, bright, and stupid. Clean wants often are.
Ciri held out the ribbon.
I took it.

The mark in my palm did not heat. The barbed star at my throat did not cool. Nothing ancient answered. Only cloth against skin, dry and frayed, smelling faintly of smoke under Triss's preservation spell.
"They wanted to learn whether you could be pulled by objects," Ciri said.
"They learned."
"No," she said. "They learned you can be hurt by them. Not the same."
The distinction mattered enough to keep me in the room.
By dawn, Ossen Birt had given us four more names and one warning. He did it after Ves placed the burned notice in front of him and Roche's countermark beside it.
"There is a man above Veyrane," he said.
"Name," Yennefer said.

Ossen shook his head. "No. Not above in rank. Above in convenience. The senior examiner carries the doctrine, but the doctrine is useful because everyone wants a piece of it. Courts want safety. Churches want meaning. Mages want classification. Soldiers want weapons. Families want their grief returned with a face. Veyrane survives by never seeming to want anything for himself."
"Everyone wants something," Ciri said.
Ossen looked at the notice. "He wants the moment a person accepts a cage because rejecting it would hurt someone else. He calls that proof of suitability."
The room held still.
That was Sorel Veyrane before I met him: not a man who built chains first, but one who waited for love to make the first link and then offered to standardize the rest.
Sorel Veyrane received the news in a clean room above a customs office that had never touched cargo.

Cleanliness suited him. Not luxury. His desk held six sharpened pens, a slate, a glass of water, and three objects removed before our arrival: a second copy of the living chamber rejection, a rubbing of Helena's clasp, and a scrap of blue thread mislabeled domestic textile fragment.
Merrow stood before him with one bandaged hand.
"They took the family effects," Merrow said.
"Not all."
"Enough."

Sorel lifted the blue thread with tweezers and set it in a small dish. He did not smile. Smiling was theatrical. Theatrical men were easy to dislike, and being disliked too clearly reduced usefulness.

"Enough to update attachment hierarchy," he said. "Mother marker first. Protector marker second. Child relic retained. Ciri's presence altering leverage rather than merely increasing risk. Geralt's restraint phrase still relevant. Objects wound him. They do not yet govern him."
Merrow's mouth tightened. "You expected theft."

"Theft is what frightened institutions call unauthorized correction." Sorel adjusted the thread so it lay straight. "They did not steal randomly. Random grief resists modeling. Ordered grief can be respected, then used."
"Respected."
"Yes. Do not confuse contempt with discipline. Contempt is lazy. These people are dangerous because they can love efficiently."
Merrow did not answer. He had learned that Sorel's gentlest sentences often carried the sharpest hooks.

On the desk lay a report for the chapel granary not yet performed, because Sorel's office drafted possible outcomes before bodies obliged. It had three columns: voluntary approach, hostile extraction, relational intervention. Under the third, someone had written probability increasing.
Sorel tapped that column once.

"Do not try to break the witcher by pain," he said. "Pain creates spectacle and shortens cooperation. Do not threaten the empress-designate directly. That creates banners. Do not provoke Geralt of Rivia unless you require an instructional massacre. Standardize love into compliance. Make the persons around him appear safer when he is nearer a cage."
Merrow's eyes lifted. "Use children."
"You object?"
"I ask for clarity."

"Good. Clarity saves lives when administered early." Sorel folded his hands. "The child must survive, be seen, and ask the correct question in the correct hearing. If Morningstar refuses a frightened child, he becomes selfish. If he accepts the metaphor, he becomes useful. If he loses temper, he becomes public risk. Each outcome has value."
Outside, a bell marked the hour. Sorel waited until the sound ended. He disliked competing with bells. They were too fond of certainty.
"And Cazren?" Merrow asked.
"Let him sing."
"He is unstable."

"So is fire. We continue using it because it cooks, warms, and reveals smoke paths. Brother Cazren will go where documents cannot. Poor rooms. Hungry mouths. Dreams that want permission to become doctrine. We will not endorse him. We will not stop him while his noise maps what our papers cannot."
Merrow looked at the blue thread. "And if Morningstar comes here?"
For the first time, Sorel looked almost sad.
"Then I will ask him whether he has noticed how many people are safer when he is near a cage."
He wrote one line on a fresh sheet, sanded it, and set it aside for later correction.
Subject displays probable vulnerability to custody framed as protection of others. Relational network not to be broken directly. Convert love into procedure where possible.
Vernon Roche had chosen a country without a throne and wore the permanent expression of a man expecting someone to send him the bill.

He waited in a ruined counting house two miles from the old road to Tretogor, on ground that had been Temerian, Redanian, Nilfgaardian, and briefly owned by deserters who discovered that collecting tolls required more arithmetic than stabbing. The counting house still had a stone strongroom, cracked floor tiles, and a painted lily hidden under soot where someone had tried to erase it without kneeling. Roche had not cleaned it. Some marks deserved to remain half-buried and stubborn.

Geralt entered first with rain on his cloak and suspicion in his boots. That was polite, by Roche's standards. I followed, then Ciri under a plain hood, Yennefer, Triss, Asha, and Ves, who had been outside checking whether anyone had remembered to be stupid. Zoltan remained with the horses because the road beyond the counting house had opinions about wheels. Dandelion had been forbidden to come and had therefore come halfway, then been intercepted by Priscilla with more sense and better timing.
Roche saw Ciri and did not bow too deeply. Men who bow too deeply to young women with too many titles usually hope the angle hides the knife in their sleeve.
"Highness," he said.
"Roche."
"This room has leaks, rats, and no imperial furniture. I apologize only for the rats."
"The rats are probably more honest than furniture."
"Temeria agrees."

I looked around. Door, window, ceiling gap, strongroom hinge, Ves's position, Geralt's distance, Ciri's sightline, Yennefer's left hand, Triss's satchel, Roche's boots. The room had five exits if a man did not insist on dignity, three if he did, and none if Yennefer decided the count offended her.
Roche watched me do it. "You trained him," he said to Geralt.
"Some."
"Vesemir hid him."
"Yes."
"And now everyone with a stamp wants him."
"Yes."
Roche grunted. "That is what happens when you let the state learn a noun."
Ciri removed her hood. "Black Ink is using Temerian corridors."
"So Ves said. Show me."

Triss spread out false transit orders, resistance countermarks, wax impressions, legal phrasing, and Ossen's livestock certificate. She did not over-explain. Many mages speak as if the world has been waiting for their footnotes. Triss spoke like someone who had learned frightened people needed the sharp end first.
Roche did not begin with permits. He began with boots.

Ves placed three pairs on the table. The first belonged to a courier: soles wrapped for silence, front leather polished, back leather cracked. A man who expected to be seen from ahead and forgotten from behind. The second were pilgrim boots, muddy above black soldier stitching. The third were small, padded on the inside, with leather loops hidden near the ankle.
Ciri's face did not change. "For restraints."
"For making restraints look like transport care," Ves said. "A child, an old woman, a wounded mage, or a man someone has decided should arrive unmarked."
"My size?" I asked.
"No," Ves said. "Smaller."
That made the room colder than yes would have.

Roche took one false permit and laid it beside the boots. "A defeated country keeps two governments. The one that signs where the victor points, and the one that remembers where the dead are buried. Sometimes they help each other. Sometimes they sell each other for flour. If Black Ink is using our quiet roads, it is not because Temeria invited them as a state. Temeria has no clean state left. It is because our old tricks have value to new cowards."
"You make compromise sound like disease," Yennefer said.
"It spreads through necessity. That is close enough."
Ciri looked at him. "You chose compromise."

"Yes." Roche did not make the mistake of dressing the word. "Temeria under vassal settlement, not ashes. Old colors in cupboards, not fields. Taxes paid to men we used to kill. Boys alive because their fathers swallowed pride until it lodged somewhere permanent. I do not regret saving what could be saved. I regret what the saving taught people to accept."
Ciri did not flinch. "Good. Then you remain useful."
Roche almost smiled. "Your father says similar things with better gloves."
"My father owns too many gloves."
"Emperors do. They dislike fingerprints."
Geralt looked at the floor because the room had too many fathers in it already.

I had said nothing. Roche noticed. Quiet men in political rooms are either bored, ignorant, or counting exits. I was counting the ways men explained necessary harm and deciding which explanations deserved to remain alive.
"You dislike this," Roche said.
"I dislike how often men say necessary after the harm is done."
"Before harm, necessary is prediction. After, defense."
"You comfortable with that?"
"No. Comfort is for people who chose less." He leaned over the table. "But if you want clean hands, witcher, wash them before touching history. It will not help. History stains through soap."
Geralt glanced between us. "Roche."
"What?"
"Less charm."
"This is my charm."
"Explains the wars."
Ves snorted despite herself.

Triss unfolded the map. "These transit routes cross three places where Black Ink could move people or objects without standard inspection: Old Alder Ford, the chapel granary near Dravik, and a ferry at Marna's Bend. Which one carries manacles?"
"All could."
"Which one would you use?" Ciri asked.

Roche pointed without hesitation. "The chapel granary. Men think chapels are watched by gods and therefore forget cart doors. Also the priest there is dead, the replacement drinks, and the grain tithe records are so badly kept a dragon could be logged as rye if it wore a sack."
Asha's face did not change at dragon. Saesenthessis was absent to object. The absence felt briefly amused.

Ves moved beside the map. "One altered mark went through a charity tied to war widows. Same charity Zoltan found. Same wax. Same clove-black compound. The courier making the last transfer wore a pilgrim badge with a blackened crown scratched on the back."
"Cult," Yennefer said.
"Or someone using cult marks to make Black Ink look less tidy," Triss said.
"Both can be true," I said.
Roche nodded once. "That is the sort of answer that gets men killed and investigations moving."

We went to the strongroom because Ves insisted the real reason for meeting was proof, not talk. Roche unlocked three bolts, removed a fourth that had not been installed by the original builder, and lifted a floor stone with Geralt's help. Beneath lay a tin box wrapped in oilcloth and a child's old cloak patched at the elbows.
"We hide things in what inspectors find sentimental," Ves said. "They dislike touching poor children's clothes. Makes their hands remember they have hands."

Inside the box were permits, wax impressions, and six names. Four clerks. One courier. One priest: Cazren of the Red Step, formerly attached to an Eternal Fire fringe house, removed for doctrinal fever after the pyres cooled.
"Cazren," Yennefer said. "Pamphlets. Apocalypse sermons. He claimed the White Frost did not end because Ciri saved the world, but because the world had been granted time to prepare for judgment."
Ciri rolled her eyes in a way that made her look younger and more tired at once. "How generous of judgment."
"He disappeared after Novigrad's sermon houses became unfashionable," Triss said.
Roche folded the permit. "Men like that do not disappear. They discover basements."
A pilgrim badge lay under the names. A simple crown, burned black at the points. Beneath it, in a poor hand, someone had scratched five words.
My palm tightened.
Ciri saw and came closer. "Do not."
"I didn't."
"You started."
Roche looked at us because tact had never been his favorite weapon. "Started what?"
"Becoming useful to the wrong sentence," Ciri said.
The counting house chose a fine silence to display its leaks.
We rode for the chapel granary before noon.

That was my mistake. Roche wanted two scouts first. Ves wanted a night watch and a false cart. Geralt wanted both. I wanted the manacles removed from the road before another pair of small boots found them. Righteous impatience is still impatience. It dresses better and kills with cleaner hands.

Ves made the impatience pay toll before it reached the granary. At Old Alder Ford, a rope crossed the track under the supervision of three men with pilgrim badges, one county seal, and the bored confidence of people who had been told legality would arrive after obedience. Their cart had fever marks painted on the side. The horse did not sweat enough for the load it claimed to carry.

Roche did not draw a sword. He gave the first man a transit order with the wrong date and watched him accept it too quickly. Ves walked behind the cart, cut one rear tie with a knife no larger than a woman's comb, and let the canvas sag just enough to show padded loops inside.
"Empty," the guard said.
"So are many heads," Roche replied. "We still inspect them when they block roads."

The cart held no child. Only restraints, drug cloth, two gray cloaks, and a ledger page naming the chapel granary as rest point instead of destination. That was worse than finding the captive there. It meant the road had stations. It meant the granary was not one crime but a room inside a method.

Ciri looked at me after Ves folded the ledger scrap. She did not say I told you. That was one of her sharper mercies. Geralt tightened Buck's girth twice, which meant he wanted to say the same thing and had chosen leather instead.

We found the granary empty enough to prove it was not empty. Old wheat dust lay thick on the floor. One cart stood under the loft with straw over its bed. The straw smelled of vinegar, fear, and iron. A painted saint watched from the wall with the bored expression of a man who had been asked to bless too much trade.
"Too quiet," Geralt said.
"I know."
I did not.

The first crossbow fired from the saint's mouth. Not a metaphor. Someone had cut a slit through the painted lips and set a spring behind the plaster. The bolt struck my shoulder guard hard enough to spin me. Pain flashed down my arm. I lost the Sign I had shaped. Ciri dragged a child from under the cart before I understood there had been a child to drag.
Small. Drugged. Breathing. Wrists bruised where padded restraints had lied about kindness.

The floor opened under Ves. She caught the edge with one hand. Roche shot the man below without looking proud of the accuracy. Yennefer turned the saint's wall inside out. Triss threw a barrier over the child as a glass bulb burst green against it. Geralt went up the ladder two rungs at a time and came down with a man who regretted having bones.
I had gone for the wrong shadow.

One pilgrim-cloaked guard slipped past me with the child's carrying strap. I caught his sleeve, missed his wrist, and took a knife across the ribs. Panic is not always loud. Sometimes it is the discovery that your body has become one heartbeat slower than your intent. He would have opened my side if Buck had not come through the granary door like an ugly law of nature.
No one had invited Buck. Buck had studied invitation at Kaer Morhen and rejected the philosophy.
He struck the guard in the back, sent him face-first into the cart wheel, and then tried to bite the saint.
"Bad saint," I told him, because speech was easier than admitting my hands were shaking.
Roche looked at the child, then at me. "This is why scouts go first."
I deserved the cut in the sentence. "Yes."
"Do not waste the lesson by bleeding dramatically."
"I will bleed with restraint."
"Try competence. It saves cloth."

The child woke before dusk. A boy, seven perhaps, with brown hair shaved badly to hide lice and eyes too calm for safety. His name was Tavin. He had been taken from a widow's house two roads west, carried as fever cargo, and told he was going to be made useful. He did not know to whom. He did know the phrase sung by the men who fed him drugged milk.
The red door walks.

Ciri sat with him while he ate. Not as princess. Not as future ruler. As someone who understood what happened when children became roads for older appetites. She did not touch him without asking. That mattered. He watched her hand longer than her face.
"Are they coming back?" he asked.
"Not the same men," Ciri said.
"Others?"
She did not lie. "We are making that harder."
Tavin looked at me. "Are you the door?"
Every adult in the granary stopped breathing for the smallest practical moment.
I crouched. My ribs hurt. My shoulder hurt. The mark in my palm was quiet. I disliked that more.
"No," I said.
Tavin studied me with the ruthless seriousness of children who have received too much truth too early. "They said doors say that before they open."
I had no clever line. Good. Cleverness would have made the boy carry more of what belonged to men who had hurt him.
"Then I will keep saying it," I told him, "and you keep not believing every hungry man who teaches doors grammar."
He considered. "Can I have more bread?"
"Yes."
Best answer I had given all day.
Tavin's mother came after dark.

She did not run into the granary weeping, which songs would have preferred. She came with a woodcutter's hatchet in one hand, two neighbors behind her, and terror packed so tightly into her face that there was no room left for tears. Her name was Mela. Widow. Weaver when there was work. Washer of soldiers' shirts when there was not. Woman who had given a child fever syrup from a charity cart because the man pouring it wore a pilgrim badge and spoke gently.
The first thing she did was strike the man Roche had kept alive.
Not hard enough to kill. Hard enough to make his lip split and his eyes learn something about consequences. Roche let it happen once. Ves stopped the second blow.
"He answers first," Ves said. "Then you may hate him more accurately."
Mela's hand shook around the hatchet. "He carried my boy."
The prisoner spat blood. "I carried fever cargo."
Mela made a sound. Not grief. Not rage. The place between.

I moved before thinking. Wrong direction. Toward the prisoner, not the mother. My body chose the throat holding the phrase, because host, cargo, asset, door, all such words had begun wearing the same face. The mark in my palm heated. The prisoner saw me coming and smiled with red teeth.
There. The trap opening.
Ciri stepped into my path and struck me in the chest with her palm.
Not hard. Enough.
"Wrong target," she said.
Every person in the granary heard it.
So did I.
The shame came hot. Better than crimson. Cleaner than power. It forced breath back into the body I had almost given to someone else's report.
I turned to Mela.
She stared at me with hatred that had no time to decide whether I deserved any of it. "Are you why they took him?"
Best answer would have been no. Accurate answer was uglier.
"Partly," I said.
Geralt's head turned. Ciri did not stop me. Good.

"They wanted a child who could ask me a question in front of witnesses. They wanted his fear to make a handle. That does not make me guilty of taking him. It does make me part of the shape that brought them here."
Mela looked as if I had given her a stone and called it bread.
"I don't care for shapes," she said. "I care that he was gone."
"Yes."
She hated that answer too, but it gave her nowhere false to stand.

Tavin called for her from behind Ciri. Not loudly. The drug still owned most of him. Mela dropped the hatchet so quickly it cut straw, then crossed the floor and stopped two feet from her son because fear of hurting him had become stronger than need to touch.
Ciri spoke softly. "Ask him."
Mela's mouth moved before sound came. "Can I?"
Tavin nodded.
Only then did she take him.

I had seen battles end with less consequence than that embrace. No music. No bright restoration. The boy stiff at first, then shaking. The mother holding too tightly, realizing it, loosening, crying without face enough left to hide it. Around them, Roche's men looked at walls. Ves cleaned her knife. Geralt watched me watch them and said nothing, which was mercy of the older kind.
Triss examined the drug vial from the cart. "Not poison. Sleep-milk, poppy, fever bitter, and something to make memory uneven."
"Can you fix it?" Mela asked.
"Some. Not all tonight."
Mela nodded as if partial mercy was still a luxury. "Then fix some."
Yennefer had found the transport ledger in a false-bottom grain bin. She opened it and read with the expression of a woman adding names to a private weather system.
"There are three more soft transport trials planned. One child, one wounded veteran, one suspected mage with no guild registration. All routed under charitable fever cargo."
Roche swore softly.
"Where?" Ciri asked.
Yennefer showed her.

That changed the night. We did not celebrate rescue. Rescue was one boy. The ledger was three doors still opening. Roche sent riders before moonrise. Ves took two. Geralt wanted to go and did not because someone had to keep me from following every road at once. That realization sat badly between us.
Mela stayed until Triss finished with Tavin. Before leaving, she came to me. Tavin slept against her shoulder.
"He asked if you were the door," she said.
"Yes."
"What are you?"
I looked at the child. No cleverness came. Good.
"Late," I said.
Mela's eyes hardened. "Be earlier next time."
She left before I could answer.
Roche watched the door close. "Widows improve most briefings."
"That was not a briefing."
"No. It was a sentence. Try serving it usefully."
I wanted to dislike him for that. I managed for perhaps five seconds.

By dawn, two of Roche's riders returned. One planned transport had been abandoned. One handler had been taken. The suspected mage had fled before anyone reached her, which meant fear had been faster than rescue and perhaps saved her life. The wounded veteran was found in a barn with fever and a false saint medal in his mouth. He lived. Barely.
The third rider did not return.
Roche said nothing for a long time.
Then he folded the map, placed one finger on the Saint Mered mark, and said, "Cazren."
The name had become less rumor than direction.
Recovered Black Ink field summary, chapel granary incident:

Unauthorized interference by Temerian residual cells, witcher-associated parties, and imperial-adjacent principal disrupted soft transport trial. Child test subject recovered by hostile actors. Subject Morningstar displayed slowed response under decoy pressure, possibly fatigue, wound response, or relational distraction. Animal interference repeated. Recommend equine classification review elevated from humorous to operational.
I was not in Saint Mered's basement when Cazren fed hunger a hymn.

Dandelion and Priscilla told us the shape of it later, each correcting the other's account in ways that proved memory is less a window than a room two people fight to furnish. Zoltan supplied the parts involving doors, horses, and the exact weight of the ledger under Priscilla's arm. He claimed such details are where truth lives. Dandelion claimed truth lives in cadence. Priscilla said both men should stop treating truth as a rented room and let it breathe.
I believed her version most.

Brother Cazren had learned, while still a priest of the Eternal Fire's outer kitchens, that hungry people listened better when the sermon smelled of bread. The trick was not kindness. Kindness gives food away and asks the soul to follow if it wishes. Cazren preferred lentils under salt, black rye, watered beer, and a room warm enough to make poverty feel briefly chosen. Men who came for food stayed for heat. Women who came for heat stayed because their sons had bad dreams. Boys who came to mock stayed because mockery is easier before a preacher names fear in a voice that does not tremble.

He had been removed from three proper pulpits and two improper ones. The first after suggesting fire did not purify enough if the world kept producing the same rot. The second after calling Radovid's death proof that kings burned poorly unless opened first. The third after a canon with soft hands told him apocalypse fatigue was not doctrine. Cazren thanked him, stole his candle money, and discovered basements.

The basement beneath Saint Mered's abandoned almshouse was excellent. Low ceiling. Good acoustics. Two exits. One dry wall for scripture. A storeroom where donated flour could be weighed beside names. A saint with ledgers was better than a saint with miracles. Miracles could not be audited.

By dusk, thirty-three people had gathered there. War widows. Dock men. Former witch hunters with insignia removed and habits intact. Two girls from a laundry who had dreamed of red stone and woken with ash on their tongues. A cooper whose son had frozen during the White Frost and who hated every survivor of prophecy with a fairness no theologian could improve. Three men who wanted violence and had learned to kneel first because kneeling made violence look like service.

There was also Old Rusk, though no one called him old to his face because he still carried barrels with one shoulder lower than the other and pride enough to make youth look wasteful. His daughter had survived the Frost and returned from a shelter speaking in half-sentences about green fire, dead horses, and a woman with ashen hair. After that, a tax man took their room for arrears and a healer charged him twice for herbs that did not work. Rusk did not need a doctrine. He needed someone to say the world had not been meaningless when it ate his child by inches.

Cazren gave him that. Not truth, exactly. A shape. Poor rooms forgive bad shapes when good ones have never arrived. The former witch hunters liked the talk of judgment. The widows liked the bread. Rusk liked that the sermon did not ask him to stop hating courts, mages, soldiers, or anyone saved by prophecy while his own table went cold. That made him dangerous because he was not stupid. Only hungry for sense.
Cazren fed them lentils. Then he let them smell the red candles.

Not ordinary tallow. Ordinary tallow comforts. These had been mixed with powdered rust, fake dragon-bone, ash from burned court records, and one black scale bought from a man who lied about draconid origin with such confidence the lie deserved respect. The candles smoked dark at the wick and red along the gutter. They made the room look wounded.

On the table lay the ledger. Names. Debts. Dreams. Witnesses. Phrases repeated across unrelated mouths: red door, walking chamber, crown under stone, hinge in blood, wolf with a throat of iron, mother of ash, father with broken sword.
Cazren had not invented all of them. Invention is for poets. Revelation is for men skilled at organizing what frightened people already bring.
"You have seen the sign," he said.
The room leaned toward him. Bodies have more honest theology than mouths.
"Not in temples. The gods do not always choose temples. Temples have schedules, roof fees, clerks, and broom cupboards full of arguments about candle wax. Judgment has better taste."
A small ripple of laughter moved through the hungry. Cazren smiled gently because hunger likes being allowed to laugh before being told it is holy.

"You have seen it in dreams, in cracked walls, in the way your children wake speaking names they never learned, in beasts hollowed from within, in the red wolf walking roads men with titles pretend are safe."
A woman near the back began to weep. Cazren accepted the tear as if he had minted it.
Dandelion and Priscilla watched through a gap above the stair. They had come for a ledger, not a sermon. Unfortunately sermons, like lice, rarely ask permission before making a body their country.
"He is setting the refrain," Priscilla whispered.

Dandelion had heard battle songs, tavern songs, coronation hymns, gutter rhymes, lullabies, funeral pieces, and the sort of ballad that makes people mistake regret for romance after the third drink. This was stranger. Cazren borrowed from harvest cadence: thresh, turn, lift, breathe. Older than doctrine. More dangerous because the body trusted it before the mind asked who held the flail.
Below, Cazren set down the ladle.
"A door is not guilty for standing in a wall."
A woman whispered, "A door opens."

"Only when taught," Cazren replied. "A hinge is not wicked for bearing weight. A chamber is not cruel for holding what would devour the house. But if a chamber walks, if a door takes flesh, if a hinge bleeds, then judgment has taken mercy by the throat and given us a shape we can follow."
"The red door," someone said.
"The red door walks," Cazren answered.

Dandelion told me later that was the moment the room stopped listening and began belonging. He tried to make the confession sound theatrical. It was not. He looked sick as he said it. Public words becoming chains will do that to a man who has spent his life selling songs and hoping the damage stayed decorative.
"We should leave," he whispered.
"We should steal the ledger," Priscilla whispered back.
"I adore you. Your timing is monstrous."
"That is why you adore me."

The ledger sat on the left table, open beside sacks of charitable flour. Names were written in columns, not merely of those fed, but of dreams reported. Ash tongue. Red stone. Black crown. Wolf with door in ribs. Girl of green fire. Sea beast hollow. Every sorrow marked for future use.

Cazren lifted a blackened crown from the table. Tin or poor iron under soot, hammered by someone with more devotion than skill. The points were uneven. Red candle wax had gathered in the dents like clotted light.

"They will call him risk," Cazren said. "Offices will call him asset. Sorceresses will call him anomaly. Kings will call him jurisdiction. But we will call him by the name the dark taught our dreams."
The room answered before he finished.
"Red door."
"Blood hinge."
"Chamber that walks."
I heard those words later and hated how well they fit the mouth. Bad ideas survive by being singable.
Dandelion descended three steps, then four. Priscilla followed, slate in hand, head down, body moving with the modesty of someone already stealing the room's attention by refusing to request it.
Cazren saw him at once. True fanatics are not fools. Fools are easier and rarely survive into ledgers.
"Inspector," Cazren said.

Dandelion bowed with the irritation of a minor official recognized incorrectly. "Brother. I am here regarding irregular flour movement under charitable exemption, devotional grain allotment, soup thickness, and possible false holiness applied to lentils."
One dock man frowned into his bowl.
Cazren smiled. "We keep careful accounts."
"So did several tyrants. It rarely improved their soup."

Priscilla marked the ledger's distance. Two men near it. One candle. One exit behind hanging cloth. A former witch hunter watched Cazren, not her. Men with old habits watch the loudest man in the room and forget women who move as if permission has already been granted.
Cazren set the crown beside the ledger. "You are not a flour man."
"Few of us are what our hats promise."
"You are a singer."
"Under favorable conditions. These are not."
Recognition moved through the room. It could save or kill depending on who gave it first.

Cazren turned to the crowd. "See how quickly the old world sends ornament to mock hunger. A feather man. A court singer. A friend of white wolves and throne girls. He comes to weigh our bread and steal our words."
Effective. Dandelion hated effective work done by bad men. It made professional disgust hard to separate from moral urgency.
"I steal only when words are mistreated," he said. "These are being beaten in a cellar. I may have to intervene."
A few people laughed. Too few.
Cazren's eyes sharpened. "Tell me then, poet. What does your red wolf call himself when no one sings?"
Dandelion let the silence hold. My name had weight now. Names could lead chains.
"Tired, probably," he said. "Most men being hunted by clerks and candles become tired."
Priscilla moved while he spoke. Three steps left. Downcast eyes. Slate close. One hand near the ledger.
"He is not a man," Cazren said.
There it was. The sentence every enemy eventually finds, the door through which ownership enters wearing different shoes.
Dandelion's performance fell from him.
"Yes," he said, very clearly, "he is. That is what has upset everyone."
The room shifted.
Priscilla took the ledger.

The former witch hunter saw too late. His hand moved. Priscilla's small knife moved first, not to flesh, but to the candle. It toppled into lentils and died with a wet hiss. Darkness broke the room's rhythm.

Dandelion shouted something about flour seizure, doctrinal contamination, and rats in the tithe sack. It was nonsense. Good nonsense. Crowds need shape, and nonsense in official posture can beat panic by three seconds.
They used the three seconds.

Up the stairs. Through the kitchen. Under laundry lines. A boy tried to bar the door and changed his mind when Priscilla gave him one calm look. Dandelion did not ask what expression she used. Some arts are private.
In the alley, Zoltan stood with two horses and the expression of a dwarf who had expected trouble and been offended by its punctuality.
"Got it?"
Priscilla held up the ledger.
"Good. Bard?"
"Insulted, threatened, theologically underestimated. Otherwise radiant."
"Mount. Radiance later."
Behind them, Saint Mered's began to sing again. Louder now. Not because Cazren had recovered control, but because disruption had made belief more vivid. The words followed them over wet stones.
The red door walks.
The blood hinge turns.
Priscilla looked back once. "We did not stop it."
Dandelion heard the crowd and felt the old horror of public words leaving their maker. "No. But we learned the tune."
"Can you break it?"

He thought of Ciri's face when public names got too close, of Geralt reading guilt into straps, of Yennefer's hatred for vessel, of Triss copying chamber until ink became a wound, of me standing in the wrong room too late.
"No," he said. "But I can make people distrust anyone who sings it too cleanly."

They read the stolen ledger in Zoltan's back room above a warehouse where the ceiling leaked in four places and one leak had been assigned a cup with a label. Dandelion objected to the label, which read leak three and implied a bureaucracy of water. Zoltan said water had better administrative discipline than most aldermen and should be encouraged.
Priscilla ignored both and turned pages.
The ledger was worse than the sermon. Sermons admitted hunger. Ledgers organized it. Each name had a debt, a grief, a dream phrase, and a usefulness mark.
Widow with dead son, hears crown in sleep, useful for weeping.
Former guard, knows south gate, useful for transport.
Laundress, two daughters, dreams red horse, useful for women's circle.
Beggar child, repeats hinge rhyme, useful if fed.
Dandelion stopped performing.
"He is scoring sorrow."

"Yes," Priscilla said. "And he understands cadence. People with similar grief receive different phrases, but phrases that complete one another when sung together. He is making a crowd that feels as if it discovered the song itself."
"Can you break that?" Zoltan asked.
"Not by mocking it," Priscilla said. "Mocking hunger makes the hungry defend the man who fed them."
Dandelion touched the ledger with one finger. He had loved audiences all his life. He had rarely respected them and feared failing them. That, he discovered, had been vanity in a better hat.
"Begin," Priscilla said.
So he did, before the door closed.
Dandelion did not begin with mockery.

That was how Priscilla knew he understood the danger. Mockery was his most convenient blade. It glittered, traveled well, and made frightened rooms remember they still had teeth. But Cazren had built his power in hunger. Laughing at hungry people would only teach them to hold the preacher tighter.
So Dandelion began with a work song.

Not pretty. He hated that. The first version had no feather in it, no clever lift for taverns, no turn clever enough to make countesses lean forward. It had boots, bowls, cold hands, and a refrain about men who weighed grief before feeding it.
Priscilla wrote beside him, crossing out every line that made him sound too pleased with himself.
"Too elegant," she said.
"It is one of my burdens."
"Burden someone else. These people have enough."
Zoltan listened from a crate, carving a splinter into something small and violent. "Needs a line about ledgers."
"Every song does not need ledgers."
"This one does. Bastard marked a beggar child useful if fed. Put that in."
Dandelion looked down at the page. The joke did not come.

They worked until the lamp burned low and the warehouse leaks found new cups. First verse for the hungry, so they would not feel mocked. Second verse for the people who fed them while counting. Third verse for the phrase red door, not denying the fear but turning the command sideways.
A door that walks may walk away.
Priscilla underlined that one.
"Good," she said.
"You sound surprised."
"I am always surprised when vanity serves truth without charging extra."
"That is almost romantic."
"Do not test me while I am armed with ink."

By morning, the first singers had it. Not the clean singers. Those would sound purchased. Zoltan chose a docker with a scarred lip, two washerwomen with strong lungs, and a child who could not hold pitch but could hold rhythm better than most priests. They took the song into bread lines and ferry queues, not noble houses. Noble houses received scandal later, when scandal had learned to walk.
The song did not defeat Cazren's hymn.
Songs rarely kill cleanly. They bruise, bother, complicate. A crowd that had begun to belong to one refrain now found another crawling under it like a stubborn root.
The red door walks, Cazren's people sang.
A door that walks may walk away, answered three boys near the fish market.
The blood hinge turns.
Whose hand oils it? asked a woman rinsing laundry with raw knuckles.
The chamber must open.
Ask the man inside, sang a dockhand before laughing as if the line had been his all along.
That was the beginning of doubt. Not noble. Not enough. Enough to make the clean refrain dirtier at the edges.
Cazren heard it before noon.
He smiled.
That was when Priscilla knew he was worse than a fool. Fools hate contradiction. Cazren tasted it and adjusted.

Cazren did not punish the room after the bard fled. Punishment wasted heat. Better to convert embarrassment. He lifted the black crown, stood among spilled lentils, and let the people see he was not angry. Anger would have made him ordinary. Mercy, performed correctly, made him necessary.
"He feared the ledger," Cazren said.
The crowd listened, hungry for humiliation to become meaning.

"He feared what your hands would write. Your dreams. Your dead. Your children waking with ash on their tongues. Why would a court singer fear poor people's pages unless poor people had found the road kings denied?"
A woman whispered, "The red door."
"Yes." Cazren lowered his voice. "The red door walks. But doors are made to open. A door that refuses must be persuaded. A hinge that resists must be oiled with what first made it turn."

In his private pocket lay the page he had not left in the ledger. He was not foolish. Scripture did not live in one book. The page had come from a dream shared by three women, one boy, and a dying draconid whose throat smoked when it opened.
It showed a road east.
It showed a canyon of stars.
It showed a man with red eyes kneeling in black sand while a crown beneath the world breathed through him.
Cazren was wrong about almost everything except the direction.
That made him difficult to kill cleanly.
Cazren sent bread the next morning.

Four baskets appeared at three poor doors, each one wrapped in clean cloth and tied with red thread. No sermon attached. No demand. Only bread, still warm, because he understood timing better than most soldiers. If a rival song taught people to distrust anyone who fed them with too clean a hand, he would feed them before the lesson settled and make hunger argue in his favor.
Inside one basket lay a scrap of vellum.
A door that walks may walk away, it said. Unless the house burns behind it.

Dandelion brought the scrap to us himself. By then we had rejoined near Marna's Bend, with rain turning the road into a contract dispute and Roche's men moving in and out of mist. The bard looked less theatrical than usual. That alone made the day feel unsafe.
"He learns quickly," Priscilla said.
"So do lice," Zoltan replied. "Still kill them."
"You cannot kill a tune by stabbing the singer," Dandelion said.
Roche looked up from the map. "You can reduce volume."
"Temerian music criticism remains direct."
The scrap smelled of bread, red wax, and smoke from cheap candles. Yennefer took it with two fingers. "This is not Black Ink phrasing."
"No," Triss said. "But look here. The vellum was cut from office waste. Same ruling marks as the archive transfer sheets."

Cazren and Black Ink had found one another without becoming the same thing. That was the ugly elegance of it. Institutions needed mouths that could reach basements. Fanatics needed papers that could open granaries. Each could despise the other while borrowing tools.
"A human weapon," Regis said later, though he had not yet arrived in our order of memory. The phrase fit backward.

Cazren did not need to be correct. He needed to make fear feel like duty and duty feel like warmth. He could turn a rescue into theft, protection into hoarding, refusal into selfishness. He could make me a door in the mouths of people Black Ink would later call witnesses.
The next message came through a boy with one shoe, which made me want to kill the sender twice.

The boy had been told to find the white wolf with red eyes and ask whether doors were allowed to leave burning houses. He delivered the line, accepted food from Geralt, and admitted, under Zoltan's gentle threat to purchase him better footwear, that the man who paid him had hands like a priest and boots like a soldier.
"Cazren is moving north and east," Ves said.
"Ahead of us?" Ciri asked.
"Beside. He does not need to reach the same places. He needs the same people to hear him before we do."
That made him more dangerous than a hunter. Hunters follow tracks. Cazren planted weather.
Asha took the red thread from the bread cloth and held it over her palm. It did not burn. It did worse: the barbed star at my throat cooled, very faintly.
"He has no old knowledge," she said. "Only crumbs from stolen rooms. But crumbs lead rats, and rats find granaries."
"What does that mean in less cheerful terms?" Zoltan asked.
"He is singing near something that answers. Badly. Not because he understands it. Because ignorance makes noise without caution."
The road east waited in the sentence.
Cazren had become a man carrying a candle into a powder room while calling it dawn.

chapters.chapter_title: REGIS AND THE QUESTION OF APPETITE
paragraphs: Regis arrived with an umbrella, which made the situation worse.

It was not large or decorative. It was plain, black, excellently maintained, and held at a sensible angle against the rain falling over Marna's Bend. The road there had become more mud than road, the ferry sat chained to the wrong bank, and a dead wyvern lay under a tarp near the willow line because everyone present had agreed not to let Dandelion see it before breakfast.
Regis stepped around a puddle, inclined his head to Geralt, and looked at the tarp with the tired courtesy of a physician invited to dinner and shown a corpse under the table.
"Geralt."
"Regis."
"You said the matter was urgent. I assumed a certain range of unpleasantness."
"And?"
"You have exceeded expectations. This is rarely a compliment."

I stood beside Buck under a willow that dripped steadily down the back of my collar. My left hand was bandaged again because the cut had opened during the granary fire. Not much. Only enough to remind me that my body had opinions about restraint. Ciri watched from the ferry post, hood low, expression caught between impatience and the stillness of a woman too used to being observed. Yennefer stood near the tarp. Triss held the living chamber copy in oilcloth. Asha stood where the road bent east, as if she had already begun leaving.
Regis saved me for last. Deliberate. I respected it despite myself. Monsters, truly old ones, know the discourtesy of immediate hunger.
"Mr. Morningstar," he said.
"Regis."
"Technically, Emiel Regis Rohellec Terzieff-Godefroy, but in present weather I will accept several abbreviations and one dry room."
"No dry room," Geralt said.
"Then we must make do with accuracy."

Regis did not examine the living chamber page first. He examined the cup beside it, which irritated nearly everyone except Geralt. Old monsters and old friends sometimes approach horror through harmless objects because harmless objects reveal who still has patience.
"Bad tea," Regis said.
"We know," Geralt replied.
"No. You suspect. I have confirmed. Willow bark, stale mint, and an unfortunate optimism about dried apple."
Zoltan grunted from the wagon. "It was boiled under pressure."
"So are confessions. That does not improve them."
Ciri laughed once before catching herself. The sound loosened the place by a thread. Regis heard it, acknowledged nothing, and set the cup aside.
Only then did he look at me.

He did not stare at my eyes. People with manners did not, and monsters with age had better manners than many kings. He looked at my bandaged hand, the line of tension along my throat where the barbed star rested hidden, the way Ciri had placed herself with sight of both me and the road, and Geralt's hand pretending not to hover near a sword.
"You have become parental in several directions," Regis told Geralt. "This seems logistically unwise."
Geralt exhaled through his nose. "Missed you too."
"I would have brought better tea had I known affection would be so badly expressed."

Yennefer stood with her fingers near the diagram. She had not sat since Regis entered. That was not discourtesy. That was Yennefer refusing to let the room decide whether civility made her less dangerous.
Regis bowed with precision. "Madam Vengerberg."
"Regis."
"Your reputation for disapproval remains restorative."
"Your reputation for politeness remains evasive."
"Then we are both consistent, a rare mercy."
Triss placed the packet before him. "We need an answer we will hate."
Regis's expression changed. The gentle surface remained, but the air beneath it cooled. "Then be careful not to reward yourselves for hating it. Some people mistake reluctance for morality."
I liked him less immediately. That proved either wisdom or bad timing.
He read the living chamber page once. Then again. No one interrupted. Even Dandelion let silence keep its profession.
"This is not a prison design," Regis said at last.
Asha's eyes narrowed. "It says chamber."

"Humans also call many marriages arrangements. We should not assume consent has improved. This is a proposed metabolism. A living chamber must receive pressure, distinguish hunger from signal, absorb injury without identifying with the injurer, and keep choosing boundaries while part of it is taught that boundaries are lies."
The rain did its best with the silence.
"You make it sound alive," I said.
"It would have to be. That is the cruelty. Dead stone can hold without understanding. A living chamber must understand what it holds without becoming the hunger's accomplice."
Geralt rubbed one hand over his mouth. "Could it work?"
Compassion crossed Regis's face. That made the answer worse before he gave it.
"Many impossible things work briefly. That is why they kill."
Yennefer's voice cut in. "Briefly is not an answer."
"No. It is a warning."
Yennefer's fingers tightened around the page. "You are avoiding the answer."
"Yes," Regis said.
That startled more honesty into the room than a defense would have done.

He set the page flat with two fingertips. "Clean answers are how decent people become comfortable beside cruel work. Yes turns horror into instruction. No turns danger into pride. Perhaps turns suffering into a waiting room. I will give you none of those as furniture. I can describe appetite, restraint, cost, and probability. I will not make the sentence easier to sit in."
Geralt looked as if he disliked the answer and trusted him more for it. I understood the feeling. It was inconvenient.

He moved to the glass bowl Triss had prepared. Inside lay a clot from one of the scale-sick draconids, sealed under spell-cold. The matter did not rot. It trembled when I entered the room and stilled when I left. Regis lifted the glass cover a finger's width.
The smell that escaped was not decay. It was hunger translated poorly into flesh: hot copper, wet ash, old reptile musk, and a sweetness that made the mouth remember blood.
Regis closed his eyes. Not revulsion. Recognition.
Geralt saw. "Regis."
"I am here."
"That wasn't my question."
"No. It was your hand on the hilt before a question found language. I appreciate the efficiency."
I watched him more closely. "You feel it."
"Yes."
"Because you are a vampire."

"Because I have been hungry," Regis corrected. "Species is a detail, significant and socially inconvenient, but still a detail. Hunger has grammar. This has grammar. It is not hunger exactly. It is dominion wearing hunger because hunger is a language bodies obey quickly."
Asha murmured something in Faithel. I knew none of the words, but the cadence cooled the star at my throat.
"What did she say?" Regis asked.
"A door is innocent until someone teaches it appetite," Asha said.
"A sensible people. Very unpleasant, I imagine, when correct."
"Often."
Ciri came to the table. "And Jack?"
No title. No file word. No asset, bearer, chamber, hinge. Just the name, placed between us like a drawn line.
Regis's attention moved from her to me. "At present, he is not appetite. He is boundary under stress. That distinction matters."
"But later?" I asked.
He did not soften the answer. "Later, if enough pressure teaches the boundary to survive by wanting what it holds, the distinction may begin to suffer."
"No," Ciri said.
Regis inclined his head. "I would be grateful if refusal could alter metaphysics. It can alter what people do before metaphysics narrows the room. That may be everything, if used early."
Yennefer took the page from him. "Then the living chamber is unacceptable."
"Morally, yes. Strategically, perhaps. Beware words like unacceptable once every other door has failed. They become monuments after the dead have no use for principles."
Triss closed her eyes once. "I hate this answer."
"Then keep it honest. Do not let hatred of the answer become hatred of the person who may one day be forced to stand near it."
"No one is forcing me," I said.
"Not yet."
Those two words struck harder than accusation. I felt Ciri turn toward me. I did not look at her because if I did, the place might discover too much.

Regis continued, quieter. "A person can be forced by chains, spells, threats, or law. He can also be forced by love if he mistakes the desire to spare others pain for a command they gave him. That coercion leaves no jailer to blame. Very efficient."
Geralt looked at me fully. The look said Ciri, Yennefer, Triss, Asha, perhaps even himself. It said every person in the room was becoming a possible lever, whether they deserved it or not.
"You speak gently," I said.
"A lifetime of evidence suggests harsh truths do not improve when shouted."
"Sometimes they move faster."
"So do fires."
Zoltan muttered, "Worse than a priest. At least priests pass a plate."
"If it comforts you," Regis said, "I can request a donation for the improvement of tea."
That earned a laugh. Brief. Necessary.
Then Regis took up Jacob's broken hilt from the table. My hand moved before I stopped it. He noticed and did not touch the hilt further.
"Your father died buying minutes," he said.
"Yes."

"Minutes are underestimated by people who have not needed them. A minute can be shelter, birth, a letter hidden, a door barred, a child lifted over a wall. If one day you are asked for more than minutes, do not let your father's courage become currency others spend from your purse."
My throat tightened. I hated that it happened in front of so many witnesses.
"He already did," I said.
"Yes. And gave you life. That is a gift, not a debt. Gifts rot when people use them as invoices."
Asha looked east. "Faithel law calls it last witness. The chamber must choose. The witnesses must refuse before they consent."
"A wise cruelty," Regis said. "Refusal proves everyone understands the horror. Consent proves they understand the alternative."
"Stop making it sound possible," Geralt said.
Regis regarded his old friend with genuine sorrow. "My dear Geralt, I am trying to make the price sound ruinous so no one mistakes possibility for solution."
Regis did not stop there.

That was another reason to trust him unwillingly. He asked for a knife, a bowl, clean water, three drops of my blood, and permission. The last came after the rest because he knew what rooms like ours noticed.
"Permission for what?" Ciri asked.
"A demonstration, if Mr. Morningstar consents. Not a test. Tests imply a correct answer known to the examiner. I claim no such comfort."
Yennefer folded her arms. "And if he refuses?"
"Then the demonstration improves by absence."
I almost liked that answer. "What happens if I agree?"
"You will bleed three drops. I will show you how quickly appetite builds a story around them. Then we destroy the evidence before anyone sentimental or administrative names it destiny."
Ciri looked at me. Not command. Not plea. Attention. That was more dangerous than either.
"Do it," I said.
"That was too fast," Triss said.
"I can wait and say it again."
"Do not mistake stubbornness for consent."
That landed. Harder because Triss had earned the right to say it.

I breathed once. The river smelled of mud and rain. The covered wyvern under the tarp smelled worse through every precaution. Buck watched from the willow line and disliked everything about the gathering except perhaps Regis's umbrella, which he seemed to consider a rival species.
"I agree," I said. "Three drops. No more. If anything answers wrong, Yennefer burns the bowl, Geralt cuts my hand away from it, and Ciri is allowed to insult my judgment."
"Allowed?" Ciri asked.
"Encouraged."
"Accepted."
Regis inclined his head. "Excellent boundaries. We may survive education yet."

He cut the pad of my thumb, not the marked palm. That mattered. Blood welled dark, too warm in the rain. One drop fell into the bowl. Then another. The third hesitated, fat and bright, before joining the water.
Nothing happened.
For one breath, disappointment moved through the room like a thief.
Then the wyvern under the tarp shifted.
Dead weight should not sound curious.

The bowl's water did not turn red. It cleared. Too clear. Beneath the surface, each drop held its shape and pulled toward the others, not mixing, not dissolving. Three small suns under water. The scale-clot beside Triss's packet trembled. My palm heated. The barbed star cooled. Ciri stepped closer before I could decide whether I wanted her nearer or farther.
Regis's eyes darkened.
Geralt's hand moved toward him.
"I am here," Regis said.
"You keep saying that when you are least convincing," Geralt replied.
Regis smiled without humor. "That is when it most needs saying."
The three drops in the bowl began to move in a slow circle. Not toward me. Toward the tarp. Toward the dead hunger. Then, just as slowly, toward Ciri's hand where it rested on the table edge.
Ciri did not move.

"There," Regis said. His voice had lost all ornament. "This is the danger. Appetite looks for shortest routes to meaning. Blood. Corpse. Beloved witness. It does not care which is cause, symptom, or hostage. It creates a triangle and calls the geometry fate."
Yennefer's face was terrible. "Destroy it."
"In a moment."
"Now."
"Look first," Regis said, and there was command under the gentleness. "All of you. If you cannot bear to see a small version, you will lie to yourselves about the large one."
The third drop stretched toward Ciri's hand.
I covered the bowl with my palm.

Pain snapped up my arm. Not heat. Hunger trying a door and finding flesh in the way. My knees flexed. Geralt caught my shoulder. Ciri caught my wrist. Yennefer's spell hit the bowl, Triss's followed, and the glass cracked into white powder under my hand without cutting me.
For a moment the world had no sound but rain.
Then Buck bit the umbrella.
Regis looked at the ruined handle with genuine regret. "That was a very good umbrella."
"Operational loss," Zoltan said.

I leaned on the table, breathing through the pain. Ciri had not let go of my wrist. Neither had Geralt of my shoulder. Two holds. Both different from chains. I needed to remember the difference before the world improved its arguments.

Regis picked up a shard of white glass and placed it in a pouch. "The chamber problem is what holding teaches hunger to associate with survival. If it learns Ciri, it reaches for Ciri. If it learns Geralt's command, it reaches for Geralt. If it learns pain, it asks for more pain. If it learns sacrifice, every exit grows need."
"Then what should it learn?" I asked.
Regis looked at my hand, then at the people around it.
"Refusal first. Consent last. Witness always."
No one spoke. There were worse commandments. There were easier commandments. This one would have to do.
Ciri released my wrist only after I straightened.
"You put your hand over it," she said.
"I noticed."
"That was stupid."
"Yes."
"And useful."
"Do not encourage me."
"I am distinguishing carefully," she said.
Triss, to my surprise, smiled a little. "Good phrase."
"I stole it from you."
"Then use it correctly."
Regis removed the ruined umbrella from Buck's reach and sighed. "A day of progress, then. At ruinous cost to equipment."
We buried the wyvern in the rain.
The work should have been ordinary.

Monster down. Body too dangerous to leave. Pit deep enough for caution, lime for flesh, iron for restless magic, wards for whatever ignorance had not named. Witchers had done uglier work for worse pay. That did not make the first spade cut easy.

The ground near Marna's Bend was river-fat, dark, and stubborn. It swallowed the shovel blade with a sound like a mouth accepting argument. Geralt dug on my left. I dug on the right. Roche's men cut turf and passed it back. Ciri held the lantern at first, then handed it to Ves and took a spade from a soldier who wisely decided rank was not worth the look she gave him.
"You do not have to," Geralt said.
"I know," she answered.
The same answer I gave too often. It sounded different in her mouth. Less defensive. More final.

Regis watched the covered carcass while we worked. Some dead things, he said, deserved not to be left alone with their worst hunger. When the tarp shifted once under rain, not with life but with corrupted muscle's last argument, he placed one gloved hand on it and waited until it stopped.
Asha spread ash around the pit and muttered that northerners dug like people negotiating with spoons.
"You are welcome to improve the hole," Zoltan said.
"I am improving the witnesses. Holes forgive less."

By the time the pit reached my chest, my ribs had begun listing complaints in old languages. The granary cut pulled. My shoulder burned. The mark under my bandage pulsed with every shove of the spade, not answering power, only pressure. That mattered. Not all pain was omen. Sometimes a wound was only a wound and still deserved respect.
I ignored it for ten more strokes.
On the eleventh, my grip failed.
The spade slipped, struck the pit wall, and sent mud down over my boot. Not dramatic. No collapse. No danger. Only a small failure in front of too many people trained to notice small failures.
Ciri set her own spade down. "Out."
"No."
"That was not a question."
"You been taking lessons from Yennefer?"
"From watching stubborn men become corpses while insisting they are nearly finished. Out."
Geralt did not help her. Worse, he agreed by silence.

Pride rose, loyal and stupid. Then Mela's voice returned from the granary: Be earlier next time. Pride had not saved her child. It had nearly made me the nearest weapon in a room designed to witness it.
I climbed out.
Badly.

Regis offered a hand. I almost refused because some part of me still believed monsters helping men made the world illegible. Then I remembered I was the one everyone kept trying to make into a door, and pettiness lost its footing.
I took his hand.
His grip was cool, exact, and very strong. He did not pull until I put weight into the choice. There was a lesson there. I resented him for making even assistance philosophical.
Ciri went into the pit in my place.

No ceremony. Mud on boots. Hair damp at her temples. Future empress with a shovel and a face that discouraged anyone from calling the image symbolic. She worked beside Geralt for twenty strokes. Then Roche's man took over. Then Zoltan. Then Ves. The pit became a communal insult to hunger.
I stood under the willow with rain in my collar and learned, unwillingly, that not every task loses meaning when taken from my hands.

When the wyvern finally slid into the hole, the whole riverbank seemed to hold breath. The body was too heavy for dignity. It went down on ropes, tarp tied around it, one malformed wing jutting hard against the cloth like a question no one wanted to answer. The scale-sickness had left red threads beneath the skin. Even covered, I knew where they pulsed.
The barbed star at my throat cooled.
Not much. Enough.
"No," I said quietly.
Ciri heard. "To what?"
"Whatever wants me to make this useful."
She looked at the pit. "Then do not. Let it be dead."
Let it be dead.

A clean command. A mercy and a refusal. I repeated it while lime went down, while Yennefer set the ward, while Triss wrote the method without turning the corpse into argument, while Regis held the tarp's last fold until mud covered it.
For once, the dead thing was allowed to be only dead.
It felt like practice for my parents.
When the body was covered, Regis placed one gloved hand on the iron bars laid across the soil.
"Rest," he said.
No one asked whether he spoke to the wyvern, the hunger, or himself.
Geralt found Regis by the river after midnight. I heard enough from the mist to know the conversation had waited years for a different subject and found me instead.
"You should have lied," Geralt said.
"To whom? Him? Ciri? You? Pick one."
"He will consider it."
"Yes."
"Too calmly."
"Yes."
"And if the numbers turn ugly past a certain point, he will choose it."
"I suspect so."
Geralt turned on him. "You could sound less resigned."
"Resignation is not agreement. It is recognition of another will. You taught me some of that while being deeply irritating and armed."
"This is different."
"Every beloved disaster is."
I stepped from the mist then because listening any longer would make hiding the cowardice, and I had met enough cowardice that day.
"You talk loudly for old monsters," I said.
"Age affects volume unpredictably," Regis replied.
Geralt said nothing.
I came to the riverbank. My left hand was wrapped too tightly. That was the sort of detail old friends and old monsters noticed. "If it comes to it, I choose."
"No," Geralt said.
"Yes."
"Not alone."
The river was easier to understand than the space between us. It kept moving, took whatever fell into it, lied about nothing except depth.
"Not alone," I said. "But mine."
Before dawn, Regis found me sitting beside the covered pit. The air above it seemed unwilling to host insects, dew, or ordinary silence.
"May I intrude?" he asked.
"You are."
"Shall I leave?"
I considered. "No."
He sat at the other end of the log. No umbrella this time. Perhaps the weather was clear. Perhaps even vampires understood when a joke had finished its work.
"If you become the last prison," he said, "what do you imagine remains yours?"
"Choice."
"Choice at the gate, perhaps. Afterward?"
Afterward had no proper shape. I could imagine pain, darkness, pressure, hunger learning me from within. I could imagine winning in the way a lock wins, by continuing to be closed.
I could not imagine what a man does after becoming a room.
"I don't know."
"Good. Certainty would worry me more." Regis folded his hands. "Restraint is not one decision. It is a civilization maintained daily inside one body."
"And if the gates hold?"
"Then one still has to live near the gates. Do not romanticize maintenance into sacrifice before you understand it."
I turned to him. "You think I want sacrifice."
"No. I think you trust loss more than comfort. That is common among people taught too early that comfort comes with hooks."
The words found places I had not named. I disliked him for that and respected him more in the same breath.
"If holding requires a man," Regis said, rising, "the man is not merely a lock. He is a citizen of his own suffering. Ask for laws before accepting the kingdom."
That was his least poetic advice.
Probably his best.
Ciri learned that her affection had become a state concern from a woman carrying pears.

I did not hear that line until later. Ciri gave it to me beside an unfinished road marker with mist under our boots and Geralt pretending not to guard us from the trees. She said it as if amused. Her hands were too still for amusement.

The woman was not actually a pear seller. The pears were real, because Ilyra Sarn disliked props that failed inspection, but the seller's hands had no fruit stains and too much knife discipline for honest market work. She approached Ciri at the morning halt outside Marna's Bend with a wicker basket, a bowed head, and a voice pitched exactly between servant humility and trained urgency.
"Highness," she said.
Ciri considered the pears. "If those explode, I will be irritated."
"Only one contains a note. The others are seasonal."
"That may be the most Nilfgaardian sentence I have heard this week."
Ilyra took one pear, turned it, found the hairline cut, and removed a roll of paper from the hollow around the stem. She gave the fruit back.
"Waste nothing."
The note was from Emhyr. Of course it was. Emperors send concern the way archers send arrows: carefully feathered, meant to appear elegant until they enter flesh.

Cirilla, the note said, the pattern around your movements has become visible. Men who fear you are now less dangerous than men who fear for you in public language. I have received inquiries using the terms anomalous protector proximity, emotional vulnerability vector, and destabilizing private attachment. I do not ask you to return because asking what you will refuse wastes ink. I do ask whether the person drawing these terms understands what your closeness will do to him. Signed: E.
Ciri read it once. Then again. She considered throwing it into the ash pit and decided the ash pit had suffered enough.
Yennefer read it and made a sound that was almost admiration and mostly contempt. "Your father has acquired a poetic bureaucrat."
"He wrote it himself."
"Worse. He is improving."
Geralt read slowly, lips barely moving at emotional vulnerability vector. "Vector."
"I know," Ciri said. "I hate that one."
"Pick a number and stand in line."

I stood by Buck with Roche's map in one hand and a look, apparently, that said I knew a message had arrived and would rather face a monster than ask whether it concerned me. Buck pushed his nose into my shoulder. He understood correspondence as a predator with poor teeth and endless patience.
Ciri folded the note and put it in her sleeve.
"They know," she said.
"They knew you cared before you did," Yennefer said. "Institutions are vulgar that way."

The second warning came in a box of pears because imperial gravity prefers sweet surfaces. The fruit were yellow, unbruised, and packed in straw too clean for the roads they claimed to have traveled. Inside the box, beneath the invoice, lay another note. No imperial seal. Seals announce power. Unsealed notes announce intimacy, or the wish to deny it later.

Cirilla, your movements have become a discussion in rooms where concern has learned to use your name softly. Return if you wish to choose the conversation. Remain if you wish others to choose its terms. Signed: E.
Ciri hated it because it was good advice.

Ilyra had more. Advisers asking whether her northern inspection had become compromised by personal sympathy. A quartermaster asking whether her escort should be expanded. A priest sending prayers for discernment, which Ilyra had quarantined on aesthetic grounds. One report noted that Ciri and I had ridden side by side for half a mile without speaking.
"The empire's capacity for boredom remains formidable," Ilyra said.

Ciri looked down into the yard where Geralt pretended not to supervise me pretending to check Buck's shoe. Yennefer and Triss spoke beneath the eaves, two forms of care that would deny kinship if accused. Asha watched the road. Regis stood in the rain with his umbrella and looked morally disappointed by weather.
"Say it," Ciri told Ilyra.

"If you love him, it is already political. If you do not love him, they will write that you do if it helps. If he loves you, he is a hostage to your choices. If he does not, he is still a man your enemies can place near you and call motive. There is no private answer now. Only more or less honest public handling."
Ciri closed her hand around a pear until the skin broke. Juice ran over her fingers. Sweet, sticky, absurd.
"I have not said love."
"No," Ilyra said. "You have said logistics several times with unusual hostility."
Ciri laughed despite herself. It came sharp as a blade.

I looked up from the yard. Not because I heard the laugh, perhaps. Because the world changed pressure around it. Our eyes met through a dirty window. Neither of us smiled. The distance between us held every word others might later weaponize.

She told me before the order left. Not in front of everyone. That would have made truth into theater. She found me behind the stable, where Buck educated a post by ignoring it with contempt. Rain had stopped. Water fell from the eaves in slow drops, each one striking mud with the patience of a clerk making a list.
"I have forbidden imperial custody action in my name," Ciri said.
I tightened a strap. "That is an order."
"Yes."
"To them."
"Yes."
"Not to me."
She heard the question hidden under grammar. Good. I had learned to make questions look like fences.
"Not to you. I do not command your body. I am warning anyone who thought my title could be used as a rope around it."
Then I let her see my face. The crimson of my eyes was duller in wet daylight, less flame than banked coal. It did not make me less frightening. Only less useful for myth.
"Thank you," I said.
The phrase looked small in the yard. I left it there anyway.
Ciri's eyes softened in a way that did not make them gentle. "That was difficult for you."
"Usually."
"Being thanked?"
"Being defended."
She came one step closer. "You defended Tavin."
"He was a child."
"And you are a man. That is not a lesser category."
I had no answer that would not insult us both.
