The order she dictated did not name me first. That was its strength. Ciri and Ilyra built it broad enough to shelter more than my blood and sharp enough to cut anyone trying to pretend that shelter was sentiment.

No person under imperial transition, vassal settlement, free company, guild license, mage-recognition process, witcher contract, non-human custodial obligation, or private citizenship shall be placed under emergency restraint, medical custody, bloodline seizure, or anomalous-host classification without named charge, witnessed consent, and review by three authorities who do not share a funding chain.

Triss wrote quickly. Yennefer changed two phrases to survive hostile interpretation. Ilyra changed one to survive imperial procedure. Geralt objected to funding chain because it sounded like something that would make clerks multiply. Ciri kept it for that reason.
I said nothing until the end.
"They will find cracks."
"Yes," Ciri replied. "But cracks slow rats if the walls are thick enough."
Ilyra sanded the page. "This will not save him."
"No," Ciri said. "But it will make theft take longer and involve witnesses. That is sometimes the beginning of civilization."
Outside, rain hardened. Inside, she signed with the long ugly line of a name the world had been trying to own since before she knew how to hold a sword.
Cirilla Fiona Elen Riannon.
She did not write Empress-designate. The absence did more work than the title would have.

The response came too quickly and not from Emhyr. That frightened Ilyra more than anger would have. The document acknowledged Ciri's draft, praised its humanitarian breadth, questioned its procedural feasibility, and suggested provisional advisory review for any order issued under conditions of emotional proximity to anomalous persons.
Yennefer read that sentence and said nothing.
I had learned to fear Yennefer's silences more than most men's shouts.
"They were waiting for her to defend someone," Ilyra said. "They did not know whom. The mechanism was prepared."
Geralt studied the settlement mark. "Can Emhyr stop it?"
Ciri laughed once. Too short for humor. "Of course. That is the problem. If he stops it openly, my protection becomes his indulgence. If he does not, the review becomes proof I need supervision."
"Then we bypass him," Yennefer said.
Ilyra's eyes lifted. "Legally?"
Yennefer's look could have stripped paint. "Do not ask questions that insult both of us."

They answered through three channels: mage humanitarian language to make refusal look cruel, witcher-adjacent contractor language to make enforcement expensive, and Ciri's order through vassal settlement before the advisory review could claim procedure had already begun. Dandelion and Priscilla would turn the cult's clean refrain dirty at the edges. Zoltan would make sure the right taverns heard which charity used grief as a ledger. Roche would leak just enough to make old Temerian roads suspicious of new stamps.
Ciri turned to me. "See? I am not spending imperial weight on you. I am spending paperwork on everyone who hates paperwork."
"Generous."
"Vindictive, actually. Generosity is less organized."
Leaving the rest unsaid did more work than speaking it.

That night, I found her by the unfinished road marker east of camp. It had once pointed toward three villages. Two names had been scratched out, not by war but taxation, which was more final in certain districts. The remaining arm leaned east and said nothing useful.

Ciri sat on the stone base with her cloak around her knees, watching mist move over low fields. She had left camp without escort because she wanted privacy and because everyone nearby was competent at pretending not to follow while following. Geralt was in the trees to the west. Yennefer watched from somewhere no one would see unless she wanted it.
"You are being guarded," I said.
"I know."
"Badly?"
"Lovingly. Related problem."
She patted the stone. I sat. Carefully. Not because of injury. Because closeness had become a political act and we were both tired of giving politics free seating.
For a while, we said nothing. Campfire glowed through mist. Buck's silhouette moved near the horses. Somewhere, Roche's men changed watch. An owl called and received no answer, which seemed sensible.
"I almost thought of the chapel today," Ciri said.
"Almost."
"Yes. Then I stopped because once I thought it, they would have won something. They would have made a private room into evidence."
"Rooms can be both."
"I know. That is what hurts."
No clean answer existed. Clean answers are what people invent to avoid washing their hands.
She studied my bandaged hand. "When I signed the order, I wanted to sign it for you. I made it broad because that was wiser. I still wanted it to be for you."
"I know."
"Do you hate that?"
I considered. She deserved that. Men answer too quickly when women ask if care has become burden. They think speed is kindness. It is usually fear wearing clean boots.
"No," I said. "I fear it."
"Good."
"Good?"

"Fear means you understand it has weight. I am tired of men treating my choices as either gifts or disasters depending on whether they benefit. Sometimes they are blades. I know. I still hand them over."
I reached for her hand, stopped halfway, and waited.
She placed her hand in mine.

No kiss. No sudden heat beyond what skin carried. That made it harder in some ways. Desire can be blamed on night, fear, bodies, wounds, the need to feel alive. Holding hands in a misty field while the world tries to classify the contact as leverage requires quieter defiance.
Ciri leaned her shoulder against mine. Barely.
It steadied me anyway.
From the trees, Geralt looked away.
Yennefer did not.
Before dawn, Ilyra burned three drafts and kept the fourth.
"Send it," Ciri said.
"As law?"
"As weather. Let them complain after it is already raining."
The complaint arrived before sunrise with six riders and an officer who believed tone could replace legality.

They wore no imperial colors. That was the point. Too much black and gold would have made the matter Ciri's. Too much northern cloth would have made it local. They chose gray cloaks, polished buckles, and a stamped packet that called itself provisional advisory authority under humanitarian review. The words were so careful they could have cut themselves.
The officer asked for Ciri by title.
Ciri came out without one.

Plain cloak. Hair tied back. Two knives visible, one hidden because court had not cured her of sense. Ilyra stood two steps behind her with a writing board. Yennefer stood where the officer could see her and regret unnecessary verbs. Geralt and I stayed by the horses because men with swords make arguments stupid faster than women with documents, though not always more effectively.
"Your Highness," the officer said, bowing exactly deep enough to be wrong either way.
"You have a packet," Ciri said.
"A clarification request."
"Requests do not ride with six men before breakfast."

His mouth tightened. "There is concern that your recent order may be compromised by emotional proximity to persons under anomalous review. Pending procedural examination, we are instructed to recommend temporary removal of such persons from immediate political influence."
I felt the sentence enter every listener differently. Geralt as threat. Yennefer as insult. Triss as procedure. Ilyra as architecture. Ciri as something she had been expecting and still despised.
In me it found an old reflex: leave, make it simpler, remove the handle.
Ciri did not look at me.
That was mercy and command in one movement.
"Name the persons," she said.
The officer hesitated. "The language allows general classification."
"Then your language can wait outside. Name the person."
He looked at me.
Buck bared his teeth.
The officer looked back at Ciri. "Jack Morningstar."
There it was. My name in a clean mouth, dressed for seizure.
"Good," Ciri said. "Now name the charge."
"There is no charge. This is protective review."
"Protective of whom?"
"Public stability. Your Highness's position. The subject's own safety."
"He is not subject to your convenience. Try again."
The officer found stiffness where courage should have been. "I am empowered to recommend escort."
"Recommend it."
"Now?"
"You rode here. Spend the effort."
He swallowed. "I recommend that Jack Morningstar submit voluntarily to neutral escorted review pending clarification of proximity concerns."
Ciri turned then. Not to me. To Ilyra.
"Record: recommendation heard. Recommendation declined by the named person unless he chooses otherwise."
Every eye found me.
The trap had changed shape. If I refused, I endangered Ciri's order. If I agreed, I gave them clean paper. If I attacked, I became their favorite word.
For a moment I hated Ciri for not saving me from the choice.
Then I understood she had saved the choice itself.
"No," I said.
Small word. Ugly word. Necessary.
The officer's shoulders loosened by half an inch. He had expected resistance and prepared three replies. "Refusal noted."
"No," I said again. "Choice noted. Refusal is what you call it so the next page can sound disappointed. I choose not to go with men who cannot name a charge, authority, victim, term, or destination."
Triss's pen moved. Yennefer's eyes warmed in the dangerous way. Geralt looked at the ground, perhaps to hide pride, perhaps to keep himself from killing a man whose only weapon was grammar.
Ciri looked at the officer. "There. You have the clarification."
He tried one more road. "Your Highness, continued proximity may create hostile interpretation."
"Hostile interpretation already came with riders," she said. "I prefer it in sight."

Ilyra gave him a copy of the order, marked with three counter-seals he had not expected and one route of appeal that would bury his request under committees for months if he insisted on being useful to it.
Then Asha stepped from the barn with Tavin's mitten in her hand.

"Your gray men passed a child road yesterday," she said. "They did not stop. Their horses had clean hooves. Their eyes had schedules. In my country, men who miss a crying child are not trusted to review safety."
The officer did not know where to put that in his hierarchy.
Roche, from behind the well, supplied assistance. "Try under local witness objection. Heavy category. Smells bad in appeals."
The riders left with their packet still clean and their authority dirtier than when it arrived.
Only after they were gone did my knees remember anger had been holding them upright.
Ciri came to me by Buck. "You said no."
"Twice. Trying to improve with practice."
"You also wanted to leave."
"Yes."
"Thank you for not making my choice into your escape."
That struck deeper than the officer's packet.
I had no answer. Buck saved me by biting at the gray rider's dropped glove and spitting it out with public disgust.
"Official opinion recorded," Geralt said.
For once, everyone agreed with the horse.
Druidic packet delivered through Kovir courier route, salt-stained and resealed twice:

To Yennefer of Vengerberg, Triss Merigold, and the white-haired witcher who still owes me a clear answer about a leshen in Ard Skellig. The sea has begun returning what it should keep. Queen Cerys demands plain truth before she sends aid into another continent's secret. I agree with her, which will surprise no one with sense.
I read Ermion's opening twice and almost liked him for it.

The packet reached us in a rain-stiffened satchel carried by a Kovir merchant who believed he transported smoked herring invoices and therefore complained the whole way with convincing sincerity. We opened it in a barn outside Vengerberg because the inn nearby had too many ears and one bard too eager to prove he knew the second verse of a song Dandelion had not yet finished corrupting.
The barn smelled of hay, damp wool, horses, and sheep resentment. Buck approved of the sheep's attitude and no other part of the arrangement.
Yennefer read Cerys's letter first. Her mouth moved at send truth, not comfort.
"She has improved," Yennefer said.
Geralt took the report. "She was always direct."
"Direct and improved are not enemies."
The report began on a Skellige shore.

The first sign, according to the fisherman who found the carcass, was that gulls would not touch it. Fishermen respect gulls the way priests respect omens: publicly with reverence, privately with insults and an eye to profit. Gulls touch everything. Bait, bread, fingers, funeral rings if widows cry too long. If gulls would not land, the thing below them had entered a category older than appetite.

Cerys an Craite arrived in riding leathers, hair braided back, crown absent because cliffs do not care for gold and neither did she when the work was honest. Wind off the sea cut through wool and made banners snap above the harbor. Ermion stood beside the covered shape on the stones with his staff planted in shingle and the grim face of a man right too early and tired of repetition.
"Draconid?" Cerys asked.
"Yes."
"Skellige kind?"
"No."
"Then why is it on my shore?"
"That is the expensive question."
"You have been speaking with witchers again."
"One learns phrases from bad company."

The carcass had once been a basilisk or near it, insulting taxonomy. Head too narrow. Chest too deep. Wing joints malformed by an inland breeding line that had no business reaching an island shore. The belly had not been opened. The skin remained whole. Yet the body sagged inward as if everything that made it hungry had been drawn through a hole smaller than thought. The eyes were intact and empty.
Not dead empty. Room-after-furniture empty.

Cerys had seen battlefields, drowned men, plague, berserker aftermath, and the Hunt's shadow when stories became hoofbeats. This was different. Not violence done to flesh. Instruction removed from flesh.
"No birds," she said.
"No lice either," Ermion replied. "No worms. No scavenger claim. Even rot is hesitating."
"Rot has more sense than half my jarls."
"Often. Less jewelry."
The smell was wrong. Brine, dead scale, and beneath both hot stone, old smoke, a forge heard from underwater.
"You said dreams," Cerys said.
Ermion nodded toward the priestess by the path. "Three women in separate villages. One priestess of Freya. One net-mender. One girl too young for politics and too old for fairy tales. Same phrase."
"Say it."
"The crown drinks through the door."

Ciri read those words in the barn and went still at door. I knew why. Gate had haunted her all her life. Door was worse in a quieter way. A gate belonged to paths, worlds, crossing. A door belonged to a house. To ownership. To rooms where someone could decide who entered.
"Door," Ciri said.
Asha closed her eyes. "Faithel teaching says gate is passage, wound is damage, door is intention. A door belongs to a maker. Or a claimant."
"Vharakthul claims," Yennefer said.
Regis, who had stayed longer than he claimed he would, studied the red pulse rubbing. "And drinks. Through hunger, through dream, through dead beasts, perhaps through fear."
I studied the scale scrap sealed in wax. It lay like a dead black leaf. My left palm ached.

Cerys's packet included more than words. A scale sealed in wax mixed with salt. A charcoal rubbing of a red pulse mark. Ragna's dream statement. Ermion's diagram showing three shapes in ash: gate, wound, door. His handwriting stayed patient only until the final note.
Gate is passage. Wound is damage. Door is intention. Morningstar's friends say man. His enemies say key. The dead beast says hunger has begun confusing the terms.
Cerys's own letter was written in a hand that made ink seem like a tool rather than decoration.
Yennefer, Geralt, Ciri, Triss, and whoever Jack Morningstar allows near his shoulder to read,

Skellige has received one hollowed draconid, three shared dream phrases, one child repeating mainland cult words without contact, and enough bad weather to make even druids look smug. The phrase here is crown drinks through the door. Ermion says door is not gate, which is the sort of distinction that usually becomes expensive. Ragna says a body can be a house in dreams, and dreams have begun trespassing.
If this is your secret, it has reached my shore. That makes it less private.

I will not sail my people blind into another hidden war. Send the facts. If aid is needed, name the need. If ships are needed, say so. If silence is needed, explain why silence is not merely another rich person's curtain. Skellige has buried enough for other people's prophecies.
Cerys an Craite, Queen of Skellige
"Direct," Geralt said.
"Restrained," Yennefer replied.
"By what?"
"Lack of larger paper."

Triss moved the scale away from her ink. "The problem is not local. Not Novigrad. Not Temeria. Not northern roads. It touches Skellige. Draconids are reacting across distance. Shared phrases are spreading without normal travel."

"The outer seal," Asha said. "If the old anchors are sick, northern doctrine will never be enough. You have fragments. Fragments helped you live this long. They will not tell you how the prison fails."
"Zerrikania," Geralt said.
No one disagreed.

Rain moved beyond the barn doors, gray and patient. The east had waited behind every answer since the first warm ground under Willenford. Helena, Jacob, Asha's scars, Saesenthessis's silences, the blue bead, the living chamber page, the draconid bodies, Cazren's red door, Cerys's weather. Evidence had become motion. Motion had become road.
"Not yet," I said.
Every face found me.
I touched the pouch where the bead lay. "Burial first."
Asha bowed her head once. Not agreement. Recognition. Geralt looked at me for a long moment, then down at the Skellige report.
"Yes."
Ciri did not speak. She understood too well that some roads become survivable only after grief is given a place to stand.
Outside, Buck kicked the barn door.
Zoltan said from the stall, "Horse votes for burial with decent oats."
"Horse votes against barns," I said.
"Horse can file complaint with Cerys," Geralt replied. "She is collecting mainland problems."
Dandelion, who had indeed come despite claiming to be elsewhere, lifted a finger. "I can make that rhyme."
Priscilla touched his wrist. "Don't."
He lowered the finger. "Wisdom arrives through cruelty."
For one moment, the world remained terrible and also populated by people refusing to let terror have the only voice.
Then we planned the burial.
First we planned how not to turn the burial into a trail.

That took longer than planning most attacks. Attacks have targets. Mourning has habits. People leave marks when they think no one is hunting grief: a stone placed too carefully, a path walked twice, a flower from the wrong region, a witness who remembers that the future empress stood in rain beside a white-haired witcher while a sorceress cursed the soil.
"No flowers," Roche said.
Ciri looked at him. "No. One. Not visible."
Roche opened his mouth, looked at her face, and chose survival. "One. Buried."
"No road approach twice," Ves said. "We split before the stream, circle in, leave by three lines."
"No fire," Yennefer said. "Smoke reports itself."
"No singing loud," Triss added, glancing toward Dandelion.
He placed a hand to his heart. "I am wounded by the assumption and guided by its accuracy."
Priscilla took his sleeve. "You will be quiet."
"Wounded further."
"Alive still."

Zoltan checked the spades and muttered that people who made graves secret deserved to be buried under bureaucracy until they apologized. Regis, who had found dry shelter and improved it by looking politely out of place, asked whether the burial needed a physician's silence or a friend's. Asha answered without looking at him.
"Witness first. Friend if the dead allow."
Regis bowed. "A wise order."

We wrote no full map. Triss made three partial sketches and gave one to each person who needed it. Yennefer altered the rain for an hour in two valleys we would not use. Ilyra sent a courier west with a sealed dispute about bridge levies to create a reason for Ciri to be elsewhere. Roche leaked a false rumor that a cache of unpaid resistance coin had been found south of the old orchard, because greed drags boots better than loyalty.
Cerys's answer arrived while we were still arguing about spades.
It was shorter than her first letter.

I have received the truth. I dislike it less than comfort and more than silence. Skellige will watch the sea, burn what should not float, and prepare two ships without naming why. If your road turns to water, send a sign that cannot be sung by priests. If it turns to death, send names. We remember names better than empires do.
Cerys an Craite
Geralt read it once and handed it to Yennefer. She read it and looked almost pleased.
"High praise?" I asked.
"From Cerys, this is practically an embrace."
"Skellige embraces with axes," Zoltan said.
"More honest than advisory review," Ciri replied.
The burial had gained one more witness who would not attend. A queen across the sea, holding ships unnamed so our dead could be placed in ground before the next road stole the hour.
I kept thinking about it.
Perhaps all mourning is partly logistics. Who knows. Who carries. Who lies well enough to keep the place safe. Who refuses to let secrecy become erasure.
I did not feel ready for any of it.
Asha gave me Helena's folded letter and Jacob's broken hilt. "Read nothing today unless it asks."
"Letters ask?"
"Some do. Some only wait. Learn the difference."
Geralt looked at the hilt, then away.
Ciri touched the pouch with the pear from Ilyra's box. "We go before morning light."
"Burials at dawn?" Dandelion asked quietly.
"Before," Asha said. "Dawn makes witnesses of everything."

The plan had to account for things that should never have belonged in the same conversation: a symbolic grave, imperial pursuit, Temerian quiet roads, Skellige omens, a cult song, Black Ink routes, horse appetite, and whether Dandelion could be trusted not to call the whole matter beautifully tragic within earshot of me.
The answer to the last question was no.
Priscilla took responsibility.

Triss spread the map on a barn door laid over barrels. "Cerys can send ships if we need them later, but east by sea risks ports, records, and too many eyes. We go overland until the road makes water unavoidable."
"Overland means Korath," Asha said.

"Eventually," Yennefer replied. "Before that it means every petty official between here and the last civilized bath asking why a future empress, two sorceresses, witchers, a Faithel survivor, and a horse with criminal tendencies are traveling together."
Buck struck the wall.
"He heard criminal," I said.
"He understood tendencies," Geralt replied.
Ciri studied the map. The route east had too many names and not enough certainty. Villages thinned. Roads lost confidence. Borders became less lines than arguments with armed witnesses.
"I cannot remain with the main party after the burial," she said.
I looked up. Geralt did too quickly.

Ciri continued before either concern could swell into something everyone had to step around. "Not far. Not gone. But visibly traveling with you gives Black Ink and the court the same handle. Ilyra can create a false westward movement. I can ride offset with two guards and rejoin at marked points."
"No," I said.
"That sounded almost like ownership. Try again."
The barn enjoyed the silence in a cruel way.
"Bad," I said after a moment.
"Better. Also true. Still necessary."
Geralt rubbed a hand over his face. "I hate plans that sound like something I would have suggested twenty years ago."
"Then improve it," Ciri said.

So we did. Marked inns. Dead drops. Bird routes Triss could trust. Witcher signs placed where only Geralt and I would look. A phrase Dandelion would carry west in case rumor needed bending. Asha's old Faithel markers for the eastern approach.
It was not safe.
It was threaded.
In this world, threaded was sometimes the nearest safety came without lying.
We buried Jacob and Helena where no one could prove they were.

The place lay three hills east of the ruined watch-house, under birch grown white and thin from poor soil. A shallow stream cut the lower field. Someone had started a stone wall there once and abandoned it halfway, leaving gray rocks that led nowhere and divided nothing.
I chose the place because the ground was quiet.
Buck approved after biting one birch branch and finding it morally acceptable. Roach grazed beside him. Ciri's gelding kept to the stream. Light rain made every object shine too clearly.
The grave needed lies to survive.

No carved names. No signpost. No heroic stones for enemies, clerks, pilgrims, or collectors to find. The world had already proved it could turn a family into doctrine if given ash and a label, so we chose a hollow between dead orchards where roots had knitted through war rubble and the road bent away.

Asha said the place had no proper eastern meaning. Geralt said western graves rarely cared for proper. Yennefer said if anyone tried to disturb it she would leave enough curse on the soil to educate future centuries. Triss asked her to make the curse subtle enough not to attract a mage with ambition. Yennefer looked offended by the implication that subtlety required request.
Buck chose the exact spot by refusing three others and standing before a thorn tree with one ear turned toward me.
"Your witness has opinions," Regis said.
"He usually does."
"Are they reliable?"
Buck bared his teeth at a branch.
"More than most councils," Geralt said.

We dug with borrowed spades and one entrenching tool Roche had given us after calling it a gift for optimism. The ground was cold under wet leaves. Not frozen. Stubborn. I worked until my palms blistered under old calluses and the red lines beneath the skin pulsed from pressure, not power. Ciri tried to take the spade once.
I let her for six strokes.
Then I took it back because the work had to pass through my hands until it became real.
She did not argue. That was how I knew she understood.

Asha prepared the bundle. Not bodies. Never bodies. The North had not given me that mercy. It gave me Jacob's broken hilt, the blue bead, Helena's daylight clasp, a strip of cloth that may have touched her sleeve, copied letters, and the Black Ink operational tag folded so terminated faced inward where earth could correct it slowly.
"The tag should not go with them," Triss said. "It is evidence."
"Copy exists."
"Evidence should remain available."
"So should insult."
She turned from me to the tag. She understood before she liked it. "You want the file buried under the names it failed to use."
"Yes."
Yennefer's mouth curved by less than a knife's edge. "A rare example of administrative justice."
Ciri knelt beside the bundle and placed one pear from Ilyra's warning box beside it. Small, yellow, bruised from travel.
I looked at her.
"It came with a leash," she said. "It can stay with people who cut one."
I did not know what to say. Good. Too many words would have made the pear ridiculous. Silence let it remain strange and therefore true.

Asha walked the circle with a copper bowl in one hand and linen in the other, singing in the same dry language she had used beneath the watch-house threshold. The song had been made for heat-holding stone and water measured by oath. Here it crossed wet grass and learned exile.
The rite did not ask us to understand it.

Faithel practice, at least this damaged remnant of it, did not explain. It assigned work. Asha gave Geralt linen for the hilt, Yennefer salt she was told not to improve, Triss rainwater from three leaves, and Ciri the pear.
That surprised me. Ciri looked down at the bruised fruit in her palm. "What do I do?"
"Cut it," Asha said. "Not cleanly. It came with a hidden message. Let it open in public."
Ciri drew a small knife and cut the pear across the middle. Juice ran over her fingers, pale and sweet. She placed half beside Helena's clasp and half beside Jacob's hilt.
"For what was used as a leash," Asha said.
Ciri's voice was low. "And for what refuses."
Asha looked at her for a long moment, then nodded.
To me she gave nothing.
That was the part that almost broke me.
Hands need tasks. Grief needs tasks more. Everyone else carried, tied, salted, held, cut, or guarded. I had only the body that had survived and the name the dead had bought time to protect.
"What do I do?" I asked.
Asha kept walking the circle. "Stand."
"That is not work."
"For you, today, it is."
Ciri looked at me then. So did Geralt. Neither spoke. They both understood too much about standing where every instinct wanted movement.

Asha's song changed on the second circle. In its pauses, she named what no file had kept: Helena burning bread because she argued while baking, Jacob cutting his sleeve for a child's bandage and complaining about waste, Asha stealing sugared figs before a ride east, and one law said without ornament: no debt on the child.
That last one hit strangely.
Evidence of a self before fear had trained me into witness posture.
"He hated quiet?" I asked before I meant to.
Asha's voice remained in the song's shape. "You hated being put down. Quiet meant hands had left."
Rain touched my face. I decided it could be rain.

Geralt turned away to give me the courtesy of not being seen by too many eyes at once. Yennefer did not. She never mistook earned witness for trespass. Triss looked into the bowl as if its surface had become suddenly important.
Ciri stayed looking at me.
On the third circle, Asha stopped before the hollow and pressed her thumb into the mud. She drew no barbed star. No dragon sign. No family crest. Only three short lines crossing unevenly.
"What is that?" Dandelion whispered.
"A door barred from inside," Asha said.
The simplest marks are often the most dangerous. They leave less room for decoration.
"Say their names," she told me.
I had said them before. In anger. In evidence. In answer to questions. Not like this.
"Helena Morningstar," I said.
The name felt too new and too old. I had no right to it. I had every right. The contradiction stood and did not ask permission.
"Jacob var Moorlen," I said.
Asha closed her eyes.
"Again," she said.
I said them again.
The second time, Geralt spoke with me. On Jacob. Not Helena. A soldier acknowledging a soldier, perhaps. Or a father acknowledging another man who had bought minutes he could not spend.
The third time, Ciri spoke too.
Not loudly. Enough.
Helena Morningstar. Jacob var Moorlen.
The rain did not stop. The world did not answer. No golden light rose from the mud. No ancient seal accepted our grief as payment. Good. The dead deserved one moment not useful to magic.
Only Buck lowered his head near the thorn tree and stood very still.
That was miracle enough.
After the first verse she translated only the parts that wounded properly.
Blood remembers work, not glory. Stone remembers weight, not praise. A hidden name is not lost if one living mouth refuses to sell it.

I stood outside the circle with Jacob's broken hilt, Helena's folded letter, the bead, and the copied operational tag wrapped in separate cloths. Geralt stood beside me. Not too close. Close. The distance meant something.
"You don't have to put the tag in," he said.
"I know."
"You can keep the anger."
"I know."
"Jack."

I looked at him then. Geralt had hidden a child because fear wore the same coat as love. He had taught me how to hold a sword, not how to hold what he had done. Now he stood in rain beside a grave without bodies and tried not to take ownership of my grief by helping too quickly.
"I am keeping the anger," I said. "I am burying the receipt."
He nodded. His jaw worked once. No speech came. Fine. Some words only exist to make silence worse.
Asha took the hilt first.
"Jacob var Moorlen," she said. "Protector by choice, not assignment. Blade broken. Minute-buyer. Father by work, not permission."
The hilt went into the hollow.
She took Helena's clasp.
"Helena Morningstar. Bearer by blood, not ownership. Mother by breath, not file. Woman of the daylight clasp. Door-closer. Debt-cutter."
The clasp went beside the hilt.
The blue bead stayed in my hand.
Asha looked at it, then at me. "A child's proof belongs first to the child. The dead can borrow memory without taking everything."

I had heard those words before at the ruin. Hearing them again did not make them easier. I lowered the bead into the ground last. My fingers did not want to open. It was a cheap blue bead from a life I had not lived. Useless, and therefore harder to surrender.
That made it harder.
Ciri's hand touched my wrist. Not taking. Not guiding. Present.
I opened my fingers.
The bead fell soundlessly.
The operational tag followed, folded inward. Terminated faced the soil.

Asha finished the rite. Yennefer placed three subtle curses and one not subtle enough to be polite. Triss wrote the true names under no official heading. Regis said nothing. Zoltan stood with his cap in both hands. Dandelion did not sing. Priscilla's fingers rested on his sleeve, and for once he understood restraint as an art form.
Saesenthessis appeared on the ridge during the final line. Human-shaped, dragon-still. She bowed her head.
A dragon's bow is terrible not because it is grand, but because it admits the scale of what even power could not undo.

Before we covered the hollow, Geralt knelt and reached toward Jacob's hilt. His mouth opened on a word that wanted to be sorry and knew it had arrived too late to be useful. He did not speak it. Instead he adjusted the linen around the broken guard so the metal would not lie crooked in the earth. Practical care. The only apology he trusted not to steal from the dead.

Ciri waited until Roche had turned away to speak with Ves. Then she took one small field flower from inside her glove, crushed from hiding and stubbornly yellow, and tucked it beneath the pear half where no scout would see color from the path. She caught me seeing it and lifted her chin as if daring me to make it soft. I did not. Some tenderness survives only by refusing audience.

Asha corrected the circle last. One salt line had been laid too close to the clasp, generous by a finger's width. She scraped it back with the edge of her nail. "Grief does not improve law by overflowing," she said. Her voice broke on neither word. That made the care sharper. Even here, especially here, accuracy was a way of refusing theft.

Afterward, we filled the grave. I stayed until the earth lost the shape of work and became ordinary ground again. My hands ached. My shoulder burned. My ribs complained. Grief had taken a body task and spent it.

We ate later by the half-wall that led nowhere: hard bread, smoked fish, sour apples, and the last decent cheese from Zoltan's pack. Asha stole a salted apple before Buck could. Buck stared at her as if she had committed war. "He may file complaint after Elskerdeg," she said.

I wanted a stone with their names. Wanting did not improve the road. So I learned the thorn tree, the crooked birch, the stream bend, Buck's bitten branch, and the place where Ciri had buried half a pear. If the world gave me no marker, I would become the marker and hate it less than the alternative.
Geralt waited until the others had gone to ready the horses before speaking to me alone.

Alone was not accurate. Ciri stood within sight near the stream, speaking with Yennefer. Triss was with Ilyra sealing copies. Asha watched the road. Regis had become interested in birch fungus. Dandelion was being prevented by Priscilla from composing a burial verse. Zoltan helped by insulting mud.
Still, the circle held a privacy of purpose.
Geralt stood by the half-wall. I checked Buck's girth though he was not saddled yet. Habit gives hands work when words become expensive.
"You care for her," Geralt said.
My fingers stopped on the strap. "Which one?"
The pause sharpened.
"Cruel question," I said. "There are several women here capable of ruining a careless answer."
"Ciri."
I resumed the strap. "Yes."
Geralt exhaled. Not relief. Not fear. Something that had both in it and disliked the compromise.
"Does she know?"
"She is not stupid."
"That isn't what I asked."
"No."
Buck turned his head and watched me with the disdain of a creature who had never hidden an emotion in his life unless biting counted as poetry.
Geralt looked toward the stream where Ciri stood with Yennefer. "She has been made into purpose too many times."
"I know."
"Do you?"

I wanted anger. He had hidden me and had no clean right to warn me about turning a woman into purpose. He also had every right, because wrong men sometimes become right in later rooms, and the universe has poor manners about granting chances.
"I am trying," I said.
The answer was smaller than pride wanted. Better for that.
Geralt nodded. "Good."
"You have advice."
"No."
"That sounded like advice preparing to ambush me."

"Fine." He looked at Buck because fathers, even the unwilling kind, sometimes need a horse to absorb the first draft. "Do not confuse making distance with giving freedom. I did that. It looked noble in bad light. It was still distance."
That found me cleanly.

I looked toward Ciri. Rain clung to her hair. Her plain cloak made her look less like a future empress and more dangerous for it, as if the titles had been stripped away and left only the woman who kept choosing to stand where power did not want her.
"And if staying becomes a chain?" I asked.
Geralt's mouth tightened. "Then you both cut it. Not one of you for the other. Both."
Practical. Terrible. Useful.
"You sound like Regis."
"I am sorry."
"You should be."
He almost smiled. I did too. Almost had become family dialect.
Ciri came after Geralt left.
"He warned you," she said.
"Several times. Inefficiently."
"About me?"
"About myself near you."
"Better."
She stood beside Buck. Buck allowed it. He had strange standards and better judgment than most courts.
"I will ride offset after the next road," she said.
"I know."
"You will dislike it."
"I have scheduled several complaints."
"File them with Buck. He enjoys procedure."
The humor landed, then faded. What remained was road, grave, east, and the knowledge that care had become both shelter and target.
I touched her hand where it rested on Buck's mane. No one owned the motion. No one named it for us.
"I am afraid," I said.
Her fingers turned under mine.
"Good," she said softly. "So am I. Stay near anyway."
That should not have steadied me. It did.
The comfort did not last cleanly.

It came with packing, with Ciri checking the eastern waypoints twice, with Geralt sharpening a blade that needed no more edge, with Yennefer revising one curse because subtlety had lost an argument with affection, and with Triss sealing copies that might outlive us if the road became hungry.
Ves gave me a strip of leather before she left.
"For the wrist," she said.
"Mine works."
"It shakes."
I looked at her.

She did not look away. Ves had the gift of making pity impossible by refusing to supply it. "Tie it before sword work. Not too tight. Men who over-tighten support straps are usually trying to strangle evidence."
"Roche teach that?"
"Experience. Roche only teaches suspicion and where to hide knives in rooms built by optimists."
I took the leather. "Thank you."
She nodded as if the phrase had been filed and would be reviewed later.

Roche said goodbye by not saying goodbye. He handed Geralt two route slips, Ciri one countermark, Yennefer a list of officers who would become temporarily busy if she wished, and me nothing until I started to turn away.
Then he said, "Do not mistake every cage for Temeria. Some cages are built because men love one thing more than freedom and are too frightened to name it."
"Advice?"
"Warning. Advice implies I expect you to improve."
"Charming to the end."
"I try to remain consistent."
He looked toward Ciri, then back to me. "The boy Tavin asked for you. I told him you had gone east to learn how not to be a door."
"That is a terrible answer for a child."
"He asked if doors can learn. I said if they are stubborn and poorly hinged."
I almost smiled. "Still terrible."
"Memorable. Better than most truth."

Regis remained until the others gave us distance by pretending to check saddles. He held the broken umbrella handle Buck had ruined and looked as though he had forgiven the horse in principle, not in detail.
"Should I go with you?" he asked.
"Do you want to?"
"Want is not the most useful category."
"Everyone keeps saying that about useful. It is becoming suspicious."
"Then let me ask more plainly. Would my presence help?"
I looked east, where the air had begun to taste of dust beneath rain. "Yes."
"And would it help enough to justify what your road may teach hunger about me?"
That was the question behind all offers now. Who becomes a handle by standing near. Who becomes safer by distance. Who gets to decide the difference.
"No," I said.
Regis inclined his head. "Then I will travel otherwise. Parallel roads have their uses. They allow friendship to avoid becoming architecture."
"You talk like a man paid by syllable."
"If only. I would be rich beyond decency."
He placed one small vial in my hand. Not blood. Not medicine. Clear liquid with a smell of bitter herbs and iron rain.
"For panic," he said. "Not to prevent it. That would be dishonest. To give the body three breaths before panic becomes monarchy. Use only when deciding matters more than pride."
"So never?"
"Try to surprise me."
He left without drama, which was polite and therefore unsettling.

By the time we reached the last inn, our company had become smaller in body and larger in consequence. Roche and Ves fell away into roads that denied them. Dandelion and Priscilla turned west with Zoltan to keep songs dirty and witnesses expensive. Regis disappeared into weather with a ruined umbrella and too much understanding. Triss stayed one more night to send the packets, then would take a separate route south before bending east by mage channels Yennefer trusted only because distrust had been built into them.
The road ahead kept Ciri, Geralt, Yennefer, Asha, Buck, Roach, and me.
It was still too many people to hide.
It was no longer enough to feel safe.

At the last northern inn before the road turned from empire's memory into trader's rumor, I bought oats, salt, two skins of vinegar, and a coil of rope from a woman who asked no questions because she charged so much that curiosity became unnecessary. Geralt bought dried meat and checked shoeing nails on every horse. Triss sent one more packet west. Yennefer argued with a map until the map lost. Ciri disappeared for an hour and returned with a plain cloak, two knives, and an expression that discouraged questions about how either had been acquired.

We spread the road east across a table sticky with spilled beer and old knife cuts. It looked less like myth there. Myth does not arrive with water skins counted twice, false names written in three hands, spare linen boiled in vinegar, and arguments about whether Buck required more grain than dignity allowed. Geralt checked hooves until Roach lost patience. Then he checked them again. Ciri's offset route went into Ilyra's cipher and one dull bridge complaint meant to travel west at the wrong speed.

Triss burned two drafts and hid a third inside a list of fever powders. Yennefer sealed the useful letters with wax that would punish curiosity without making a spectacle of it. Asha inspected our skins, rejected one for a seam I could barely see, and made me smell the leather until I understood sour water before it reached my mouth. Politics became folded paper. Grief became oilcloth. Zerrikania became weight on a saddle, not a song on the horizon.
Asha watched all this with the air of a woman seeing northerners prepare for heat by purchasing objects that would later teach humility.
"Too much?" I asked.
"Wrong much," Asha said. "But learning begins when leather cracks."
Buck bit the rope.
"Your witness is impatient," she added.
"He dislikes philosophical supplies."
"He will dislike Korath more."
I looked east. For the first time, the road ahead did not smell of rain. It smelled of dust under wet air, as if another country had sent a warning small enough to fit through weather.

Behind us, the inn kept the North in small noises: rain under the eaves, men arguing over ale, a dog sleeping too close to the hearth, wet cloaks steaming by the door. Ordinary sounds. I listened too hard because I knew I would miss them once heat began making different demands.

Ciri left the yard by a side track before us, as planned. Not gone. Offset. The distinction was sensible and therefore hateful. Geralt watched the track until Yennefer said his name, and he stopped watching without stopping at all.

Buck disliked the first dry mile. Mud at least had the decency to show prints. Dust lifted around his hooves and vanished too quickly, a witness with no loyalty. He sneezed, shook his mane, and tried to bite the future by taking a mouthful of road grass that had already begun to go thin.
I did not feel ready.
That was probably the first honest preparation.
We rode east until the wet northern light thinned behind us and the road began to smell, faintly and impossibly, of dust.

part_subtitle: The land that made the bloodline will either claim Jack or reveal him.

paragraphs: Extract from a trader's weather account copied at the southern caravanserai:

Northerners ask where the desert begins. The correct answer is not a line on a map. The desert begins when water stops being something you own and becomes something that decides whether you are worth carrying farther.
Korath began before the sand.

Grass thinned into gray wire under the horses' hooves; stones took heat from a sun still too low to deserve such confidence. Buck gave up on mud and began hating dust, because horses, like priests and kings, preferred known grievances to new governments.

The reins told me first. Leather dried faster here. Sweat left salt along my glove seams before I had finished pretending the morning was tolerable. The air entered the mouth clean, hot, and accusing, and every old wound in my body woke as if a clerk had opened a ledger and requested payment in skin.

Asha rode ahead in a hood the color of baked clay. She had said little since the last northern inn, which was not unusual, but the silence had changed. In the North she withheld answers. Here she withheld memory. The distinction was small unless one had made a profession of listening to breath, hands, and the angle of a horse's ear.

Ciri rode beside me for the first hour, then dropped back to argue with Yennefer about the map. It was not a loud argument. Yennefer made loudness feel vulgar by sharpening every word until volume had nothing to do. Ciri answered with the clipped patience of a ruler who had learned that if she shouted, men would call it temperament instead of proof that the room had become stupid.
"The map says a dry wash bends south," Ciri said.
"The guide is riding east," Yennefer replied.
"I noticed. That is why I mentioned it."

"The guide has a cousin whose wrist is still whole and a sister's son whose freedom depends on us reaching Elskerdeg alive. He does not look at ink. He looks at dune color. Try not to be jealous of paper losing an argument."

Geralt rode behind me with Roach and watched the horses. Triss watched the riders. Regis appeared where shade should not have held a person and made polite observations about heat as if heat might apologize. Saesenthessis had left three mornings earlier, claiming Zerrikanian skies disliked witnesses who remembered older scales.
By noon, the first water seller refused coin.

His stall stood under a patched canopy where two paths met and immediately regretted the intimacy. Three clay jars sat behind him in shadow. Two boys with knives at their belts watched the jars, not us, which told me what mattered in the scene. The old man himself was brown as roasted bark, thin without weakness, and tired of travelers before our dust reached him.
"Water," Geralt said.
"Memory," the old man answered.
Ciri looked at me. Yennefer looked as if she had heard a legal argument disguised as folklore and was preparing to kill both.
Asha dismounted before either could speak. "He asks custom."
"He asks for a memory," I said.

"Custom is often inconvenient when translated accurately. Coin buys from wells owned by cities. Memory buys from wells that survived cities. You give what water can carry. If it rejects you, we buy dust instead. Dust is cheaper and less useful."
The old man smiled with four teeth and no apology. "The witness remembers. Good."
Geralt measured the jars. "I have several bad memories. How picky is the well?"
"Very," Asha said.
"Then it has standards. Unlike some innkeepers."
The old man did not laugh. The boys did, briefly, before their grandfather restored the regional government of silence.

Asha put two fingers on the nearest lid and spoke in Zerrikanian. I understood none of the words. I understood the shape. Introduction. Restraint. An apology not for wrong done today, but for failing to return when expected.
She spoke long enough for the heat to gather between us. Her shoulders did not bend. Her voice did. When she finished, the old man lifted the lid.
"She gave enough," he said in the common tongue. "Not all. That will do."
"You sell water with judgment," Yennefer said.
"I sell water with memory. Judgment is free."
Ciri almost smiled. "Expensive gift."
"For rulers, always."

The line entered the shade and stayed there. Ciri's face did not change. Stillness replaced expression, which with her was worse than anger. I knew the shape because I had seen it in soldiers, girls with knives, and people who had survived being called destiny by men who did not have to bleed for it.
I gave the well no heroic memory. I gave it Buck refusing the bridge at Willenford.
The old man listened through Asha's translation and looked disappointed in the way craftsmen look when a tool does not break as expected.
"A horse," he said.
"A good one."
"You cross a desert with horse memory?"
"Horses have kept more people alive than emperors."
Buck, who understood praise badly and suspicion perfectly, tried to bite the old man's sleeve. The water seller moved his arm without surprise.
"The well accepts," he said. "Perhaps the horse is wiser than the rider."
"Often," Geralt said.
We watered the horses first. That impressed the boys. Or perhaps it amused them. In Korath, those two expressions shared a narrow face.

After the horses drank, people drank by arithmetic. Ciri refused the extra swallow Nadir offered her and passed the cup to the youngest pack handler before anyone could turn the gesture into nobility. The boy took it with both hands and looked at the cup, not her. That was wise. Gratitude becomes dangerous when aimed too high. Yennefer watched the exchange, mouth tight, because the heat had made magic feel less like command and more like negotiation with a fever. Her fingers left faint white marks on the water skin before she noticed and released it.

Triss changed my bandage in the shadow of a leaning rock while the light went copper around us. Bad light makes wounds more honest. The cut under the wrapping had salt at the edge, grit in the fold, and a pulse that answered the land before it answered pain. She cleaned it without comment until the cloth came away redder than expected. Geralt saw that from Roach's side, checked a hoof twice, then checked Buck's for the third time because worry in him preferred iron, nails, and straps to speech.

At the next shelter, a stone shelf under a cliff lip, Triss checked my palm. The red lines had darkened during the day. Not flared. Thickened, as if heat had made the blood remember old grammar. She used cloth soaked in bitter water and touched only the edge.
"It is responding to the land," she said.
Asha looked from the basin. "No. The land is responding to him. There is a difference, and both are impolite."
"That should comfort me?"
"Comfort is not among the desert's gifts."
"It has gifts?"
"Thirst. Truth. Sand in places you cannot negotiate with."
Geralt looked up from Roach's hoof. "Charming country."
"It did not invite you."
Nadir el-Kharim, our guide, placed a clay cup before me. The drink smelled of smoke, salt, and something root-bitter enough to discourage hope.
"Tea," he said.
I lifted it. "This is punishment."
"Medicine. In Korath the distinction is mostly marketing."
I drank. It tasted like burnt rope steeped in regret. My stomach objected, then settled. The pulse in my palm eased by a fraction.
Nadir watched too closely.
"You expected something," I said.
"I always expect something. It gives disappointment a schedule."
"Try again."

His eyes went to Asha, then to the darkening east. "Men came through twelve days ago. Black coats under pilgrim brown. They paid in northern silver and asked where a red-eyed witcher would enter the Frying Pan. I sold them a lie."
"Generous," Geralt said.
"Expensive," Nadir corrected. "They knew one of my debts. A sister's son. Taken for taxes that were not taxes by men who used a seal no one local recognized."
Black Ink had crossed the maps before us.

The old file had not taught them the desert. It had taught them what to ask. Current reports supplied my fatigue, route habits, the mark's reaction near old stone, and the names of people who would spend themselves to keep me from becoming an office.
That was the danger of an institution with patience. It did not need prophecy. It needed old failure, fresh evidence, and enough coin to make strangers repeat the correct questions.
Black Ink did not cross Korath with honest noise. It arrived ahead of us as debt, question, bought silence, and a boy's absence in a guide's mouth.

Fresh reports had taught them what old files could not: how long I rode before my left shoulder stiffened, which names made me turn too quickly, when Ciri rode near enough to change my choices, and how Geralt's silence shifted when restraint looked like a cage. Local debt gave those facts legs. A missing nephew here, a water lien there, a tax company with no office but excellent handwriting. Black Ink's true desert weapon was not soldiers. It was making strangers ask the correct question and then selling them the shame of having answered.
Nadir showed us how quickly that worked.

He led us after sunset to a hollow called the Beggar's Bowl, though no bowl had ever deserved such heat. The place was a shallow ring of stone where caravans rested when they had failed to deserve better shade. Old fire pits marked the center. Around the edges, families had scratched signs into rock: one line for safe water, two for illness, three for burial, five for do not sleep here unless your enemy is thirst.
Asha read the marks before she dismounted. "Two caravans last month. One northern party. One missing child. One debt taken in water measure."
"You can read all that from scratches?" Dandelion asked.
"No. I read scratches, ash, hoof drag, and where men thought fear would not leave prints. You read audiences. Try not to become provincial because the walls stopped having curtains."
Zoltan laughed until the heat punished him for it.
Nadir knelt by the fire pit and sifted gray sand through his fingers. "They burned paper here. Not all. Enough to claim they tried."
Yennefer came down beside him and lifted one blackened strip with a spell so thin it looked like refusal. The fragment had no seal, only three words visible where the ash had held.
...bearer fatigue assessment...
Triss did not curse. That was how I knew she wanted to. She took the fragment, turned it once, and looked at my bandaged palm as if the hand had become a road map again.

"They are not only tracking route," she said. "They are tracking tolerance. Heat, thirst, proximity to old sites, contact with local rites. They want to know which pressure makes the seal answer first."
"Kind of them to conduct science," I said.
"Bad science," Yennefer replied. "No controls. No ethics. Ugly handwriting."
Geralt looked at the dark beyond the hollow. "Good enough to kill people."

Ciri had been quiet through the reading. She took the ash strip from Triss and held it near the fire, dust on her cheek, one knuckle cracked. Court portraits never bothered with cracked knuckles. That was how portraits lied.
"They will not get fatigue as evidence," she said.
"Fatigue has a habit of arriving whether or not we endorse it," I said.
"Then we change what it means before they do. Tired does not mean pliable. Wounded does not mean owned. Thirsty does not mean ready to kneel."
Nadir watched her as if revising a bad assumption. "Your empire teaches good sentences?"
"No," Ciri said. "It teaches why sentences need guards."

We slept in watches after that. Slept is generous. I closed my eyes while heat moved around the camp like a patient animal. Ciri took first watch with Tala's courier tag in hand; Asha took second and sang under her breath, rhythm without words.
Near midnight, Triss sat beside me with her knees drawn up and her hair braided out of the dust.
"Mara would hate this place," she said.
The name came without warning. I should have disliked that. I did, then did not.
"She would complain about cracked skin, contaminated water, and everyone pretending grit was character."
"She wrote back," Triss said.
My head turned too quickly.

"Not through unsafe channels," she added before I could sharpen. "One line only. Sent through a fever report that does not exist. It says: Tell him care is not recalled by distance. Tell him I burned what needed burning."
The desert moved between us.

A man can be wounded by a sentence that gives him exactly what he asked for. Mara was alive. Mara had burned duplicates. Mara had not forgiven me into comfort. She had left care standing where evidence could not easily steal it.
"That is two lines," I said.
Triss smiled with tired mercy. "I thought you would need something trivial to survive the rest."
"You were right. Do not enjoy it."
"Too late."

By morning, the Beggar's Bowl had given us three facts: Black Ink had crossed with debt records, Cazren's hymn had reached the caravanserai, and the old roads remembered my blood well enough for guides within two days to charge more for fear.
Ciri's hands went still in her lap. Yennefer's head turned slightly. Triss stopped wrapping my palm and began listening with her whole face.
"You guide us because?" I asked.
"Because if you die in the wrong place, they keep the boy and sell his debt to a man with softer hands and worse imagination. If you live, perhaps the account changes."
"So I am payment."
"No. You are trouble. I am hoping trouble falls in the correct direction."
Asha looked toward the stars. "He was always this honest when cornered."
"You liked me better silent," Nadir said.
"I liked your cousin better with two working wrists."
"Most of us did."
An hour before dawn, Buck woke me by stepping on my boot.

That is not a noble alarm, but nobility tends to arrive late and overstate itself. The horse had lowered his head and pinned both ears toward the east. Roach was awake too, still as stone. Ciri's gelding trembled without moving. Asha's mare watched the dark with the patient hatred of a creature deciding whether to run.
I reached for silver.

The draconid came out of the dry wash low and wrong. It had been a scorpion-tailed wyvern once, perhaps young, perhaps starved, but hunger had been removed from it. Its chest was flat under unbroken scales. No heart. Its wings dragged as if the joints had forgotten sky. The mouth opened and closed without sound, drawing dust inward in small breaths.
"Down," Geralt said.
Everyone moved except me. Not because I had chosen to stand bravely. Because the barbed star at my throat went cold enough to put a hook in my spine.
The wyvern turned its blind head toward me.
I saw the pattern late. Again. The dry wash was not a path. It was a throat. Red grit lay in five narrow streams around the creature, all pointing at my boots.
Ciri saw my delay and shoved me hard enough to insult several ribs. The wyvern's tail punched through the air where my chest had been. Venom struck the stone shelf and made it smoke.
I hit the ground, tasted dust, lost my grip on the knife, and hated needing the help before I had finished needing it.
"Move," Ciri snapped.
I moved. Not elegantly.

Geralt took the foreclaw aside with silver and nearly lost the edge when the scale flexed around the blade. Yennefer's spell struck the tail and made the venom gland burst in a line of black steam. Triss threw a ward over Nadir and the horses. Asha cut her thumb and flung blood into the dust, speaking three words that sounded older than language and angrier than prayer.
The wyvern did not die. It emptied.
The body folded inward as if something behind it had stopped remembering the shape. Scales collapsed. Bone softened. A final black breath left the mouth and went east.
Saesenthessis descended through red dawn before anyone had lowered a weapon. She wore human shape, but the air around her had the pressure of wings.
"Vharakthul's hunger is teaching itself flesh again," she said. "Lesser draconids are becoming rehearsal."
I spat dust and blood. "Good morning to you too."
Her gold eyes found my palm. "You answered before you moved."
"I was pushed before I answered."
Ciri looked down at me. "You are welcome. Again."
I had a reply. It was probably good. I swallowed it, which improved it beyond recognition.
"Thank you," I said.
Ciri blinked once. Geralt pretended to study the dead wyvern. Asha's mouth twitched. Buck, satisfied the governing bodies had learned humility, stepped off my boot.

By sunset we reached the first caravanserai, where a dispute over stolen shade cloth had become a trial before anyone had been granted water. A blue canvas strip lay between two families, one knife, four witnesses, and a guard young enough to believe judgment could be tidy.

Shade cloth, I learned, was not cloth in the way northerners used the word. It was water that had not yet entered the mouth. A strip large enough to cover two jars could keep a fevered child breathing until dusk. A strip cut badly could spoil dates, sour medicine, or make a guard leave his post early because his skull had begun to cook. Outsiders heard fabric and thought price. The caravanserai heard shade and thought survival arithmetic. Ciri understood that before speaking. She watched the women first: which one stood near the well, which one held the torn edge, which one kept looking toward the courier tag as if a false seal might drink from her house next.

Asha translated only the necessary lies. Nadir translated the profitable ones, then stopped when Tala's seal appeared on a courier tag carried by the man who claimed to have lost the cloth. The man's hands feared the tag more than the knife. That improved the question.

A dust-colored supply cart arrived while the guard was deciding whether truth required witnesses or only better posture. Zoltan climbed down first, beard full of road grit and temper fully loaded. Dandelion followed with a scarf over his hair and the pained dignity of a man who had been told to dress like cargo for survival.
"If this country charges for shade," Zoltan said, looking at the blue canvas, "I hope it issues receipts for bad decisions."
Dandelion touched the torn edge. "At last, politics with fabric. I can almost understand it."

By nightfall, the canvas had been returned and the courier tag taken. Zoltan brought wax samples, coin, and three names from the rumor trail. Dandelion brought two songs, one wrong on purpose and one wrong because the world had paid a better liar.

Women sold flatbread from stone griddles. Men patched wheels under lanterns hung low to conserve oil. Children ran messages between stalls with the silent competence of people who had learned that a shout wasted water. A singer with a cracked reed flute played the same four notes beside the well until Dandelion went pale from professional distress.
"Someone should help him," he whispered.
"Someone should stop you," Zoltan replied. "Both hopes are old and unlikely."

The stolen shade cloth affair opened into more than cloth. Tala's seal on the courier tag had been copied badly, then used to move three sealed jars through the pass as water medicine. Nadir opened one under Asha's direction and found no medicine. Only black wax pellets, copper shavings, and folded strips of prayer-cloth printed with Cazren's refrain in Zerrikanian script.
The translation was poor. That made it more dangerous. Bad translations travel faster because they fit more mouths.
Asha read the line once and spat into the dust. "They turned maintenance into obedience."
"Can people tell?" Ciri asked.
"Some. Not enough. Hunger does not check grammar before it kneels."

Yennefer burned the prayer-cloth after copying the mistakes. Triss kept the jar. Geralt kept the names of the men who had carried it. Zoltan kept the wax because he said one day he would like to know whether evil could be traced by smell and invoice together. Dandelion kept silent for nearly six minutes, which was how we all knew Cazren had done damage.

At the far end of the yard, Buck stood over a water trough like a tyrant with a provincial court. A smaller horse tried to drink. Buck allowed it only after looking at me as if I were responsible for the decline of border discipline.
"He is popular," Ciri said.
"He is armed with teeth and opinions. That carries in most cultures."
"So do you. Yet here we are arguing with water sellers."
"Buck has better diplomacy. He bites before making promises."
She touched the red thread at my wrist. Not the mark. Always the thread. "Do you feel it more here?"
I looked toward the pass. The hills ahead stood black against the last light. They did not look like home. They looked like a mouth deciding whether to admit taste.
"Yes."
"What does it want?"
"Old things rarely want cleanly. It recognizes. It pulls. It waits for me to mistake recognition for instruction."
Ciri's fingers tightened. "Then do not mistake it alone."

The answer should have been easy. I had been given too many easy exits in life and taken most of them at speed. Instead I let her hand remain where it was while the caravanserai shouted, bargained, cooked, bled, prayed, and lied around us.
"I will try," I said.
She looked almost satisfied. "Better. Still not good."
"Your standards survived the desert. Tragic."
"So did your mouth. Equally tragic."

That night, the courier tag was placed under three stones and one bowl of water. Asha said the water would remember who had lied with Tala's seal. Yennefer said water had no memory, only useful magical behavior under appropriate conditions. Asha said northern arrogance had a long tradition of mistaking different words for correction. Triss wrote both statements down and labeled them potentially explosive.
I slept after that, briefly, with my hand wrapped, my sword near my knee, and Ciri close enough that leaving would have woken her.
That was not safety.
It was worse. It was trust with witnesses.
Ahead lay Elskerdeg Pass, water law, Faithel judgment, and a sanctuary that had survived by learning whom not to welcome.
Behind us, the emptied wyvern cooled under sand, proof that the Crown's hunger had entered flesh badly and intended to keep practicing.
Pass-keeper proverb, translated by a northern scholar and corrected in three hands:
A gate that opens for pity will one day open for fire. A gate that never opens becomes a tomb. The keeper's sin is choosing which dead can be counted.
Elskerdeg Pass sold safety with the manners of a knife merchant.

It rose from Korath in tiers of red stone, pale stair cuts, wind-polished towers, and hanging bridges strung between cliffs too narrow for armies and too honest for diplomacy. The road bent three times before the first gate, so every traveler arrived tired, measured, and smaller than pride preferred.
Above the gate, bronze mirrors flashed in the sun. Not decoration. Signals.
I counted six watchers before Nadir lifted one hand and told me to stop being obvious.
"They know," I said.
"Yes," he replied. "But there is politeness in not proving it. In Korath, suspicion is a guest. Paranoia is a cousin who sleeps too long and eats all the dates."
Buck stopped before the first toll line and breathed at the sand with disgust.
A guard in linen and bronze looked at him. "Your beast has opinions."
"He has standards."
"Does he pay toll?"
"He bites receipts."
The guard considered this with admirable seriousness. "Critique is recognized currency in small amounts."
That almost made me like the place. Then the gate opened and three elders were waiting with the kind of stillness people use when they have already decided you are evidence.
They did not call me witcher first.
They did not call me Jack.
A herald, young and pale under the sun, read from a strip of treated leather.
"Jack of the Morning Star House. Hidden bearer. Untested return. Last Warden possibility. Admitted under dispute."
Geralt's hand moved a finger's width toward his sword.
Ciri's expression cooled into court stone. "He has a name. You read it first. Try trusting your own mouth."
One elder, a woman with skin lined like dried riverbeds, inclined her head. "I am Mother Varda of Maintenance. Names are not denied here. They are weighed."
"Then use fewer stones," I said.
Asha made a soft sound that might have been warning. Or prayer. With her, the two occasionally shared boots.

They brought us to a shade court cut into the middle tier. Water ran in a narrow floor channel, guarded by two girls with hooked knives. The seats named the factions before anyone did: Maintenance in gray, Passage in sand-white, Trade in dyed blue, Purge in unmarked black.

Before anyone named law, the pass named thirst. A clerk marked mouths, beasts, and wounded on a water slate while an old woman corrected Geralt's knot for wasting a thumb's worth of water. Above the court, girls scraped salt bloom from copper screens and sang softly: one cup for labor, one for fever, none for pride.

The slate had more columns than a northern court would have tolerated without inventing fees. Mouths. Beasts. Wounded. Oath-bound. Disputed. Children too young to carry debt were marked with blue chalk. Guides with unpaid water loans were marked in red. I received no color at first, only a blank space under disputed while two clerks argued whether a bearer counted as one mouth, one risk, or a debt the pass had inherited from dead people with poor timing. Mother Varda let them argue for exactly seven breaths before saying, 'Names are weighed here. They are not divided until they stop resembling people.'

No faction agreed about me. Maintenance wanted measurement before judgment. Passage wanted roads closed until the old pull quieted. Trade wanted terms. Purge did not waste language. Their knives were clean.
"Dead, undecided, or wisely absent?" Ciri asked.
Nadir leaned against a pillar. "In politics those are cousins."

Asha stood before the elders and gave them her return without kneeling. Her Zerrikanian came faster here, less careful, more dangerous. I caught only names I knew. Helena. Jacob. Villentretenmerth. Black Ink. Vharakthul. My own name, placed like a blade on a table.
A man from Trade asked whether the lock-force could be observed under managed contract.
Geralt said, "No."
The man blinked. "Witcher, this is not your court."
"No. Yours has better ventilation. Same kind of fools."
Mother Varda looked at Geralt as one might look at a dog that had bitten the correct stranger. "Let the bearer answer."
I stood too quickly. Heat gathered under the bandage on my palm. Ciri saw and shifted half a step, not in front of me, beside me. That helped more than I wanted to admit.

"I did not come for a throne," I said. "Or worship. Or a room full of people improving the word cage until it passes for mercy. I came because something under your stone has been reaching through my blood since the Broken Crown, and because the North is full of men who would rather file me than ask what they are filing."
"That is not an argument," said Soren of Purge, a thin man with a voice like sand in a cup.
"No," I said. "It is information you should have before making policy with my bones."
The court did not like that. Courts rarely enjoy being reminded that bones are involved. It makes upholstery harder to trust.
Soren rose. "Every key can corrupt the lock. Every living bearer invites the Crown to learn refusal. A dead key cannot betray."
"Dead men teach plenty," Geralt said.
"Usually bad lessons," Zoltan added from the side, where no one had invited him and no one had been foolish enough to remove him.
Mother Varda lifted two fingers. Silence returned with discipline.
Tala entered through the side gate while they were still deciding whether to kill me as policy or delay as courtesy.

She was younger than Asha and older than confidence. Her hair was wrapped in red cloth. Her left cheek carried a white scar that vanished beneath the jaw. She wore no ornaments except a copper ring at her throat and a red thread wound around two fingers. Her spear had seen use and no vanity.
Her eyes went first to my hands.
"This is the last bearer?" she asked in the common tongue. Her voice was low, practical, and unimpressed.
"Efficient," I said.
"That is a northern word."
"It is a tired word. Travel improved it."
She came close enough that Buck, tethered beyond the court rail, lifted his head and considered biting through jurisdiction.
"Rules," I said.

Tala lifted the red thread before answering. Every child in the court knew what it meant: witness under stress, a hand tested without being owned, a record of whether fear, insult, or danger opened the old pressure first.
Tala stopped. "You ask that before every room?"
"Rooms lie less when forced to define themselves."
"Good. No killing. No maiming unless stupidity demands education. No crimson. No Elder Blood. No mage ward. No father stepping in first."
Geralt's eyes narrowed. "Father?"
"If the word offends, prove it irrelevant by obeying."
I almost laughed. Geralt did not. That improved the room.
The test was not a duel. I had expected a duel. That was my first mistake.
Tala struck once with the spear butt, low toward the knee. I turned it aside. She did not follow. She stepped back and dropped her own guard.
It made no sense.
My body moved before judgment caught up. A gap is a question. Training answers. I went in, flat of the blade toward her ribs, light enough not to break bone.
The red thread snapped between her fingers.

Pain flashed through my palm. Not much. Enough. The barbed star cooled. The court vanished for half a breath and left only stone, heat, and the old inward pull. I checked myself too late. The blade stopped a finger from her side, but the point of my control had moved elsewhere.
Tala did not flinch.
"There," she said. "The lock answers insult faster than danger."
I stepped back, breathing through my teeth. "You baited it."
"Yes. And you followed."
Ciri's face had gone still. Geralt looked murderous. Yennefer looked as if she were deciding whether to educate a nation.
Tala tied the broken red thread around my wrist, not gently. "You are not ready."
I hated her. Then I hated that she was right.
"Good," Mother Varda said. "Now we can begin without theater."

After the test, the factions stopped decorating fear. Trade wanted access. Purge wanted my throat. Maintenance wanted records opened. Passage wanted no foreign army crossing their water lines because a northern man had brought dragon hunger home under his skin.
Ciri let them speak until they began pretending I was not in the room.
Then she stood.
She did not announce her titles. That was the first dangerous thing. Anyone can hide behind titles. Ciri used absence as a blade.

"I have what happened," she said. "Reports, copies, witness testimony, and surviving objects. Black Ink tried to classify him before asking his name. The North tried to use contracts as traps. My father's empire has not yet decided whether it wants jurisdiction, custody, or plausible ignorance. If you think killing him frees you from politics, you are children. His death would become a road. Men would march down it with cleaner boots than mine."
Soren of Purge folded his hands. "And if leaving him alive opens the Crown?"
Ciri looked at me once. Not for permission. For fact.
"Then we answer that," she said. "But we do not begin by becoming the same thing hunting him."
There was no applause. Good courts do not applaud. Bad ones do, then hang someone. This one stayed quiet long enough for Mother Varda to reach a decision.
"He enters the sanctuary under Maintenance protection," she said. "He is neither throne nor prisoner. He is a man under test. If the anchors fail, we reconvene."

"Maintenance has protected failure for five generations," he said. "The outer ring weakens. Draconids hollow. Children dream northern words. A bearer comes late, trained by witchers, touched by empire, loved by dangerous women, watched by a dragon, and you call that a man under test. I call it a door wearing mercy."
Ciri's chin lifted by one fraction.
"Careful," I said.
The court looked at me. So did Ciri.
"That was for me," I added. "I nearly proved him useful."
That quieted the room in a different way. Anger expected resistance. Honesty made everyone check the floor beneath their opinions.
Tala watched me from the side gate, arms folded, spear resting against one shoulder. "He learns after pain. Slowly."
"Do all of you use encouragement like a dull hook?" I asked.
"Only on people who mistake sharp hooks for respect."

Mother Varda tapped the staff once against stone. Water in the floor channel trembled. Not magic, perhaps. Or magic so old it had stopped announcing itself. "The court will record three conditions. First, the bearer will not touch anchor stone without Maintenance witness. Second, no external authority will claim custody within the pass. Third, no one will use affection as leverage in this court and call it prudence."
Her gaze moved to Soren, then to Geralt, then to Ciri, then to me. Fair cruelty. Efficiently distributed.
"And if he runs?" asked the Trade elder.
"Then he proves fear," Varda said. "Not guilt. We will not become northern paper because travel tired us."
Asha closed her eyes for one breath.

That was the first time I understood that returning had hurt her before it helped anyone. She had carried the names north for years, carried the shame of living, carried my existence as rumor and debt, then brought me back to people who might kill me because their old duty had become exhausted enough to resemble fear.
I wanted to thank her. The room was too full. Gratitude can become spectacle under the wrong roof.
So I only said, "Asha."
She looked at me.
I touched Helena's pouch at my belt.
Her face changed. Not much. Enough.
Tala noticed that too. She noticed everything worth resenting.
After the court broke, it leaked into corridors, whispers, knives left unbelted, and children moved from lower dormitories before anyone named why.
Dandelion watched them go and went quiet.
"Do not write that," I told him.
He looked offended, then tired. "Not everything I remember becomes a song."
"Since when?"
"Since hungry children learned Cazren's refrain faster than mine."
There are apologies men make without saying sorry. That was one. I accepted it by not looking at him too kindly.
Zoltan passed with two sacks over his shoulder. "The south has bad ale, good knives, and politics that make the North look like a tavern fight with stationery. I may retire here and become worse."
"Impossible," Geralt said.
"Aim high or stay home, wolf."
Then the lower bells rang once.
Not alarm.
Counting.
Mother Varda looked toward the sound and said, softly enough that only witcher ears and frightened hearts caught it, "One anchor heard him."
