No one asked who she meant.
"If the anchors fail," Soren said, "there may be no court left."
"Then you are spared minutes of speech."
I decided Mother Varda might be survivable.

That night they gave us rooms cut into red stone. Mine had a bed too narrow for dignity, a water bowl guarded by custom, one lamp set behind copper mesh, and a window slit facing the lower road. Heat stayed in the walls after sunset. The stone breathed it back slowly, dry and patient, until the room smelled of dust, clean linen, leather, and the bitter oil painted into the doorframe to keep old pressure from listening too closely.
I did not enter at first.

Elskerdeg had made me visible in too many useful languages. Bearer. Untested return. Man under test. A door presented as mercy. Every name had left a finger mark. I wanted air, or something near enough to air that the pass would not tax it as a luxury.
Tala found me beside the third water court.

Ciri had gone with Mother Varda to turn her protection speech into written condition before some clerk improved it into leash. Geralt had taken Buck's saddle apart because fear, in him, often disguised itself as leatherwork. Yennefer and Triss were copying court testimony with the kind of silence that meant two intelligent women had agreed not to murder anyone until ink dried. Asha had vanished into the returning corridors, where old shame knew her name and kept saying it.

The water court sat between two sandstone walls open to a strip of dark sky. Copper reeds screened the eastern side, thin enough for air and thick enough for privacy if no one wished to be rude. Water moved below in disciplined threads. The lamps were low. Their red glass made the stone look warm and the shadows look almost alive.
Tala brought two cups of water and one strip of salted date bread.
"This is not courtship," she said.
"Good. I was afraid tradition had underfed me."
"Ration law. You missed evening measure. I dislike waste."
"Romance survives another wound."
"Northern word."
She sat anyway.

For a while, neither of us spoke. The pass breathed through vents and copper. Stone held heat from the day and grief from five centuries. Below us, the channels murmured like something disciplined because everyone alive had agreed to make discipline cheaper than disaster.
Tala ate her half of the date bread slowly. I ate mine too fast. She judged me without moving her face.
"You eat like someone expects the food to be taken away," she said.
"Often accurate."
"Not here. Here food is taken away if you waste it, insult the water, or listen badly to elders."
"I am in danger from two of those."
"Three. You waste yourself."

I looked at her. The lamp made the white scar along her cheek sharper. It vanished under her jaw, then reappeared when she swallowed. She was not dressed for ceremony. Linen shirt, loose trousers, spear calluses, a bandage above one arm where the court test had not cut her but old duties had already taken bites. Nothing ornamental except the copper ring at her throat.
"That is a hard accusation to answer with bread in my mouth," I said.
"Then swallow first."
I did.
"Proceed."
She looked at the water instead of me. "I was not always Maintenance."
"No?"

"Purge took me first. My mother believed the old line had become too dangerous to preserve. She thought mercy was a gate left unguarded. I learned knife work there. Silence. How to look at one person and decide if ten others would live more easily with that person dead."
The water below kept moving.
"What changed?" I asked.

"A boy. Not you. Do not become vain. He was thirteen, fevered, born with old gold pressure in his lungs but no bloodline to carry it. Purge wanted him ended before he became a crack. A Maintenance keeper made me sit with him three nights first. By the second, he was no longer a crack. He was a boy who hated bitter tea and lied badly about being afraid. By the third, killing him would have required me to become less accurate."
"Did he live?"
"No."
No ornament. No appeal. The word stood hard and small.
"But he died as himself," she said. "Not as evidence for my fear. Maintenance took me after that. Or I took it. The order depends on who is telling the story."
I looked at her hands. Spear callus. Red-thread scars. Small burns from copper work. Hands trained to end a life and then trained harder to keep one from becoming an argument.
"Is that why you test me?"
"I test you because you are dangerous. I stay because you answer badly and then try again."
It should not have been enough. It was.
The silence changed. Not into comfort. Comfort would have cheapened it. Into permission. The kind that made no promise of safety and therefore felt less like a trap than mercy usually did.
I set my cup down first, away from the edge of the channel.
Tala noticed. Of course she did.
"Good," she said.
"Water before speeches. I learn slowly."
"Slow learning is still learning if the cup remains unbroken."
"Rules," I said.

She looked at me, and for the first time I saw amusement arrive unarmed. "No promises made to avoid grief. No touch used as proof of belonging. No pretending tomorrow is not coming. No lying to Ciri by omission if this changes what she has a right to know."
That last rule cut cleanest.
"She knows there is a road here," I said.
"Then do not hide where you step."
Tala set her own cup down with care. Water law made even desire move respectfully around objects that kept people alive.
"More rules?" I asked.
"If I say stop, you stop. If you say stop, I stop. If pain speaks before either of us does, we listen to pain. If fear speaks, we make it name itself before obeying."
"Efficient."
"Necessary."
"Are you certain?"
"No," she said. "I am aware. Certainty is what fools bring to wells."
I believed her. That was the beginning of danger.

Tala touched my wrist, above the red thread, not on the mark. I let her. The letting mattered more than the heat that followed. Her thumb found the place where her test-thread had left a shallow crease in my skin.
"Be here," she said.
"I am."
"Not because tomorrow frightens you?"
"Tomorrow frightens me very thoroughly. That is not why."
Her eyes held mine in the low red light. "Say the why."

I could have said desire. True, and too easy. I could have said gratitude. True, and dangerous in the wrong way. I could have said I wanted to feel human before the pass improved me into a function. True, and therefore almost a lie because it leaned too close to using her as proof.
"Because you see the part that wants to become useful," I said, "and you do not flatter it."
Her breath changed. Barely. Enough.
"Good," she said. "Now stop talking like a witness before a tired court."
I closed the distance.
Not fast. Not theatrical. I moved as I would move toward a drawn blade held by someone who had already told me the rule of the room. Refusal could have lived in every inch between us. It did not.
Tala let me come to her.

The kiss was blunt, hot, and exact. Her mouth met mine with the directness of a spear thrust stopped exactly where training intended. No conquest. No apology. No softness pretending the room contained no consequences.
She tasted of salt, date bread, and water measured carefully enough to become law.
Her hand stayed around my wrist above the red thread. Not on the mark. The distinction was deliberate.
I placed my other hand on her shoulder and waited until she shifted closer.
That was her answer.
"There," she said against my mouth.
Not coy. A location confirmed.
Heat entered quickly. Fear followed. I drew back before either could disguise itself as certainty.
Tala let me go.
She did not chase, soothe, or punish the retreat. She sat beside the water court and watched me find my breathing.
"Say it."
"If this becomes goodbye, stop me."
"I planned to."
"If I make you permission to die, hit me."
"Hard."
My breath changed.
Tala noticed. "That interests you?"
"Your concern has unusual architecture."
"You mistake correction for cruelty because northern affection is badly trained."
"And Zerrikanian affection?"
"Carries water before making speeches."
She lifted both cups and moved them beyond reach of an accidental foot.
Only then did she return.
"Chosen?" she asked.
"Yes."
"Then stand."
I stood.
This time I kissed her first.
Copper reeds clicked in the desert wind. Below us, water traveled through disciplined channels. The pass had survived five centuries by giving pressure somewhere lawful to go.
Tala treated desire the same way.
Her fingers found the buckle at my shoulder.
"This?"
"Yeah."
She opened it with one hand. The strap loosened. Her palm remained against the leather over my chest, feeling the movement beneath.
"Pain?"
"No... no."
"Fear?"
"…yes."
"Useful."
"Everyone I want has disturbing opinions about fear."
"Then improve your taste."
I smiled despite myself, small and dangerous. "Too late."
For the first time that night, Tala almost smiled back.
She turned and led me behind the copper screen.
The sleeping space held a woven mat, folded linen, a clay lamp, a shallow basin, and no decoration beyond workmanship. Tala placed her spear within reach. Her knife beside it. She looked at my sword.
I set it beside hers.
"Closer," she said.
"I trust you."
"The pass contains other people."
I moved it closer.
"Better."

She wore what work required: loose trousers, a linen shirt repaired at one shoulder, belt, bandage above one arm, copper ring at her throat. Spear calluses marked her palms. Fine red-thread scars crossed one wrist. The white line along her cheek disappeared under her jaw.
Nothing ornamental. Nothing offered for approval.
I wanted her with an intensity made worse by accuracy.
"What?" she asked.
"You."
"Broad."
"You brought ration bread to a dangerous man and called it waste prevention."
"It was."
"You sat down."
"You were wasting yourself where I could see."
"Romantic."
"Northern word."
I reached for the next buckle myself.
Her eyes narrowed, measuring, not forbidding.
"This?" I asked.
"Yes. Do it properly."
"Cruel standard."
"Low standard."
Armor came away according to utility. Shoulder strap. Bracer. Knife belt. Coat. Each item placed for retrieval. Each injury checked without transforming the act into medicine.
When a sleeve dragged across my shoulder, pain crossed my face.
Tala stopped.
"Careful," she said.
"That was me."
"Then be careful with yourself. It is shared tonight."
The sentence struck beneath the ribs.
She saw it and did not apologize.

Her fingers entered my open collar and moved over scarred skin with practical attention. She learned where muscle had tightened around old damage, where the crimson had once heated flesh, and where the necklace made touch feel like trespass.
At the chain she stopped.
"No," I said.
"No."
She moved beside it and placed her palm over my heart.
"Fast."
"You are very close."
"Accurate cause."
My hand went to the tie at her throat.
"This?"
"Yes."
The knot resisted. I started to force it, then stopped before she could correct me.
Tala's mouth moved once. "Learning."
"Slowly."
"Visible."
I worked the leather loose properly and opened the shirt.
The linen parted over sun-warmed skin. An old scar crossed her collarbone. Her pulse moved beneath it.
I did not touch the scar first. I looked at her.
She gave one short nod.
Only then did I trace beside it.
Her breath left through her teeth. Controlled. Physical. She did not transform the reaction into embarrassment.
"There," she said.
I kissed the scar.
Her hand entered my hair and held me there. The pressure was clear without being force. When my mouth moved beneath her ear, her head tilted and a rough sound escaped before she caught it.
"Again," she said, clipped and low.
I listened.
She drew me upright and opened my shirt. Her hands found each old injury without lingering sentimentally over any of them.
"You carry damage like rank," she said.
"Cheaper than gold."
"Not praise."
"Nothing from you is."
Her mouth moved once. Almost a smile.

We removed the remaining armor and clothing without performance. Belts loosened. Boots placed near the mat. Linen lifted carefully around her bandaged arm. My injured hand failed a fastening; she took over without pretending the failure meant anything beyond weakness.
Tala stood before me in red lamplight with strong shoulders, spear-trained arms, old scars, and a bruise near her ribs. She did not cover herself or arrange her body for admiration.
She waited to see whether I would remain honest under wanting.
I approached the bruise and stopped.
"Painful?"
"If pressed."
"Then I will not press it."
"You may forget."
"Tell me."
"I will."
Her hands moved over my chest. Not gentle in the northern sense. Attentive. Better word. She found where ribs complained and where scars had tightened. Each touch asked without ornament.
I answered by placing her hand more firmly where I wanted it.
"There," I said.
Tala nodded. "Useful answer."
She took my marked wrist and turned the palm upward. The red thread crossed it above the scar.
"Chosen warning," she said.
"Not restraint."
"If it becomes restraint?"
"I tell you."
She placed my open hand against her shoulder. "Hold me."
I did.
She leaned into the grip.
Trust expressed as weight. Tala's language.
We lowered ourselves onto the narrow mat and lost balance once. The woven surface shifted. Her shoulder struck the copper screen, which whispered reproach.
Tala laughed once into my mouth.
"Poor equipment," I said.
"Maintenance will review it."
"Urgently?"
"After the next court decides not to kill you."
Tomorrow remained in the room. Good. Desire without tomorrow is merely appetite pretending not to understand time.
I supported my weight away from her bruised side.
Tala caught the hesitation. "Closer."
"Your ribs."
"I will speak. Trust the rule."
I moved closer.

Heat passed between us, dry and startling. Her body was built around balance; even lying down, she adjusted with trained precision, shifting my injured arm where it carried less weight and setting herself where leverage belonged.
No passive yielding.
No performance.
She guided pressure. Corrected balance. Pulled me back when caution became distance.
"Not away."
"I am here."
"Then be here."
I was.
Her hand found mine and guided it lower with exact pressure.
"There," she said, clipped.

I followed, fingers tracing the slick heat of her, learning the places that made her breath sharpen. She was wet, the arousal clear and unhidden. When I slid two fingers inside the tight clench of her she made a low, rough sound.
"Mmmh... yes."

Her hips moved with precise rolls against my hand, directing the depth and curl. Her free hand at my shoulder gripped when it pleased her. I lowered my mouth to her breast, tongue circling the nipple, saliva leaving a wet trail as I sucked gently. Her body trembled in small waves. The wet clench around my fingers pulsed. "Ah... there. Harder."
When the first climax took her it came in long, precise pulses. Her body locked around my fingers. A sharp low sound escaped as she trembled and held my gaze.
"Jack..."

She pulled me up after, eyes fierce in the red lamplight, and guided me between her thighs. The thick length of me met the slick heat of her. I pressed in slowly. The wet clench gripped every inch as I buried myself. She adjusted the angle with her hand at my hip.

"Slower," then "There," and I obeyed, moving with measured strokes while she met every thrust with precise rolls of her hips. Her legs wrapped around me, guiding depth. Sweat cooled between us. Her low sounds broke more often. Breath hot against my jaw.
"Mmmh... deeper."

Her second build came with her body tightening in long waves around the thick length of me. The wet clench pulsed hard as she trembled. "Yes... like that." I followed her over. Control fraying as the heat of my release surged into her in strong pulses. Her body still gripping me through the last tremors.

We did not stop at one. She rolled us when breath allowed, taking the lead with the same disciplined grace. Riding with measured rolls of her hips. The slick heat of her dragged along every inch. I held her waist, following her rhythm. Her hand guided mine to where she wanted pressure. Another build. Another climax for her with low rough sound and trembling.
"Ah... Jack." as she moans while mine is hitting the spot.

We changed positions with the same ruthless attention. Her on her side. Me behind driving deeper while her hand stayed at my hip directing. Later her guiding me above again until exhaustion claimed us both. Sweat-slick and breathing hard. The mat shifted. Copper screen whispering every adjustment.
Afterward was not soft enough to be easy.

Afterward was water from one shared cup, a shaking hand, a tightened bandage, a shoulder checked in lamplight, a bruise she had hidden under discipline until I saw it and she gave me an offended look for noticing late. Afterward was me cleaning a shallow cut near her ribs with the corner of my shirt because the proper cloth was out of reach and neither of us wished to stand yet. Afterward was her taking the cloth from me and doing it correctly because tenderness did not excuse incompetence.
"You are terrible at wound cleaning from this angle," she said.
"I usually have a table."
"You usually have excuses."
She smiled then. Not much. Enough to make the room warmer than the lamps deserved.

We lay on the narrow sleeping mat behind the screen of copper reeds while the channels murmured below us. The world remained unsaved. My palm still ached. The sanctuary still waited beyond court words and pass law. Her shoulder was warm under my hand. Sweat cooled along my back. Every breath reminded me I had not become a lock yet. Every silence reminded me the stone below wanted an answer.
Tala drew one finger along the red thread at my wrist.
"If you choose death because it is easier than being held," she said, "I will curse your name in three languages and teach the children the rude version."
"That seems fair."
"Not fair. Necessary."
"And if every other door burns?"
Her face changed in the low light. The change was not softness. It was the cost arriving early and asking to sit.
"Then I will stand where I can see your face," she said. "And I will not call it beautiful."
That was more intimate than anything the night had given us.
When I returned to the room cut into red stone, Ciri was waiting beside the window.

She knew before I spoke. Of course she did. Her face tightened, hurt moving through it like a blade under cloth. But she listened. That was the courage of her. Not that she felt less. That she did not make feeling into law.

The room smelled of clean linen, hot stone, bitter door oil, and the dust I had carried back on my boots. Ciri stood with both hands on the sill, looking down at the gate lamps as if one of them had personally offended her. She had changed into a plain linen shirt and dark trousers, her hair braided badly enough to prove she had done it herself. Heat had put color along her throat. Dust still clung to one cheek where she had wiped sweat with the wrong part of her sleeve.
"Did it make leaving easier?" she asked.
"No."
"Good. Then it was not cowardice."
I had no answer that did not deserve silence.

She gave me one anyway. She turned from the window, saw the loosened strap, the red thread, the place where Tala's knot no longer bit but still remembered. Pain moved across her face. She did not make it mine to solve.
"I hate this," she said.
"Yes."
"I hate that I understand it."
"That may be worse."
"It is."

For a moment the pass outside sounded too large for the room. Ropes creaked. A mule complained. Somewhere below, a clerk discovered that Zoltan had opinions about barricade nails and would now be forced to survive them.
"Do not make distance and call it freedom," Ciri said.
Geralt's words from my parents' grave came back with poor timing.
"I was not."
"You were preparing to."
I wanted to lie because the lie had manners. Instead I said, "Yes."

She came close enough that the room lost a careful inch of air. Not close enough for claim. Close enough for consequence. Her fingers found the red thread at my wrist. She did not touch the mark beneath it. She touched the chosen warning, the thing put there to keep me human.
"Better," she said. "Not good."
"You have all been saying that lately."
"Then learn faster."
I let her hold the thread a moment longer, then turned my hand so my fingers closed lightly around hers.
Ciri looked down at the contact.
"I will not ask you to be noble about this," I said.
Her throat moved. "Good. I would refuse badly."
"I know."
"Do you?"
"Enough to stay in the room while you hate it."
That answer landed harder than comfort would have. She drew one breath through her nose and let none of it become grace.
"I intend to be difficult," she said.
"You have trained for it."
Her laugh was small, wounded, and real.

I touched her cheek with the backs of my fingers. Not a claim. Not apology. A visible thing. She leaned into it for one heartbeat, then caught herself before comfort became permission for either of us to pretend the room was stronger than the world outside it.
"Rules," she said.
"No hiding. No calling desire strategy. No using anyone else to make tomorrow simpler. No dying to make anyone's feelings cleaner."
"That last one deserves repetition."
"Everyone seems fond of it."
"Because you keep trying to make death sound organized."
She looked at my mouth, then back at my eyes, and anger crossed her face because the body had a poor sense of timing and the heart had worse.
"Ciri," I said.
"Yes."
"If this is anger, keep it anger. I know how to stand near that."
"It is anger," she said. "It is also not only anger."

Her hand rose to the side of my neck. Not soft. Not hesitant. Exact. For a breath, nothing moved except the water in the wall channels and whatever foolish part of me still believed restraint could keep a man unwounded.
"If I kiss you," she said, "it is not forgiveness."
"Good."
"It is not proof that I understand enough to hurt less."
"No."
"It is not a contest."
"I know."
"With me?" she asked.
"With you."
I kissed her before either of us could turn the question into another council.

The kiss was brief and not gentle enough to become consolation. It carried heat, yes, but the heat was leashed by grief and choice. I kept one hand against the wall beside her shoulder and the other open where she could see it until she took it and put it back on her wrist herself.
"No distance," she whispered.
"No distance."

Her mouth trembled against mine, then steadied because she forced it to. When the second kiss threatened to become a road neither of us had agreed to walk tonight, she stopped it by resting her forehead against my chest.
"Not tonight," she said.
"No."
"Not because I do not want you."
"I know."
"Because if we let this room become proof, tomorrow will use it badly."
"Then we disappoint the room."
She stayed close for one breath more, hand locked around my wrist, eyes bright and furious and hurt. Then she stepped back.
"Good," I said, too tired and too grateful to choose a safer word.
"No," she said. "Not good. Visible."
That was the most honest comfort Elskerdeg gave me before the gate shouted.
A shout rose from the lower gate.
The postern key had been sold.

Black Ink did not attack like soldiers. Soldiers shout because fear needs company. These men came with muffled boots, hooked knives, glass bulbs, and three local guides who had decided debt was stronger than shame. One carried a restraint rig padded at the wrists.
The court learned before dawn that policy could bleed.

Ves, who had arrived with Roche's final courier and a disposition improved by the chance to stab men in offices, caught the first intruder on the stair. Geralt took the second at the gate arch. Zoltan met the third with an axe and a sentence too dwarven to translate politely.
I went for the postern.
Wrong choice.
The man with the padded restraints had not come for my throat. He came for the red thread. He hooked it with a curved blade and pulled.
Pain went through my palm and into the stone.
For one breath, Elskerdeg answered. Lamps bent. Water in the floor channel rose in a thin line. The pass itself seemed to inhale through my hand.
Tala struck the man from the side and drove him into the wall hard enough to crack teeth. Ciri caught my wrist with both hands.
"Hold," she said.
Not Geralt's voice. Not the same word. Same shape.
I held.
The pass exhaled.

Afterward, Asha named the traitor who had sold the postern key. She did it coldly, without satisfaction. That made the man look smaller than anger would have. Mother Varda ordered him bound, watered, and kept alive for questioning, which proved this country could be cruel in ways that respected logistics.
Tala wiped blood from her spear and looked at my wrist.
"You needed help."
"I noticed."
"Did you?"
I looked at Ciri's hand still around mine. "Eventually."
The court admitted us to the sanctuary at first light.
No one mentioned that the gate had nearly used me as a bell.
That was how I knew everyone had noticed.
The morning after the postern attack, Elskerdeg made us watch consequence before giving us shelter.

The traitor who sold the key was brought to the lower shade court bound in white cord, given water, and made to name every debt that had found his throat: wife's burial fee, brother's gambling loss, a nephew taken by a tax company under a dead name, three loans recorded by men with northern ink, and one Black Ink contact who had never said Black Ink aloud.
"Why keep him alive?" I asked Tala.
She stood beside me with her spear across both hands. "Dead men stop telling us which hunger bought them."
"The North occasionally remembers that. Usually late."
"The North likes executions because they make lines look clean." Her eyes went to the bound traitor. "Our lines live in sand. Cleanness insults them."

Ciri stood with Mother Varda while the testimony was taken. She did not command the court. She did something more dangerous. She listened with the bearing of someone who could command later. Men adjusted themselves around that. Women too. A ruler who listens before speaking makes every liar choose whether to improve or panic.
Geralt leaned near the gate, arms folded, eyes on me rather than the prisoner.
"You are doing it," I said.
"What?"
"Watching whether I turn myself into an errand."
"Yes."
The clean answer annoyed me into almost smiling. "At least pretend to be subtle."
"Too hot."
Yennefer passed behind us carrying a strip of the restraint rig in a glass tube. "Subtlety is frequently used by men afraid their motive would look foolish in good light. Geralt is simply obvious."
"Thank you," Geralt said.
"It was not a compliment."
"I know. They last longer from you."

Triss stood by the water channel with Sera, comparing Black Ink's restraint padding with Faithel anchor cloth. Her anger had become work, and work had become mercy. She looked up once when Geralt and Yennefer spoke, aware of history standing in the same corridor and refusing to die neatly.
The traitor named the phrase he had been given as assurance.
The bearer will choose the smallest chain if the room contains enough people he loves.
The court heard it. Ciri heard it. Geralt heard it. Asha's mouth went hard. Tala looked at me, and for the first time since we met, there was no test in her face.
Only recognition.
"They know your wound," she said.
"Several people have taken turns pointing at it."
"No. They know the part that wants to become useful before it becomes honest. That wound is older than you."
"Comforting. I have inherited structural stupidity."
"You have inherited maintenance," Tala said. "There is stupidity in mistaking the two."
At first light, before the sanctuary gate opened, Mother Varda ordered the postern sealed and the traitor's testimony copied three times. One copy for the court. One for Ciri. One for me.
"Why me?" I asked.
"Because documents have hurt you enough that you should own one that hurts them back."
I took it.
The paper did not feel clean.
Good. Clean paper had been the problem from the start.
Fragment from a Faithel teaching tablet, later recited by a child who did not know why the adults wept:
A house that keeps a lock is not a palace. A hand that tends a wound is not a crown. Blood is not privilege. Blood is maintenance.
The sanctuary did not rise from the desert.

It had been cut into the place where desert, mountain, and old fear shared a wall. From outside it looked like stepped sandstone, copper vents, shadowed colonnades, and water channels too narrow to waste a prayer in. The lower gates bore no statues. I approved of that. Statues are how the dead begin collecting rent.

Inside, the air changed. Cooler. Not kind. Kindness was not an architectural principle here. The halls held the smell of salt, stone, old oil, bruised mint, and iron that had not yet decided whether to be tool or weapon. Water ran beneath floor grates in guarded threads.
"Beautiful," Triss said.
"Desperate," Yennefer replied.
"Those often share a tailor," Geralt said.
Dandelion, who had been allowed in only after promising not to rhyme sanctuary with perfumery, whispered, "I write those down."
"You should," Zoltan said. "They will not fill a large book."

A woman in gray robes met us beyond the third gate. She was broad-shouldered, severe, and held a staff tipped with black iron. Her hair had gone white not with age, but with the sort of work that makes age look like an amateur.
"I am Sera of the Third Maintenance," she said. "Asha returns late. The northern company arrives attached. The bearer comes breathing. Good. We can still disagree usefully."
"I like her," Ciri murmured.
"That may pass," Geralt said.
"You say that often. It rarely does."

Sera's gaze rested on me. She did not look at my eyes first. She looked at the red thread, the bandaged palm beneath it, the way my shoulder sat slightly higher from the postern wrench, and the hidden place under my shirt where the barbed star had started to cool again.
"He is not to be left alone with old stone," she said.
"I have been left alone with worse," I said.
"Yes. That is why you answer badly."
Asha lowered her head. Not bowing. Returning. It hurt to watch. Some rooms make grief visible by refusing to make space for it.
Sera took her hand once, briefly. "You lived."
"Not here."
"That is still a kind of living. We will argue later about whether it was well done."
Asha's mouth trembled and steadied. "I missed your kindness."
"Then your memory has become decorative."

Before the old rooms, Sera made us wait in an ordinary corridor and let the sanctuary happen around us: a gatekeeper with one arm in a sling losing an argument over mint water, apprentices with raw hands being sent to drink first, children copying ration marks onto wax tablets small enough not to steal from the next mouth.

The gatekeeper with the sling had lost two fingers, not the will to accuse cooks of extravagance. He held up a chipped cup and argued that mint water for fever apprentices required three leaves, not four. The cook, a square woman with flour on one wrist and a burn along her thumb, answered that a child coughing blood had earned the luxury of a fourth leaf and that Maintenance could fine her after the cough stopped. Sera did not intervene. Law here seemed to trust argument more than sentiment.

The apprentices had raw hands from copper scraping. They were not allowed to pretend toughness made thirst smaller. A gray-robed teacher sent them to the wall basin before the older workers, and when one boy objected, she made him hold out both palms. The skin had split at the thumb joint. 'A cracked hand wastes blood,' she said. 'A wasted hand wastes water. Drink.' He drank with the furious dignity of a child caught being cared for.

Farther down the corridor, children copied ration marks onto wax tablets with bone styluses. One girl drew a generous line on a water measure because her brother was ill. The teacher took the tablet, scraped it clean, and made her draw again. Not cruelly. Worse, accurately. 'A generous mark steals from the next mouth if the cistern does not agree,' she said. The girl cried once, silently, then redrew the line smaller. I disliked the lesson. I disliked more that it was true.

Then the sanctuary stopped being an ancient secret and became a place where tired people maintained survival with cups, scoldings, tablets, bad tempers, and hands too young for the work they already knew. Mystical nobility would have been easier to resent. Maintenance under pressure was harder. It looked too much like people trying to keep one another alive without having enough kindness to waste on lies.

They showed me the water walls first because the Faithel believed in explaining danger through plumbing. The sanctuary had five outer anchor lines, each a channel cut through stone, lined with copper, salt, and old draconic ash. The channels did not hold Vharakthul by strength. They gave the pressure somewhere to go, the way a ditch gives floodwater a path that is not your bed.
The second thing they showed me was breakfast.

The sanctuary ate by work, not rank. Bread came flat and salted; dates were quartered with violent fairness; lentils moved clockwise, water counterclockwise, because even generosity here kept discipline.
A little girl with two copper beads in her hair sat across from me and stared at my eyes with complete professional interest.
"Are you the lock?" she asked.
The hall went still in the small radius around us.
"No," I said.
She considered. "Are you the man with the lock?"
"Closer."
"My grandmother says closer is where most mistakes live."
"Your grandmother sounds expensive to argue with."
The girl nodded solemnly. "She charges in chores."
Zoltan nearly choked on lentils. Dandelion covered his mouth in a way that suggested a rhyme had tried to escape and been killed for mercy.
Sera, seated three places away, did not rescue me. Faithel training apparently began with letting children ask the worst question in the room.
"What is your name?" the girl asked.
"Jack."
"That is short."
"I travel. Long names cost saddle room."
She accepted this with the grave skepticism children reserve for adult nonsense that entertains them. "I am Iren. I carry water cups on third mornings. If you break the channel, I will be angry."
"Reasonable."
"Do not break it."
"I will try."
"Trying is what people say before chores get larger."

Ciri laughed then, sudden and bright enough that three people looked at her as if she had broken court etiquette by becoming human in public. The sound did more damage to my defensive plans than Tala's spear had.
After breakfast, Tala took me through the sleeping tiers.

Not sacred chambers. Sleeping tiers. Tala made me see children arguing over blankets, old women mending screens, a one-legged man grinding herbs, boys failing at staff forms, and mothers measuring water into bowls marked by family scratches. The sanctuary was chores under doom. That made it harder to leave behind as myth.
"This is not for guilt," Tala said.
"No?"
"Guilt makes northerners dramatic and therefore unreliable. This is for weight. If you decide anything here, decide with weight, not fever."
A boy ran past carrying a copper cup. He slowed when he saw me, almost tripped, recovered, then pretended the stumble had been planned. I respected the effort.
"Do they know what I am?" I asked.
"They know too many stories. We are trying to replace some with one man walking badly in heat."
"Unkind. Accurate."
"Accuracy is kindness when fear has become decorative."

She stopped at a high balcony overlooking the inner water court. Below, five channels met around a circular stone basin. Each line entered separately. None touched. Copper plates along the rim had been polished by generations of hands.

"Every family here gives one month a year to Maintenance," she said. "Not because they are noble. Because if they do not, the water stinks, the copper pits, the salt cakes wrong, and old hunger finds a crack. People like heroic stories because they end before sweeping. We sweep."
I looked down at the channels. "House Morningstar swept too?"
"House Morningstar was not a house first. It was a duty that got roofed because rain annoyed people. Later men made names. Later still, northerners found names easier to steal than work."
The barbed star under my shirt cooled.
"That meant yes," I said.
"That meant yes, and do not look pleased. Maintenance is not nobility."
"I am rarely in danger of feeling noble."
"Good. Nobility wastes water on mirrors."
At noon, Sera made me carry two buckets from the eastern cistern to the healing room.
Geralt watched this with the stillness of a man considering whether the world had improved while he was not looking.
"He is injured," he said.
"So are the channels," Sera replied. "They still carry."
"Careful."
"No. Measured. Careful is what frightened people say when they want work done by someone else."

I carried the buckets. One sloshed onto my boot because my left hand shook halfway up the stair. No one helped. I hated them for it, then understood, then hated understanding because it refused to be simple.
At the top, Tala took one bucket only after I set it down.
"Good," she said.
"Not good. Wet boot."
"Visible."
I had heard that word before from Ciri, Yennefer, Asha, and now Tala. Perhaps everyone in the world had formed a committee while I slept badly through my own life.
The first channel steamed when I approached.
Tala stepped between me and the copper. "No closer."
"Your hospitality remains warm."
"Yes. It tries to cook guests."
Triss crouched near the channel, careful not to touch. "This is not only binding. It is circulation. The prison needs maintenance because the Crown is not inert. It pushes, learns, reacts."
"All prisons teach the prisoner their walls," Yennefer said.
Sera looked at her with some respect. "You are less ornamental than your clothing suggests."
"Often."
Geralt studied the channel. "Bad place to put a monster."
"There was no good place," Asha said.
Sera took us to the lower cistern before dusk.

The descent went through three locked doors, two false turns, and one corridor so narrow Zoltan accused the architects of harboring personal grudges against shoulders. The air cooled with each step until sweat became salt on the skin. Lamps burned behind red glass. Their light made every face look wounded before anything had happened.

At the bottom, the cistern opened into a long chamber half filled with dark water. The ceiling hung low. Copper ribs crossed it like the inside of some old beast. Along the walls, names had been carved by hand. Not rulers. Not heroes. Maintainers. People who had cleaned, replaced, watched, died, failed, repaired, and returned to work before anyone remembered to praise them.
Asha touched one name near the door.
"My mother," she said.
No one answered too quickly. Even Dandelion had learned that some silences should not be improved.

Tala walked to the water's edge and knelt. "This cistern listens to old pressure. When the Crown pushes, the water blackens first. When the bearer comes close, it should remain still if the anchors are strong."
"Should," I said.
"A beautiful word for people who dislike responsibility."
"Everyone here teaches with insults."
"You learn with resistance. We adapt."
Sera gestured me forward.
The first step did nothing. The second made the red thread at my wrist tighten. The third made the water draw back from the stone lip as if the cistern had inhaled.
Geralt moved.
Tala lifted one hand without looking at him. "No father stepping in first. That rule did not expire."
"Not his father," Geralt said.
"Then prove it better."
He stopped. Not because he agreed. Because Ciri touched his sleeve.
I took the fourth step.

Blackness rose under the water. Not ink. Ink would have been almost comforting by then. This was shadow with appetite, gathering beneath the surface, folding itself into a shape that almost became a crown before the copper ribs overhead rang once.
I tasted ash.
A voice came with it, not loud, not outside me.
Little lock.

My knees bent. Not from fear. Recognition struck the body before thought arranged itself. I saw Helena's room. Jacob's hilt. Ciri's hand on red thread. Geralt's fingers on a stirrup. Buck's teeth. Mara's unsent care. Every person who had made me heavier than survival.
Little lock, it said again, and I understood the cruelty. It did not offer power. Power is for fools and young kings. It offered relief.
Open, and no one will have to hold you anymore.
The water climbed the steps.
Ciri's voice reached me through stone and blood. "Jack."
Not hold. Not stop. My name.
I took one step back.

The cistern struck the copper ribs hard enough to make lamps jump. Water slapped the walls, black at the center, clear at the edges. Triss threw up a ward around the nearest lamp. Yennefer anchored it. Sera drove the butt of her staff into a floor notch and shouted a Faithel command that made my teeth hurt.
The blackness sank.

Only after it vanished did I realize Tala had been beside me, one hand on the back of my belt, not pulling, not holding, simply ready to keep my body from falling into the water if my will lost the argument.
"That was Vharakthul," Yennefer said.
Saesenthessis answered from the door. "That was his courtesy."
"He has courtesy?" Zoltan asked.
"All old predators do. It gets them closer before the teeth."
Sera studied the water. "The outer ring is weaker than we feared."
"Say it plain," I said.

She did. Faithel kindness had no cushions. "If we only repair stone, he learns the repair. If we move you away, he pulls through what follows you. If we kill you, your blood becomes a road through death and someone else will try to own the corpse."
"Efficient list. Missing cheerful options."
"There are none in this room."
Ciri crossed to me, ignoring every custom about water lines, and took my hand. The cistern did not stir.
"Then we find another room," she said.
Sera looked at our joined hands. "That is what hope often says before it begins counting bodies."
"Then hope will learn arithmetic," Ciri replied.
No one improved that.
"There are graves."
"We tried those first," Sera replied. "He made them doors."
The sentence had no ornament. That gave it teeth.
They took us to Helena's room last.

I knew before they opened it. Not because of magic. Because Asha slowed, Sera stopped speaking, and Tala's hand moved near mine as if the thread could hold something that had begun moving under my skin.

The room was small. That offended me. I had expected, perhaps hoped, for grandeur, because grandeur gives anger a bigger target. Helena Morningstar had spent her last days in a room with a low bed, one writing table, a water basin, a narrow window, and a shelf where three clay cups still sat. Someone had kept them clean.

The three clay cups on the shelf undid me more efficiently than the table. One had a nick near the rim. One had been repaired with a dark mineral seam. The third was small enough for a woman who had been told to rest and had apparently ignored the instruction with household precision. Someone had washed them recently. Not ceremonially. Correctly. Dust had been kept from the rims. The basin had been scrubbed where water rings usually leave pale ghosts. A room preserved too grandly becomes a shrine. This one had been kept ready, as if Helena might return irritated by poor housekeeping.

No one rushed me. It unsettled me more than pressure. Ciri stood near the window and let her hands remain visible. Geralt stayed at the threshold as if crossing without invitation would make him another man with a claim. Yennefer examined the wall rather than my face, because pride can become mercy when placed correctly. Triss looked at the notes and not the trembling in my fingers. Tala watched the room the way Maintenance watched water: not soft, not distant, responsible for what attention might break.
On the table lay copies of her last notes.
I did not touch them immediately.
That was new.
Ciri noticed. So did Yennefer. Geralt stood at the threshold with his hands hanging open, a posture I had seen only around graves and sleeping children.
"She was supposed to rest," Asha said. "Jacob brought her pillows every morning and checked the knives every night."
"Did she rest at all?" I asked.
"Only when sleeping."
Tala leaned against the wall. "She made him carry the basin."
"He was a good guard," Asha said.
"He was a terrible guard," Tala answered. "He fell in love with the assignment."
"Many did," Asha said. "It made losing her less efficient."
I picked up the first note.
Helena's hand was steadier than mine.

Jacob, if the northern men come again, count blades before titles. Men with clean titles often hide dirty knives because they believe grammar washes steel. If our son survives this, do not let anyone name him before he has had a chance to be inconvenient.
The next line made my throat close.
If he has your stubbornness, forgive him early. If he has mine, forgive him often.
I set the page down because my hand had begun to shake. Not much. Enough.
"Continue," I said.
No one moved.
I hated them for the kindness. Then I hated the need for it.

Yennefer took the next page and read where my eyes could not. "Helena rejected the word vessel. She rejected host. She rejected chamber unless paired with chosen, temporary, and reversible. She wrote in the margin, any doctrine that requires a child to understand sacrifice is doctrine written by adults who should be kept from children."
"She was right," Ciri said.
"Frequently," Asha replied. "Annoyingly."
Geralt looked toward the window. "And Jacob?"
Sera brought a smaller bundle.

My father's notes were worse because they were practical. He counted water skins, guard shifts, copper nails, oil, wounded hands, enemy routes, and the cost of replacement hinges. Love appeared only by what he counted too carefully.

Another page listed hinges. Not weapons. Not heirs. Hinges. Door to upper stair: oil nightly. Window shutter: sticks in heat, plane lower edge. East knife rack: move higher before child walks. Beneath that, in a different pressure of the same hand, Jacob had written: Helena sleeps when the room believes I have gone. Return quietly. Bring pillow before argument begins. Love, apparently, had hidden in the inventory because soldiers trust lists more than declarations.
One margin note, scratched beside an inventory of grain, read:
A clean conscience is what officers call an empty room after they have removed the people.
I almost laughed. It came out wrong.
"Your father had good advice," Ciri said.
"Which part?"
"The part about annoying enemies."
"He also called one Nilfgaardian assessor an imperial ass with a borrowed vocabulary," Asha said.
"Also accurate," Yennefer said.
I breathed until the room stopped leaning.
The day between Helena's room and the second archive belonged to ordinary things that had no mercy because they were ordinary.

Asha took Helena's ribbon to the washing court and asked permission before placing it near steam. Sera granted it with a nod. Tala brought cedar soap. Ciri stood beside Asha, sleeves rolled, and helped wash cloth that had survived fire, archive, theft, and my failure to know my mother's hands.
I watched from the doorway until Asha noticed me.
"Do not haunt a washing court," she said. "Help or leave."
I helped badly.

Helena's ribbon bled smoke into the basin. The water turned gray. Ciri's fingers were careful. Asha's were less careful because memory had earned the right to touch firmly. Tala stood behind me and corrected how I wrung the cloth.
"You will tear it," she said.
"I have killed less fragile things."
"That is visible."

She took my hands and changed the pressure of my grip. Her fingers were callused along the spear line, warmer than mine, dry from desert air. The contact was practical. That made it more dangerous. I had been handled as patient, target, son, lover, subject, and risk. This was different. This was someone teaching a man to hold what should not be broken.

Ciri saw. Her face did not close. Desire did not make ownership honest simply because it was mutual. She looked at Tala, then at me, and there was pain in the look, yes, but not accusation. The road between us had never promised simplicity. It had promised choice, and choices cost more when everyone remained awake for them.
After the ribbon dried, Asha folded it into three turns and tucked it beside Helena's notes.
"She would have laughed at this," Asha said.
"At what?" I asked.
"At all these dangerous people trying to save a ribbon and nearly failing at domestic competence."
Geralt, from the hallway, said, "Fair."
"You do not get to agree," Asha told him. "You look like a man who folds shirts under duress."
"Under Triss," Geralt said.
Yennefer passed behind him. "That was not nearly as clever as you think."

Dandelion opened his mouth. Priscilla, who had arrived by southern courier with Zoltan's last convoy and had already taken charge of not letting him become entirely useless, closed it with two fingers on his sleeve.
The sanctuary, for one hour, became crowded with the living.

It is one thing to reject sacrifice as policy before diagrams. It is another to watch Ciri rinse smoke from your mother's ribbon, Geralt take water from a child without spilling it, Yennefer argue over copper ratios, Triss help a wounded boy write his name, Zoltan fix an offensive door, Dandelion carry lentils because Priscilla told him art could wait, and Buck lower his ugly head for Iren's blue beads.

Yennefer read the chamber doctrine again in the alcove outside, not because she expected mercy from rereading, but because anger needed employment before it became weather. Triss cataloged Helena's notes with the care of a healer washing instruments after a death: too late to save, still necessary if the next wound was to be treated honestly. Geralt fixed a buckle on Buck's bridle that had not been broken. Buck allowed three stitches before biting the air near his sleeve, which everyone accepted as a professional review.

Tala did not comfort with softness. She stood near the washing court door and made sure no one turned the hour into legend. When two apprentices slowed to stare at me, she sent them to carry lentils. When I stopped eating after three bites, she placed the bowl back in front of me and said, 'Grief does not exempt the stomach. It only lies to it.' I hated the accuracy enough to finish half.
Buck allowed it for six breaths, then shook them off and looked insulted by beauty.
Iren laughed until she had to sit down.
The sanctuary truth came later, under the mountain, where the second archive waited behind a copper door and three Faithel who looked ready to kill anyone who called it sacred.
The old diagrams were not Black Ink's copies. They were the thing Black Ink had tried to understand badly.
Five anchors. One outer ring. One inner lock. One living hinge.
The phrase sat in Faithel script, not imperial. That made the room worse.
"Say it," Ciri said.

Sera looked at me. "A living chamber is a bearer capable of receiving the Crown's pressure internally, not as a slave, not as a sacrifice by default, but as a conscious seal. Old doctrine held it as impossible to use ethically. Newer panic forgot the ethics and kept the shape."
"Black Ink stole your impossible and filed off the shame," I said.
"Yes."
"And my blood?"
Asha looked at the floor. "Morningstar blood was bred from maintenance, not rule. The line was not noble. It was made responsible. There is a difference."
"Made," I said.
The word hurt more than it should have.
Sera did not soften it. "Yes. Made. Also taught. Also loved. Those truths have always hated sharing a room."
"Can the anchors be repaired without me?" I asked.
No one answered quickly enough.
That was an answer.
Ciri stepped closer. "We find another way."
Sera closed the diagram. "Then we look at the canyon. If the stars still hold, there may be enough outer structure to restore the ring."
"And if not?" Geralt asked.
Saesenthessis spoke from the doorway. No one had heard her enter. Dragons enjoyed arriving as punctuation.
"Then someone will finally say aloud what everyone here is swallowing."
"No," Ciri said.
"I had not said it."
"Good. Keep not saying it."
Saesenthessis looked at me, and in her eyes I saw old gold, old ash, and something like apology dragged over broken glass.
The sanctuary had shown us a possible road, and the ground had begun drawing it under my boots.
Druidic report delivered to Queen Cerys by sea courier, salt-damaged:

The drowned draconid had no heart, though the chest was unbroken. The priestesses heard a phrase in sleep, not Skellige speech, not Elder Speech. Old wall learning. Old wall learning. I advise that we do not ask the sea what it means unless we are ready to dislike the answer.
The Canyon of Stars did not look like a wound until night.

By day it was stone, heat, and distance. Red cliffs split by a river that no longer ran. Wind scraping dust into the teeth. Lizards vanishing under flat rocks. A path so narrow the horses considered religion and so wide no man could call it impossible. The Faithel moved through it with quiet economy, every step placed where generations had learned not to fall.
The northerners moved with more caution and less dignity.
I include myself in that. Anyone who says witchers do not sweat has never put one in Zerrikania with a water ration and a saddle sore.

The canyon earned its name after sunset. Stars appeared in the cliff walls, not above them. Tiny mineral seams caught the last light, then answered with a pale glow that turned the rock into a map of frozen sparks. Copper bands crossed those sparks in five old lines. Anchor roads. Vharakthul's cage written through stone by people who had not trusted one wall to do all the work.
"It is beautiful," Dandelion whispered.
"Do not flirt with architecture," Zoltan said. "It always outlives you."

Tala led us toward the third marker. Sera had sent eight wardens, three scholars, and one boy whose only task was to tell the scholars when they were standing too close to an edge. That made him the most useful scholar present.
My job was simple: stand where told, touch nothing unless ordered, and report every pull, pressure, cold, heat, scent, or unwanted philosophical awakening.
I failed within the hour.

The first anchor stone looked dormant. I said so. The copper band lay dull. The star seams around it glowed evenly. No smell of burned iron. No inward pressure. My medallion remained still. Buck, brought only as far as the lower basin, had not screamed, though he had made his low opinion of canyons available to all.
"Dormant," I said.
Tala did not move. "Again."
"It is not pulling."
"Again."
I put my hand nearer.
The stone did nothing.
Then Ciri's nose began to bleed.
She was twenty paces behind me. Too far for my hand to matter, which meant the anchor was not answering me. It was waiting for Elder Blood to come into the same geometry.
"Back," Yennefer said.
Too late.
The canyon floor opened along the old riverbed.

Not dramatic. No great roar, no noble crack. The sand simply went thin under our boots and dropped. A scholar screamed. Geralt caught him by the collar. Triss threw a net of light under two wardens. Tala shoved me hard enough to send me into Ciri instead of the gap.
For one humiliating heartbeat, we both went down tangled in cloak, steel, and dust.
"Stop saving me," I said into her shoulder.
"Stop needing it," she snapped, then held me tighter as the stone under us shivered.
A thing crawled out of the dry channel.

It had once been a sand drake, small by draconid measure, which meant large enough to make human confidence negotiable. Half its scales had turned black. The rest were peeling, each scale underlined by red thread. Its throat pulsed inward. When it opened its mouth, no roar came out. Only a command without sound.
Three wardens dropped their spears.
Not fear. Obedience.
Tala cursed and struck one across the face before he walked into the gap. Asha sang one sharp line that made the other two stumble back. Geralt and I went for the drake.
It hit me first.

I would prefer to say I allowed it. I did not. The thing came through dust faster than scale had any right to move. Its shoulder struck my hip. My left leg folded. The sword cut air. Its jaw closed on my pauldron and shook. Bone in my shoulder gave a wet complaint.

Panic is not noble. Panic is the animal inside the ribs declaring politics suspended. I drove my knife into the drake's eye and missed the socket because it moved under the blade. Teeth scraped toward my throat.

Ciri's sword flashed green-silver over my face. The drake's head jerked aside. Geralt drove silver under its jaw. Yennefer pinned the tail with a violet spike. Triss's light net dragged two wardens clear as the gap widened.
The drake did not die until Saesenthessis landed on the ledge above us and spoke one word in a language I felt more than heard.
Every red thread under the scales burst black.
The body emptied. Again.
I lay on my back, tasting blood and grit, with Ciri crouched over me and fury shaking her hands.
"You said dormant," she said.
"It was."
"You were wrong."
"Yes."
That answer cost less than the first time. Progress, perhaps. Or exhaustion.
Tala hauled one of her stunned wardens away from the fissure and looked at me with no triumph at all. "It hid from you. It listened for her."
Ciri wiped blood from her mouth. "Then I should not be here."
"No," I said too quickly.
Everyone heard it.
Ciri's eyes found mine. "That sounded less tactical than you intended."
"I have other flaws."
"Keep the useful ones."
We found the sabotage at the fourth anchor.

Not much. That was the clever part. No shattered stone. No broken copper. Only a pilgrim charm tucked beneath a lip of mineral seam, a coil of blackened thread around a sliver of bone. The charm had been soaked in draconid blood and dried under salt. It did not break the anchor. It taught it a false rhythm.
"Cult work," Sera said when the runner brought it back. "But the pattern is Black Ink's."
"Convenient partnership," Zoltan said.
"No partnership," Yennefer said. "Mutual use. Worse. Cleaner."

The name attached to the cult was Brother Cazren. He had been Faithel once, Maintenance-trained, dismissed after arguing that Vharakthul was not prisoner but rightful crown. Every prison breeds at least one person who falls in love with the thing inside it. Some call that compassion. Some call it worship. The dead rarely care about the distinction.
At night, the stars in the canyon walls flickered in the wrong order.
Asha heard it first. Not sound. Rhythm. She stood from the small fire and turned toward the inner gorge with a face I had never seen on her: child and elder at once.
"The song is moving," she said.
"Toward what?" Triss asked.
Asha did not answer.
From the far ridge came a voice made thin by distance.
"The crown is not worn," it called. "It wears. The throne is not built. It teaches the world to kneel."
Brother Cazren stood silhouetted against the star-lit rock. Around him, seven figures in pilgrim brown lifted copper rods. Black thread fluttered from each rod like dead hair.
Geralt had a knife in hand before the second line.
"Alive if possible," Ciri said.
"I dislike possible," Geralt replied.

The fight on the ridge was all bad footing and worse choices. Dandelion, who had been told to stay with the horses, screamed useful warnings from below. Zoltan reached the first cultist at knee height and solved the theological debate with an axe haft. Tala took the left slope, spear low. Asha and Sera sang counter-lines that made my teeth ache.
I tried to climb toward Cazren and found the canyon pulling through my palm.
Not hard. Persuasive.
The black threads on the rods bent toward me. Cazren smiled as if we had rehearsed.
"Last Warden," he shouted. "The Crown remembers your room."
The word room entered me badly.
For a moment I saw a black stone floor, a gold-veined table, a child's hand reaching through ash. My boot slipped. The ridge vanished from beneath me.
Ciri blinked to me and caught my harness with both hands. Elder Blood cut the air green-white. The world lurched. We hit the lower ledge hard enough to make my shoulder flare white.
"I had him," I said.
"No," she said, breath shaking. "You had an opening and he had your name."
Above us, Cazren escaped into the upper dark because I had given him the breath to do it.
My mistake left with him.
The next morning, Sera placed the sabotaged charm in a copper bowl and watched it smoke.
"The anchors are not only failing," she said. "They are being taught."
Regis, kneeling beside the dead drake's emptied body, looked at me with the quiet horror of a physician who had just watched a disease learn medicine.
"Then no repair," Yennefer said.
Saesenthessis's silence became heavier.
Geralt saw it. "Still not saying it?"
"No," the dragon said.
"Good," Ciri replied, voice raw. "Keep not saying it."
In the canyon walls, the stars flickered again, one by one, like a lock considering which tooth to break first.
Asha's private testimony, never entered into the sanctuary archive:

The child did not cry when the dragon died. That was the first horror. A baby should have wept at the heat, the smoke, or the sound of stone shifting. Instead he watched the gold scales turn to charcoal and reached out his small, soot-stained hand as if trying to catch the ash.
I think he knew, even then, that ash was the only thing his mother had left him to wear.
I did not dream the massacre.

Dreams have mercy. They allow the dreamer to believe, if only for a second, that the road might turn before the cliff. The sanctuary gave me no dream. It gave me memory without ownership, pictures cut so deep into stone that the heat of my hands woke them.

The ritual chamber sat under the lowest tier, where limestone went black with five centuries of oil smoke. One gold-veined table stood in the center. Copper bowls circled it. Salt lines crossed the floor in patterns that looked decorative until one understood decoration had been the first lie ritual ever learned.
Regis warned me before I touched the stone.
"Memories kept in stone are not like memories in the mind," he said. "A mind forgets to survive. Stone survives by refusing to forget. Do not let it think for you."
"That advice arrives late in my life."
"Most useful advice does. We dislike it earlier."

Triss tied a warming field around my wrist. Yennefer anchored my breathing with one hand at the back of my neck and the expression of a woman threatening my lungs into obedience. Ciri stood where I could see her. Geralt stood where I could pretend I did not need him.
Asha and Sera began the old song.
I placed my hand on the table.
The room changed without moving.

Asha was younger first. Barefoot, thin, hair cut unevenly, carrying a basket too large for her arms and a knife too sharp for a servant. Helena sat on the low bed in the room above, one hand on her swollen stomach, mending a tear in a sleeve with the grim focus of a woman refusing to admit the world had narrowed around her.
Jacob stood by the door, counting sounds outside.
"You stop at the same line," young Asha said.
Helena looked up. "Because the old song has a leak."
"Songs do not leak."
"All useful things leak eventually. Walls, vows, governments, husbands asked to carry basins."
Jacob did not turn. "I heard that."
"Good. It will improve your posture."
I wanted to laugh. The wanting hurt.
The memory shifted.

Fire under the upper gates. Men in black under pilgrim brown. Others in imperial leather, no banners, because banners could later be denied. Jacob's sword broke at the third man and kept killing after the break. Helena ran with blood down one leg and me against her chest. Asha, small and terrified, tried to help and was struck hard enough to fall.
"Go!" Jacob roared.
"No," young Asha said.
"Go!"
That was the terrible thing about command when spoken by someone who loves you. It can save you and ruin you in the same breath.

The memory did not spare me because I was watching from within it. I felt Helena's breath. I felt my own infant weight against her. I heard the black-star necklace strike the clasp at her throat. The chamber below opened like a wound with manners.
The golden dragon lay dying there.

Villentretenmerth had burned already. Not with ordinary fire. His scales had gone black at the edges, gold becoming charcoal, eyes still bright enough to shame the lamps. He lowered his head toward Helena.
His voice entered the room without needing air.
The old anchors fail. The Crown has learned the outer wall. It will rise through blood roads and make kingdoms into nesting grounds.
"Then rebuild them," Helena said.
The dragon's eye turned toward the infant in her arms.
No.
I did not know who said it. Helena. Asha. Me. Ciri in the present. Perhaps all of us.
Villentretenmerth said, The living chamber is not a prison if chosen by one who can refuse. But a child cannot choose.
"Let him live," Helena whispered. "Please. Let him live before anyone decides what he is for."
The dragon closed his eyes. I understood then why mercy could become cruel. It often arrives carrying a knife it hopes you will call a tool.
I saw what he did.

Not made me a prison. Not fully. Not cleanly. He gave the bloodline an architecture it could grow into or reject, if the world left enough of the man intact to choose. Helena sealed the first door with her life. Jacob held the outer stair. Asha carried me through smoke and ash because command had broken her and duty used the crack.
The last thing Helena sang was not a spell.
It was my name.
Jack.
I tore my hand from the table.

The present returned badly. My knees struck stone. Ciri caught one shoulder. Geralt caught the other. Yennefer swore at the table with impressive variety. Triss pressed cloth under my nose, which had begun bleeding without permission.
Asha stood frozen.
Saesenthessis had entered during the memory. Her face was human. Her eyes were not.
"You knew," Geralt said.
The dragon looked at him. "I knew my father gave the boy a capacity to hold. I did not know what Black Ink made of the absence afterward."
"Capacity," Yennefer said, voice cold enough to change weather. "That is a polished word for stealing a child's future."
"My father believed the world would die without it."
"Many men have believed that before putting children on altars," Ciri said.
Saesenthessis's jaw tightened. "He was not a man."
"Then he had fewer excuses."
The room went very quiet.
I had expected rage. Mine, perhaps. Geralt's. Ciri's. What came was smaller and more difficult to carry.
"How much of me," I asked, "was permission?"
No one answered.
It was the worst answer yet.
Asha made a sound and turned away. "I carried you out. I thought that was enough. I thought if you lived, the old sin had failed."
"It did," I said.
She shook her head. "No. It moved north. It learned new paper."

Tala stood near the door, pale under her desert skin. "A living chamber requires a chooser. Old doctrine says the choice must be made by a grown bearer, witnessed by blood, love, enemy, and law. The rite was forbidden for that reason. No one ever agreed who was allowed to say yes."
"Convenient problem," Zoltan said, voice low. "Saved them from admitting no was easier."

Sera leaned on her staff. "The sanctuary kept the doctrine as warning. Black Ink found the warning and kept the shape. Cazren found the shape and called it worship. Vharakthul has learned the repair song through centuries of our maintenance. The outer anchors may not hold another breach."
There it was. Not said fully. Said enough.
Ciri gripped my sleeve. "No."
"I did not speak," Sera said.
"Everyone is speaking around it," Ciri snapped. "That is worse."
I stood. My legs disagreed but accepted the decision after some internal politics.

"We check the remaining anchors. We kill Cazren if he is kind enough to stand still. We stop Black Ink from helping the Crown by trying to own the key. We do not build the forbidden thing because the room has started to smell inevitable."
Geralt looked at me.
"What?"
"That sounded like a plan."
"I am tired. It may pass."
Saesenthessis found me above the sanctuary before dawn.

The pass below was dark. The desert held its heat badly at night, losing it in thin breaths that made stone creak. Buck stood in a lower yard under a reed awning, glaring upward as if he knew I was considering foolishness beyond his jurisdiction.
"My father would have lied less," Saesenthessis said.
"About what?"
"Hope. He preferred brutal honesty. I have often preferred silence."
"You call that an apology?"
"No. Dragons apologize badly. Usually by standing where arrows can reach."
"There are not enough arrows."
"No. There are not."
We stood with that for a while.
"If it comes to it," I said, "you will say the words."
Her eyes changed. "You have learned cruelty from us quickly."
"No. I learned assignment."
"I will not ask you."

"I know. That is why I am asking you to name it if everyone else cannot. I will not ask Ciri. I will not ask Geralt. Asha would break on the old sin. Tala would call it by the pass name and hate herself for accuracy. Yennefer would find a better word and suffer because it was not better enough."
"And Triss?"
"Triss would ask whether it hurts first. That may be worse."
Saesenthessis looked toward the lower yard. Buck stamped once, possibly on behalf of moral clarity.
"If the living chamber becomes the last door," she said, "I will name it. I will not make it clean."
That night, Tala found me again beside the third water court.
No salted bread this time. No excuse of ration law. The sanctuary had passed beyond the need for polite disguises, and she had never had much patience for them anyway.

Ciri had gone to argue with Mother Varda about evacuation routes. Geralt had taken Buck's saddle apart for the third time, which meant he was frightened enough to become unreasonable in leather. Yennefer and Triss were under the mountain with Sera, disputing anchor mathematics in two languages and three insults. Asha slept at last in Helena's old room, not peacefully, but sleep does not need peace to become mercy.

Tala stood beside me without touching me. Since Elskerdeg, that restraint had become its own kind of honesty. What had happened between us there had not made the road easier. It had made every clean answer heavier, which meant it had done its proper work.
"You asked the dragon to name the chamber if everyone else cannot," she said.
"Yes."
"Cruel assignment."
"Accurate one."
"Accuracy is not innocence."
"No."

She looked at the water threads moving under copper and stone. "If you choose death because it is easier than being held, I will curse your name in three languages and teach the children the rude version."
"You said that before."
"You are the kind of man who requires repetition when the lesson threatens your favorite wound."
"And if every other door burns?"
Her face changed in the low light. The change was not softness. It was the cost arriving early and asking to sit.
"Then I will stand where I can see your face," she said. "And I will not call it beautiful."

Ciri entered before I could answer. She saw us, saw the space deliberately left between us, and understood more than either of us had spoken. Hurt moved across her face. So did steadiness. The road had made none of us simple, but at least it had stopped rewarding lies.
"Good," Ciri said quietly.
"No," Tala answered. "Visible."
For once, Ciri did not correct her.

We stood there under the red lamps while the channels murmured below, three people with too much truth and too little room for comfort. Desire had already had its witness. Grief had not been cheated. Tomorrow remained armed, and none of us pretended otherwise.
That was the most honest comfort I received before the siege.
Recovered Black Ink field order, edges burned:

Authority is clearest at crisis. Local objections, religious panic, and familial attachments must be converted into preservation language. Subject is to be acquired alive if containment remains viable. If hostile draconic manifestation prevents acquisition, priority shifts to preventing uncontrolled ownership by cult, Faithel, or imperial faction.
The last ordinary morning began with bitter tea.
Ordinary is a cruel word for the hour before ruin. It lets the cups look like cups.

The sanctuary woke under a red sky that every local pretended not to read. Children were moved from the lower tiers before breakfast. The old were given double water and told it was because the day would be hot, which fooled no one and comforted several. Zoltan inspected the western barricade and declared it built by people who understood duty but not dwarven standards. Sera told him standards could be improved if he used his mouth less and his hands more. He fell in love with her immediately and called it professional respect.

Dandelion and Priscilla took their place in the echo hall with six Faithel singers, two drums, and a boy whose voice had not yet decided whether to remain a child's. Their task was not inspiration. Inspiration was for cavalry charges and bad theater. Their task was counter-cadence. Cazren's hymn moved bodies toward obedience. Priscilla had found the harvest rhythm under it, the borrowed shape, the place where hunger accepted command because command had learned to smell like bread.
"We cannot outshout him," she said. "We have to give the body another road."
Dandelion looked wounded by the tactical use of music. "I have been saying this for years, though usually in better clothes."
"Then prove it in worse ones," Ciri said.
He bowed. For once, no flourish. "Highness. Jack. Try not to die before the refrain. It has an excellent turn in the third measure."
"Motivating," I said.
"Art often is when not interrupted by bleeding."

Geralt distributed blades. Not dramatically. He checked edges, straps, buckles, weights. To Tala he gave a spare knife he said had belonged to no one important, which meant it had belonged to someone very important and he did not trust the room with that wound. To Ciri he gave no blade. He only checked the one she already carried, because he had learned, finally and imperfectly, that love was not issuing equipment to a woman who had chosen her own steel.
Yennefer and Triss stood over the central anchor diagram, not touching hands, but close enough for their spells to share breath.
"If the western channel breaks first, we bleed pressure into the dry wash," Triss said.
"Which kills everyone near the west barricade," Yennefer replied.
"Unless Sera's spill line holds."
"It will not hold long."
"Then long is what we buy."
Yennefer looked at her. Old history moved between them, no longer rivalry, not comfort either, but two forms of care forced to spend the same coin well.
"We buy long," she said again.
Yennefer nodded. "Then we spend it well."
Asha came to me last. She carried Helena's ribbon, Jacob's broken hilt, and a strip of new cloth dyed with desert red.
"Your mother would have argued with every person here," she said.
"Useful trait."
"Your father would have checked every exit twice and then pretended he did not trust the third."
"Also useful."
She tied the red cloth around my upper arm. Not family color. Not rank. Maintenance mark.
"This is not blessing," she said.
"No one here blesses cleanly anyway."
"Good. Blessings make people stupid. This is work. If you fall, someone sees where to grab. If you live, someone sees where to scold."
I looked at the cloth. "And if I choose the chamber?"
Asha's hand stilled.
For all her hard language, all her scars, all her years carrying duty like a blade hidden in bread, that question reached the woman who had once failed to carry a child from fire.
"Then I will sing you in," she said. "And hate the song forever."
Ciri found me at the lower stair while the first distant bells began counting movement in the canyon.
"I have orders ready," she said.
"For evacuation?"

"For evacuation, for witness protection, for denying Nilfgaard jurisdiction over your body, for condemning Black Ink, for recognizing Faithel custodial sovereignty, for arresting three men who will pretend not to know Sorel Veyrane."
"Prepared."
"Terrified. The difference is paperwork."
"Do I get an order?"
She folded one sheet and put it in my coat. "You get a blank one."
"Dangerous."
"Yes. If you return, write what you choose to be called. If you do not, I will write Jack and dare any empire, court, cult, office, or grieving idiot to improve it."
I touched the paper once.
The first alarm bell rang properly then, not counting, not warning.
Arrival.
The ordinary morning ended with cups still warm on the table.
Asha handed it to me in a clay cup and watched until I drank. The liquid was dark, sour, and thick with ground seeds that clung to the tongue like bad law.
"This is vile," I said.
"It keeps blood from listening too quickly."
"By frightening it?"
"By reminding the body that destiny is not its oldest enemy."
Geralt took my harness and adjusted the left shoulder strap. Again.
"Stop," I said.
"Stop is vague."
"You dislike vagueness now?"
"In straps. Vague straps kill."
"You have checked it five times."
"Six. You were asleep for one."
That almost hurt more than the strap. He had watched me sleep because old guilt repaired buckles when it could not repair years.

Ciri came in as Geralt finished. She carried her sword, two knives, and no crown. Her hair was bound tight. A smudge of ash crossed her cheek. She had been helping Sera mark the second channel, which was either leadership or avoidance. With Ciri, those often wore the same boots.
"You missed a strap," I said.
She looked down at the harness. "No. I did not."
"Strategic restraint?"
"I have been practicing. The rewards are poor."
Her fingers checked the strap anyway. Briefly. Intimately. Then she tied a small knot in the red thread at my wrist, beside Tala's uglier one.
"What is that?"
"A complaint."
"From whom?"
"Me. It says return alive enough to be insulted."
"High standard."
"I lowered it for you."

Yennefer entered with Triss behind her and brought the room back to work before it became too honest. They had built three overlapping fields: a warming lattice for blood stability, a deflection ring to prevent the Crown from using my pulse as map, and a mercy clause Yennefer refused to call by name.
"You are doing that thing," I said.
"I do many things," Yennefer replied, taking my wrist. "Specificity is civilized."
"Pretending medical attention is not worry."
"Too late," Triss murmured.
Yennefer gave her a look. Triss smiled without apology.
Yennefer's fingers rested over my pulse. Her face did not soften. Her steadiness told me she was frightened.
"If the pressure rises, you tell us before it becomes theatrical," she said.
"I dislike theater."
"You travel with Dandelion. That argument died months ago."
Outside, the pass bells began.
Not one bell. Five. Water-line bells. Gate bells. Alarm bells. A sound like metal learning panic.
The first Black Ink envoy reached the second gate under a white cloth and three lies.

He was bald, narrow, and dressed in dust-colored travel linen that failed to hide northern boots. Behind him stood twelve field men, two carts, a medic's chest, and restraints folded under canvas. I had seen that canvas shape before at the Broken Crown. Some nightmares save money by reusing props.
Ciri met him at the gate with Mother Varda, Sera, Geralt, Yennefer, and two wardens whose spears did not care for paperwork.
I stood behind them because the envoy had asked to see the subject and Ciri had said no in a tone that made grammar limp.
